A delta is dominated by deposition, whereas an estuary is associated with tidal or drowned-mouth processes. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xs: An **estuary** is the drowned river mouth — option **(1)**.
An estuary is associated with **tidal** or **drowned-mouth processes**, whereas a **delta** is **dominated by deposition**.
xa: A **spit** **projects from the coast**; a **tombolo** **connects an island to the mainland**.
A **barchan** is **crescent-shaped**; a **seif** is **longitudinal**.
**V-shaped** valleys are fluvial; **U-shaped** glacial.

8.s:
Assertion (A): Horsts and grabens are associated with block mountains.
Reason (R): Horsts are uplifted fault blocks, while grabens are down-faulted blocks.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
8.x: Both are true and R explains A: block mountains are uplifted horsts beside sunken grabens.
8.tq: Check whether R is the cause of A.
n: Horsts and grabens are associated with block mountains. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xs: **Both A and R are true**, and R is the **correct explanation** of A — option **(1)**.
A **horst** is an **uplifted fault block** and a **graben** a **down-faulted block** (rift valley); block mountains are **uplifted blocks** **linked with rift valleys**.
**Horsts = block mountains** (APPSC **2022**).
xa: **Vosges** (France) and **Black Forest** (Germany) are horsts flanking the **Rhine rift valley**.
**Death Valley** (USA) is a graben; **Lake Malawi** lies in the **Great Rift Valley**.
**Narmada** and **Tapi** flow west through **rift valleys**.

8.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Western Ghats rivers are short and swift.
II. Western Ghats rivers generally have estuarine mouths.
III. Longshore drift forms spits.
IV. A spit connects an island to the mainland.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
8.x: I, II and III are correct: Western Ghats rivers are short, swift and end in estuaries, and longshore drift builds spits. IV is false because a tombolo, not a spit, joins an island to the mainland.
8.tq: Discriminate tombolo from spit.
n: Western Ghats rivers are short and swift. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Longshore drift forms spits. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xs: Statements **I, II and III** are correct as keyed — option **(4)** I, II and III only.
I and II: per the key, **Western Ghats rivers** are **short and swift** and end in **estuarine mouths** — an estuary is a **drowned-mouth** feature.
III: **longshore drift** forms **spits**, which **project from the coast**.
IV wrong: a **tombolo**, not a spit, **connects an island to the mainland**.
xa: A **delta** is **dominated by deposition**; an **estuary** by **tidal** processes.
A **barchan** is **crescent-shaped**; a **seif dune** is **longitudinal**.
A **stalactite** hangs from a roof; a **stalagmite** rises from a floor.

8.s:
How many of the following are examples of block mountains?
1. Sierra Nevada
2. Vosges
3. Black Forest
4. Fuji
8.x: Three are block mountains: Sierra Nevada, Vosges and Black Forest. Fuji is a volcanic mountain.
8.tq: Discriminate block from volcanic mountains.
n: The Sierra Nevada are block mountains. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
The Vosges are block mountains. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
The Black Forest is a block mountain range. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Fuji is a volcanic mountain. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xs: **Only three** are block mountains — option **(3)**: **Sierra Nevada**, **Vosges** and **Black Forest**.
**Fuji** is a **volcanic mountain**, built by **lava accumulation**.
Block mountains form by **faulting** — **uplift and downthrow** along faults, with **steep fault scarps**.
xa: ⚠ **Sierra Nevada** in "young folded" lists is a **block (fault) mountain** (MPPSC **2021**).
Block mountains are associated with **horsts and grabens**.
Other volcanic mountains: **Kilimanjaro**, **Mount St. Helens**, **Cotopaxi**.

8.s: Which mountain range is identified as the longest major mountain range?
8.x: The Andes, about 7,000 km long, are the longest mountain range. The Himalayas are the highest.
8.tq: Discriminate longest from highest.
n: The Andes are the longest major mountain range. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
The Andes are in South America. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xs: The **Andes** (**South America**) are the **longest major mountain range** — option **(3)**.
The **Andes** and **Himalayas** are **young fold mountains**; so are the **Alps** and **Rockies**.
xa: The **world's highest peaks** mostly lie in young fold mountains — **Himalaya**, **Everest**.
The **Himalaya** uplift began ~**70 million years ago** and continues.
**Aravalli** — one of the oldest fold mountains, now residual (**300–900 m**).

8.s:
Consider the following statements about old fold mountains:
I. They result from ancient folding and prolonged denudation.
II. They are lower than young fold mountains.
III. They have rounded forms.
IV. They are highly eroded.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
8.x: All four are correct: old fold mountains come from ancient folding and long denudation, so they are lower, rounded and highly eroded.
8.tq: Recall the features of old fold mountains.
n: Old fold mountains formed through ancient folding and prolonged denudation. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Old fold mountains are lower than young fold mountains. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Old fold mountains are rounded. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Old fold mountains are highly eroded. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Young fold mountains are high and rugged, whereas old fold mountains are low and rounded. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xs: **All four statements are correct** — option **(2)** I, II, III and IV.
Old fold mountains result from **ancient folding and prolonged denudation**.
They are **lower** than young fold mountains, **rounded** and **highly eroded**.
xa: Examples: **Aravallis**, **Appalachians**, **Urals**, **Pennines**.
**Aravalli** — about **570 million years** old; highest peak **Guru Shikhar** (**1,722 m**).
Young fold mountains are **high and rugged**; old ones **low and rounded**.

8.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Residual mountains
(b) Dome mountains
(c) Block mountains
(d) Volcanic mountains

List-II
(i) Remnants of older elevated surfaces left by erosion
(ii) Magma pushes the crust upward without erupting
(iii) Uplift of crustal blocks between faults
(iv) Accumulation of lava and volcanic material
8.x: Residual mountains are erosional remnants of older surfaces, dome mountains form when magma bulges the crust without erupting, block mountains are uplifted between faults and volcanic mountains build from lava, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
8.tq: Match each mountain type to the process that forms it.
n: Residual mountains are remnants of older elevated surfaces. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
The Appalachians are residual mountains. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
The Pennines are residual mountains. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Dome mountains form when magma pushes upward without erupting through the crust. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xs: **Residual** = remnants left by erosion, **dome** = magma pushes up **without erupting**, **block** = uplift between faults, **volcanic** = accumulation of lava — option **(3)** a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
Residual examples: **Aravallis**, **Appalachians**, **Pennines**; dome: **Black Hills**, **Bighorns**.
xa: Block examples: **Sierra Nevada**, **Vosges**, **Black Forest**.
Volcanic examples: **Kilimanjaro**, **Fujiyama**, **Mount St. Helens**, **Cotopaxi**.
Volcanic mountains have **conical peaks** and **craters**.

8.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Dome mountains have dome-shaped uplift.
II. The Black Hills are dome mountains.
III. The Bighorns are dome mountains.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
8.x: All three are correct: dome mountains are dome-shaped uplifts, as in the Black Hills and Bighorns.
8.tq: Recall an example of each mountain type.
n: Dome mountains have dome-shaped uplifts. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
The Black Hills are dome mountains. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
The Bighorns are dome mountains. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xs: **All three statements are correct** — option **(2)** I, II and III.
**Dome mountains** form when **magma pushes upward without erupting**, giving **dome-shaped uplifts**.
Examples: the **Black Hills** and **Bighorns**.
xa: **Volcanic mountains** form by **accumulation of lava** — **Kilimanjaro**, **Fuji**.
**Residual mountains** are **remnants of older elevated surfaces**.
**Block mountains** form by **faulting** — **Sierra Nevada**, **Vosges**.

8.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Compression is the main force for fold mountains.
II. Faulting is the main force for block mountains.
III. Volcanism is the main force for volcanic mountains.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
8.x: All three are correct: compression makes fold mountains, faulting block mountains and volcanism volcanic mountains.
8.tq: Recall the force behind each mountain type.
n: Compression is the main force in fold mountains. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Faulting is the main force in block mountains. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Volcanism is the main force in volcanic mountains. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Block mountains are formed by faulting. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Fold mountains result from compression, whereas block mountains result from faulting. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xs: **All three statements are correct** — option **(2)** I, II and III.
**Compression** forms **fold mountains**; **faulting** forms **block mountains**; **volcanism** forms **volcanic mountains**.
xa: Fold mountains: **rugged, parallel ranges** (**Himalaya**, **Alps**, **Andes**).
Block mountains: **fault scarps**, **horsts and grabens** (**Sierra Nevada**, **Vosges**).
Volcanic mountains: **cone shape**, **craters** (**Fuji**, **Kilimanjaro**).

8.s:
Assertion (A): A rift valley is an elongated depression associated with faulting.
Reason (R): In rift formation, the central block subsides after divergence and faulting.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
8.x: Both are true and R explains A: the central block sinks between faults as the crust pulls apart, forming the long depression.
8.tq: Check whether R is the cause of A.
n: A rift valley is an elongated depression associated with faulting. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Rift valleys form through divergence or tension. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Divergence or tension causes faulting in rift-valley formation. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Faulting causes the central block to subside in rift-valley formation. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Tectonic faulting forms rift valleys. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
A hanging valley is glacial, whereas a rift valley is tectonic. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xs: **Both A and R are true**, and R is the **correct explanation** of A — option **(1)**.
**Divergence or tension causes faulting**, and **faulting** makes the **central block subside** — producing an **elongated depression**.
xa: A **graben** is a **down-faulted block** (rift valley); a **horst** an **uplifted** one.
Examples: **Death Valley** (USA), **Rhine Rift Valley**, **Narmada** and **Tapi** valleys.
⚠ A **rift valley** is **tectonic**; a **hanging valley** is **glacial**.

8.s: Which is the highest peak of the Aravalli Range?
8.x: Guru Shikhar, 1,722 m at Mount Abu, is the highest Aravalli peak.
8.tq: Recall the highest peak of each range.
n: Guru Shikhar is the highest peak of the Aravalli Range. [Indian Geography · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 41-46]
Guru Shikhar is located in Sirohi district. [Indian Geography · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 41-46]
Sirohi district is located in Rajasthan. [Indian Geography · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 41-46]
xs: **Guru Shikhar** (**1,722 metres**) is the **highest peak** of the Aravalli Range — option **(3)**.
It lies in **Sirohi district**, **Rajasthan**.
xa: The Aravalli lies in **Rajasthan**, **Haryana** and **Delhi**; its northern extension **reaches Delhi**.
Geological age about **570 million years**; a **residual mountain range** formed from **Dharwar** sediments.
SC (Nov **2025**) definition: an Aravalli hill rises **100 m** above local relief.
MoEF&CC banned new Aravalli mining leases on **24 Dec 2025**.

8.s:
How many of the following are examples of volcanic mountains?

1. Fujiyama
2. Mount St. Helens
3. Cotopaxi
4. The Urals
8.x: Three are volcanic: Fujiyama, Mount St. Helens and Cotopaxi. The Urals are old fold mountains.
8.tq: Discriminate volcanic from fold mountains.
n: Fujiyama is an example of a volcanic mountain. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 18-20]
Mount St. Helens is an example of a volcanic mountain. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 18-20]
Cotopaxi is an example of a volcanic mountain. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 18-20]
xs: **Only three** are volcanic — option **(3)**: **Fujiyama**, **Mount St. Helens** and **Cotopaxi**.
**The Urals** are **old fold mountains**, like the **Appalachians** and **Aravallis**.
Volcanic mountains form by **accumulation of lava and volcanic material** and have **conical peaks**.
xa: Other volcanic mountains: **Kilimanjaro** (Africa), **Etna** (Italy).
⚠ **Sierra Nevada** is a **block (fault) mountain**, not young fold.
**Dome mountains** form when magma pushes up **without erupting** — **Black Hills**, **Bighorns**.

9.s: Which one of the following correctly describes a caldera?
o: A horizontal sheet of magma between rock layers
A narrow vertical intrusion cutting across strata
A funnel-shaped mouth at the top of a volcanic cone
A cauldron-shaped depression formed after chamber emptying and summit collapse
9.x: A caldera is a cauldron-shaped depression formed when a large eruption empties the magma chamber and the summit collapses. A funnel-shaped summit mouth is a crater.
9.tq: Distinguish crater and caldera by formation process and shape.
xs: A **caldera** is a **cauldron-shaped depression** formed when the magma chamber empties and the **summit collapses** — option **(4)**.
It follows a **big eruption**.
A **funnel-shaped mouth** at the top is a **crater** — option (3) is the trap.
xa: **Magma** = molten rock below the surface; **lava** = magma at the surface.
Lava reaches the surface through the **vent**.
**Pyroclasts**: ash, **lapilli**, volcanic bombs.

9.s:
Consider the following statements about monitoring instruments:
1. A tiltmeter measures ground tilt over faults and volcanoes.
2. A creepmeter measures slip along a fault.
3. An anemometer measures wind direction.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
9.x: Statement 1 is correct: a tiltmeter records ground tilt over faults and volcanoes. Statement 2 is correct: a creepmeter records fault slip. Statement 3 is wrong: an anemometer measures wind speed, not direction. So '1 only' misses statement 2, and the options with statement 3 are wrong; the answer is 1 and 2 only.
9.tq: Classic APPSC trap: anemometer = wind SPEED, not direction.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: a **tiltmeter** measures **ground tilt** over faults and volcanoes.
Statement 2 correct: a **creepmeter** measures **fault slip**.
Statement 3 wrong: an **anemometer** measures wind **speed**, not direction.
xa: These instrument matches were asked in APPSC **2018**.
⚠ **Trap:** anemometer = wind **speed**, not direction.
Most abundant volcanic gas: **water vapour**.

9.s: Which statement best describes acidic or felsic lava?
o: It always flows farther than basic lava.
It is silica-poor, fluid and generally forms broad shield volcanoes.
It is silica-rich, viscous and often associated with explosive eruptions.
It is composed only of water and volcanic gases.
9.x: Acidic or felsic lava is silica-rich and viscous, making eruptions more explosive. It commonly produces steep cones and stratovolcanoes.
9.tq: Use the contrast between silica content, viscosity and eruptive behaviour.
xs: **Acidic (felsic) lava** is **silica-rich, viscous and explosive** — option **(3)**.
It builds **steep cones** and **stratovolcanoes** (andesitic magma).
Option (2) describes **basic (mafic) lava**: silica-poor, fluid, forms **shield volcanoes**.
xa: Basic lava **flows far**, building **shield volcanoes and lava plateaus** (basalt).
⚠ **Shield** = fluid basalt, gentle; **composite** = lava + ash layers, steep, explosive.
Stratovolcanoes produce **pyroclastic flows** and **lahars**.

9.s: Pyroclastic flows and lahars are particularly associated with:
9.x: Pyroclastic flows and lahars, or volcanic mudflows, are associated particularly with stratovolcanoes.
9.tq: Link hazardous volcanic products to the volcano type that generates them.
xs: **Pyroclastic flows** and **lahars** are associated with **stratovolcanoes** — option **(4)**.
**Lahars** are **volcanic mudflows**.
Stratovolcanoes are **steep, explosive** cones of alternating lava and ash.
xa: Pyroclasts: **ash, lapilli, volcanic bombs**.
Examples: **Fuji, Vesuvius, St Helens, Fuego, Taftan**.
Stratovolcanoes form from **andesitic magma**.

9.s:
Consider the following statements about volcanic gases and ejecta:
1. Water vapour is the most abundant volcanic gas.
2. Sulphur dioxide forms aerosols that scatter sunlight and can cool the Earth for years.
3. Volcanic ash stays in the atmosphere for years and is the main cause of post-eruption cooling.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
9.x: Statement 1 is correct: water vapour is the most abundant volcanic gas, followed by CO2 and SO2. Statement 2 is correct: SO2 forms aerosols that scatter sunlight and cool the Earth for years. Statement 3 is wrong: ash falls back within weeks; the long cooling comes from SO2 aerosols. Hence 1 and 2 only; '1 only' omits a true statement and the options with 3 include a false one.
9.tq: Cooling for years = SO2 aerosols; ash settles within weeks.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: **water vapour** is the most abundant gas, then **CO2**, **sulphur dioxide**.
Statement 2 correct: **SO2** forms **aerosols** that scatter sunlight and **cool Earth for years**.
Statement 3 wrong: **ash falls back within weeks**; the long cooling is from SO2.
xa: Pyroclasts: **ash, lapilli, volcanic bombs**.
Mud volcanoes emit gases such as **methane, CO2, nitrogen**.
**Tiltmeter** monitors ground tilt over volcanoes.

9.s:
Consider the following statements about volcanoes classified by activity:
1. An active volcano is one that is erupting or has erupted recently.
2. A dormant volcano has been quiet for a long time but may erupt again.
3. An extinct volcano is one that is expected to erupt again after a long quiet spell.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
9.x: Statement 1 is correct: active = erupting or recently erupted. Statement 2 is correct: dormant = quiet for long but may erupt. Statement 3 is wrong: that describes a dormant volcano; an extinct volcano is one from which no eruption is expected. Hence 1 and 2 only.
9.tq: Dormant may wake; extinct never expected to.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: **active** = erupting or recently erupted.
Statement 2 correct: **dormant** = quiet for long but may erupt.
Statement 3 wrong: an **extinct** volcano is one with **no eruption expected**.
xa: **Barren Island** is **India's only active volcano**.
**Narcondam** is **dormant**; **Dhinodhar** (Kutch) is **extinct**.
**Hayli Gubbi** erupted in **Nov 2025** after **10,000-12,000 years** dormant.

9.s: Hayli Gubbi, which erupted in November 2025 after remaining dormant for approximately 10,000–12,000 years, is an example of which type of volcano based on its form?
9.x: Hayli Gubbi in Ethiopia is identified as a shield volcano. Its eruption in November 2025 followed a dormant period of approximately 10,000–12,000 years.
9.tq: Combine the numerical time period with the volcano-type identification.
xs: **Hayli Gubbi** (Ethiopia) is a **shield volcano** — option **(3)**.
It erupted in **Nov 2025** after **10,000-12,000 years** dormant.
Shield volcanoes are **broad, gentle slopes** of **fluid basalt**.
xa: The other shield example: **Mauna Loa**.
**Complex volcanoes**: **Taal, Dukono**.
**Composite**: **Fuji, Vesuvius, St Helens, Fuego, Taftan**.

9.s:
With reference to composite or stratovolcanoes, consider the following statements:
1. They generally have steep cones.
2. They are built from alternating layers of lava and ash.
3. Their eruptions may be explosive.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
9.x: All three statements are correct. Composite or stratovolcanoes are steep, consist of alternating lava and ash layers, and are associated with explosive eruptions.
9.tq: When all three statements describe the defining characteristics, select the complete combination.
xs: All three — **1, 2 and 3** — are correct — option **(4)**.
**Composite/stratovolcanoes** are **steep cones** of **alternating lava + ash layers**.
Their eruptions are **explosive**.
xa: Examples: **Fuji, Vesuvius, St Helens, Fuego, Taftan**.
They come from **andesitic magma** and produce **pyroclastic flows and lahars**.
⚠ **Shield** = fluid basalt, gentle; **composite** = steep, explosive.

9.s: Lava plateaus such as the Deccan Plateau commonly weather into:
9.x: Basaltic lava plateaus such as the Deccan weather to form fertile black soil.
9.tq: Connect the volcanic rock province with the soil produced by its weathering.
xs: Lava plateaus such as the **Deccan** weather into **fertile black soil** — option **(1)**.
They are built by **basic (basalt)** lava.
xa: In AP, **Deccan Trap basalts** (**Prakasam, Palnadu, Guntur**) give **black cotton soil**.
The Deccan Traps are **fissure (flood-basalt)** eruptions of the end-**Cretaceous** (about **65 million years**).
They are linked to the **Reunion hotspot**.

9.s:
Consider the following pairs (hot spring / geothermal site : State):
1. Tattapani : Odisha
2. Taptapani : Odisha
3. Vajreshwari : Maharashtra
Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
9.x: Pair 1 is wrong: Tattapani is in Chhattisgarh. Pair 2 is correct: Taptapani is in Odisha. Pair 3 is correct: Vajreshwari is in Maharashtra. So only 2 and 3 are correctly matched; any option containing pair 1 is wrong.
9.tq: Tattapani = Chhattisgarh, Taptapani = Odisha - the near-identical names are the trap.
xs: Pairs **2 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Pair 1 wrong: **Tattapani** is in **Chhattisgarh**.
Pair 2 correct: **Taptapani** — **Odisha**.
Pair 3 correct: **Vajreshwari** — **Maharashtra**.
xa: ⚠ **Tattapani** = Chhattisgarh; **Taptapani** = Odisha.
**Manikaran**: Himachal Pradesh (**Kullu valley**).
**Puga Valley, Chumathang**: **Ladakh**.

9.s: Which belt is associated with the greatest concentration of volcanic eruptions and earthquakes?
9.x: The Pacific Ring of Fire has the greatest concentration of volcanic eruptions and earthquakes. It includes volcanoes such as Fuji and Mount St. Helens.
9.tq: Identify the global belt from its combined volcanic and seismic activity.
xs: The **Pacific Ring of Fire** has the most eruptions and earthquakes — option **(3)**.
Its volcanoes: **Fuji, St Helens, Fuego, Mayon, Dukono, Popocatepetl**.
xa: **Mid-Atlantic belt**: Iceland - **Hekla**.
**Mediterranean belt**: **Vesuvius, Etna, Stromboli**.
**East African Rift**: **Kilimanjaro**; intraplate hotspot: **Hawaii**.

9.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
9.x: Stromboli belongs to the Mediterranean volcanic belt. The East African Rift is associated with Kilimanjaro and the Afar triple junction.
9.tq: Find the location that belongs to a different volcanic belt.
xs: **East African Rift — Stromboli** is wrongly matched — option **(4)**.
**Stromboli** is in the **Mediterranean belt**; the East African Rift has **Kilimanjaro**.
**Hawaii** (intraplate hotspot), **Hekla** (Mid-Atlantic), **Vesuvius, Etna** (Mediterranean) are correct.
xa: The **Pacific Ring of Fire** has most eruptions and earthquakes.
Ring of Fire volcanoes: **Fuji, St Helens, Fuego, Mayon**.
**Hekla** lies in **Iceland**.

9.s:
Which of the following statements about Indian volcanic features are correct?
1. Barren Island is India's only active volcano.
2. Narcondam is a dormant volcanic island.
3. Dhinodhar is an extinct volcanic hill in Kutch, Gujarat.
4. Baratang is known for mud volcanoes.
9.x: All four statements are correct. Barren Island is India's only active volcano, Narcondam is dormant, Dhinodhar is an extinct volcanic hill, and Baratang has mud volcanoes.
9.tq: Separate active, dormant, extinct and mud-volcano features before choosing the combination.
xs: All four — **1, 2, 3 and 4** — are correct — option **(4)**.
**Barren Island** (Andaman Sea) is **India's only active volcano**.
**Narcondam** is **dormant**; **Dhinodhar** (Kutch) is an **extinct** volcanic hill.
**Baratang** (Middle Andaman) has **mud volcanoes** and limestone caves.
xa: Barren Island's last eruption in the notes: **2017**.
**Narcondam** is a wildlife sanctuary with the endemic **Narcondam Hornbill**.
⚠ APPSC GS **2021** key gave "Barren island" for mud volcanoes — the right answer is **Baratang**.

9.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes Baratang from Barren Island?
o: Baratang has a magmatic active volcano, whereas Barren Island has mud volcanoes.
Baratang has mud volcanoes, whereas Barren Island is India's only active magmatic volcano.
Both are extinct volcanic hills of Gujarat.
Both are dormant volcanic islands of the Andaman Sea.
9.x: Baratang is associated with mud volcanoes, while Barren Island is India's only active magmatic volcano. Mud volcanoes erupt mud, water and gases rather than lava.
9.tq: Discriminate between two frequently confused Andaman volcanic features.
xs: **Baratang** has **mud volcanoes**; **Barren Island** is India's only **active magmatic volcano** — option **(2)**.
Option (1) reverses them.
Mud volcanoes erupt **mud, water, gases**, not lava.
xa: ⚠ APPSC GS **2021** key gave "Barren island" for mud volcanoes — correct answer **Baratang**.
Fresh mud volcano eruption at **Diglipur** (North Andaman).
Mud volcanoes are **cool and shallow**.

9.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the Deccan Traps?
o: Fissure-related flood-basalt outpourings on the Maharashtra Plateau near the end of the Cretaceous
An intrusive granite batholith formed in Ladakh during the Cenozoic Era
A chain of dormant volcanic cones formed in the Andaman Sea during the Quaternary period
A group of extinct volcanic hills confined to Kutch
9.x: The Deccan Traps are fissure or flood-basalt outpourings on the Maharashtra Plateau that occurred at the end of the Cretaceous and are linked to the Reunion hotspot.
9.tq: Use origin, location and geological age together rather than a single keyword.
xs: The **Deccan Traps** are **fissure (flood-basalt)** outpourings on the **Maharashtra plateau** at the end of the **Cretaceous** — option **(1)**.
They date to about **65 million years** ago.
**Dhinodhar** is the extinct hill of **Kutch** — option (4) wrong.
xa: Linked to the **Reunion hotspot**.
In AP: **Prakasam, Palnadu, Guntur**.
They weather into **fertile black soil**.

9.s: The Deccan Traps are linked in origin with the:
9.x: The Deccan Traps are linked to activity of the Reunion hotspot near the end of the Cretaceous.
9.tq: Discriminate among similarly named hotspot examples using the associated landform.
xs: The **Deccan Traps** are linked to the **Reunion hotspot** — option **(2)**.
They were flood-basalt eruptions at the end of the **Cretaceous** (about **65 million years**).
xa: They lie on the **Maharashtra plateau**; in AP in **Prakasam, Palnadu, Guntur**.
**Hawaii** is an **intraplate hotspot** volcano.
**Iceland** lies on the **Mid-Atlantic belt** (Hekla).

9.s: A mud volcano at Diglipur is distinguished from a lava volcano because it ejects:
9.x: The Diglipur mud volcano ejects mud, water and methane rather than lava. Its activity is driven by tectonic pressure on the active Andaman Arc subduction zone.
9.tq: Distinguish a process by its actual ejecta rather than by the word volcano.
xs: The **Diglipur** mud volcano ejects **mud, water and methane**, not lava — option **(4)**.
It is driven by tectonic pressure on the active **Andaman Arc** subduction zone.
xa: Mud volcanoes erupt gases such as **methane, CO2, nitrogen**; they are **cool and shallow**.
**Diglipur** is in **North Andaman**; **Baratang** (Middle Andaman) also has mud volcanoes.
⚠ **Baratang** = mud volcanoes; **Barren Island** = magmatic active volcano.

9.s: Volcan de Fuego, which erupted again in June 2026, is associated with the subduction of which plate beneath which other plate?
o: The Nazca Plate beneath the Cocos Plate
The Pacific Plate beneath the Nazca Plate
The Cocos Plate beneath the Caribbean Plate
The Caribbean Plate beneath the Cocos Plate
9.x: The renewed eruption of Guatemala's Volcan de Fuego is associated with the Cocos Plate subducting beneath the Caribbean Plate.
9.tq: Keep the direction of subduction in the correct order: subducting plate first and overriding plate second.
xs: **Volcan de Fuego** (Guatemala) erupts as the **Cocos plate** subducts under the **Caribbean plate** — option **(3)**.
It erupted again in **June 2026**.
xa: **Fuego** is a **composite/stratovolcano** on the **Pacific Ring of Fire**.
First 3D image of Mexico's **Popocatepetl**: magma pools down to **18 km**.
Ring of Fire also has **Fuji, St Helens, Mayon, Dukono**.

9.s:
Which of the following statements regarding geothermal exploration in India are correct?
1. ONGC drilled India's first and deepest geothermal wells at Puga Valley.
2. The wells reached a depth of 1,000 metres.
3. The wells were associated with a 1 MW pilot project.
4. The Puga Valley is located in Ladakh.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
9.x: All four statements are correct. ONGC drilled India's first and deepest geothermal wells at Puga Valley in Ladakh to a depth of 1,000 metres for a 1 MW pilot project.
9.tq: Check the institution, location, depth and project capacity together before selecting the complete combination.
xs: All four — **1, 2, 3 and 4** — are correct — option **(4)**.
**ONGC** drilled India's first and deepest geothermal wells at **Puga Valley**, **Ladakh**.
The wells reached **1,000 m**, for a **1 MW** pilot.
xa: GSI has identified **340** geothermal sites.
**Chumathang** is another Ladakh geothermal site.
⚠ **Tattapani** = Chhattisgarh; **Taptapani** = Odisha.

9.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Molten material below Earth’s surface is called magma.
Statement B: Molten material that reaches Earth’s surface is called lava.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
9.x: Both are true: molten rock below the surface is magma, and once it reaches the surface it is lava.
9.tq: Discriminate magma from lava.
n: Molten material below Earth’s surface is magma. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Molten material that reaches Earth’s surface is lava. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xs: **Both statements are true** — option **(1)**.
A: **magma** is **molten rock below Earth's surface**.
B: **lava** is magma **after it reaches Earth's surface** through the **vent**.
xa: ⚠ Below surface = **magma**; at surface = **lava**.
**Acidic (felsic) lava** is silica-rich, viscous, explosive; **basic (mafic) lava** is fluid and flows far.
A **caldera** forms when the magma chamber empties and the summit collapses.

9.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
 a. Magma
 b. Mantle
 c. Volcano
 d. Water vapour

List-II
 i. Produces volcanism
 ii. Layer below the crust
 iii. Releases lava, ash and gases
 iv. Most abundant volcanic gas
9.x: Magma produces volcanism, the mantle lies below the crust, a volcano releases lava, ash and gases and water vapour is the most abundant volcanic gas, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
9.tq: Recall the features of volcanism.
n: Magma produces volcanism. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
The layer below the crust is the mantle. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
A volcano releases lava, ash, and gases. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Water vapour is the most abundant volcanic gas. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xs: **Magma** **produces volcanism**, the **mantle** is the **layer below the crust**, a **volcano** **releases lava, ash and gases**, and **water vapour** is the **most abundant volcanic gas** — option **(3)** a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
After water vapour come **CO2** and **sulphur dioxide**.
xa: **SO2** forms aerosols that scatter sunlight and cool Earth for years.
**Barren Island** (Andaman Sea) is **India's only active volcano**.
**Pacific Ring of Fire** has most eruptions and earthquakes.

10.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The epicentre is located on the Earth's surface directly above the focus.
2. Shaking is generally strongest at the epicentre.
3. The focus is necessarily located at the Earth's surface.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
10.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The focus is an underground point where rupture begins and may be shallow or deep; it is not located at the surface.
10.tq: Find the false statement by testing the precise location of the focus.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: the **epicentre** is the surface point **directly above the focus**.
Statement 2 correct: shaking is **strongest at the epicentre**.
Statement 3 wrong: the **focus** is a point **inside Earth**, shallow or deep.
xa: Typical crustal quakes: **10-29 km** deep.
**Intensity** falls with **distance from the epicentre**.
**Seismic doublet**: two independent quakes of **similar magnitude**, in quick succession, close together.

10.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
10.x: The Ring of Fire is associated mainly with volcanic and convergent-margin activity, not with the San Andreas-type transform setting. The San Andreas Fault is the transform-boundary example.
10.tq: Find the incorrectly assigned boundary type rather than choosing a familiar place name.
xs: **Transform boundary — Ring of Fire** is wrongly matched — option **(4)**.
The **Ring of Fire** is a **convergent** (subduction) setting; the transform example is **San Andreas**.
**Mid-Atlantic Ridge** = divergent; **Himalaya** = convergent — both correct.
xa: **Tectonic** quakes: fault stress exceeds rock strength and the rock ruptures.
The **Pacific Ring of Fire** is the **most active belt**.
**Bhuj 2001** (Kutch) is a tectonic example.

10.s:
Consider the following statements about the causes of earthquakes:
1. Tectonic earthquakes occur when stress on a fault exceeds rock strength and the rock ruptures.
2. Volcanic earthquakes can result from rising magma fracturing rocks or the collapse of volcanic structures.
3. Tectonic earthquakes occur only at convergent plate boundaries.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
10.x: Statement 1 is correct: a tectonic quake is fault rupture when stress exceeds rock strength. Statement 2 is correct: rising magma fracturing rock or collapse of volcanic structures causes volcanic quakes. Statement 3 is wrong: tectonic quakes occur at divergent (Mid-Atlantic Ridge), convergent (Himalaya) and transform (San Andreas) boundaries. Hence 1 and 2 only.
10.tq: Watch for 'only' - tectonic quakes occur at all three boundary types.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: **tectonic** quakes occur when **fault** stress **exceeds rock strength** and the rock ruptures.
Statement 2 correct: **volcanic** quakes come from **rising magma** fracturing rock or volcanic structures collapsing.
Statement 3 wrong: tectonic quakes occur at **divergent**, **convergent** and **transform** boundaries.
xa: **Reservoir-induced**: weight of water — **Koyna 1967**.
**Intraplate**: old hidden faults — **Latur (Killari) 1993**, **Jabalpur**.
Induced (other): **mining**, **fracking** — usually low magnitude.

10.s: The 1993 Latur earthquake is significant in the study of earthquake causes because it demonstrated that
o: earthquakes may occur in stable regions along hidden faults
earthquakes occur only at convergent plate boundaries
all intraplate earthquakes are caused by volcanic eruptions
stable continental regions cannot experience damaging earthquakes
10.x: The Latur earthquake occurred far from a plate boundary and showed that stable continental regions can experience earthquakes along concealed or old faults.
10.tq: Use the exception to the plate-boundary rule as the deciding clue.
xs: **Latur 1993** showed quakes strike **stable areas along hidden faults** — option **(1)**.
It lay **far from any plate boundary** (APPSC **2025**).
It struck a zone then rated low-risk (**Zone I**), with **M 6.2** and **~10,000 dead**.
xa: After Latur, **IS 1893: 2002** merged **Zone I into Zone II**.
Latur is also called **Killari**.
⚠ **Koyna** = reservoir-induced; **Latur** = intraplate.

10.s: Which one of the following is regarded as India's classic example of a reservoir-induced earthquake?
10.x: The Koyna earthquake of 1967 is the classic Indian example of reservoir-induced seismicity, associated with the filling and weight of a large reservoir.
10.tq: Link the named event and year with the specific earthquake mechanism.
xs: **Koyna 1967** (Maharashtra) is India's classic **reservoir-induced** quake — option **(1)**.
Cause: the **weight of water** when large reservoirs are filled.
**Latur 1993** was **intraplate**; **Bhuj 2001** tectonic.
xa: Reservoir-triggered tremors possible near **Nagarjuna Sagar, Srisailam and Polavaram**.
⚠ **Koyna** = reservoir-induced; **Latur** = hidden faults.
Koyna is also listed with intraplate quakes in the peninsula.

10.s:
Which of the following activities may also induce earthquakes, usually of low magnitude?
1. Mining
2. Hydraulic fracturing
3. Filling of large reservoirs
4. Movement along the San Andreas Fault
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
10.x: Mining and hydraulic fracturing are other induced causes, generally producing low-magnitude earthquakes. Reservoir filling is another induced cause, whereas San Andreas movement is tectonic.
10.tq: Group the human-induced causes and exclude the natural transform-boundary example.
xs: **Mining, fracking and reservoir filling** (**1, 2 and 3**) induce quakes — option **(2)**.
Mining and **fracking** usually give **low magnitude** quakes.
**Reservoir-induced**: weight of water — **Koyna 1967**.
**San Andreas** is a **tectonic** (transform) fault, not induced.
xa: Intraplate quakes: **Latur 1993**, **Jabalpur**.
**Volcanic** quakes: rising magma fractures rock.
Tectonic quakes occur at divergent, convergent and transform boundaries.

10.s: A seismic doublet is best described as
o: two volcanic eruptions separated by a long interval
two independent earthquakes of similar magnitude occurring close together in time and space
a main shock followed by aftershocks that gradually become weaker
two waves arriving at the epicentre at exactly the same time
10.x: A seismic doublet consists of two independent earthquakes of similar magnitude occurring in quick succession and close together. This differs from an aftershock sequence, which generally tapers off.
10.tq: Distinguish a doublet from the familiar mainshock–aftershock pattern by focusing on independence and similarity of magnitude.
xs: A **seismic doublet** is **two independent quakes of similar magnitude**, in quick succession, close together — option **(2)**.
An **aftershock sequence** tapers off — option (3) describes that, not a doublet.
xa: Example: **Venezuela (M 7.1 and 7.5)** on the Caribbean-South American **strike-slip** boundary.
Toll: **589 dead**.
**USGS** described it as a "seismic doublet" (**26 Jun 2026**).

10.s:
With reference to seismic waves, consider the following statements:
1. S-waves are transverse waves.
2. S-waves can propagate through liquids.
3. The absence of S-waves beyond about 105° from the epicentre is evidence that the outer core is liquid.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
10.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct: S-waves are transverse (shear motion perpendicular to travel), and their absence beyond about 105° from the epicentre shows the outer core is liquid. Statement 2 is wrong: S-waves travel through solids only, which is exactly why the liquid outer core stops them.
10.tq: Eliminate the statement that reverses the solid-only property of S-waves.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: **S-waves** are **transverse** (shear, **perpendicular** to travel).
Statement 2 wrong: S-waves travel through **solids only**.
Statement 3 correct: no S-waves beyond about **105°** proves the **outer core is liquid**.
xa: **P-waves** arrive **1st**, push-pull, through solid, liquid, gas.
**Surface (L)** waves arrive **last** and **cause most damage**.
⚠ **Love** = side to side; **Rayleigh** = rolling.

10.s: Love and Rayleigh waves are collectively classified as:
10.x: Love and Rayleigh waves move along the Earth's surface and are classified as surface waves.
10.tq: Test the exact classification of closely related seismic waves.
xs: **Love** and **Rayleigh** waves are **surface waves** — option **(1)**.
They **move along the surface** and arrive **last**.
xa: ⚠ **Love** = side to side; **Rayleigh** = rolling, like ocean waves.
Surface (L) waves **cause most damage**.
**P** (1st) and **S** (2nd) waves travel through the Earth's interior.

10.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the magnitude of an earthquake from its intensity?
o: Magnitude denotes observed damage at a place, whereas intensity denotes energy released at the focus
Magnitude varies from place to place, whereas intensity has one value for the entire earthquake
Magnitude denotes energy released at the focus, whereas intensity denotes the observed effects at a particular place
Both magnitude and intensity denote the energy released at the focus
10.x: Magnitude is the quantitative measure of energy released at the focus and has one value for an earthquake. Intensity is the qualitative measure of observed effects at a particular place and varies with distance from the epicentre.
10.tq: Split the options by matching each term with its defining measure.
xs: **Magnitude** = **energy released at the focus**; **intensity** = **observed effects at a place** — option **(3)**.
Magnitude has **one value per quake**; intensity **varies from place to place**.
Options (1) and (2) swap the two.
xa: Magnitude: **Richter scale**, now **Moment Magnitude (Mw)**.
Intensity: **Modified Mercalli (MMI)** and **MSK**, both **I to XII**.
APPSC **2025**: magnitude = energy at focus; intensity = effect at a place.

10.s:
With reference to earthquake measurement, consider the following statements:
1. The Richter scale was developed by Charles F. Richter in 1935.
2. The Richter scale is used to measure earthquake intensity.
3. Moment magnitude is based on the rupture area of the fault and the size of seismic waves.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
10.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. The Richter scale measures magnitude, not intensity; intensity is measured using scales such as Modified Mercalli and MSK.
10.tq: Use the magnitude–intensity distinction to reject the swapped measurement statement.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(3)**.
Statement 1 correct: **Charles F. Richter** devised the scale in **1935**.
Statement 2 wrong: the Richter scale measures **magnitude**, not intensity.
Statement 3 correct: **Mw** is based on **rupture area** of the fault + size of seismic waves.
xa: Mw has largely **replaced Richter** for strong quakes.
Intensity is measured on **MMI** and **MSK** scales.
⚠ APPSC **2022**: "Richter scale measures intensity" is wrong.

10.s: An earthquake increases from magnitude 5 to magnitude 6 on the Richter scale. Which one of the following best describes the change?
o: Its wave amplitude becomes 6 times and energy becomes 36 times
Its wave amplitude becomes 31 times and energy released becomes 10 times
Its wave amplitude becomes 10 times and energy released becomes approximately 31 times
Both its wave amplitude and energy released become 10 times
10.x: An increase of one magnitude unit on the Richter scale represents a tenfold increase in wave amplitude and an approximately 31-fold increase in energy released.
10.tq: Separate the amplitude factor from the energy factor instead of treating both as identical.
xs: One step up gives **10x amplitude** and about **31x energy** — option **(3)**.
The **Richter scale** is **logarithmic** and measures wave amplitude.
Option (2) swaps the two numbers; option (4) ignores the bigger energy jump.
xa: **Mw** (Moment Magnitude) is based on **rupture area** and has largely replaced Richter.
Richter devised the scale in **1935**.
Magnitude has **one value per quake**.

10.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below.

List-I (Instrument)
a. Seismograph
b. Seismometer
c. Seismoscope
d. Tiltmeter

List-II (Function)
i. Sensor used in a seismograph
ii. Shows that a tremor occurred and records its time
iii. Records and measures earthquakes
iv. Measures ground tilt at faults and volcanoes
10.x: A seismograph records and measures earthquakes; a seismometer is its sensor; a seismoscope only indicates that a tremor occurred and its time; and a tiltmeter measures ground tilt.
10.tq: Start from the sure instrument–function pair and eliminate codes containing mismatches.
xs: **a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv** — option **(1)**.
**Seismograph** records and measures earthquakes (APPSC **2025**); **seismometer** is its **sensor**.
**Seismoscope** only shows a tremor occurred and its **time**; **tiltmeter** measures **ground tilt**.
xa: **Creepmeter**: slow slip (**creep**) along a fault.
India's national network uses **broadband seismometers**.
⚠ Earthquakes **still cannot be predicted accurately** (APPSC **2022**).

10.s: Which one of the following statements about earthquake prediction is correct?
o: Earthquakes are accurately predicted through the Richter scale
Earthquakes still cannot be predicted accurately
Earthquakes can be predicted accurately only in stable continental regions
Earthquakes can currently be predicted accurately for a precise time and place
10.x: Despite monitoring and seismological research, earthquakes cannot yet be predicted accurately in terms of their precise time, location and magnitude.
10.tq: Reject the extreme claim that a measurement scale can provide precise prediction.
xs: Earthquakes **still cannot be predicted accurately** — option **(2)** (APPSC **2022**).
The **Richter scale** only measures **magnitude** — it does not predict quakes.
xa: ⚠ "Richter scale measures intensity" is wrong — it measures **magnitude**.
Monitoring: **NCS** runs the **National Seismological Network** of **160 observatories**.
Public alerts: **IndiaQuake** app; MoES app **RISEQ**, now "**Bhookamp**".

10.s: Which one of the following belts is associated with the greatest concentration of earthquakes in the world?
10.x: The Circum-Pacific belt, also called the Ring of Fire, contains the world's greatest concentration of earthquakes and is associated largely with subduction around the Pacific basin.
10.tq: Use the ranking of earthquake belts to select the most active belt.
xs: The **Circum-Pacific belt (Ring of Fire)** has the most earthquakes — option **(3)**.
The **Mid-Continental (Alpine-Himalayan)** belt comes next.
**Mid-oceanic ridges** give **shallow, milder** quakes.
xa: The Ring of Fire is driven by **subduction** around the Pacific basin.
Examples: **Japan, Philippines, Indonesia, Chile, Andes, Alaska**.
**2026** Ring of Fire quakes: **Flores M 7.7**, **Colombia M 7.4**, **Kyushu M 7.1**.

10.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Belt)
a. Pacific Ring of Fire
b. Mid-Atlantic belt
c. Mediterranean-Himalayan belt
 d. Hotspot belt

List-II (Plate setting or process)
i. Mantle plume beneath a moving plate
 ii. Divergent ridge
 iii. Subduction around a basin
 iv. Continental collision

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
10.x: The Pacific Ring of Fire is linked to subduction, the Mid-Atlantic belt to a divergent ridge, the Mediterranean-Himalayan belt to continental collision, and hotspots to mantle plumes.
10.tq: Start with the sure plate-setting pair and eliminate codes containing a wrong association.
xs: **a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i** — option **(1)**.
**Ring of Fire** = **subduction**; **Mid-Atlantic** = **divergent** ridge.
**Mediterranean-Himalayan** = **continental collision**; **hotspots** = **mantle plume** under a moving plate.
xa: Hotspot examples: **Hawaii, Galapagos**, Reunion.
Mid-Atlantic example: **Iceland**.
Mediterranean-Himalayan: **Italy, Türkiye, Himalayas / India**.

10.s: The earthquakes associated with mid-oceanic ridges are generally:
10.x: Mid-oceanic ridge earthquakes are generally shallow and milder, reflecting activity at divergent plate boundaries.
10.tq: Use the depth-and-severity comparison among the major earthquake belts.
xs: Mid-oceanic ridge quakes are **shallow, milder** — option **(4)**.
The ridges are **divergent** settings, not collision zones.
xa: Ranking: **Circum-Pacific** (most) → **Alpine-Himalayan** → **mid-oceanic ridges**.
**Mid-Atlantic belt** example: **Iceland**.
Tsunamis need a focus shallower than **~70 km** and **vertical seafloor uplift**.

10.s: The 1993 Latur earthquake was significant because it occurred in an intraplate region that had earlier been rated as which risk zone?
10.x: The Latur earthquake occurred in an intraplate region that was then classified as low-risk Zone I.
10.tq: Use the numerical-zone clue to distinguish a low-risk intraplate event.
xs: **Latur 1993** struck a zone then rated **Zone I** (low-risk) — option **(3)**.
It was an **intraplate** quake, **M 6.2**, **~10,000 dead**.
xa: After Latur, **IS 1893: 2002** merged **Zone I into Zone II** → four zones.
⚠ **Bhuj 2001** → **DM Act 2005**; **Latur 1993** → Zone I merged into Zone II.
Latur showed quakes strike **stable areas along hidden faults** (APPSC **2025**).

10.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Gorkha earthquake:
1. It occurred in Nepal in 2015.
2. It had a magnitude of 7.8.
3. It occurred along the Main Himalayan Thrust.
4. It caused liquefaction in Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
10.x: All four statements are correct. The 2015 Gorkha earthquake in Nepal had a magnitude of 7.8, occurred along the Main Himalayan Thrust and caused liquefaction in parts of the Gangetic plain.
10.tq: Verify the event through its year, magnitude, tectonic setting and secondary effect.
xs: All four — **1, 2, 3 and 4** — are correct — option **(4)**.
On the **Main Himalayan Thrust**; caused **liquefaction** in **Bihar, UP, WB**.
xa: Liquefaction hits the **soft soils of the Indo-Gangetic plain**.
**Uttarkashi** (**1991**, M ~**6.8**) also lay in the **Himalayan thrust zone**.
Indian plate pushes north at about **5 cm/year**.

10.s:
Match List-I (Earthquake) with List-II (Tectonic setting):
List-I
a. Tohoku, Japan (2011)
b. Turkey-Syria (Feb 2023)
c. Myanmar, Mandalay (2025)
List-II
i. East Anatolian Fault (Anatolian-Arabian plates)
ii. Sagaing Fault - strike-slip, Indian vs Eurasian plate
iii. Pacific plate subduction
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
10.x: Tohoku 2011 (M 9.0) was a Pacific plate subduction quake (tsunami, Fukushima) = iii. Turkey-Syria 2023 (M 7.8) was on the East Anatolian Fault = i. Myanmar 2025 (M 7.7) was on the strike-slip Sagaing Fault between the Indian and Eurasian plates = ii. Option B swaps Tohoku and Turkey-Syria, option C swaps Turkey-Syria and Myanmar, option D mismatches all.
10.tq: Japan = subduction; Turkey = East Anatolian; Myanmar = Sagaing strike-slip.
xs: **a-iii, b-i, c-ii** — option **(1)**.
**Tohoku (2011)** = **Pacific plate subduction** (tsunami, **Fukushima**).
**Turkey-Syria (Feb 2023)** = **East Anatolian Fault**; **Myanmar (2025)** = **Sagaing Fault**, strike-slip.
xa: Tohoku: **M 9.0**; Turkey-Syria: **M 7.8**; Myanmar: **M 7.7**, **2,000+** dead.
**Seismic seiches** were reported during the **Myanmar** earthquake.
The **Sagaing Fault** is the **Indian-Eurasian** boundary.

10.s: Seismic seiches are
o: standing waves in rivers, reservoirs and ponds
waves generated only by volcanic ash
10.x: Seismic seiches are standing waves that may develop in enclosed or partly enclosed water bodies such as rivers, reservoirs and ponds. They were reported during the Myanmar earthquake.
10.tq: Distinguish a water-body phenomenon from earthquake source types and fault movements.
xs: **Seismic seiches** are **standing waves** in rivers, lakes, reservoirs, ponds — option **(3)**.
They were reported during the **Myanmar earthquake**.
Slow slip along a fault is **creep** — option (1) wrong.
xa: **Landslides**: fragile **Himalaya** and **North-East**.
**Liquefaction**: soft soils of the **Indo-Gangetic plain**.
**Fires**: from **broken gas and power lines**.

10.s: Which combination of conditions is most conducive to the generation of a tsunami?
o: Magnitude below 5.0, deep focus and horizontal movement only
Magnitude above 6.5, shallow focus and vertical uplift of the sea floor
Volcanic ash fall without any displacement of water
Deep continental earthquake and subsidence of an inland basin
10.x: A tsunami generally requires an earthquake of magnitude greater than 6.5, a focus shallower than approximately 70 km and vertical uplift of the sea floor.
10.tq: Apply the necessary-condition test instead of relying on magnitude alone.
xs: A tsunami needs **M > 6.5**, a **shallow focus** and **vertical seafloor uplift** — option **(2)**.
The focus must be shallower than **~70 km**.
Horizontal movement or a deep focus will not do — option (1) wrong.
xa: Over **80%** of tsunamis come from **megathrust subduction** quakes.
**Kamchatka (Aug 2025)**: **M 8.8** megathrust quake caused only a **limited tsunami**.
The **Tsunami Early Warning System** was built after the **2004 Sumatra** quake.

10.s:
Match the earthquake effect with the region or cause most closely associated with it:

List-I (Effect)
a. Landslides
b. Liquefaction
c. Seismic seiches
 d. Fires

List-II (Associated setting or cause)
i. Broken gas and power lines
 ii. Lakes and reservoirs
 iii. Fragile Himalaya and North-East
 iv. Soft soils of the Indo-Gangetic Plain

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
10.x: Earthquakes trigger landslides in the fragile Himalaya and North-East, liquefaction in soft Indo-Gangetic soils, seiches in lakes and reservoirs, and fires through broken gas and power lines.
10.tq: Match each hazard with its distinctive physical setting or immediate cause.
xs: **a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i** — option **(1)**.
**Landslides** = fragile **Himalaya and North-East**; **liquefaction** = soft soils of the **Indo-Gangetic plain**.
**Seiches** = rivers, **lakes, reservoirs**; **fires** = **broken gas and power lines**.
xa: Seiches were reported during the **Myanmar earthquake**.
**Gorkha (2015)** caused liquefaction in **Bihar, UP, WB**.
**95%** of quake deaths occur in poorly built **1-3 storey houses**.

10.s: India forms part of which major seismic belt?
10.x: India lies in the Alpine-Himalayan seismic belt, which extends eastward through the North-East into Myanmar.
10.tq: Recall the major global seismic belt associated with India.
xs: India lies in the **Alpine-Himalayan belt** — option **(1)**.
The **Indian plate** pushes north at about **5 cm/year** into the **Eurasian plate**.
The belt continues east through the **North-East** into **Myanmar**.
xa: **Sagaing Fault** = Indian-Eurasian boundary in Myanmar.
**Zone V** runs along the Himalayan front, where **magnitude-8** quakes have struck.
The **Circum-Pacific** belt has the most quakes; Alpine-Himalayan is **next**.

10.s: Which of the following regions is NOT identified as a prone area for significant earthquake activity in India?
10.x: Kutch, the North-East and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands are earthquake-prone areas. Visakhapatnam is cited as an example of a low-risk stable-shield area.
10.tq: Find the location that does not belong to the group of earthquake-prone regions.
xs: The **stable shield around Visakhapatnam** is not a prone area — option **(2)**.
**Visakhapatnam** lies in **Zone II** (low risk).
**Kutch**, the **North-East** and **Andaman & Nicobar** are prone areas, all in **Zone V**.
xa: ⚠ **Visakhapatnam** = Zone II; **Vijayawada** = Zone III.
AP is mostly in **Zones II and III**.
**Koraput-Jeypore quake (6 Apr 2026)**: **M 4.4**, shook **Araku** and **Paderu**.

10.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Liquefaction is a particular concern in the Indo-Gangetic plain.
2. Peninsular faults associated with Latur and Koyna can produce earthquakes.
3. The Himalaya, North-East and Andaman and Nicobar Islands are among the earthquake-prone regions of India.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
10.x: All three statements are correct. Earthquake vulnerability in India is associated with Himalayan and North-Eastern regions, liquefaction-prone alluvial plains, peninsular faults and the Andaman and Nicobar region.
10.tq: Combine regional distribution with the associated hazard or geological setting.
xs: All three — **1, 2 and 3** — are correct — option **(4)**.
Statement 1 correct: the **Indo-Gangetic plain** (Bihar, UP, WB) is highly prone to **soil liquefaction**.
Statement 2 correct: peninsular faults (**Latur, Koyna**) can give severe **intraplate** quakes.
Statement 3 correct: the **Himalaya**, **North-East** and **Andaman & Nicobar** are prone areas.
xa: **Kutch** is another prone area (**Zone V**).
**Jabalpur** is also an intraplate example.
Indian plate pushes north at about **5 cm/year**.

10.s: Under IS 1893:2016, which sequence correctly represents the seismic zones from lower to higher risk?
o: Zone II, Zone III, Zone IV, Zone V
Zone V, Zone IV, Zone III, Zone II
Zone III, Zone II, Zone V, Zone IV
Zone II, Zone IV, Zone III, Zone V
10.x: Under the four-zone map in force, Zone II represents low risk, Zone III moderate risk, Zone IV high risk and Zone V very high risk.
10.tq: Arrange the zones by increasing risk rather than by geographical location.
xs: Low to high risk: **Zone II, Zone III, Zone IV, Zone V** — option **(1)**.
The map in force (**IS 1893: 2016**) has **four zones**; **Zone II is the calmest**.
xa: **Zone V** runs along the Himalayan front where **magnitude-8** quakes have struck.
**Zone VI** came in the **2025** code, **withdrawn on 3 Mar 2026**.
**Zone I** was merged into Zone II after **Latur 1993**.

10.s: Which of the following areas is included in Zone V under the seismic zoning map in force?
10.x: Kutch is included in Zone V, the very-high-risk zone. Visakhapatnam and Hyderabad are examples of Zone II, while Vijayawada is cited under Zone III.
10.tq: Distinguish locations by their assigned seismic-risk zones.
xs: **Kutch** (Gujarat) is in **Zone V** — option **(3)**.
**Visakhapatnam** and **Hyderabad** are **Zone II**; **Vijayawada** is **Zone III**.
xa: Zone V also covers the **entire North-East**, **J&K, Ladakh, HP, Uttarakhand**, north **Bihar**, **Andaman & Nicobar**.
The withdrawn **2025** code placed parts of **Kutch** in **Zone VI**.

10.s:
Consider the following statements about seismic zones under IS 1893: 2016:
1. Delhi lies in Zone IV.
2. Vijayawada lies in Zone III.
3. Visakhapatnam lies in Zone III.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
10.x: Statement 1 is correct: Delhi, the rest of the Himalayan foothills and the Indo-Gangetic belt are Zone IV (high). Statement 2 is correct: Vijayawada is cited under Zone III (moderate). Statement 3 is wrong: Visakhapatnam is on the stable shield in Zone II (low). Hence 1 and 2 only.
10.tq: AP cities: Visakhapatnam = Zone II, Vijayawada = Zone III; AP has no Zone V.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: **Delhi** is in **Zone IV** (high).
Statement 2 correct: **Vijayawada** is in **Zone III** (moderate).
Statement 3 wrong: **Visakhapatnam** is in **Zone II** (low), on the stable shield.
xa: ⚠ **Visakhapatnam** = Zone II; **Vijayawada** = Zone III.
Zone III also includes **Chennai**, the **Latur-Koyna** belt and the **Amaravati** region.
AP has **no area in Zone V**.

10.s: Which of the following States or Union Territories has no area in Zone V?
10.x: Andhra Pradesh has no area in Zone V. Assam, Bihar and Jammu and Kashmir are identified as having areas in Zone V.
10.tq: Use the exception-based regional comparison to identify the outlier.
xs: **Andhra Pradesh** has **no area in Zone V** — option **(3)** (APPSC **2024**).
**Assam, Bihar and J&K** do have Zone V areas.
AP lies mostly in **Zones II and III** (low to moderate risk).
xa: **Visakhapatnam** = Zone II; **Vijayawada** = Zone III.
Reservoir-triggered tremors possible near **Nagarjuna Sagar, Srisailam and Polavaram**.
Old **Eastern Ghats** faults can also trigger tremors.

10.s: Zone I was merged into which zone after the 1993 Latur earthquake?
10.x: After the 1993 Latur earthquake, Zone I was merged into Zone II, resulting in the four-zone classification under IS 1893:2002.
10.tq: Link a classification change to the event that prompted it.
xs: After **Latur 1993**, **Zone I** was merged into **Zone II** — option **(3)**.
This came in **IS 1893: 2002**, giving **four zones**.
xa: **IS 1893 (Part 1): 2025** (BIS, **6 Nov 2025**) added **Zone VI** using a **probabilistic (PSHA)** model.
BIS **withdrew** it on **3 Mar 2026**; the **2016** four-zone map is back in force.
The 2025 map put **over 60%** of India's land in moderate-to-high zones.

10.s:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
A. Withdrawal of IS 1893 (Part 1): 2025
B. Notification of IS 1893 (Part 1): 2025
C. 1993 Latur earthquake
D. Bhuj earthquake
10.x: The correct order is the 1993 Latur earthquake, the 2001 Bhuj earthquake, notification of the 2025 revision on 6 November 2025, and its withdrawal on 3 March 2026.
10.tq: Use the first and last events, then place the two intermediate dates.
xs: Order: **Latur (1993) → Bhuj (2001) → notification of 2025 code → its withdrawal** (**C, D, B, A**) — option **(1)**.
**Latur 1993** came first; **Bhuj** struck on **26 Jan 2001**.
BIS notified **IS 1893 (Part 1): 2025** on **6 Nov 2025** and **withdrew it on 3 Mar 2026**.
xa: After Latur, **IS 1893: 2002** merged **Zone I into Zone II**.
⚠ **Bhuj 2001** → **DM Act 2005**; **Latur 1993** → Zone I merged into Zone II.
After the withdrawal, **IS 1893 (Part 1): 2016** was restored.

10.s: Which feature was introduced by the IS 1893 (Part 1): 2025 revision?
o: The abolition of all seismic zones in India
The exclusion of the North-East from the highest-risk category
The restoration of Zone I as the lowest zone
A new top Zone VI covering parts of Kashmir, the North-East and Kutch
10.x: The 2025 revision introduced a new top Zone VI for parts of Kashmir, the North-East and Kutch, and placed more than 60% of India’s landmass in moderate-to-high zones.
10.tq: Identify the distinctive institutional change rather than a reversed zoning claim.
xs: The **2025** revision added a new top **Zone VI** for parts of **Kashmir, the North-East and Kutch** — option **(4)**.
It used a **probabilistic (PSHA)** model.
It put **over 60%** of India's landmass in moderate-to-high zones.
xa: The map was built by **IIT-Madras** for **NDMA**; **PGA 0.15-0.75 g** from Zone II to Zone VI.
Basis: **69,519 events** and **36 seismogenic zones**.
BIS **withdrew** it on **3 Mar 2026**.

10.s: The 2025 revision of IS 1893 was withdrawn on 3 March 2026 primarily after objections relating to which issue?
o: The inability to identify earthquakes of magnitude 3.0 and above
The absence of earthquake data from the North-East
The replacement of the National Seismological Network
The cost implications raised by MoHUA, Metro Rail corporations and the NDSA
10.x: The 2025 revision was withdrawn after MoHUA, Metro Rail corporations and the NDSA objected to the cost implications. The 2016 code was restored.
10.tq: Match the policy rollback with the specific administrative objection.
xs: The 2025 code was withdrawn after **cost objections** from **MoHUA, Metro Rail corporations and the NDSA** — option **(4)**.
BIS **withdrew it on 3 Mar 2026**; the **2016** code was restored.
xa: A **review panel** is to report to the **Cabinet Secretariat**.
Debate: safer **PSHA-based codes** vs **construction cost**.
Experts call the restored 2016 values **too low for the Himalaya**; NDMA called the new ones "**too high**".

10.s: The National Centre for Seismology detects which combination of earthquakes through its monitoring network?
o: Only earthquakes capable of producing tsunamis
Indian earthquakes of magnitude 3.0 and above and global earthquakes of magnitude 6.0 and above
Indian earthquakes of magnitude 1.0 and global earthquakes of magnitude 3.0 and above
Only earthquakes occurring in the Himalayan region
10.x: The network detects every Indian earthquake of magnitude 3.0 or above and global earthquakes of magnitude 6.0 or above, including tsunami-capable events.
10.tq: Separate the two magnitude thresholds instead of treating them as identical.
xs: NCS detects every **Indian** quake of **M 3.0+** and **global** quakes of **M 6.0+** — option **(2)**.
Global coverage includes **tsunami-capable** quakes.
xa: NCS runs the **National Seismological Network** of **160 observatories**.
Public alerts: **IndiaQuake** app.
**Tsunami Early Warning System** was built after the **2004 Sumatra** quake.

10.s: The first seismological observatory in India was established at which place in 1898?
10.x: India’s first seismological observatory was established at Alipore in Calcutta in 1898.
10.tq: Recall the earliest observatory by combining its place and year.
xs: India's **first observatory** was at **Alipore, Calcutta (1898)** — option **(2)**.
**New Delhi** is the seat of the **National Centre for Seismology**, not the first observatory.
xa: NCS is attached to **MoES**.
The National Seismological Network has **160 observatories**.
MoES app **RISEQ** is now "**Bhookamp**".

10.s: RISEQ, the earthquake-related app of the Ministry of Earth Sciences, is now known by which name?
10.x: The MoES app RISEQ is now called “Bhookamp.” IndiaQuake is the public-alert app of the National Centre for Seismology.
10.tq: Discriminate between two similarly themed earthquake applications.
xs: The MoES app **RISEQ** is now "**Bhookamp**" — option **(1)**.
**IndiaQuake** is the separate **public alerts** app.
xa: NCS (New Delhi) is an attached office of **MoES**.
First observatory: **Alipore, Calcutta (1898)**.
NCS detects Indian quakes of **M 3.0+**.

10.s: India developed its Tsunami Early Warning System after which event?
10.x: India built its Tsunami Early Warning System after the 2004 Sumatra earthquake and tsunami.
10.tq: Match the warning-system initiative with the triggering disaster.
xs: India's **Tsunami Early Warning System** was built after the **2004 Sumatra quake** — option **(3)**.
**Bhuj 2001** led to the **DM Act 2005** and **NDMA** instead.
xa: Tsunamis need **M > 6.5**, focus shallower than **~70 km**, **vertical seafloor uplift**.
Over **80%** come from **megathrust subduction** quakes.
**Tohoku (2011)**: tsunami and **Fukushima**.

10.s: Which gas is present in the greatest proportion among the principal gases released by volcanoes?
10.x: Volcanic gases consist mostly of water vapour, followed by carbon dioxide, sulphur dioxide and hydrogen sulphide.
10.tq: Recall the stated order of abundance rather than confusing gases with solid volcanic products.
xs: **Water vapour** is the most abundant volcanic gas — option **(3)**.
It is followed by **CO2**, **SO2** and **H2S**.
xa: Products: **pyroclastic debris, ash, volcanic bombs, lava**.
**Vulcanian** eruptions are **more explosive** than Strombolian.
**Shield** volcanoes have **fluid basaltic lava**.

10.s:
Consider the following statements about composite or stratovolcanoes:
1. They generally have thick and viscous lava.
2. They commonly form steep cones.
3. They are associated with explosive eruptions.
4. They constitute approximately 60% of the Earth's volcanoes.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
10.x: All four statements are correct. Composite or stratovolcanoes have viscous lava, steep cones, explosive activity and constitute approximately 60% of Earth's volcanoes.
10.tq: Test a group of defining characteristics together, including the quantitative share.
xs: All four — **1, 2, 3 and 4** — are correct — option **(4)**.
**Composite/stratovolcanoes** have **thick, viscous lava**, **steep cones** and **explosive** eruptions.
They form **~60%** of Earth's volcanoes.
xa: Examples: **Etna, Mayon, Fuego**.
**Mayon** (Philippines) is a **symmetrical composite cone**.
**Fuego** gives **Strombolian** eruptions every **15-20 min**.

10.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Mauna Loa — caldera formed by explosive collapse
Mount Aso — one of the world's largest calderas
Etna — complex volcano with several overlapping vents only
Dukono — shield volcano with gentle basaltic slopes
10.x: Mount Aso is one of the world's largest calderas. Mauna Loa is a shield volcano, while Dukono is listed as a complex volcano.
10.tq: Start with the distinctive example of a landform and then eliminate type-example reversals.
xs: **Mount Aso — one of the world's largest calderas** is correct — option **(2)**.
**Mauna Loa** is an active **shield** volcano — option (1) wrong.
**Etna** is a **stratovolcano**; **Dukono** a **complex** volcano — options (3) and (4) wrong.
xa: A **caldera** is a large depression from **collapse** after an explosive eruption.
**Taal** is listed both as a caldera and a **complex** volcano.
**Dukono** is on **Halmahera, Indonesia**.

10.s: Which of the following is correctly matched with a complex or compound volcano?
10.x: Taal in the Philippines is a complex or compound volcano. Dukono is in Indonesia, while Mount Aso is a caldera in Japan.
10.tq: Use the sure example-location pair and reject nearby country substitutions.
xs: **Taal — Philippines** is the complex (compound) volcano match — option **(3)**.
Complex volcanoes have **several vents, overlapping cones, lava domes**.
**Dukono** is in **Halmahera, Indonesia**, not Guatemala; **Mount Aso** is a **caldera**.
xa: The other complex example is **Dukono**.
**Mayon** (Philippines): **symmetrical composite cone**.
**Volcan de Fuego** is the Guatemala volcano.

10.s: Which statement correctly distinguishes Strombolian and Vulcanian eruptions?
o: Vulcanian eruptions consist only of gentle lava flows.
Strombolian eruptions are frequent and mild, whereas Vulcanian eruptions are more explosive.
Strombolian eruptions are always more explosive than Vulcanian eruptions.
Both terms refer exclusively to dormant volcanoes.
10.x: Strombolian eruptions involve frequent, mild bursts of bombs and ash, whereas Vulcanian eruptions are more explosive.
10.tq: Compare the intensity and nature of the two similarly named eruption styles.
xs: **Strombolian** = frequent, **mild** bursts; **Vulcanian** = **more explosive** — option **(2)**.
Strombolian bursts throw **bombs and ash**.
Option (3) reverses the two.
xa: **Stromboli** (Italy) gives its name to **Strombolian** eruptions.
**Volcan de Fuego** has Strombolian eruptions every **15-20 min**.
Stromboli is the "**Lighthouse of the Mediterranean**".

10.s: A large, often dome-shaped mass of granite occurring at great depth and exposed after denudation is called:
10.x: A batholith is a huge mass of granite emplaced at depth. It may become exposed after denudation removes the overlying rocks.
10.tq: Identify the intrusive landform from its scale and depth.
xs: A huge dome-shaped **granite** mass cooled deep in the crust is a **batholith** — option **(3)**.
It forms **mountain cores** and is **exposed after denudation**.
**Sill** = horizontal sheet; **lopolith** = saucer; **phacolith** = wavy, lens-shaped mass.
xa: Intrusive bodies form from magma that **cools inside the crust**.
The **Ladakh Magmatic Arc** went through a **batholith phase**.
**Laccolith**: dome with a **flat base**, fed by a pipe.

10.s:
Consider the following statements about intrusive volcanic forms:
1. A laccolith is a dome-shaped body with a flat base.
2. A lopolith is a saucer-shaped body, concave upward.
3. A sill is a vertical wall cutting across the rock beds.
4. Dykes fed the Deccan Traps.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
10.x: Statement 1 is correct: a laccolith is dome-shaped with a flat base, fed by a pipe. Statement 2 is correct: a lopolith is saucer-shaped (concave upward). Statement 3 is wrong: a sill is a horizontal sheet parallel to the beds; the vertical wall cutting across beds is a dyke. Statement 4 is correct: dykes fed the Deccan Traps. Hence 1, 2 and 4 only.
10.tq: Sill = horizontal/parallel; dyke = vertical/across.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 4** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: a **laccolith** is **dome-shaped** with a flat base.
Statement 2 correct: a **lopolith** is **saucer-shaped** (concave upward).
Statement 3 wrong: a **sill** is **horizontal**; the vertical wall is a **dyke**.
Statement 4 correct: **dykes** fed the **Deccan Traps** (western Maharashtra).
xa: **Phacolith**: wavy mass at the base of a **syncline** or top of an **anticline**.
Thin sills are called **sheets**.
⚠ APPSC G1 **2024**: domes are **laccoliths**, not phacoliths.

10.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Lopolith — wavy mass in a folded structure
Phacolith — wavy mass at the base of a syncline or top of an anticline
Laccolith — vertical wall cutting across rock beds
10.x: A phacolith is a wavy intrusive mass occurring at the base of a syncline or the top of an anticline. A lopolith is saucer-shaped, a laccolith is dome-shaped with a flat base, and a dyke is a vertical wall.
10.tq: Match each intrusive form with its distinctive shape or structural position.
xs: **Phacolith — wavy mass at the base of a syncline or top of an anticline** is correct — option **(3)**.
**Batholith** is a huge granite mass, not saucer-shaped; the **lopolith** is the saucer — options (1), (2) wrong.
A **laccolith** is a **dome**; the vertical wall is a **dyke** — option (4) wrong.
xa: ⚠ APPSC G1 **2024**: "phacoliths are large domed mounds" is the wrong statement.
**Sill / sheet**: **horizontal**, parallel to the beds.
**Dykes** fed the **Deccan Traps**.

10.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the geological development of the Ladakh Magmatic Arc?
o: It formed when the Neo-Tethys plate subducted under Eurasia and underwent a batholith phase from about 160 Ma to less than 45 Ma.
It formed from the Reunion hotspot during the end of the Cretaceous and consists only of flood basalts.
It formed at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge through present-day divergent movement.
It developed when the Indian plate subducted beneath the Pacific plate during the Quaternary period.
10.x: The Ladakh Magmatic Arc formed through subduction of the Neo-Tethys plate beneath Eurasia and experienced a batholith phase from approximately 160 Ma to less than 45 Ma.
10.tq: Combine the tectonic process with the geological time interval and reject unrelated settings.
xs: The arc formed as the **Neo-Tethys plate subducted under Eurasia**, with a **batholith phase** from **~160 Ma** to **<45 Ma** — option **(1)**.
Flood basalts belong to the **Deccan**, not Ladakh — option (2) wrong.
xa: It lies in the **Trans-Himalaya** between the **Indus and Shyok** suture zones.
**Batholith**: dome-shaped granite mass exposed after **denudation**.
Extrusive landforms include **lava plateaus (Deccan)**.

10.s: Which one of the following is an extrusive volcanic landform?
10.x: Lava plateaus, cinder and composite cones, craters, calderas and lava flows are extrusive volcanic landforms. Batholiths, lopoliths and phacoliths are intrusive forms.
10.tq: Separate surface-formed extrusive features from underground intrusive bodies.
xs: A **lava plateau** is an **extrusive** landform — option **(2)**.
Other extrusive forms: **cinder and composite cones, craters, calderas, lava flows**.
**Lopolith**, **phacolith** and **batholith** are **intrusive** — magma cooled inside the crust.
xa: Example lava plateau: the **Deccan**.
**Dykes** fed the Deccan Traps.
⚠ **Sill** = horizontal; **dyke** = vertical.

10.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Stromboli — Lighthouse of the Mediterranean
2. Hekla — Iceland
3. Mauna Loa — Hawaii, USA
4. Tungurahua — Ecuador
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
10.x: All four pairs are correctly matched. Stromboli is known as the Lighthouse of the Mediterranean, Hekla is in Iceland, Mauna Loa is in Hawaii, and Tungurahua is in Ecuador.
10.tq: Check each country or regional location before selecting the coded combination.
xs: All four pairs — **1, 2, 3 and 4** — are correct — option **(4)**.
**Stromboli** (Italy) = "**Lighthouse of the Mediterranean**"; **Hekla** = **Iceland** (Mid-Atlantic Ridge).
**Mauna Loa** = **Hawaii, USA** (shield); **Tungurahua** = **Ecuador** (active).
xa: Stromboli gives its name to **Strombolian** eruptions.
⚠ **Kilimanjaro** and **Fuji** = dormant; **Etna, Stromboli, Vesuvius** = active (all Italy).
**Ojos del Salado** (Chile) is the **world's highest active volcano** (**6,893 m**).

10.s: Which one of the following statements regarding Mount Etna is correct?
o: It is Europe's largest and most active volcano, rises to about 3,300 m and became a UNESCO site in 2013.
It is Africa's highest peak and has been dormant since 1707.
It is the world's highest active volcano at 6,893 m.
It is an extinct volcano that buried Pompeii in AD 79.
10.x: Etna is Europe's largest and most active volcano, is approximately 3,300 m high and has been a UNESCO site since 2013.
10.tq: Distinguish closely related volcano facts by checking the continent, height, status and historical association.
xs: **Etna** is **Europe's largest and most active** volcano, **~3,300 m**, a UNESCO site since **2013** — option **(1)**.
**Africa's highest peak** is **Kilimanjaro**; dormant since **1707** is **Fuji** — option (2) wrong.
The **world's highest active volcano** (**6,893 m**) is **Ojos del Salado** — option (3) wrong.
**Pompeii (AD 79)** was buried by **Vesuvius** — option (4) wrong.
xa: Etna is in **Sicily**, an active **stratovolcano**.
APPSC G1 **2018** cited Etna as a classic **volcanic mountain**.
