2. It will map energy and water budgets, land surface temperature and urban heat islands.
3. It was launched on a PSLV in 2025.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
15.x: Statement 1 is correct: TRISHNA is an ISRO-CNES thermal-infrared mission. Statement 2 is correct: it will map energy/water budgets, land surface temperature and urban heat islands. Statement 3 is wrong: its PSLV launch is due in 2027. Hence 1 and 2 only.
15.tq: TRISHNA = thermal IR, India + France, launch due 2027.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: **TRISHNA** is an **Indo-French** thermal-infrared satellite (**ISRO-CNES**).
Statement 2 correct: it will map **energy and water budgets**, **land surface temperature** and **urban heat islands**.
Statement 3 wrong: its **PSLV** launch is due in **2027**, not done in 2025.
xa: Urban heat island: **concrete and asphalt** store heat; Hyderabad UHI intensity **5.74-6.82 °C**.
Oceans took up a record **+23 zettajoules** of heat in **2025**.
A **heat dome** = stalled high pressure under a slowed, meandering **jet stream**.

15.s: A heat dome is best described as a situation in which:
o: A cold ocean current remains below a stationary cyclone
A low-pressure system forms over a rapidly moving jet stream
A monsoon trough shifts permanently towards the poles
A stalled high-pressure system remains under a slowed, meandering jet stream
15.x: A heat dome develops when a high-pressure system stalls beneath a slowed and meandering jet stream, producing persistent heat.
15.tq: Select the option that correctly links the pressure system with the jet-stream condition.
xs: A **heat dome** is a **stalled high-pressure system** under a **slowed, meandering jet stream** — option **(4)**.
It caused a record early heatwave in **Western Europe** (**27 May 2026**).
It involves high pressure, not a low-pressure system or cyclone.
xa: Oceans absorbed a record **+23 ZJ** of heat in **2025** (~**90%** of excess heat).
IMD heatwave thresholds: **40°C plains / 37°C coast / 30°C hills**.
AP 2026: **El Nino** intensified the heat (**22-23 May 2026**).

15.s:
Assertion (A): Cloudy nights are generally warmer than clear-sky nights.
Reason (R): Clouds reduce terrestrial heat loss at night.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
15.x: Both are true and R explains A: clouds trap outgoing heat at night, keeping cloudy nights warmer.
15.tq: Check whether R is the cause of A.
n: Cloudy conditions reduce terrestrial heat loss at night. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Cloudy conditions produce warmer nights. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Cloud cover affects day and night temperature. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
xs: **Both A and R are true**, and R is the **correct explanation** of A — option **(1)**.
At night, clouds **reduce terrestrial heat loss** — they **trap outgoing radiation** and send heat back — so cloudy nights are **warmer**.
**Clear nights** lose more heat by radiation (cold nights, **frost**).
xa: By day, clouds **reduce incoming solar radiation** — **cooler days**.
**High, thin clouds trap heat**; **low, thick clouds reflect sunlight**.
**Planetary albedo** about **35%**.

15.s:
Consider the following statements:

I. Cloudy conditions reduce incoming solar radiation during the day and make daytime conditions cooler.
II. Clear skies produce greater solar heating during the day.
III. Clear skies produce greater terrestrial cooling at night.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
15.x: All three are correct: clouds cut daytime sunshine, while clear skies allow more daytime heating and more night-time cooling.
15.tq: Relate cloud cover to heating and cooling.
n: Cloudy conditions reduce incoming solar radiation during the day. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Cloudy conditions produce cooler daytime temperatures. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Clear skies allow greater solar heating during the day. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Clear skies cause greater terrestrial cooling at night. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Cloud cover affects day and night temperature. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
xs: **All three statements are correct** — option **(4)** I, II and III.
I: **cloudy** skies **reduce incoming solar radiation** — **cooler daytime**.
II: **clear** skies give **greater solar heating** by day.
III: clear skies give **greater terrestrial cooling** at night.
xa: **Cloudy nights** stay warmer.
Annual range is **minimum at the equator**; largest in high-latitude interiors (**Siberia**).
Seasonal differences are **maximum in high latitudes** (APPSC-G1 **2023**).

15.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the minimum threshold temperature used in IMD heatwave criteria:

I. For plains, the minimum threshold temperature is 40°C.
II. For coastal areas, the minimum threshold temperature is 37°C.
III. For hilly regions, the minimum threshold temperature is 30°C.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
15.x: All three are correct: a heatwave needs at least 40°C in the plains, 37°C on the coast, and 30°C in the hills.
15.tq: Recall the 40–37–30 thresholds.
n: The minimum threshold temperature for declaring a heatwave in plains is 40°C. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 70-72]
The minimum threshold temperature for declaring a heatwave in coastal areas is 37°C. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 70-72]
The minimum threshold temperature for declaring a heatwave in hilly regions is 30°C. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 70-72]
xs: **All three statements are correct** — option **(4)** I, II and III.
IMD minimum thresholds: **plains 40°C**, **coastal areas 37°C**, **hilly regions 30°C**.
⚠ Memory aid: **40 – 37 – 30** = **plains – coast – hills**.
xa: Heatwave = departure of **4.5°C to 6.4°C**; severe = **more than 6.4°C**.
An actual maximum of **45°C** or more is a heatwave on its own.
**NDMA heat-wave guidelines:** **2019**; AP **Heat Wave Action Plan** since **2016**.

15.s:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
 a. Heatwave in plains
 b. Severe heatwave in plains
 c. Heatwave in coastal areas
 d. Severe heatwave in plains based on actual maximum temperature

List-II
 i. Departure from normal of 4.5°C or more when the maximum is at least 37°C
 ii. Departure from normal is more than 6.4°C
 iii. Departure from normal is 4.5°C to 6.4°C
 iv. Actual maximum temperature of 47°C or more
15.x: In the plains a heatwave is a departure of 4.5–6.4°C and a severe one more than 6.4°C, or an actual maximum of 47°C or more; on the coast a 4.5°C departure counts once the maximum reaches 37°C, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-i, d-iv.
15.tq: Separate departure-based criteria from actual-temperature criteria by region.
n: A heatwave in plains is declared when the temperature departure from normal is 4.5°C to 6.4°C. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 70-72]
A severe heatwave in plains is declared when the temperature departure from normal is more than 6.4°C. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 70-72]
A heatwave in coastal areas is declared when the temperature departure from normal is 4.5°C or more. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 70-72]
A heatwave in hilly regions is declared when the temperature departure from normal is 4.5°C to 6.4°C. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 70-72]
xs: Plains heatwave = departure **4.5°C to 6.4°C**; plains severe = **more than 6.4°C**; coastal heatwave = **4.5°C or more** at **37°C**; plains severe by actual maximum = **47°C** — option **(2)** a-iii, b-ii, c-i, d-iv.
Thresholds: **plains 40°C**, **coast 37°C**, **hills 30°C**.
xa: Plains heatwave by actual maximum: **at least 45°C**.
⚠ Sources differ: other notes apply **4.5 to 6.4 °C** to all regions, coast included.
AP **2026** peak: **48.1 °C** at **Piduguralla**; **45 °C** crossed in **18** districts.

15.s:
Match the condition with the corresponding actual maximum temperature criterion in plains.

List-I
 a. Heatwave identified by actual maximum temperature
 b. Severe heatwave identified by actual maximum temperature

List-II
 i. At least 45°C
 ii. At least 47°C
15.x: In the plains, an actual maximum of 45°C or more counts as a heatwave, and 47°C or more as a severe heatwave. The answer is a-i, b-ii.
15.tq: Recall the 45°C and 47°C rules.
n: A heatwave in plains is also identified when the actual maximum temperature is at least 45°C. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 70-72]
A severe heatwave in plains is also identified when the actual maximum temperature is at least 47°C. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 70-72]
xs: In the plains, a **heatwave** is identified at **at least 45°C** and a **severe heatwave** at **at least 47°C** — option **(3)** a-i, b-ii.
This applies to **plains only**, using the **actual maximum temperature**.
xa: Otherwise a heatwave needs a **40°C** threshold plus a departure of **4.5–6.4°C**.
Coastal threshold **37°C**; hilly **30°C**.
IMD criteria updated **Apr 2026**.

15.s:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the declaration of cold waves:

List-I
 a. Plains: minimum-temperature threshold
 b. Plains: cold-wave departure
 c. Plains: severe cold-wave departure
 d. Hilly regions: minimum-temperature threshold
 e. Hilly regions: cold-wave departure
 f. Hilly regions: severe cold-wave departure

List-II
 i. 0°C or below
 ii. 10°C or below
 iii. Negative departure of 4.5°C to 6.4°C
 iv. Negative departure greater than 6.4°C

Select the correct answer using the code below:
o: a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i, e-iii, f-iv
a-i, b-iii, c-iv, d-ii, e-iii, f-iv
a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i, e-iv, f-iii
a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i, e-iii, f-iv
15.x: The plains threshold is 10°C or below and the hills 0°C or below; a cold wave is a departure of −4.5 to −6.4°C and a severe one more than 6.4°C. The answer is option A.
15.tq: Recall the cold wave thresholds.
n: The minimum-temperature threshold for declaring a cold wave in plains is 10°C or below. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-74]
In plains, a cold wave is declared when the minimum temperature has a negative departure of 4.5°C to 6.4°C. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-74]
In plains, a severe cold wave is declared when the minimum temperature has a negative departure greater than 6.4°C. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-74]
The minimum-temperature threshold for declaring a cold wave in hilly regions is 0°C or below. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-74]
In hilly regions, a cold wave is declared when the minimum temperature has a negative departure of 4.5°C to 6.4°C. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-74]
In hilly regions, a severe cold wave is declared when the minimum temperature has a negative departure greater than 6.4°C. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-74]
xs: Plains threshold **10°C or below**, hills **0°C or below**; cold wave = **4.5°C to 6.4°C** negative departure; severe = **greater than 6.4°C** — option **(1)** a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i, e-iii, f-iv.
The same departures apply in both **plains** and **hilly regions**.
xa: **Coastal stations:** threshold **15°C or below**; cold wave at **4.5°C or more** departure.
Plains by actual minimum: **cold wave** at **4°C or below**; **severe** at **2°C or below**.
India's coldest: **Dras** (Ladakh), **-45°C** (**1908**).

15.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: Temperature generally decreases from the equator towards the poles.
The sea moderates temperature, making coastal climates more equable.
Interior areas generally have a smaller annual temperature range than coastal areas.
Temperature generally decreases with increasing altitude.
15.x: Option C is incorrect: interior areas have a larger annual range, because land heats and cools fast. Coasts are equable because the sea moderates them.
15.tq: Check for a reversed comparison.
n: Temperature generally decreases from the equator toward the poles. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Temperature generally decreases with increasing altitude. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
The sea moderates temperature. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Coastal climates are equable. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Interior temperatures are more extreme. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Coastal regions have a smaller annual temperature range. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Interior regions have a larger annual temperature range. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
xs: The incorrect statement is that **interior areas** have a **smaller annual temperature range** than **coastal areas** — option **(3)**: interiors have a **larger** range.
**Land heats and cools rapidly**, while the **sea heats and cools slowly** and **moderates temperature** — so coasts are **equable**, interiors **extreme (continental)**.
The others are correct: temperature **decreases toward the poles** and **with altitude**.
xa: **Warm currents raise** coastal temperatures; **cold currents lower** them.
The **annual range** is generally **greater toward higher latitudes**.
**Hottest latitudes:** **subtropical deserts** (about **20–30° N**), not the equator.

15.s: Which climatic control explains why the Himalayas are cooler despite their lower latitude?
15.x: Altitude makes the Himalayas cool despite their low latitude, since temperature falls about 6.5°C per km.
15.tq: Recall the effect of each climatic control.
n: Altitude is a factor or control of climate. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Temperature generally decreases with increasing altitude. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
The Himalayas are cooler despite having a lower latitude. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
xs: **Altitude** explains it — option **(1)**: temperature **decreases with increasing altitude**, so the **Himalayas** are **cooler despite a lower latitude**.
**Distance from sea** moderates range; **ocean currents** raise or lower coastal temperatures; **cloud cover** modifies day and night heating.
xa: Normal lapse rate **6.5 °C/km**.
Higher air is **thinner**, with **less water vapour and dust**, so it absorbs less heat.
Air is heated **from below** by terrestrial radiation.

15.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Continentality
(b) Cloud cover
(c) Warm ocean currents
(d) Cold ocean currents

List-II
(i) Extreme interior climates with a large annual range
(ii) Reduces daytime heating and night-time cooling
(iii) Raise coastal temperatures
(iv) Lower coastal temperatures and favour west-coast deserts
15.x: Continentality makes interiors extreme, cloud cover cuts both daytime heating and night cooling, warm currents raise coastal temperatures and cold currents lower them and help form west-coast deserts, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
15.tq: Do not swap the effects of warm and cold currents.
n: Distance from the sea or continentality is a factor or control of climate. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Interior climates are extreme. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Cloud cover modifies heating and cooling. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Warm ocean currents raise coastal temperatures. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Cold ocean currents lower coastal temperatures. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Relief alters temperature and air movement. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Mountain slopes and aspects affect temperature. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Cold currents combined with subtropical highs are often associated with arid west-coast climates. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Cloud cover affects day and night temperature. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
xs: **Continentality** = **extreme interiors** with a **large annual range**; **cloud cover** = **reduces daytime heating and night cooling**; **warm currents** = **raise** coastal temperatures; **cold currents** = **lower** them — option **(3)** a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
Interiors are **extreme**; coasts **equable**.
xa: Continental interiors have **large annual and daily ranges** — hot summers, cold winters.
**Cloudy nights** stay warmer; **clear nights** lose more heat.
**Relief** alters **temperature** and **air movement**.

15.s:
Consider the following statements:

I. Latitude provides solar control of climate.
II. The equator receives more direct rays, producing greater heating.
III. The poles receive oblique rays, producing lower heating.
IV. Seasonal variation and the annual temperature range generally increase towards higher latitudes.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
15.x: All four are correct: latitude sets the Sun's angle, giving strong heating at the equator, weak heating at the poles and larger seasonal ranges at high latitudes.
15.tq: Recall the effect of latitude.
n: Latitude is a factor or control of climate. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
The equator receives more direct rays. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
More direct rays at the equator produce greater heating. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
The poles receive oblique rays. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Oblique rays at the poles produce lower heating. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Seasonal variation increases with latitude. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Annual temperature range is generally greater toward higher latitudes. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
xs: **All four statements are correct** — option **(4)** I, II, III and IV.
I: **latitude** controls temperature through the **solar angle**.
II and III: the **equator** gets **more direct rays** (greater heating); the **poles** **oblique rays** (lower heating).
IV: **seasonal variation** and the **annual temperature range** **increase** toward **higher latitudes**.
xa: Annual range is **minimum at the equator**.
The **equator** receives the **most annual insolation**; the **poles** the least.
**Perihelion** ~**3 Jan**, **147 million km**; **aphelion** ~**4 Jul**, **152 million km**.

15.s: Which climatic control can alter both temperature and air movement?
15.x: Relief changes both temperature, through height, and air movement, by blocking or channelling winds.
15.tq: Recall the effect of each climatic control.
n: Relief or topography is a factor or control of climate. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Relief alters temperature and air movement. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
xs: **Relief or topography** alters both **temperature** and **air movement** — option **(3)**.
**Mountain slopes** and **aspects** affect temperature.
**Latitude** works through the **solar angle**; **distance from the sea** moderates temperature.
xa: **Altitude:** temperature generally **decreases** with height — the **Himalayas** are cooler.
**Ocean currents:** **warm** raise, **cold** lower coastal temperatures.
Insolation factors also include **slope/aspect of land**.

16.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Pressure gradient is the fall of pressure per unit distance and it sets wind speed.
2. Air generally moves from low pressure to high pressure.
3. Closely spaced isobars indicate a steep pressure gradient and strong winds.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
16.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is wrong: air moves from high pressure to low pressure. So '1 only' misses statement 3, while '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' include the false statement 2.
16.tq: Air flows high to low; close isobars = strong wind.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(3)**.
Statement 1 is correct: **pressure gradient** is the **fall of pressure per unit distance**, and it sets **wind speed**.
Statement 2 is wrong: air moves from **high pressure to low pressure**, not the reverse.
Statement 3 is correct: **closely spaced isobars** mean a **steep gradient** and **strong wind**.
xa: **Isobars** join places of **equal pressure**, reduced to **sea level**.
**Standard sea-level pressure** = **1013.25 mb (hPa)**.
The pressure-gradient definition was asked in **APPSC-G2 2011**.

16.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Isobars join places having equal atmospheric pressure reduced to sea level.
2. The standard sea-level pressure is about 1013.25 mb (hPa).
3. A steady fall in the barometer reading generally indicates fair and settled weather.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
16.x: Statement 1 is correct: isobars join places of equal pressure reduced to sea level. Statement 2 is correct: standard sea-level pressure is 1013.25 mb. Statement 3 is wrong: a falling barometer means low pressure, with cloud, rain or storm; a RISING barometer indicates fair, settled weather. Hence 1 and 2 only.
16.tq: Barometer falling = storm coming; rising = fair weather.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: **isobars** join places of **equal pressure** reduced to **sea level**.
Statement 2 is correct: **standard sea-level pressure** is **1013.25 mb (hPa)**.
Statement 3 is wrong: a **falling** barometer means **low pressure** → cloud, rain, storm; a **rising** barometer means **fair, settled weather**.
xa: **Pressure gradient** = fall of pressure per unit distance → sets **wind speed** (**APPSC-G2 2011**).
**Closely spaced isobars** = steep gradient = **strong wind**.
Barometer (**mercury**, **aneroid**) and **barograph** measure pressure in **millibar/hectopascal**.
⚠ **Anemometer** = wind **speed**; **wind vane** = wind **direction**.

16.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
16.x: An anemometer measures wind speed, generally in kilometres per hour or knots. A barometer or barograph measures pressure, while a wind vane shows wind direction.
16.tq: Start with the direct instrument–measurement association and eliminate swapped functions.
xs: **Anemometer — wind speed** is correctly matched — option **(2)**.
**Barometer** and **barograph** measure **pressure**, not wind direction or rainfall.
**Wind vane** shows **wind direction**, not atmospheric pressure.
xa: ⚠ **Anemometer** = speed; **wind vane** = direction.
Wind speed is given in **km/h** or **knots**; pressure in **millibar/hectopascal**.
Barometer types: **mercury** and **aneroid**; the **barograph** records pressure continuously.

16.s:
Consider the following statements about the Coriolis force:
1. Caused by the Earth's rotation, it deflects winds to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere (Ferrel's law).
2. It is maximum at the equator and zero at the poles.
3. It is directly proportional to wind speed.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
16.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is wrong: the Coriolis force is zero at the equator and maximum at the poles. So '1 only' misses statement 3, and '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' include the false statement 2.
16.tq: Coriolis: zero at the equator, which is why cyclones form only beyond 5°.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 is correct: the **Coriolis force** comes from the **Earth's rotation** and deflects winds **right in the NH, left in the SH** (**Ferrel's law**).
Statement 2 is wrong: it is **zero at the equator** and **maximum at the poles**.
Statement 3 is correct: it is **directly proportional to wind speed**.
xa: Because it is zero at the equator, **cyclones form only beyond 5°** latitude.
The deflection rule was asked in **APPSC-G1 2019**.
**Wind modifiers:** **Coriolis force** changes direction; **friction** changes speed.

16.s: Which one of the following statements regarding friction is NOT correct?
o: It is negligible in the upper air.
It increases the speed of surface winds.
It is stronger over land than over a smooth water surface.
16.x: Friction slows surface winds; it is stronger over land and becomes negligible in the upper air. It does not increase wind speed.
16.tq: Find the statement that reverses the established effect of friction.
xs: The statement that is NOT correct: friction **increases the speed of surface winds** — option **(2)**.
**Friction slows surface winds**; it is **stronger over land** and **negligible in the upper air** — so options (1), (3), (4) are true.
xa: **Coriolis force** modifies wind **direction**; **friction** modifies wind **speed**.
With no friction aloft, the **geostrophic wind** blows **parallel to isobars**.
**Pressure gradient** sets **wind speed**; air moves from high to low pressure.

16.s: A geostrophic wind develops when:
o: Coriolis force is absent and air moves vertically
Friction alone drives air parallel to the equator
Pressure gradient force and Coriolis force balance each other, with no frictional effect
Pressure gradient force becomes zero near the poles
16.x: A geostrophic wind is an upper-air wind blowing parallel to isobars when the pressure gradient force and Coriolis force are balanced and friction is negligible.
16.tq: Identify the force balance and the resulting direction of upper-air flow.
xs: A **geostrophic wind** forms when the **pressure gradient force and Coriolis force balance**, with **no friction** — option **(3)**.
It is an **upper-air wind** blowing **parallel to isobars**, since friction is negligible aloft.
The Coriolis force is not absent — it is one of the two balancing forces.
xa: **Coriolis force** is caused by the **rotation of the Earth**; deflects **right in NH, left in SH** (**Ferrel's law**).
Coriolis is **zero at the equator**, **maximum at the poles**.
**Friction** slows surface winds, more over **land**.

16.s: Tropical cyclones do not normally form within about 5° of the Equator. The main reason is that near the Equator:
o: The Coriolis force is zero or negligible
Friction over the ocean is very high
Trade winds are absent throughout the year
16.x: The Coriolis force, caused by the Earth's rotation, is zero at the equator and maximum at the poles, so the rotation needed for a cyclone cannot develop within about 5° latitude. Equatorial seas are warm, not cold; friction is low over the ocean, not high; and the trade winds do blow towards the equatorial low, so the other options are wrong.
16.tq: Coriolis zero at equator → no cyclones within 5°.
xs: Near the equator **the Coriolis force is zero or negligible** — option **(2)**.
The **Coriolis force** is **zero at the equator** and **maximum at the poles**, so cyclones form only beyond **5°** latitude.
xa: Coriolis force is caused by the **rotation of the Earth** and deflects winds **right in NH, left in SH** (**Ferrel's law**).
It is **directly proportional to wind speed**.
**Trade winds** push tropical cyclones **westward** to east coasts; **westerlies** turn mature cyclones **north-east**.

16.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the pressure belts of the Earth:
1. The equatorial low-pressure belt extends approximately from 0° to 5° on either side of the Equator.
2. The subtropical high-pressure belt occurs approximately between 30° and 35° latitudes in both hemispheres.
3. The subpolar low-pressure belt is found approximately between 60° and 65° latitudes in both hemispheres.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
16.x: All three statements correctly give the approximate latitudinal locations of the equatorial, subtropical and subpolar pressure belts.
16.tq: Read the latitude ranges carefully and eliminate options containing a misplaced belt.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
**Equatorial low**: **0-5°** N and S; **subtropical high**: **30-35°** N and S; **subpolar low**: about **60-65°** N and S.
xa: Equatorial low = **Doldrums / ITCZ**; subtropical high = **Horse latitudes**.
**Polar high** lies at the **poles (90°)**: cold, dense, sinking air.
Belts shift about **5-10° north in NH summer** and **south in winter**, following the overhead sun.

16.s: The term ‘horse latitudes’ refers to which one of the following?
o: The subpolar low-pressure belt between 60° and 65°
The equatorial low-pressure belt between 0° and 5°
The subtropical high-pressure belt between 30° and 35°
16.x: The subtropical high-pressure belts at approximately 30°–35° N and S are known as the horse latitudes.
16.tq: Match the alternate name with its precise latitude range.
xs: **Horse latitudes** = the **subtropical high-pressure belt between 30° and 35°** — option **(4)**.
It is a belt of **calm, weak winds** and **sinking dry air** that gives **hot deserts**.
The **equatorial low (0-5°)** is the **Doldrums**; the subpolar low (60-65°) is where westerlies meet polar easterlies.
xa: Asked in **APPSC 2019** and **APPSC-GS 2019**.
**Trade winds** blow from the subtropical high to the equatorial low; **westerlies** to the subpolar low.
**Hadley cell** air **sinks near 30°** and returns as trade winds.

16.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Pressure belt)
a. Equatorial low
b. Subtropical high
c. Subpolar low
d. Polar high

List-II (Characteristic)
i. Cold and sinking air
ii. Meeting of westerlies and polar easterlies
iii. Calm, rising air and convergence of trade winds
iv. Sinking dry air and hot deserts

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
16.x: The equatorial low has calm rising air; the subtropical high has sinking dry air; the subpolar low is a meeting zone of westerlies and polar easterlies; and the polar high has cold sinking air.
16.tq: Start from the sure pair and complete the one-to-one matching.
xs: Correct code: **a–iii, b–iv, c–ii, d–i** — option **(1)**.
**Equatorial low** → calm, rising air, trade winds converge; **Subtropical high** → sinking dry air, hot deserts.
**Subpolar low** → westerlies meet polar easterlies (storms); **Polar high** → cold, dense, sinking air.
xa: Latitudes: equatorial low **0-5°**, subtropical high **30-35°**, subpolar low **~60-65°**, polar high **90°**.
Other names: equatorial low = **Doldrums/ITCZ**; subtropical high = **Horse latitudes**.

16.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The doldrums are a belt of strong winds on both sides of the Equator.
2. The trade winds of the Northern Hemisphere blow from the north-west.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
16.x: Statement 1 is wrong: the doldrums extend on both sides of the equator but are a belt of calm, not strong winds. Statement 2 is wrong: Northern Hemisphere trade winds are north-easterly, not north-westerly. So '1 only', '2 only' and 'Both' are wrong; the answer is neither (APPSC-G1 2024).
16.tq: Doldrums = calm; NH trades = NE. Both traps false.
xs: **Neither** statement is correct — option **(4) Neither 1 nor 2**.
Statement 1 is wrong: the **doldrums** lie on both sides of the equator but are a belt of **calm**, not strong winds.
Statement 2 is wrong: NH **trade winds** are **north-easterly**, not north-westerly.
xa: This was the **APPSC-G1 2024** question; answer = **neither**.
SH trade winds are **south-easterly**; NH **westerlies** are **south-westerly**.
Doldrums = **equatorial low** = **ITCZ**, where trade winds converge.

16.s:
Consider the following statements about the seasonal shift of the pressure belts:
1. The belts shift about 5°–10° northward during the Northern Hemisphere summer.
2. The belts shift southward during the Northern Hemisphere winter.
3. The seasonal shift of the belts is about 25°–30°.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
16.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the belts follow the apparent movement of the overhead sun, shifting about 5°–10° north in the NH summer and south in winter. Statement 3 is wrong: the shift is only about 5°–10°, not 25°–30°. So 2 and 3 only, 1 and 3 only, and 1, 2 and 3 are all wrong.
16.tq: Belts follow the overhead sun, but only by 5–10°.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statements 1 and 2: belts shift about **5-10° north in NH summer** and **south in winter**, following the **overhead sun** (apparent movement).
Statement 3 is wrong: the shift is only about **5-10°**, not 25-30°.
xa: In NH summer the **ITCZ** shifts north over the Indian plains (**monsoon trough**) — this drives the monsoon.
In winter the ITCZ migrates **south of India** → **north-east monsoon**.
Southward shift of the doldrums → heavy rain in **southern states** (**bimodal rainfall**).

16.s: The Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone is best described as:
o: A high-pressure zone near the poles where polar easterlies diverge
A low-pressure zone at 60°–65° where polar highs converge
A high-pressure zone at 30°–35° where westerlies originate
A low-pressure zone near the Equator where the trade winds converge
16.x: The ITCZ is the equatorial low-pressure zone formed where the trade winds from the two hemispheres converge.
16.tq: Distinguish the ITCZ from the subtropical and subpolar pressure belts by location and pressure type.
xs: The ITCZ is **a low-pressure zone near the Equator where the trade winds converge** — option **(4)**.
**ITCZ** = **Inter Tropical Convergence Zone**, the **equatorial low** (doldrums).
**30-35°** is the subtropical high and **60-65°** the subpolar low — not the ITCZ.
xa: Asked in **APPSC 2019** and **APPSC-GS 2019**.
In NH summer the ITCZ shifts north over the Indian plains as the **monsoon trough**.
The **modern monsoon theory (1957)** is built on the **northward shift of the ITCZ**.

16.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Northern Hemisphere winter:
1. The southward migration of the ITCZ, together with high-pressure cells over Tibet and Siberia, helps establish the north-east monsoon.
2. The southward shift of the doldrums is associated with heavy rain in the southern states and a bimodal rainfall pattern.
3. The ITCZ shifts northward over the Indian plains as the monsoon trough.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
16.x: Statement 3 is wrong: the northward shift over the Indian plains (monsoon trough) happens in the NH SUMMER; in winter the ITCZ moves south of India. Statement 1 is correct: the southward ITCZ plus highs over Tibet and Siberia set up the north-east monsoon. Statement 2 is correct: the southward shift of the doldrums brings heavy rain to the southern states (bimodal rainfall). Hence 1 and 2 only.
16.tq: ITCZ follows the sun: north in summer (SW monsoon), south in winter (NE monsoon).
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — so option **(3)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: in winter the **ITCZ** migrates **south of India**; with **high-pressure cells over Tibet and Siberia** it sets up the **north-east monsoon**.
Statement 2 is correct: the **southward shift of the doldrums** brings **heavy rain in southern states** (**bimodal rainfall**).
Statement 3 is wrong: the ITCZ shifts **north over the Indian plains** (**monsoon trough**) in the **NH summer**, not winter.
xa: **ITCZ** = **Inter Tropical Convergence Zone**, a low-pressure zone near the **equator** where **trade winds converge**.
Pressure belts shift about **5-10°** **north in NH summer** and **south in winter**, following the **overhead sun**.
The ITCZ's **northward shift** in summer **helps monsoon circulation**.
**Winter cooling** reverses the pressure pattern → **seasonal wind reversal**.

16.s: Which of the following correctly represents the direction of the trade winds?
o: From the subtropical high to the subpolar low; south-westerly in the NH and north-westerly in the SH
From the subtropical high to the equatorial low; north-easterly in the NH and south-easterly in the SH
From the equatorial low to the subtropical high; north-westerly in the NH and south-westerly in the SH
From the polar high to the subpolar low; north-easterly in the NH and south-easterly in the SH
16.x: Trade winds blow from the subtropical high-pressure belts towards the equatorial low-pressure belt. They are north-easterlies in the Northern Hemisphere and south-easterlies in the Southern Hemisphere.
16.tq: Separate the source-to-destination relationship from the hemispheric wind direction.
xs: **Trade winds** blow **from the subtropical high to the equatorial low**; **north-easterly in the NH**, **south-easterly in the SH** — option **(2)**.
Option (1) describes the **westerlies**; option (4) describes the **polar easterlies**.
xa: Trade winds are also called the **easterlies**.
⚠ **APPSC-G1 2024** trap: "NH trade winds blow from the north-west" is **wrong**.
Trade winds push tropical cyclones **westward** onto east coasts.
**Hadley cell**: air sinks near **30°** and returns as **trade winds**.

16.s:
Consider the following statements about the planetary winds:
1. In the Northern Hemisphere the westerlies blow from the south-west.
2. The westerlies blow from the subtropical high towards the subpolar low.
3. The polar easterlies blow from the subpolar low towards the polar high.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
16.x: Statement 2 is correct: westerlies blow from the subtropical high to the subpolar low (35-60°). Statement 3 is wrong: polar easterlies blow FROM the polar high TO the subpolar low (north-easterly in the NH, south-easterly in the SH). Statement 1 is correct: westerlies are south-westerly in the NH and north-westerly in the SH. Hence 1 and 2 only.
16.tq: Winds always blow from a high-pressure belt to a low-pressure belt.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — so option **(3)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: the **westerlies** are **south-westerly** in the **NH** (north-westerly in the SH).
Statement 2 is correct: westerlies blow from the **subtropical high → subpolar low** (**35-60°**).
Statement 3 is wrong: **polar easterlies** blow **from the polar high to the subpolar low**.
xa: **Trade winds** blow from the **subtropical high → equatorial low**: **north-east** in the NH, **south-east** in the SH.
**Hadley cell:** air rises near the **equator**, sinks near **30°**, returns as **trade winds**.
**Walker circulation** = east-west (zonal) **Pacific** cell.
Westerlies are **stronger and steadier in the Southern Hemisphere**.

16.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the Hadley cell from the Walker circulation?
o: Hadley circulation is mainly meridional between the Equator and subtropics, whereas Walker circulation is an east–west zonal circulation over the Pacific.
Hadley circulation is an east–west Pacific circulation, whereas Walker circulation is a polar circulation.
Hadley circulation occurs only in the Southern Hemisphere, whereas Walker circulation occurs only in the Northern Hemisphere.
Both are names for the same local wind system over mountain valleys.
16.x: In the Hadley cell, air rises near the Equator, moves poleward aloft, sinks near 30° and returns as trade winds. Walker circulation is the east–west zonal cell over the Pacific.
16.tq: Separate the two circulations by direction and geographical scale.
xs: **Hadley** is mainly **meridional (Equator–subtropics)**; **Walker** is an **east–west zonal Pacific cell** — option **(1)**.
**Hadley cell**: air rises near the equator → moves poleward aloft → sinks near **30°** → returns as **trade winds**.
**Walker circulation** is the **east-west (zonal) Pacific** cell — not polar, not a valley wind.
xa: Walker circulation was in the news in **Apr 2026**.
Hadley-cell sinking at about **30°** matches the **subtropical high / horse latitudes**.
The **modern monsoon theory** includes **ENSO**.

16.s: Which planetary winds push tropical cyclones westward towards the east coasts of continents, and which winds later turn mature cyclones towards the north-east?
o: Westerlies push them westward; polar easterlies turn them north-east
Trade winds push them westward; westerlies turn them north-east
Polar easterlies push them westward; trade winds turn them north-east
Westerlies push them westward; trade winds turn them north-east
16.x: Trade winds (easterlies) steer tropical cyclones westward onto east coasts; on reaching higher latitudes the westerlies turn mature cyclones north-east. Westerlies do not push cyclones west, and polar easterlies do not act in the tropics, so the other options are wrong.
16.tq: Trades steer west; westerlies recurve north-east.
xs: **Trade winds push them westward; westerlies turn them north-east** — option **(2)**.
**Trade winds (easterlies)** steer tropical cyclones **westward to east coasts**; the **westerlies** then turn mature cyclones **north-east**.
xa: Example: **Cyclone Montha** (**Nov 2025**), **Kakinada** coast.
AP cyclones peak **October-December** (**Hudhud**, **Titli**, **Michaung**).
Cyclones form only beyond **5°** latitude, where the **Coriolis force** is enough.

16.s:
Consider the following statements about the westerlies of the Southern Hemisphere:
1. They are weaker than in the Northern Hemisphere because of greater land friction.
2. The Roaring Forties blow between 40° and 50° S.
3. The Furious Fifties blow between 50° and 60° S.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
16.x: Statement 1 is wrong: the westerlies are STRONGER and steadier in the Southern Hemisphere because it is mostly open ocean with little land friction. Statements 2 and 3 are correct: Roaring Forties 40-50° S, Furious Fifties 50-60° S (Shrieking Sixties around 60° S). Hence 2 and 3 only.
16.tq: Open southern ocean, little friction = strongest westerlies: Roaring 40s, Furious 50s, Shrieking 60s.
xs: Statements **2 and 3** are correct — so option **(3)** is correct.
Statement 1 is wrong: SH westerlies are **stronger and steadier**, as the SH is mostly **open ocean** with **little land friction**.
Statement 2 is correct: **Roaring Forties** = **40-50° S**.
Statement 3 is correct: **Furious Fifties** = **50-60° S**.
xa: **Shrieking/Screaming Sixties** blow around **60° S**.
Westerlies blow from the **subtropical high → subpolar low** (**35-60°**).
Westerlies turn mature cyclones **north-east** (**Cyclone Montha**, **Kakinada** coast, Nov **2025**).

16.s:
Consider the following statements about jet streams:
1. They first became widely known through high-flying aircraft during the First World War.
2. They were first identified by Wasaburo Ooishi of Japan in the 1920s.
3. They are narrow, high-velocity upper-level winds found at about 10-12 km.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
16.x: Statement 3 is correct: jet streams are narrow, fast upper-level winds at about 10-12 km. Statement 2 is correct: Wasaburo Ooishi first identified them in the 1920s. Statement 1 is wrong: they became widely known during the SECOND World War, noticed by high-flying bomber pilots. Hence 2 and 3 only.
16.tq: Ooishi 1920s found them; WWII bombers made them famous.
xs: Statements **2 and 3** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is wrong: jet streams became widely known during **World War II**, noticed by **high-flying bomber pilots**.
Statement 2 is correct: first identified by **Wasaburo Ooishi** (**Japan**, **1920s**).
Statement 3 is correct: jet streams are **narrow, high-velocity upper-level winds** at **10-12 km**.
xa: **Sub-Tropical Westerly Jet (STJ)** lies south of the Himalayas in **winter**, carries **western disturbances**; shifts **north of the Himalayas** in summer.
**Tropical Easterly Jet (TEJ)**: summer only, **5-20°N**, **strengthens the SW monsoon**.
**Somali (Findlater) Jet** is a **low-level** jet off the **East African coast**.
⚠ **STJ** = westerly, winter; **TEJ** = easterly, summer.

16.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the Sub-Tropical Westerly Jet over India?
o: It lies north of the Himalayas in winter and south of them in summer.
It remains north of the Himalayas throughout the year.
It remains south of the Himalayas throughout the year.
It lies south of the Himalayas in winter and shifts north of them in summer.
16.x: The Sub-Tropical Westerly Jet lies south of the Himalayas in winter and shifts north of them in summer.
16.tq: Test the seasonal reversal and location of a closely associated jet stream.
xs: The **STJ** lies **south of the Himalayas in winter** and shifts **north of them in summer** — option **(4)**.
Options (1), (2) and (3) reverse or freeze this seasonal shift.
xa: The STJ carries **western disturbances**; its **withdrawal** lets the monsoon **"burst"**.
It **returns in October** to end the monsoon.
The **TEJ** is the summer jet at **5-20°N**, June to early October.

16.s:
Consider the following statements about the Sub-Tropical Westerly Jet:
1. It carries western disturbances.
2. Its withdrawal is associated with the burst of the monsoon.
3. Its return in October is associated with the end of the monsoon.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
16.x: The Sub-Tropical Westerly Jet carries western disturbances, withdraws before the monsoon burst and returns in October as the monsoon ends.
16.tq: Check each seasonal role separately before selecting the coded combination.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
The **STJ** carries **western disturbances**; its **withdrawal** lets the monsoon **"burst"**; it **returns in October** to end it.
xa: STJ lies **south of the Himalayas in winter**, **north** in summer.
Western disturbances come from the **Mediterranean**; they worsened extremes in the **2026** monsoon.
⚠ **STJ** = westerly, winter; **TEJ** = easterly, summer.

16.s:
Consider the following statements about the Tropical Easterly Jet (TEJ):
1. It is a summer jet found between about 5°N and 20°N from June to early October.
2. It extends from the South China Sea to East Africa.
3. It strengthens the south-west monsoon by creating a surface anticyclone and an upper-air low over the Indian plains.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
16.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: the TEJ creates an upper-air anticyclone and a surface low (not the reverse) over the Indian plains. Hence '1 only' leaves out a true statement, and '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' include the false statement 3.
16.tq: TEJ: high up = anticyclone, at the surface = low.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: the **TEJ** is a summer jet at **5-20°N**, **June to early October**. Statement 2: it runs from the **South China Sea to East Africa**.
Statement 3 is wrong: it creates an **upper-air anticyclone** and a **surface low** over the Indian plains — not the reverse.
xa: The TEJ comes with and **strengthens the SW monsoon**.
**Somali (Findlater) Jet**: low-level, off the **East African coast**, intensifies monsoon winds.
⚠ **TEJ** = easterly, summer; **STJ** = westerly, winter.

16.s:
Consider the following statements about the Somali (Findlater) Jet:
1. It is a low-level jet off the East African coast.
2. It intensifies the monsoon winds together with the Labrador Current.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
16.x: Statement 1 is correct: the Somali Jet is a low-level jet off East Africa. Statement 2 is wrong: it strengthens monsoon winds together with the Somali Current, not the Labrador Current. So '2 only', 'Both' and 'Neither' are wrong.
16.tq: Somali Jet goes with the Somali Current.
xs: Only statement **1** is correct — option **(1) 1 only**.
Statement 1: the **Somali (Findlater) Jet** is a **low-level jet** off the **East African coast**.
Statement 2 is wrong: it intensifies monsoon winds together with the **Somali current**, not the Labrador Current.
xa: The **TEJ** (**5-20°N**) runs from the South China Sea to **East Africa** and strengthens the SW monsoon.
The **STJ** carries **western disturbances**; its withdrawal lets the monsoon burst.
Jet streams in general blow at **10-12 km**.

16.s:
Consider the following statements about the polar vortex:
1. It is a year-round cold, low-pressure region around the poles.
2. It is strongest during winter.
3. Its anticlockwise flow helps keep cold air near the poles.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
16.x: The polar vortex is a year-round cold, low-pressure region, becomes strongest in winter and its anticlockwise circulation confines cold air near the poles.
16.tq: Verify the nature, seasonal strength and circulation effect of the same atmospheric system.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
The **polar vortex** is a **year-round low-pressure, cold-air** reservoir around the poles, **strongest in winter**.
Its **anticlockwise flow** keeps **cold air locked near the poles**.
xa: A **strong vortex** keeps the cold air up north and warm air to the south (**APPSC 2018**; **APPSC-GS 2018**).
Layers: tropospheric up to **15 km**; stratospheric **15-50 km** (seasonal).
**Sudden stratospheric warming** / **Rossby waves** weaken it → cold air spills into mid-latitudes.

16.s: What may happen when Rossby waves weaken the polar vortex?
o: The vortex becomes permanently stationary and cold air remains confined to the poles.
The tropical easterly jet disappears and the equator cools permanently.
The polar region changes into a high-pressure warm region throughout the year.
The winds may reverse, the vortex may split and cold air may spill into the mid-latitudes.
16.x: Weakening by Rossby waves can reverse the winds, split the vortex and allow cold air to move into the mid-latitudes, producing cold spells.
16.tq: Follow the cause–effect chain from weakened circulation to mid-latitude cold spells.
xs: **The winds may reverse, the vortex may split and cold air may spill into the mid-latitudes** — option **(4)**.
**Rossby waves** or **sudden stratospheric warming** weaken the vortex → **cold spells** in mid-latitudes.
A strong vortex, not a weakened one, keeps cold air confined to the poles.
xa: The vortex's **anticlockwise flow** locks cold air near the poles (**APPSC 2018**).
It is a **low-pressure, cold-air** reservoir, strongest in **winter**.
Tropospheric part to **15 km**; stratospheric part **15-50 km**.

16.s:
Which of the following factors are included in the modern monsoon theory formulated in 1957?
1. Northward shift of the ITCZ
2. Jet streams
3. Tibet Plateau
4. ENSO

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
16.x: The modern monsoon theory of 1957 considers the northward shift of the ITCZ together with jet streams, the Tibet Plateau and ENSO.
16.tq: Treat the complete set of listed monsoon controls as the key when all components are supported.
xs: All four are included — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
The **modern monsoon theory (1957)** is built on the **northward shift of the ITCZ** + **jet streams** + **Tibet plateau** heating (heat island) + **ENSO**.
xa: **Halley's theory (1686)**: monsoon = **giant land-sea breeze**.
**TEJ** strengthens the SW monsoon; **STJ** withdrawal lets the monsoon **burst**.
**Monsoon** = Arabic **"mausim"** (season) = seasonal wind reversal.

16.s: Halley’s theory of 1686 regarded the Indian monsoon primarily as a:
16.x: Halley’s 1686 theory explained the monsoon as a giant land-sea breeze.
16.tq: Associate the earlier theory with its simple explanatory model and distinguish it from the modern theory.
xs: **Halley (1686)** saw the monsoon as a **giant land-sea breeze** — option **(1)**.
That is, the land-sea breeze on a large scale: seasonal heating of land and sea instead of daily heating.
xa: The **modern monsoon theory** dates from **1957**: **ITCZ** shift + jet streams + **Tibet** + **ENSO**.
**Sea breeze** blows by **day** (sea → land); **land breeze** by **night** (land → sea).
"Monsoon" is from Arabic **"mausim"** = season.

16.s: During the daytime, a coastal city experiences air moving from the sea towards the land. The immediate reason is that
o: the land cools faster than the sea and develops relatively higher pressure
the pressure over land and sea remains identical throughout the day
the sea heats faster than the land and develops relatively lower pressure
the land heats faster than the sea and develops relatively lower pressure
16.x: During the day, land heats faster than the sea, producing relatively lower pressure over land and drawing air from the sea. This is the sea breeze.
16.tq: Infer the breeze from the differential heating and pressure pattern.
xs: By day **the land heats faster than the sea and develops relatively lower pressure** — option **(4)**.
Air moves from **high to low pressure**, so cooler sea air flows to the hotter land: the **sea breeze**.
The land **cools faster** only at **night** — that gives the **land breeze**, not this daytime flow.
xa: Land and sea breezes are marked along **AP's coast** and **moderate coastal temperatures**.
Sea breeze cools coastal cities like **Mumbai** (**Mar 2026**).
**Halley (1686)** called the monsoon a **giant land-sea breeze**.

16.s: Which of the following correctly describes mountain and valley breezes?
o: Valley breeze blows downhill during the day, while mountain breeze blows uphill at night.
Valley breeze blows uphill during the day, while mountain breeze blows downhill at night.
Both breezes blow uphill because slopes are heated throughout the day and night.
Both breezes blow downhill because cold air rises along mountain slopes.
16.x: Valley or anabatic breeze rises uphill during the day. Mountain or katabatic breeze descends downhill at night.
16.tq: Use the day–night reversal to separate anabatic and katabatic winds.
xs: **Valley breeze blows uphill by day; mountain breeze blows downhill at night** — option **(2)**.
**Valley (anabatic)** breeze flows **uphill by day**; **mountain (katabatic)** breeze flows **downhill at night**.
Option (1) reverses the two.
xa: ⚠ **Anabatic** = valley breeze, uphill; **katabatic** = mountain breeze, downhill.
At night cold air collects in valleys → **temperature inversion, frost**.
**Sea breeze** by day, **land breeze** by night.

16.s: At night, cold air descending from mountain slopes collects in valleys. Which one of the following effects may result?
o: Permanent low pressure and intense convection
The formation of the equatorial low-pressure belt
16.x: The nocturnal mountain or katabatic breeze carries cold air downhill, where it accumulates in valleys and may produce temperature inversion and frost.
16.tq: Link the wind process with its immediate atmospheric effect.
xs: Cold air pooling in valleys causes **temperature inversion and frost** — option **(3)**.
This is the **mountain (katabatic) breeze**, flowing **downhill at night**.
xa: The **valley (anabatic) breeze** flows **uphill by day**.
⚠ Anabatic = uphill/day; katabatic = downhill/night.
**Land breeze** at night: cooler land → warmer sea.

16.s: The word ‘monsoon’ is derived from the Arabic word ‘mausim’, which means
16.x: 'Monsoon' comes from the Arabic 'mausim', meaning season; the term refers to the seasonal reversal of winds, but the word itself means season, not reversal, storm or ocean.
16.tq: Test the exact meaning of the terminology rather than its climatic effect.
xs: Arabic **"mausim"** means **season** — option **(3)**.
A **monsoon** is a **seasonal wind reversal**; the word itself means season, not reversal.
xa: **Halley's theory (1686)**: monsoon = giant land-sea breeze.
**Modern monsoon theory (1957)**: **ITCZ** northward shift + jet streams + **Tibet** + **ENSO**.
SW monsoon **2026** reached AP on **6 June** (normal **4 June**; **26 May** in 2025).

16.s: Which of the following is a significant climatic effect of sea and land breezes along the Andhra Pradesh coast?
o: They eliminate all seasonal variations in rainfall.
They create permanent westerlies over the coast.
They prevent the formation of any local pressure differences.
16.x: The alternating sea and land breezes moderate temperatures along the coast, including the coastal areas of Andhra Pradesh.
16.tq: Identify the practical coastal effect of periodic thermal winds.
xs: Sea and land breezes **moderate coastal temperatures** along AP's coast — option **(3)**.
**Sea breeze** by day (sea → hotter land) and **land breeze** by night (cooler land → warmer sea) alternate.
xa: Sea breeze cools coastal cities like **Mumbai** (**Mar 2026**).
AP coastline: **1,053.07 km**, **3rd longest** in India (AP Survey 2025-26); older figure **974 km**.
AP cyclones peak **October-December** (**Hudhud**, **Titli**, **Michaung**).

16.s: Which one of the following local winds is a hot, dry summer wind that affects North India as well as Rayalaseema?
16.x: The Loo is a hot and dry summer wind affecting North India and also Rayalaseema.
16.tq: Use the region–effect association to identify the local wind.
xs: The **Loo** is the hot, dry summer wind of **North India** and **Rayalaseema** — option **(4)**.
It is a hot, dry, dusty **summer afternoon** wind of the north and north-west plains; causes **heatstroke**.
**Mistral** is a cold northerly of the **Rhone valley**; **Harmattan** blows from the **Sahara to West Africa**; **Bora** is a cold wind of the **Adriatic**.
xa: **Harmattan** is called **"the doctor"** — relief from humidity.
East India's pre-monsoon storms: **Nor'westers / Kaal Baisakhi**; north-west dust storms: **"aandhi"**.
**Mango showers** in the south (Kerala, Karnataka, AP) aid mango ripening.

16.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Foehn is a warm, dry wind descending the leeward slope of the Alps.
2. Chinook is associated with the Rockies and is popularly called the ‘snow eater’.
3. Both winds can cause the melting of snow.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
16.x: Foehn occurs in the Alps, while Chinook occurs in the Rockies; both are warm, dry descending winds capable of melting snow.
16.tq: Combine region, nature and effect statements before selecting the coded option.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
**Foehn**: warm, dry wind descending the leeward slope of the **Alps**; **melts snow**, ripens grapes.
**Chinook** ("**snow eater**"): warm, dry descending wind on the eastern slopes of the **Rockies**; melts snow, helps ranching.
xa: ⚠ **Foehn** = Alps; **Chinook** = Rockies; **Harmattan** = "the doctor".
**Santa Ana** (Southern California): hot, dry, spreads **wildfires**.
**Sirocco** (Sahara → Italy) brings **"blood rain"**.

16.s:
Match List-I (Local wind) with List-II (Feature):
List-I
a. Mistral
b. Sirocco
c. Harmattan
d. Santa Ana
List-II
1. Hot, dry wind of West Africa called 'the doctor'
2. Cold, dry northerly wind down the Rhone valley to the Mediterranean
3. Hot, dry wind of southern California that spreads wildfires
4. Hot, dusty wind from the Sahara to Italy that can cause 'blood rain'
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
16.x: Mistral = cold, dry northerly wind of the Rhone valley (2); Sirocco = hot, dusty Saharan wind reaching Italy, 'blood rain' (4); Harmattan = hot, dry West African wind called 'the doctor' (1); Santa Ana = hot, dry southern California wind that spreads wildfires (3). Option B swaps Mistral and Sirocco, option C swaps Harmattan and Santa Ana, and option D mismatches all four.
16.tq: Mistral = Rhone (cold); Sirocco = blood rain; Harmattan = doctor; Santa Ana = wildfires.
xs: The correct match is **a-2, b-4, c-1, d-3** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Mistral** = cold, dry northerly wind of the **Rhone valley** to the **Mediterranean**; **Sirocco** = hot, dusty **Sahara → Italy** wind giving **"blood rain"**.
**Harmattan** = hot, dry **West African** wind called **"the doctor"**; **Santa Ana** = hot, dry **southern California** wind that spreads **wildfires**.
xa: **Foehn** = warm, dry wind of the **Alps**; **Chinook** = **"snow eater"** of the **Rockies**.
**Bora** = cold, dry, gusty wind of the **Adriatic** coast; **Leveche** = hot, dry wind of **Spain**.
**Brickfielder** = hot, dusty wind of **south-east Australia** (**Victoria**); **Shamal** = hot, dusty north-westerly of **Iraq/Persian Gulf**.
**Loo** = hot, dry summer wind of north-west Indian plains, also **Rayalaseema**.

16.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Wind)
A. Leveche
B. Brickfielder
C. Blizzard
D. Shamal

List-II (Region)
1. Spain
2. South-east Australia
3. Polar lands and North America
4. Iraq and the Persian Gulf

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
16.x: Leveche is associated with Spain, Brickfielder with south-east Australia, Blizzard with polar regions and North America, and Shamal with Iraq and the Persian Gulf.
16.tq: Start from distinctive regional pairs and verify the remaining matches.
xs: Correct code: **A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4** — option **(1)**.
**Leveche** → **Spain**; **Brickfielder** → **South-east Australia** (Victoria); **Blizzard** → **polar regions, North America**; **Shamal** → **Iraq, Persian Gulf**.
xa: Blizzard in **Siberia** is called the **buran**.
Shamal is a hot, dusty **north-westerly**; Brickfielder blows hot and dusty from the **interior**.
**Mistral** (Rhone valley) and **Bora** (Adriatic) are **cold, dry** winds.

16.s: Which one of the following statements regarding local winds is correct?
o: They are temporary, predictable and region-specific winds caused by local temperature and pressure differences.
They occur only over oceans and are unrelated to relief.
They are permanent global winds caused only by the rotation of the Earth.
They are seasonal winds that reverse direction over the entire Indian subcontinent.
16.x: Local winds are temporary, predictable and region-specific. They arise from factors such as differential heating, pressure gradients, relief, surface cover and season.
16.tq: Distinguish local winds from planetary and seasonal winds by scale and cause.
xs: Local winds are **temporary, predictable and region-specific**, caused by **local temperature and pressure differences** — option **(1)**.
Causes: **differential heating**, **pressure gradient**, **relief**, **surface cover**, **season** — so they are not unrelated to relief.
Permanent winds driven by the Earth's rotation are the **planetary winds**; a seasonal reversal over the subcontinent is the **monsoon**.
xa: Indian pre-monsoon local storms: **Nor'westers / Kaal Baisakhi** (east), **"aandhi"** (north-west), **Mango showers** (south).
**Loo**: hot, dry, dusty summer afternoon wind of the north plains and **Rayalaseema**.
⚠ **Foehn** = Alps; **Chinook** = Rockies.

16.s:
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?

1. Aandhi — north-west India — dust storms
2. Nor’wester or Kaal Baisakhi — Bihar, Odisha, West Bengal and Assam — violent pre-monsoon thunderstorms
3. Mango showers — Kerala and Karnataka — pre-monsoon showers aiding mango ripening
16.x: All three pairs are correctly matched. Aandhi consists of dust storms, Kaal Baisakhi consists of violent pre-monsoon thunderstorms, and mango showers aid mango ripening.
16.tq: Check each region–phenomenon–effect combination independently.
xs: All three pairs are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
**Aandhi** = **dust storms** of **north-west India**.
**Nor'wester / Kaal Baisakhi** = violent **pre-monsoon thunderstorms** in **Bihar, Odisha, West Bengal, Assam**.
**Mango showers** = pre-monsoon (**convectional**) showers in **Kerala, Karnataka** (and AP) aiding mango ripening.
xa: **Kaal Baisakhi** benefits **tea, jute, rice**.
**Loo**: hot, dry, dusty summer wind of the north and north-west plains; also **Rayalaseema**; causes **heatstroke**.

16.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Western disturbances mentioned in connection with the 2026 monsoon:
1. They are carried eastward from the Mediterranean region by the Subtropical Westerly Jet.
2. They worsened weather extremes during the 2026 monsoon.
3. They may have contributed to flash floods in Nepal and Tibet.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
16.x: All three statements are correct: the Subtropical Westerly Jet carries the disturbances eastward, and they were associated with intensified weather extremes and possible flash floods in Nepal and Tibet.
16.tq: Check each statement separately, especially the linked cause-and-effect statements.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
**Western disturbances** are carried east from the **Mediterranean** by the **Subtropical Westerly Jet (STJ)**.
They **worsened weather extremes** in the **2026** monsoon and may have fed **flash floods in Nepal and Tibet** (**28 Aug 2026**).
xa: The STJ lies **south of the Himalayas in winter**, **north** in summer.
Its **withdrawal** lets the monsoon **"burst"**; it **returns in October** to end it.
⚠ **STJ** = westerly, winter; **TEJ** = easterly, summer, strengthens SW monsoon.

16.s: With reference to the expected southwest monsoon rainfall in Andhra Pradesh under El Nino conditions, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: Below-normal rainfall was expected, with short and intense low-pressure spells providing some offset.
Normal rainfall was expected because El Nino strengthens the southwest monsoon over Andhra Pradesh.
The monsoon was expected to produce above-normal rainfall through prolonged low-pressure activity.
Below-normal rainfall was expected exclusively because of Western disturbances.
16.x: El Nino was expected to contribute to below-normal southwest monsoon rainfall in Andhra Pradesh, although short and intense low-pressure spells could partly offset the deficiency.
16.tq: Apply the stated relationship between El Nino, monsoon rainfall and episodic low-pressure systems.
xs: **Below-normal rainfall was expected**, offset by **short and intense low-pressure spells** — option **(1)**.
The **IMD** expected below-normal SW monsoon rain in AP under **El Nino** (**5 Jun 2026**).
El Nino weakens rather than strengthens the monsoon here, and western disturbances were not the cited cause.
xa: UK Met Office expects the **biggest El Nino in over a century** (peak **above 3 °C**) → **2027** possibly the hottest year.
A low over the **north Andaman Sea** brought heavy rain to AP from **19 Sep 2026**.
The **modern monsoon theory (1957)** includes **ENSO**.

16.s:
With reference to Andhra Pradesh, consider the following statements:
1. As per the AP Socio-Economic Survey 2025-26, its coastline of about 1,053 km is the third longest in India.
2. Hudhud, Titli and Michaung are examples of the State's peak-season cyclones.
3. Cyclones affecting the State peak during July-September.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
16.x: Statement 1 is correct: the AP coastline is 1,053.07 km, third longest in India. Statement 3 is wrong: AP's cyclones peak in OCTOBER-DECEMBER (post-monsoon). Statement 2 is correct: Hudhud, Titli and Michaung are the cited examples. Hence 1 and 2 only.
16.tq: AP cyclone season = Oct-Dec (Hudhud, Titli, Michaung).
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: AP's coastline is **1,053.07 km**, **3rd longest** in India (**AP Survey 2025-26**).
Statement 2 is correct: **Hudhud**, **Titli** and **Michaung** are cited AP cyclones.
Statement 3 is wrong: AP's cyclones peak in **October-December**, not July-September.
xa: The earlier coastline figure **974 km** is still used in other chapters.
SW monsoon **2026** reached AP on **6 June 2026**, two days late, entering through **Rayalaseema**.
A **low-pressure area** over the **north Andaman Sea** brought heavy rain to AP from **19 Sep 2026**.

16.s: According to the indicated forecast, the projected El Nino event was expected to have which combination of characteristics?
o: The strongest La Nina in over a century, with a peak above 3 °C, possibly making 2027 the hottest year
The biggest El Nino in over a century, with a peak above 3 °C, possibly making 2027 the hottest year
A neutral phase, with no measurable temperature anomaly and no effect on 2027
The weakest El Nino in a century, with a peak below 1 °C, making 2027 cooler than usual
16.x: The forecast referred to the biggest El Nino in over a century, with a peak above 3 °C, and suggested that 2027 could become the hottest year.
16.tq: Pair the event type with both its intensity threshold and projected consequence.
xs: **The biggest El Nino in over a century**, peak **above 3 °C**, possibly making **2027 the hottest year** — option **(2)**.
This is the **UK Met Office** forecast (**25 Aug 2026**); it is an El Nino, not La Nina, and not weak.
xa: IMD expected **below-normal** SW monsoon rain in AP under El Nino (**5 Jun 2026**).
**ENSO** is part of the **modern monsoon theory (1957)**.
**Walker circulation** is the east-west (zonal) **Pacific** cell.

16.s:
Consider the following statements about the south-west monsoon of 2026 in Andhra Pradesh:
1. It reached the State on 6 June 2026, two days later than the normal date.
2. It entered the State through Coastal Andhra.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
16.x: Statement 1 is correct: the monsoon reached AP on 6 June 2026 against a normal date of 4 June, two days late. Statement 2 is wrong: it entered through RAYALASEEMA. Hence 1 only.
16.tq: 2026: 6 June, two days late, via Rayalaseema.
xs: Only statement **1** is correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: the monsoon reached AP on **6 June 2026** against a normal **4 June** — **two days late**.
Statement 2 is wrong: it entered the State through **Rayalaseema**, not Coastal Andhra.
xa: In **2025** the monsoon had come on **26 May**.
IMD expected **below-normal** SW monsoon rain in AP under **El Nino** (**5 Jun 2026**).
UK Met Office expects the **biggest El Nino in over a century** (peak above **3 °C**).

16.s:
Assertion (A): Monsoon winds reverse their direction according to the season.
Reason (R): Differential heating and cooling of land and sea produces seasonal pressure reversal.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
16.x: Both are true and R explains A: land and sea heat and cool differently, reversing pressure and therefore the monsoon winds.
16.tq: Check whether R is the cause of A.
n: The main mechanism of monsoons is differential heating and cooling of land and sea. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
Monsoonal winds reverse direction according to the season. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
Seasonal pressure reversal produces monsoons. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
**Differential heating and cooling of land and sea** is the main monsoon mechanism: summer heating → **low pressure**, winter cooling → **high pressure**.
This **seasonal pressure reversal** makes monsoon winds **reverse direction** with the **season**.
xa: **Monsoon** comes from the **Arabic** word **Mausim**, meaning **season**.
Summer monsoon winds blow **sea to land**; winter winds **land to sea**.
**Halley's theory** (**1686**): monsoon = **giant land-sea breeze**.
**Modern monsoon theory** (**1957**): built on the **northward shift of the ITCZ**, jet streams, **Tibet** heating and ENSO.

16.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Monsoonal winds reverse direction according to the season.
II. Summer monsoonal winds blow from sea to land.
III. Winter monsoonal winds blow from land to sea.
IV. Land and sea breezes are annual rather than daily phenomena.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
16.x: I, II and III are correct: monsoons reverse, blowing sea to land in summer and land to sea in winter. IV is false because land and sea breezes are daily.
16.tq: Discriminate daily from seasonal winds.
n: Monsoonal winds reverse direction according to the season. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
In summer, monsoonal winds blow from sea to land. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
In winter, monsoonal winds blow from land to sea. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
Land and sea breezes are daily or diurnal rather than annual. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
xs: Statements **I, II and III** are correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Monsoonal winds** **reverse direction** according to the **season** (I).
In **summer** they blow **sea to land** (II); in **winter** **land to sea** (III).
IV is wrong: **land and sea breezes** are **daily** or **diurnal**, **rather than annual**.
xa: ⚠ **Mountain and valley breezes** are **periodic** winds.
**Sea breeze** blows by **day** (land heats faster); **land breeze** by **night**.
**Monsoonal climate** has **wet and dry seasons**.

16.s:
Assertion (A): Monsoons produce wet and dry seasons.
Reason (R): Monsoonal climate has seasonal rainfall.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
16.x: Both are true and R explains A: seasonal rainfall is what gives monsoon lands their wet and dry seasons.
16.tq: Check whether R is the cause of A.
n: Monsoonal climate has wet and dry seasons. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
Seasonal rainfall is associated with the Indian monsoon. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
**Monsoonal climate** has **seasonal rainfall**, which produces its **wet and dry seasons**.
**Seasonal rainfall** is associated with the **Indian monsoon**.
xa: Monsoon = a **seasonal reversal of wind pattern** (Arabic **Mausim** = season).
Main mechanism: **differential heating and cooling of land and sea**.
⚠ **Land and sea breezes** are **diurnal**, not annual.

16.s:
Match the phenomenon with its climatic connection.
List-I
(a) El Niño
(b) Positive IOD
(c) Southern Oscillation
(d) Western Disturbances

List-II
(i) Winter rain and snow over north-western India
(ii) See-saw of sea-level pressure between the eastern Pacific and the Indian Ocean
(iii) Warming of the eastern Pacific that generally weakens the Indian monsoon
(iv) Warmer western Indian Ocean that can partly offset El Niño's effect
16.x: El Niño warms the eastern Pacific and usually weakens the monsoon; a positive IOD (warmer western Indian Ocean) can offset it; the Southern Oscillation is the Pacific–Indian Ocean pressure see-saw; Western Disturbances bring winter rain to the north-west, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
16.tq: Separate the ocean-temperature signals from the pressure see-saw and the winter systems.
n: ENSO or El Niño generally weakens the Indian monsoon. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
A positive IOD can partly offset the effect of El Niño. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
The IOD modulates monsoon variability. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
SST anomalies influence atmospheric circulation. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
SST anomalies influence rainfall. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**El Niño** (ENSO) generally **weakens the Indian monsoon**; a **positive IOD** can **partly offset** El Niño's effect.
**Southern Oscillation** = pressure **see-saw** between the **eastern Pacific** and the **Indian Ocean**.
**Western Disturbances** bring **winter precipitation** over **north-western India**.
xa: The **Subtropical Westerly Jet** is connected with **winter weather** and **Western Disturbances**.
The **Tropical Easterly Jet** supports **summer monsoon circulation**.
**SST anomalies** influence **atmospheric circulation** and **rainfall**.
**IOD** **modulates monsoon variability**.

16.s: During summer, what pressure condition over heated land helps monsoon circulation?
o: Low pressure over cooled land, reversing seasonal winds
Low pressure over heated land, drawing moisture-bearing winds
High pressure over heated land, drawing dry winds
High pressure over heated land, suppressing the pressure gradient
16.x: In summer heated land develops low pressure, which draws moist winds in from the sea and drives the monsoon.
16.tq: Relate heating to pressure.
n: Summer heating produces low pressure over heated land. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
A pressure gradient draws moisture-bearing winds. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
The northward shift of the ITCZ helps monsoon circulation. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
xs: **Low pressure over heated land, drawing moisture-bearing winds** — option **(2)** is correct.
**Summer heating** produces **low pressure** over **heated land**; the **pressure gradient** draws **moisture-bearing winds**.
High pressure develops with **winter cooling**, not summer heating.
xa: The **ITCZ shifts northward** in summer, helping **monsoon circulation**.
**Winter cooling** reverses the pressure pattern → **seasonal wind reversal**.
In NH summer the ITCZ lies over the **Indian plains** as the **monsoon trough**.

16.s:
Assertion (A): The ITCZ shifts northward during the northern summer.
Reason (R): The northward shift of the ITCZ helps monsoon circulation.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
16.x: Both are true but R does not explain A: helping the monsoon is a result of the shift, not why the ITCZ moves north; it follows the overhead Sun.
16.tq: Ask whether R gives the cause of A or one of its effects.
n: The ITCZ shifts northward during summer. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
The northward shift of the ITCZ helps monsoon circulation. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
xs: **Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A** — option **(2)**.
A is true: the **ITCZ shifts northward** in the **NH summer**, following the **overhead sun**.
R is true: this **northward shift helps monsoon circulation** — but that is a result of the shift, not its cause.
xa: Pressure belts shift about **5-10°** north in NH summer and south in winter.
In **winter** the ITCZ migrates **south of India**; with highs over **Tibet** and **Siberia** → **north-east monsoon**.
**ITCZ** = **Inter Tropical Convergence Zone** where **trade winds converge**.

16.s:
Assertion (A): Increasing temperature can lead to low pressure.
Reason (R): Heated air expands, its density decreases, and it produces low pressure.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
16.x: Both are true and R explains A: heated air expands and becomes less dense, which lowers pressure.
16.tq: Check whether R is the cause of A.
n: Increasing temperature causes air to expand. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Expansion of air decreases air density. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Decreased air density produces low pressure. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
**Increasing temperature** → air **expands** → **density decreases** → **low pressure**.
So **temperature differences** **create pressure differences**.
xa: **Decreasing temperature** → air **contracts** → density increases → **high pressure**.
**Higher altitude** gives **lower atmospheric pressure**.
**Standard sea-level pressure** = **1013.25 mb (hPa)**.

17.s:
Consider the following statements about measures of humidity:
1. Absolute humidity is the actual water vapour per unit volume of air (g/m³).
2. Specific humidity is the water vapour per unit weight of air (g/kg) and changes when the volume of air changes.
