3. Relative humidity is the actual vapour as a percentage of what the air can hold at that temperature.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
17.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is wrong: specific humidity (g/kg) is unaffected by volume changes. So '1 only' misses statement 3, while '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' include the false statement 2.
17.tq: Absolute = per volume; specific = per weight (volume-proof); relative = percentage.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 is correct: **absolute humidity** = actual water vapour **per unit volume** (**g/m3**).
Statement 2 is wrong: **specific humidity** (**g/kg**) is **unaffected by volume changes**.
Statement 3 is correct: **relative humidity** = actual vapour as a **%** of what air can hold at that temperature.
xa: ⚠ **Absolute** = per volume (g/m3); **specific** = per kg (g/kg).
RH = **100%** means **saturation**.
**Dew point**: temperature at which air becomes saturated and condensation begins.

17.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Dew point is the temperature at which air becomes saturated and condensation begins.
2. Air is saturated when its relative humidity reaches 75 per cent.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
17.x: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is wrong: saturation means relative humidity of 100 per cent. So '2 only', 'Both' and 'Neither' are wrong.
17.tq: Saturation = 100% RH, reached at the dew point.
xs: Only statement **1** is correct — option **(1) 1 only**.
Statement 1: **dew point** is the temperature at which air becomes **saturated** and **condensation** begins.
Statement 2 is wrong: air is saturated at **RH = 100%**, not 75 per cent.
xa: RH **falls when temperature rises** and rises on cooling (same vapour).
**Fog** forms when air is cooled **below its dew point**.
**Frost** forms when the dew point is **at or below 0 °C**; **dew** when it is above **0°C**.

17.s: If the actual amount of water vapour in the air remains unchanged and the air temperature rises, what happens to relative humidity?
o: It remains unchanged because the vapour content is constant
It falls because the moisture-holding capacity of air increases
It becomes 100 per cent in all cases
It rises because warm air contains more vapour
17.x: Warm air can hold more water vapour. Therefore, with the same actual vapour content, relative humidity falls as temperature rises and increases on cooling.
17.tq: Apply the same-vapour rule rather than confusing moisture content with relative humidity.
xs: RH **falls because the moisture-holding capacity of air increases** — option **(2)**.
**Warm air holds more vapour**, so with the same vapour RH **falls as temperature rises** and **rises on cooling**.
Option (4) is the trap: warm air can hold more vapour, but it does not contain more when the vapour is unchanged.
xa: RH = **100%** = **saturation**; reached at the **dew point**.
RH is **higher over oceans**, lower over continents.
AP: **Coastal Andhra** RH **70-90%**; **Rayalaseema** often **below 30%** in peak summer.

17.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Latent heat is absorbed during evaporation.
2. Latent heat is released during condensation.
3. The release of latent heat contributes to the energy of thunderstorms and cyclones.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
17.x: Evaporation absorbs latent heat, while condensation releases it. This released energy helps power thunderstorms and cyclones.
17.tq: Follow the phase-change direction—absorption in evaporation and release in condensation—to verify all three statements.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
**Latent heat** is **taken in during evaporation** and **released on condensation**.
This released heat **powers thunderstorms and cyclones**.
xa: **Dew point** marks where **condensation** begins.
**Cumulonimbus** clouds give **thunderstorms**, hail and **cloudbursts**.
**Evaporation + transpiration** = **evapotranspiration**.

17.s:
Consider the following statements about atmospheric water vapour:
1. It is up to about 4 per cent by volume in the warm, humid tropics and under 1 per cent in deserts and polar areas.
2. It increases with altitude.
3. Relative humidity is generally higher over oceans than over continents.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
17.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is wrong: water vapour falls with altitude (and with latitude). So '1 only' misses statement 3, while '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' include the false statement 2.
17.tq: Water vapour falls with both latitude and altitude.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 is correct: water vapour is **up to 4%** by volume in the humid tropics, **under 1%** in deserts and polar areas.
Statement 2 is wrong: water vapour **falls with altitude** (and with **latitude**).
Statement 3 is correct: RH is **higher over oceans**, lower over continents.
xa: RH **falls when temperature rises** (same vapour) — warm air holds more vapour.
**Coastal Andhra** RH **70-90%** year-round → high **heat index**.
**Rayalaseema** RH is often **below 30%** in peak summer.

17.s: Which one of the following regional humidity statements is correct?
o: Rayalaseema records 70–90 per cent relative humidity in peak summer
Coastal Andhra generally records below 30 per cent relative humidity throughout the year
Coastal Andhra generally records relative humidity of 70–90 per cent, whereas Rayalaseema may fall below 30 per cent in peak summer
Both coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema normally record identical relative humidity throughout the year
17.x: Coastal Andhra has high relative humidity of about 70–90 per cent, contributing to a high heat index. Rayalaseema often records below 30 per cent in summer.
17.tq: Use the coastal–interior contrast and check the numerical ranges before selecting the pair.
xs: **Coastal Andhra** has RH **70–90%**, while **Rayalaseema** may fall **below 30%** in peak summer — option **(3)**.
Options (1) and (2) swap the two regions; RH is not identical across them.
xa: Coastal Andhra's high RH gives a **high heat index**.
RH is **higher over oceans**, lower over continents.
**Rayalaseema** lies in the **rain shadow**; the hot, dry **Loo** also reaches it.

17.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the hydrological cycle:
1. Evapotranspiration combines evaporation and transpiration.
2. Sublimation can form part of the hydrological cycle.
3. Groundwater flow is included in the movement of water through the cycle.
4. Combustion is a normal stage of the hydrological cycle.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
17.x: Evapotranspiration, sublimation and groundwater flow are components of the hydrological cycle. Combustion is not a stage of the cycle.
17.tq: Separate the listed cycle processes from the biological or unrelated distractor.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(1)**.
**Evapotranspiration** = **evaporation + transpiration**; **sublimation** and **groundwater flow** are part of the cycle.
Statement 4 is wrong: **combustion** is not in the cycle — like **photosynthesis** and **respiration**, it is a distractor.
xa: Other cycle processes: **condensation**, **precipitation**, **infiltration/percolation**, **surface runoff**.
**Hydrometeorology** studies water and energy transfer between land surface and **lower atmosphere**.
**Lysimeter** measures **evapotranspiration** / water percolating through soil.

17.s: Hydrometeorology is primarily concerned with the study of
o: the transfer of water and energy between the land surface and the lower atmosphere
the movement of tectonic plates beneath the oceans
the chemical composition of ocean water alone
the geological evolution of mountain ranges
17.x: Hydrometeorology studies the transfer of water and energy between the land surface and the lower atmosphere, including rainfall, floods and droughts.
17.tq: Match the specialised discipline with its exact field of study.
xs: **Hydrometeorology** studies **the transfer of water and energy between the land surface and the lower atmosphere** — option **(1)**.
It covers **rainfall, evaporation, floods and droughts** — not plate tectonics, ocean chemistry or mountain building.
xa: India gets about **4,000 BCM** of precipitation a year; **1,139 BCM** is utilisable.
Heavy rain bursts exceed **infiltration capacity** → aquifer recharge falls (**Nature** study, **7 Jun 2026**).
**Evapotranspiration** is measured by the **lysimeter**.

17.s: In India, the approximate annual precipitation and utilisable water resources are respectively:
17.x: India receives about 4,000 BCM of precipitation annually, of which approximately 1,139 BCM is utilisable, including 690 BCM of surface water and 449 BCM of groundwater.
17.tq: Read the paired figures carefully and distinguish total precipitation from utilisable resources.
xs: About **4,000 BCM** precipitation and **1,139 BCM** utilisable — option **(3)**.
Utilisable **1,139 BCM** = **690 BCM surface** + **449 BCM groundwater** — so 690 or 449 alone is only a part.
xa: **Natural runoff** after evaporation: **1,999.20 BCM**.
These are India's **2026** water-budget figures.
Heavy rain bursts reduce **aquifer recharge** by exceeding **infiltration capacity**.

17.s: Frost differs from dew because frost
o: is a cloud at ground level with visibility below 1 km
forms only when the dew point is above 0°C
forms as ice crystals when the dew point is at or below 0°C
consists of rain drops larger than 0.5 mm
17.x: Frost forms as ice crystals when the dew point is at or below 0°C. Dew is liquid moisture condensed on cool surfaces with a dew point above 0°C.
17.tq: Use the temperature condition to distinguish two closely related forms of condensation.
xs: **Frost** forms **as ice crystals when the dew point is at or below 0°C** — option **(3)**.
**Dew** forms when moisture condenses on cool surfaces with the dew point **above 0°C**.
Ground-level cloud with visibility under **1 km** is **fog**; drops over **0.5 mm** are **rain**.
xa: **Lambasingi** ("**Kashmir of AP**") sees frost at about **2 °C**.
Ideal for dew/frost: **clear sky, calm air, high RH, cold long nights**.
**Snow** = condensation below **0 °C** as ice crystals.

17.s:
Consider the following statements about fog and mist:
1. Mist is thinner and wetter than fog.
2. Fog has visibility over 1 km, whereas mist has visibility under 1 km.
3. Fog is a cloud at ground level that forms when air is cooled below its dew point, often under an inversion.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
17.x: Statement 3 is correct: fog is a ground-level cloud formed when air cools below its dew point, often under an inversion. Statement 2 is wrong: it reverses the rule; fog means visibility under 1 km and mist over 1 km. Statement 1 is correct: mist is thinner and wetter. So '3 only' misses statement 1, and options with statement 2 are wrong.
17.tq: Fog = under 1 km visibility; mist = over 1 km.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: **mist** is like fog but **thinner, wetter** with **better visibility**.
Statement 2 is wrong: it reverses the rule — **fog** = visibility **under 1 km**; **mist** = **over 1 km**.
Statement 3 is correct: **fog** is a **cloud at ground level**, air cooled **below dew point**, often under **inversion**.
xa: **Smog** = fog + smoke/pollutants; ⚠ **London** smog = **sulphurous**, **Los Angeles** smog = **photochemical** (forms **PAN**).
**Frost** forms when the **dew point** is at or below **0 °C**.
Dew/frost need **clear sky, calm air, high RH, cold long nights**.

17.s:
Which of the following correctly distinguishes London smog from Los Angeles smog?
1. London smog is sulphurous, cool and humid.
2. Los Angeles smog is photochemical and requires sunlight.
3. Photochemical smog can involve the formation of PAN.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
17.x: London smog is sulphurous and associated with cool, humid conditions. Los Angeles smog is photochemical, requires sunlight and can produce PAN.
17.tq: Use the source-condition-product distinction between two types of smog.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
**London** smog: **sulphurous**, cool and humid.
**Los Angeles** smog: **photochemical**, needs **sunlight**, forms **PAN**, carries ground-level **ozone** (UPSC).
xa: **Smog** = **fog + smoke/pollutants**.
⚠ London = sulphurous; Los Angeles = photochemical.
**Acid rain** (pH **below 5.6**) comes from **SO2** and **NOx**.

17.s:
Consider the following statements about forms of precipitation:
1. Sleet forms when rain freezes into ice pellets as it falls through a cold layer.
2. Hail consists of layered ice balls formed in nimbostratus clouds with weak updrafts.
3. Snow forms when condensation takes place below 0°C as ice crystals.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
17.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is wrong: hail forms in cumulonimbus clouds with strong updrafts. So '1 only' misses statement 3, while '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' include the false statement 2.
17.tq: Hail needs the strong updrafts of a cumulonimbus.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 is correct: **sleet** = rain **freezing into ice pellets** as it falls through a cold layer.
Statement 2 is wrong: **hail** forms in **cumulonimbus** with **strong updrafts**, not nimbostratus with weak updrafts.
Statement 3 is correct: **snow** = condensation **below 0 °C** as ice crystals.
xa: **Rain**: drops **over 0.5 mm**; **drizzle**: fine drops **under 0.5 mm**, from **stratus**.
**Nimbostratus** gives **steady, continuous rain**.

17.s: Dew and frost are favoured by which combination of conditions?
o: Clear skies, calm air, high relative humidity and long cold nights
Continuous rainfall, turbulent winds and high atmospheric pressure
High daytime temperature, strong convection and dry air
Cloudy skies, strong winds, low humidity and short nights
17.x: Clear and calm nights allow surfaces to cool efficiently, while high humidity and long cold nights favour dew or frost formation. Clouds and wind tend to prevent them.
17.tq: Select the complete set of conditions favourable to surface condensation.
xs: Dew and frost need **clear skies, calm air, high relative humidity and long cold nights** — option **(1)**.
They are **prevented by cloudy skies, wind and low humidity** — option (4) lists exactly those.
xa: **Dew**: dew point **above 0°C**; **frost**: dew point **at or below 0 °C**.
**Lambasingi** ("Kashmir of AP") sees frost at about **2 °C**.
Fog forms when air is cooled **below dew point**, often under an **inversion**.

17.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Drizzle — drops exceeding 5 mm from cumulonimbus clouds
Sleet — ice crystals deposited directly on surfaces
17.x: Rain consists of drops exceeding 0.5 mm. Drizzle has fine drops under 0.5 mm and commonly comes from stratus clouds; snow consists of ice crystals formed below 0°C.
17.tq: Use the drop-size threshold to separate rain from drizzle and other forms.
xs: **Rain — drops exceeding 0.5 mm** is correct — option **(1)**.
**Drizzle** has fine drops **under 0.5 mm** from **stratus**, not cumulonimbus.
**Snow** is **ice crystals** formed **below 0 °C**; **sleet** is rain freezing into **ice pellets** as it falls.
xa: **Hail**: layered ice balls from **cumulonimbus** with strong updrafts.
**Rain gauge** measures rainfall depth; **isohyets** join places of equal rainfall.

17.s: The phenomenon known as ‘blood rain’ may occur when
o: sunlight is refracted through hexagonal ice crystals
raindrops freeze into transparent ice pellets
dust or spores become mixed with raindrops
sulphur dioxide dissolves in snow crystals
17.x: Coloured rain can result when dust or spores mix with raindrops. Sirocco dust over Italy and Kerala’s red rain of 2001 are examples associated with this phenomenon.
17.tq: Match the unusual colour of rain with its suspended material.
xs: 'Blood rain' occurs when **dust or spores become mixed with raindrops** — option **(3)**.
Example: **Sirocco** dust over **Italy**.
Refraction through **hexagonal ice crystals** makes a **halo**; freezing drops make **sleet**.
xa: **Kerala's red rain** of **2001** is another coloured rain.
The **Sirocco** blows hot and dusty from the **Sahara** towards Italy.
**Acid rain** (pH **below 5.6**) comes from **SO2** and **NOx**.

17.s:
Match List-I (Cloud) with List-II (Appearance):
List-I
(a) Cirrus
(b) Cirrostratus
(c) Cirrocumulus
(d) Cumulus
List-II
(i) Small globular masses or ripples
(ii) Thin, feathery, silky
(iii) Heaped cauliflower tops with a flat base
(iv) Thin milky sheet that causes a halo
17.x: Cirrus is thin, feathery and silky; cirrostratus is a thin milky sheet that produces a halo; cirrocumulus forms small globular masses or ripples (mackerel sky); cumulus has heaped cauliflower tops and a flat base. So a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii. The second option swaps cirrus with cirrostratus, the third swaps cirrocumulus with cumulus, and the fourth swaps cirrus with cirrocumulus.
17.tq: APPSC-G1 2024 pairs: cirrus silky, cirrostratus milky, cirrocumulus globular, cumulus cauliflower.
xs: The correct match is **a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Cirrus** = thin, feathery, **silky**; **cirrostratus** = thin **milky** sheet causing a **halo**.
**Cirrocumulus** = **small globular masses**, ripples (**"mackerel sky"**); **cumulus** = heaped **cauliflower** tops, flat base.
xa: This match was asked in **APPSC-G1 2024**.
High clouds (cirrus family) lie above **~6 km** and are made of **ice crystals**.
**Nimbostratus** gives **steady, continuous rain**; **cumulonimbus** gives **thunderstorms** and **hail**.
**Cumulonimbus** towers can reach **15 km**.

17.s:
Consider the following statements about clouds:
1. Nimbostratus is a low, dark, thick and shapeless cloud layer that gives steady, continuous rain.
2. The term 'nimbus' denotes a rain-bearing cloud.
3. Cirrus is a rain-bearing cloud of the middle level.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
17.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: cirrus is a high cloud (thin, feathery, silky) associated with fair weather and no rain. So '1 only' misses statement 2, while '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' include the false statement 3.
17.tq: 'Nimbus' in the name = rain; cirrus = high, silky, fair weather.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: **nimbostratus** is low, dark, thick, shapeless and gives **steady, continuous rain**. Statement 2: **"Nimbus"** = rain-bearing cloud.
Statement 3 is wrong: **cirrus** is a **high** cloud — thin, feathery, silky — with **fair weather; no rain**.
xa: **Rain-bearing** clouds: **nimbostratus** and **cumulonimbus**.
**Cumulonimbus produces rainstorms** (**APPSC 2019**; APPSC-GS 2019).

17.s:
With reference to cumulus clouds, consider the following statements:
1. They generally have a heaped, cauliflower-like form.
2. They usually have a flat base.
3. They are associated with fair weather but may grow into cumulonimbus clouds.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
17.x: Cumulus clouds have heaped cauliflower tops and generally flat bases. They are commonly associated with fair weather but can develop vertically into cumulonimbus clouds.
17.tq: Check whether the statements describe the complete life and appearance of a cumulus cloud.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
**Cumulus**: heaped **cauliflower** / cotton-wool tops with a **flat base**.
It brings **fair weather** but can **grow into cumulonimbus**.
xa: Cumulus has vertical growth from **4,000-7,000 m**.
**Cumulonimbus** towers reach about **15 km** with an **anvil** top.
**APPSC-G1 2024**: cumulus = **cauliflower**.

17.s: Which one of the following statements about cumulonimbus clouds is correct?
o: They are low, shapeless clouds producing only light drizzle.
They are middle-level clouds through which the Sun appears like ground glass.
They are towering clouds that may extend up to about 15 km and have an anvil-shaped top.
They are thin, silky clouds restricted to the upper troposphere.
17.x: Cumulonimbus clouds have marked vertical development, may reach about 15 km, and commonly have a towering anvil-shaped top.
17.tq: Use the extreme vertical extent and anvil top as decisive identifiers.
xs: **Cumulonimbus** are **towering clouds up to about 15 km** with an **anvil-shaped top** — option **(3)**.
They give **thunderstorms, rainstorms, hail and cloudbursts**.
Ground-glass sun is **altostratus**; thin silky clouds are **cirrus**.
xa: Cumulonimbus towers reaching **15 km** were noted on **31 Jul 2026**.
**Hail** forms in cumulonimbus with **strong updrafts**.
Orographic lifting in the **Himalaya** builds cumulonimbus → **cloudbursts**.

17.s: The sun halo is generally observed as
o: a semicircular arc produced by reflection from raindrops
a ring of about 22° formed by refraction through ice crystals in high cirrostratus clouds
a coloured ring produced by diffraction near the Sun or Moon
a white ring caused by dust particles in the lower atmosphere
17.x: A sun halo is typically a ring of about 22° produced when sunlight is refracted through millions of hexagonal ice crystals in thin, high cirrostratus clouds.
17.tq: Use the distinctive combination of angle, cloud type and ice-crystal mechanism.
xs: A **halo** is **a ring of about 22°** from **refraction through ice crystals** in high **cirrostratus** — option **(2)**.
Sunlight refracts through **millions of hexagonal ice crystals** in thin, high cloud.
Coloured rings from **diffraction** close to the sun are a **corona**; raindrop arcs are a **rainbow**.
xa: ⚠ **Halo** = refraction through ice crystals; **corona** = diffraction by water droplets.
**APPSC-G1 2024** key on the halo: statements **I and II**.
A cirrostratus halo signals a **warm front** approaching.

17.s: A corona around the Sun or Moon is formed mainly by
o: dispersion in raindrops when the Sun is behind the observer
diffraction by small water droplets in thin clouds
refraction through large hexagonal ice crystals
17.x: A corona consists of coloured rings close to the Sun or Moon and is produced by diffraction by small water droplets in thin clouds.
17.tq: Discriminate corona from halo by matching it with diffraction and water droplets.
xs: A **corona** is formed by **diffraction by small water droplets in thin clouds** — option **(3)**.
It appears as **coloured rings close to the sun/moon**.
Refraction through **ice crystals** makes a **halo**; dispersion in raindrops with the sun behind makes a **rainbow**.
xa: ⚠ **Halo** = refraction through ice crystals; **corona** = diffraction by water droplets.
Halo is about **22°** and forms in **cirrostratus**.

17.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Equatorial regions may receive convectional rain almost every day throughout the year.
2. Pre-monsoon mango showers are an example of convectional precipitation.
3. Convectional precipitation is caused by warm air being lifted over cold air along a front.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
17.x: Equatorial daily rainfall and pre-monsoon mango showers are examples of convectional precipitation. Warm air rising over cold air along a front describes frontal precipitation, not convectional precipitation.
17.tq: Separate heating-driven uplift from frontal uplift when evaluating the statements.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statements 1 and 2: **convectional** rain falls **almost every day, all year** in the **equatorial belt**; **mango showers** are convectional too.
Statement 3 is wrong: warm air **lifted over cold air along a front** is **cyclonic/frontal** precipitation.
xa: Convection: strong heating → air rises, cools, condenses → **cumulonimbus**; **afternoon** downpours.
**Orographic** rain: moist wind forced up a barrier; heavy on the **windward** side.

17.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Western disturbances — 10–15 cm winter precipitation in north-western India
Mango showers — frontal precipitation in temperate belts
Ruyli — wettest location of the Western Ghats
17.x: Western disturbances give about 10-15 cm of winter precipitation to north-western India, useful for rabi crops. Mango showers are pre-monsoon convectional (not temperate frontal) rain, Mawsynram is on the windward side (orographic rain), and Ruyli in Jaisalmer is India's driest place, not a wet Western Ghats station (those are Agumbe and Hulikal).
17.tq: Start from the distinctive rainfall amount and then eliminate reversed location–phenomenon pairs.
xs: **Western disturbances — 10–15 cm winter precipitation in north-western India** is correct — option **(1)**.
It is **cyclonic/frontal** rain that helps the **rabi** crop.
**Mango showers** are pre-monsoon **convectional** rain; **Mawsynram** is an **orographic** windward site; the wettest Western Ghats stations are **Agumbe** and **Hulikal**.
xa: Western disturbances are carried east by the **Subtropical Westerly Jet** from the **Mediterranean**.
**Rain shadow** lies on the **leeward** side.

17.s:
With reference to rainfall in the Western Ghats, consider the following statements:
1. The eastern side receives scanty rainfall as it lies on the leeward side.
2. Peninsular rainfall generally decreases from west to east.
3. The eastern side receives more rainfall than the western side because descending air is moist.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
17.x: The eastern side of the Western Ghats is in the rain shadow and receives scanty rainfall. Peninsular rainfall generally decreases from west to east; descending air is warm and dry, not moist.
17.tq: Test the relief-related reversal between windward and leeward sides.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statements 1 and 2: the **eastern side** of the Western Ghats is **leeward** and gets **scanty rain**; peninsular rainfall falls **west → east**.
Statement 3 is wrong: **descending** air on the leeward side **warms and dries** — it is not moist.
xa: Interiors of **Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana, AP and Tamil Nadu** lie in the rain shadow.
Wettest windward stations: **Agumbe**, **Hulikal**.

17.s:
Consider the following statements about rainfall in Andhra Pradesh:
1. Rayalaseema lies in a rain-shadow region.
2. The Hagari valley records the highest rainfall in the State.
3. The Sileru and Sabari valleys receive about 140–152 cm, aided by the south-west monsoon and the orographic effect of the Eastern Ghats.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
17.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is wrong: the Hagari valley has the lowest rainfall in AP (below 51 cm). So '1 only' misses statement 3, while '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' include the false statement 2.
17.tq: Hagari = driest (<51 cm); Sileru–Sabari = wettest (140–152 cm).
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 is correct: **Rayalaseema** lies in the **rain shadow**.
Statement 2 is wrong: the **Hagari valley** has the **lowest** rain (**< 51 cm**).
Statement 3 is correct: **Sileru and Sabari valleys** get **140-152 cm** from the SW monsoon + **Eastern Ghats** orographic effect.
xa: AP average rainfall is **~966 mm** — about two-thirds from the **SW monsoon**, one-third from the **NE monsoon**.
**Sri Sathya Sai** district had a **57%** deficit in the **2026 El Nino** year.

17.s:
Consider the following statements about cloud seeding:
1. Silver iodide, dry ice and common salt may be used as cloud-seeding agents.
2. Cloud seeding can produce rainfall even when suitable clouds are completely absent.
3. Silver iodide is useful because its crystal structure mimics that of ice.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
17.x: Silver iodide, dry ice and common salt may be used for cloud seeding, and silver iodide resembles ice crystallographically. Cloud seeding requires suitable supercooled clouds already to exist; it cannot work in their complete absence.
17.tq: Spot the false absolute claim about cloud seeding and retain the two mechanism-based statements.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: **silver iodide**, **dry ice** and **common salt** (sodium chloride) are seeding agents. Statement 3: **AgI**'s crystal structure **mimics ice**.
Statement 2 is wrong: seeding works **only when suitable supercooled / moist clouds already exist**.
xa: Other agents: **potassium iodide**, **liquid propane** — they act as **condensation nuclei**.
**Kazakhstan** began seeding with **UAE** help for drought-hit **Turkestan** (**13 Aug 2026**).

17.s:
Consider the following statements about acid rain:
1. It is precipitation with a pH below 5.6.
2. The term was coined by Robert Angus Smith in 1872.
3. It is caused mainly by carbon monoxide and methane.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
17.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: acid rain comes mainly from SO2 and NOx. So '1 only' misses statement 2, while '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' include the false statement 3.
17.tq: Acid rain: pH < 5.6, SO2 + NOx, Angus Smith 1872.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(3)**.
Statement 1: acid rain has **pH below 5.6**. Statement 2: the term was coined by **Robert Angus Smith (1872)**.
Statement 3 is wrong: acid rain comes from **SO2** and **NOx**, not carbon monoxide and methane.
xa: **London** smog is **sulphurous**; **Los Angeles** smog is **photochemical**.
Coloured rain: **Kerala's red rain** of **2001**.

17.s: A cloudburst is generally defined as rainfall of about:
o: 10 mm per hour over 200-300 sq km
100 mm per hour or more over 20-30 sq km
100 mm per day over a whole district
50 mm per hour over 1,000 sq km
17.x: A cloudburst is rainfall of about 100 mm per hour or more over a small area of 20-30 sq km, usually from cumulonimbus clouds. The other options give the wrong intensity, a daily rather than hourly rate, or far too large an area.
17.tq: Cloudburst = 100 mm/hour, 20-30 sq km.
xs: A **cloudburst** is about **100 mm per hour or more over 20-30 sq km** — option **(2)**.
It comes from **cumulonimbus**; the other options give the wrong intensity, a daily rate, or too large an area.
xa: Himalayan cloudbursts: **June-August**, at **1,000-2,500 m**.
Example: **Dharali, Uttarkashi** (**Aug 2025**).
**16th Finance Commission** recommended adding **heatwaves and lightning** to notified disasters (**Apr 2026**).

17.s: Which instrument is used to determine the moisture or humidity present in the air?
17.x: A hygrometer measures moisture or humidity in the air. A hydrometer measures the density of a liquid.
17.tq: Separate the look-alike terms hygrometer and hydrometer by their measured quantities.
xs: The **hygrometer** measures **moisture (humidity)** in the air — option **(4)**.
⚠ The **hydrometer** measures **liquid density** — the classic distractor for hygrometer.
**Rain gauge** measures **rainfall depth**; **barometer** measures **pressure**.
xa: Asked in **APPSC-G1 2018**.
**Sling psychrometer** gives humidity from **wet- and dry-bulb** readings (**APPSC 2018**).
**Lysimeter** measures **evapotranspiration** / water percolating through soil.

17.s: A sling psychrometer determines atmospheric humidity primarily by using
o: rainfall depth and wind speed readings
17.x: A sling psychrometer estimates humidity from the difference between wet-bulb and dry-bulb temperatures.
17.tq: Identify the instrument from the pair of observations required for its operation.
xs: The **sling psychrometer** uses **wet-bulb and dry-bulb temperature readings** — option **(3)**.
The gap between the two readings gives the **humidity** (**APPSC 2018**).
xa: **Wet-bulb temperature** = lowest temperature air can reach by **evaporation**.
Wet-bulb equals dry-bulb at **100% RH**.
Above **31.5°C** wet-bulb, the body **cannot cool itself by sweating**.

17.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
17.x: An isobar joins places of equal atmospheric pressure, not equal temperature. An isotherm joins places of equal temperature.
17.tq: Find the swapped meaning in the pair of commonly confused isolines.
xs: NOT correctly matched: **Isobar — places of equal temperature** — option **(1)**.
An **isobar** joins places of **equal pressure**; places of equal temperature are joined by the **isotherm**.
**Rain gauge — rainfall depth** and **Isohyet — equal rainfall** are correct.
xa: **Isoneph** joins places of **equal cloudiness** (**APPSC 2019**).
⚠ **Isohyet** = rainfall; **isoneph** = cloudiness.
**Hygrometer** measures humidity; **lysimeter** measures evapotranspiration.

17.s:
Consider the following statements about wet-bulb temperature:
1. It is the lowest temperature air can reach by evaporation.
2. It equals the dry-bulb temperature when relative humidity is zero.
3. Above a wet-bulb temperature of about 31.5°C, the human body cannot cool itself by sweating.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
17.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is wrong: wet-bulb equals dry-bulb at 100% relative humidity (saturated air, no evaporative cooling), not at zero. So '1 only' misses statement 3, and '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' include the false statement 2.
17.tq: Saturated air (100% RH) means no evaporative cooling, so the two bulbs read the same.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(4)**.
Statement 1 is correct: **wet-bulb temperature** is the **lowest temperature air can reach by evaporation**.
Statement 2 is wrong: wet-bulb equals dry-bulb at **100% RH**, not at zero.
Statement 3 is correct: above **31.5°C** the body **cannot cool itself by sweating**.
xa: The **sling psychrometer** reads **wet- and dry-bulb** temperatures to give humidity.
RH = **100%** = **saturation**.

17.s:
Arrange the following rain-gauge milestones in chronological order:
A. Castelli’s rain gauge
B. Rain gauge described in the Mauryan Arthashastra
C. Korea’s Cheugugi
Which one of the following is the correct sequence?
17.x: The Mauryan Arthashastra description predates Korea’s Cheugugi of 1441, which in turn predates Castelli’s rain gauge of 1639.
17.tq: Fix the earliest historical reference first and then place the dated instruments in sequence.
xs: Correct order: **B, C, A** — option **(2)**.
**Mauryan Arthashastra** gauge (earliest) → Korea's **Cheugugi (1441)** → **Castelli (1639)**.
xa: The Arthashastra gauge measured in **drona** (about **13.2 kg** of water).
A modern **rain gauge** measures **rainfall depth**.
**Isohyet** = line of equal rainfall.

17.s: Lines drawn on a map joining places having equal cloudiness are called:
17.x: Isonephs join places of equal cloudiness (APPSC 2019). Isohyets join places of equal rainfall, isotherms equal temperature and isobars equal pressure.
17.tq: Neph = cloud → isoneph.
xs: Lines of equal cloudiness are **isonephs** — option **(2)**.
**Isohyets** = equal rainfall; **isotherms** = equal temperature; **isobars** = equal pressure.
xa: Isoneph was asked in **APPSC 2019**.
⚠ **Isohyet** = rainfall; **Isoneph** = cloudiness.
**Hygrometer** measures humidity (**APPSC-G1 2018**).

17.s: A waterspout is best described as:
o: A horizontal ocean current generated by tides
A snowstorm occurring over high mountain ranges
A dust column formed over a dry desert surface
A funnel-shaped phenomenon extending from a cumulus or cumulonimbus cloud over water
17.x: A waterspout is a funnel extending from a cumulus or cumulonimbus cloud over a water body.
17.tq: Distinguish the water-based funnel phenomenon from land-based dust and snow events.
xs: A **waterspout** is **a funnel extending from a cumulus or cumulonimbus cloud over water** — option **(4)**.
It is not an ocean current, a snowstorm or a desert dust column.
xa: One was recorded over the **Brahmaputra** in **Barpeta, Assam** (**26 Aug 2026**).
**Cumulonimbus** also gives thunderstorms, hail and **cloudbursts**.
**Cumulus** (fair weather) can grow into cumulonimbus.

17.s: The 16th Finance Commission recommended adding which of the following to the list of nationally notified disasters?
17.x: The 16th Finance Commission recommended the addition of heatwaves and lightning to the nationally notified disasters.
17.tq: Use the paired current-affairs terms together; do not substitute already familiar disaster categories.
xs: The **16th Finance Commission** recommended adding **heatwaves and lightning** — option **(4)**.
They would join the **nationally notified disasters** (**Apr 2026**).
xa: **Cloudburst** at **Dharali, Uttarkashi** (**Aug 2025**).
**Wet-bulb** above **31.5°C** → the body cannot cool by sweating.
**Cumulonimbus** clouds produce **thunderstorms** and lightning-bearing rainstorms.

17.s:
Consider the following statements about rainfall in Andhra Pradesh:
1. The average annual rainfall of Andhra Pradesh is approximately 966 mm.
2. About two-thirds of the rainfall is received from the South-West monsoon.
3. About one-third of the rainfall is received from the North-East monsoon.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
17.x: Andhra Pradesh receives about 966 mm of average annual rainfall, with approximately two-thirds from the South-West monsoon and one-third from the North-East monsoon.
17.tq: Check the total figure and the complementary monsoon shares together.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
AP's average rainfall is **~966 mm**: about **two-thirds** from the **SW monsoon** and **one-third** from the **NE monsoon**.
xa: **2026 El Nino year**: **Sri Sathya Sai** district had a **57%** deficit (CDCA, Aug 2026).
**North Coastal AP** (Sileru, Sabari) gets the most (**140-152 cm**); **Hagari valley** the least (**< 51 cm**).

17.s:
Match List-I with List-II.
List-I
(a) Absolute humidity
(b) Relative humidity
(c) Dew point
(d) Condensation

List-II
(i) Temperature at which air becomes saturated
(ii) Water vapour changing into liquid or solid
(iii) Actual mass of water vapour per unit volume
(iv) Actual moisture divided by moisture-holding capacity × 100
17.x: Absolute humidity is vapour mass per volume, relative humidity is the percentage of capacity, dew point is the saturation temperature and condensation turns vapour to liquid or ice, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
17.tq: Recall the definition of each humidity term.
n: Absolute humidity is the actual mass of water vapour per unit volume. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Relative humidity is actual moisture divided by moisture-holding capacity, multiplied by 100. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
The dew point is the temperature at which air becomes saturated. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Condensation changes water vapour into liquid or solid form. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Absolute humidity** = **actual mass of water vapour per unit volume**; **relative humidity** = **actual moisture ÷ capacity × 100**.
**Dew point** = temperature at which **air becomes saturated**; **condensation** changes **vapour into liquid or solid**.
xa: ⚠ **Absolute** = per volume (**g/m3**); **specific** humidity = per kg (**g/kg**).
**RH = 100%** means **saturation**; RH **falls when temperature rises**.
**Coastal Andhra** RH **70-90%**; **Rayalaseema** often **below 30%** in peak summer.
Water vapour is up to **4%** by volume in humid tropics.

17.s:
Match the precipitation type with its mechanism or typical association.
List-I
(a) Convectional precipitation
(b) Cyclonic or frontal precipitation
(c) Orographic (relief) rainfall
(d) Rain-shadow area

List-II
(i) Moist air forced to rise over a mountain barrier
(ii) Strong heating, rising air, cooling and condensation
(iii) Convergence or frontal uplift causing rising air
(iv) Dry leeward side of a mountain range
17.x: Convectional rain comes from strong heating and rising air, frontal rain from convergence and frontal uplift, orographic rain from moist air forced up a mountain, and the rain-shadow area is the dry leeward side, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv.
17.tq: Identify what lifts the air in each case: heat, a front or a mountain.
n: Convectional precipitation results from strong heating, rising air, cooling and condensation. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Cyclonic or frontal precipitation results from convergence or frontal uplift, rising air, cooling and condensation. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Relief-induced precipitation occurs when topography modifies rainfall distribution. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Relief-induced precipitation differs between windward and leeward locations. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Windward slopes receive orographic rainfall. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
xs: The correct match is **a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv** — so option **(3)** is correct.
