18.x: The transport of warm air masses into the Arctic by a meandering jet stream drives Arctic amplification.
18.tq: Match the atmospheric process with its named climatic consequence.
xs: It drives **Arctic amplification** — option **(4)**.
A **meandering jet stream** carries **warm air masses into the Arctic** (UPSC Env p.220).
**cP** air forms over **Siberia/Canada**, not Arabia (Arabia gives **cT**).
xa: An air mass is **modified** when it leaves its source region.
**Frontolysis** = weakening of a front as temperature contrast is lost.

18.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Cold front — gentle slope — prolonged light rain ahead
Warm front — steep slope — sudden heavy showers
Stationary front — neither air mass advances — rain may persist for days
Occluded front — warm air remains at the ground — no mixed weather
18.x: At a stationary front neither air mass advances, and cloud and rain may persist for days. Cold fronts are steep, warm fronts have gentle slopes, and occlusion lifts warm air off the ground.
18.tq: Match the front type with its defining movement rather than only its cloud type.
xs: **Stationary front — neither air mass advances — rain may persist for days** — option **(3)**.
Winds blow **parallel to the front**, so cloud and rain linger.
**Cold** fronts are **steep** with short heavy showers; **warm** fronts are **gentle** with prolonged rain; an **occluded** front **lifts warm air off the ground**.
xa: **Occluded** front = **last stage** of a temperate cyclone; gives mixed cloud and rain.
⚠ Cold = steep; warm = gentle.

18.s: A cold front is characterised by which one of the following combinations?
o: Warm air riding gradually over retreating cold air and prolonged light rain
Cold air advancing and lifting warm air sharply, with heavy short showers and a sudden temperature fall
A faster warm front overtaking a cold front
Neither air mass advancing and rainfall persisting for several days
18.x: In a cold front, advancing cold air forms a steep wedge and lifts warm air sharply, producing cumulonimbus, heavy short showers, thunder, squalls and a sudden temperature fall.
18.tq: Use the movement of the advancing air mass as the key discriminator.
xs: A **cold front**: **cold air advancing and lifting warm air sharply**, with **heavy short showers and a sudden temperature fall** — option **(2)**.
It has a **steep** slope and brings **cumulonimbus**, thunder and **squalls**.
Option (1) is a **warm front**; option (4) a **stationary front**.
xa: After the cold front passes: **cold, clear air**, wind shift.
**Arcus (shelf/roll) clouds** form at the leading edge of cold fronts.
An **occluded** front forms when a faster cold front overtakes the warm front.

18.s: Arcus or shelf/roll clouds commonly form:
o: Behind every warm front after skies clear
At the leading edge of thunderstorm outflows or cold fronts
At the top of the stratosphere
Only at the centre of an anticyclone
18.x: Arcus clouds form along the leading edge of thunderstorm outflows or cold fronts and mark the boundary between warm and cool air.
18.tq: Associate the cloud form with its leading-edge boundary location.
xs: **Arcus (shelf/roll) clouds** form **at the leading edge of thunderstorm outflows or cold fronts** — option **(2)**.
They **mark the warm/cool air boundary** (**Jul 2025**).
xa: A **cold front** brings **cumulonimbus**, heavy short showers, **squalls**.
Polar anticyclones + polar fronts form **cold fronts** → storms and temperature drops.
The cold front's slope is **steep**.

18.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes frontolysis from frontogenesis?
o: Frontolysis strengthens a front, whereas frontogenesis dissolves it
Frontolysis is weakening and dissolution as temperature contrast is lost, whereas frontogenesis forms or sharpens a front
Both terms describe the overtaking of a warm front by a cold front
Both terms refer only to cloud development at a stationary front
18.x: Frontolysis occurs when a front weakens and dissolves because temperature contrast is lost; frontogenesis involves formation or sharpening through convergence of contrasting air masses.
18.tq: Compare the opposite processes by their changes in temperature contrast.
xs: **Frontolysis** = **weakening and dissolution** as **temperature contrast is lost**; **frontogenesis** = **forms or sharpens** a front — option **(2)**.
Option (1) reverses the two terms.
xa: Frontogenesis happens where **contrasting air masses converge**.
A **front** is a sloping boundary between air masses of different **temperature and density**.
Occluded front: faster **cold front** overtakes the **warm front**.

18.s: Which sequence of clouds is normally associated with the approach of a warm front?
18.x: The usual sequence ahead of an approaching warm front is cirrus, cirrostratus, altostratus and nimbostratus.
18.tq: Remember the cloud sequence from high, thin clouds to lower rain-bearing cloud.
xs: Ahead of a warm front: **cirrus → cirrostratus → altostratus → nimbostratus** — option **(2)**.
Clouds thicken and lower as the front nears; **pressure falls** and **steady, widespread rain** follows.
xa: **Warm sector**: clearing, some **stratus**; warmer, humid, rain eases.
**Cold front** passes with **cumulonimbus**, heavy showers, thunder; then **cold, clear air**.
**Cirrostratus** causes a **halo** — a sign of an approaching warm front.

18.s:
Consider the following statements about the passage of a frontal system:
1. Pressure falls as a warm front approaches.
2. The warm sector is warmer and humid, and rainfall generally eases.
3. Passage of a cold front is followed by cold, clear air.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
18.x: All three statements are correct. A warm front brings falling pressure and steady widespread rain, the warm sector brings warmer humid conditions with easing rain, and the cold front is followed by cold clear air.
18.tq: Follow the complete frontal sequence rather than isolating one cloud stage.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Approaching warm front: **pressure falls**; **warm sector**: warmer, humid, **rain eases**; after the **cold front**: **cold, clear air**.
xa: Warm-front cloud order: **cirrus → cirrostratus → altostratus → nimbostratus**.
Cold front: **cumulonimbus**, heavy showers, thunder, **wind shift**.
⚠ Cold = steep, short heavy showers; warm = gentle, prolonged light rain.

18.s:
Consider the following statements about the Polar Front Theory:
1. It was put forward by Vilhelm and Jacob Bjerknes of the Bergen School, Norway.
2. Western disturbances reach north-west India at the warm-sector stage, before fronts develop.
3. It holds that temperate (wave) cyclones form along the polar front, where cold polar air meets warm westerly air.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
18.x: Statement 1 is correct: the theory came from Vilhelm and Jacob Bjerknes of the Bergen School around the end of World War I. Statement 3 is correct: wave cyclones form on the polar front where cold polar air meets warm westerly air. Statement 2 is wrong: western disturbances reach north-west India at the occluded-front stage. So '1 only' misses statement 3, and options with statement 2 are wrong.
18.tq: Bjerknes = polar front (Bergen); Bergeron = air-mass codes. WDs arrive occluded.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: proponents were **Vilhelm and Jacob Bjerknes** (**Bergen School, Norway**), around the end of **World War I**.
Statement 3 is correct: **temperate (wave) cyclones** form along the **polar front** where **cold polar air** meets **warm westerly air**.
Statement 2 is wrong: western disturbances reach north-west India at the **occluded-front stage**.
xa: **Life cycle:** wave on the front → warm and cold fronts → **occlusion** → dissipation.
⚠ **Bjerknes** = polar front theory; **Bergeron** = air-mass classification.
**Frontogenesis** = formation of a front; **frontolysis** = its weakening and dissolution.

18.s:
Arrange the stages in the life cycle of a temperate cyclone in the correct chronological order:
A. Occlusion
B. Dissipation
C. Wave on the front
D. Development of warm and cold fronts
18.x: The sequence is wave on the front, development of warm and cold fronts, occlusion and finally dissipation.
18.tq: Fix the initiating wave and terminal dissipation before arranging the middle stages.
xs: Correct order: **C, D, A, B** — option **(1)**.
**Wave on the front** → **warm and cold fronts** develop → **occlusion** → **dissipation**.
xa: **Occlusion**: a faster cold front overtakes the warm front, lifting warm air off the ground.
Theory by **Vilhelm and Jacob Bjerknes** (Bergen School, Norway).
**Western disturbances** reach NW India at the occluded stage.

18.s: Because the Himalayas block cold, dry continental air from Central Asia, north India is approximately how much warmer than places on the same latitude during winter?
18.x: The Himalayan barrier makes north India about 3–8°C warmer than places on the same latitude during winter.
18.tq: Choose the correct numerical range by separating it from the rainfall and snowfall figures.
xs: North India is about **3–8°C warmer** in winter — option **(2)**.
The **Himalayas** block **cold, dry continental air from Central Asia** (UPSC Geo p.42; IYB).
xa: Winter **anticyclonic cell** over India: **clear skies**, light **northerly** winds, low humidity, **large daily range**.
Summer: moist maritime air from the **Indian Ocean**, fed by the **Somali Jet**.
**cP** air comes from snow-covered continents like **Siberia**.

18.s: The winter anticyclonic cell of sinking air over India is associated with:
o: Heavy convection, cumulonimbus and sudden temperature falls everywhere
Clear skies, light northerly winds, low humidity and a large daily temperature range
Persistent cloud and rain caused by a stationary front
Continuous south-westerly winds, high humidity and widespread monsoon rain
18.x: The winter anticyclonic cell produces clear skies, light northerly winds, low humidity and a large daily temperature range.
18.tq: Recognise the stable, sinking-air weather pattern of an anticyclone.
xs: **Clear skies, light northerly winds, low humidity and a large daily temperature range** — option **(2)**.
This comes from the winter **anticyclonic cell of sinking air** over India (IYB p.19; UPSC Geo p.41).
South-westerly winds and monsoon rain belong to **summer** maritime air.
xa: The **Himalayas** keep north India **3-8 degC warmer** than places on the same latitude.
Sinking-air highs give **clear skies, fog, frost**, sharp night cooling.

18.s: The south-west monsoon over India is primarily associated with:
o: Arctic air transported by the polar front
Cold dry continental air from Central Asia
Moist maritime air from the Indian Ocean fed by the low-level Somali Jet
Sinking air in the winter anticyclonic cell
18.x: The south-west monsoon is produced by moist maritime air from the Indian Ocean, supplied by the low-level Somali Jet.
18.tq: Identify the source and feeding current of the monsoon air mass.
xs: The SW monsoon comes from **moist maritime air from the Indian Ocean fed by the low-level Somali Jet** — option **(3)**.
**Cold, dry Central Asian** air and the **winter anticyclonic cell** belong to **winter**.
xa: AP has a **dual influence**: SW monsoon (summer maritime air) and **NE monsoon** (winter air returning over the **Bay of Bengal**).
Winter: Himalayas block **Central Asian** air → north India **3-8 degC** warmer.
**mT** air = warm, humid, from tropical/subtropical oceans.

18.s: Which statement correctly describes the climatic influence on Andhra Pradesh?
o: Andhra Pradesh receives rainfall only from western disturbances.
Andhra Pradesh is influenced only by the north-east monsoon.
Andhra Pradesh is under the dual influence of the south-west monsoon in summer and the north-east monsoon when winter air returns over the Bay of Bengal.
Andhra Pradesh is influenced only by the south-west monsoon.
18.x: Andhra Pradesh experiences the dual influence of the south-west monsoon and the north-east monsoon, the latter involving winter air returning over the Bay of Bengal.
18.tq: Apply the seasonal source-and-return pattern to the regional climate.
xs: AP has a **dual influence**: **SW monsoon in summer** and **NE monsoon** when winter air **returns over the Bay of Bengal** — option **(3)**.
Options (2) and (4) name only one of the two monsoons; western disturbances are not AP's rain source.
xa: SW monsoon = **summer maritime air** from the **Indian Ocean**, fed by the **Somali Jet**.
Source: **Block14 AP Climate**.
About **two-thirds** of AP rain is from the SW monsoon, **one-third** from the NE monsoon.

18.s: Which of the following recent atmospheric events is correctly associated with its reported consequence?
o: An Antarctic high reaching unusually far north — snow in Chile's Atacama Desert after more than a decade
A stationary low over Europe — record early heatwave in Western Europe
A Siberian High over India — first snowfall in the Sahara in a century
A meandering jet stream over Australia — permanent rainfall in the Atacama Desert
18.x: An Antarctic high extending unusually far north brought snow to Chile's Atacama Desert for the first time in over a decade.
18.tq: Match the unusual pressure-system displacement with its reported regional effect.
xs: **Antarctic high far north — snow in Chile's Atacama Desert** after more than a decade — option **(1)**.
It was the **first time in over a decade** (**Jul 2025**).
Western Europe's record early heatwave came from a stalled **high-pressure heat dome**, not a low.
xa: The heat dome event was reported on **27 May 2026**.
The **Antarctic High** is a **cold-core polar anticyclone**, like the **Siberian** and **Canadian Highs**.

18.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Wind is the horizontal movement of air from high pressure to low pressure.
Statement B: A greater pressure gradient produces stronger winds.

Which of the following is correct?
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
18.x: Both are true: wind blows from high to low pressure, and a steeper pressure gradient makes it stronger.
18.tq: Check each statement separately.
n: Wind is the horizontal movement of air. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Wind moves from high pressure toward low pressure. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
A greater pressure gradient produces stronger winds. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are true** — option **(1)** is correct.
A: **wind** is the **horizontal movement of air** from **high pressure** toward **low pressure**.
B: a **greater pressure gradient** produces **stronger winds**.
xa: **Atmospheric pressure** = the **force exerted by air**; varies with **temperature** and **altitude**.
**Insolation** = **incoming solar energy**, which **controls heating**.
**Temperature range** = difference between **maximum** and **minimum** temperature.

18.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Temperature
(b) Atmospheric pressure
(c) Humidity
(d) Cloudiness

List-II
(i) Water vapour present in the atmosphere
(ii) Force exerted by air
(iii) Degree of heat
(iv) Condensed water or ice particles in the atmosphere
18.x: Temperature is the degree of heat, pressure the force of air, humidity water vapour and cloudiness condensed droplets or ice, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-i, d-iv.
18.tq: Recall the definition of each element.
n: Temperature measures the degree of heat. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Atmospheric pressure is the force exerted by air. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Humidity is the water vapour present in the atmosphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Cloudiness consists of condensed water or ice particles in the atmosphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-ii, c-i, d-iv** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Temperature** = **degree of heat**; **atmospheric pressure** = **force exerted by air**.
**Humidity** = **water vapour present** in the atmosphere; **cloudiness** = **condensed water or ice particles**.
xa: **Precipitation** = water falling as **rain, snow, sleet and hail**.
**Wind** = **horizontal movement of air** from high to low pressure.
**Sunshine/insolation** = incoming solar energy that **controls heating**.

18.s:
Assertion (A): Temperature includes daily and annual ranges.
Reason (R): Temperature is controlled by latitude and altitude.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
18.x: Both are true but R does not explain A: what controls temperature does not explain that it has daily and annual ranges.
18.tq: Check whether R is the cause of A.
n: Temperature includes daily and annual ranges. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Temperature is controlled by latitude and altitude. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
xs: **Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A** — option **(2)**.
A is true: **temperature** includes **daily and annual ranges**.
R is true: temperature is **controlled by latitude and altitude** — but controls do not explain why ranges exist.
xa: **Temperature range** = difference between **maximum and minimum temperature**.
**Atmospheric pressure** varies with **temperature and altitude**.
**Insolation** **controls heating**.

18.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Mountains can block or redirect air masses.
II. The windward slope is associated with orographic rainfall.
III. The leeward slope is associated with a rain shadow.
IV. The Western Ghats produce no rainfall contrast across their slopes.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
18.x: I, II and III are correct: mountains block winds, windward slopes get orographic rain and leeward slopes lie in rain shadow. IV is false because the Western Ghats show a sharp wet–dry contrast.
18.tq: Check for an absolute claim.
n: Mountains block or redirect air masses. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Windward slopes receive orographic rainfall. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Leeward slopes form rain shadows. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
The Western Ghats produce a strong rainfall contrast across their slopes. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
xs: Statements **I, II and III** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
I: **mountains** **block or redirect air masses**.
II and III: **windward slopes** get **orographic rainfall**; **leeward slopes** form **rain shadows**.
IV is wrong: the **Western Ghats** produce a **strong rainfall contrast** across their slopes.
xa: The **Himalayas** **block cold continental winds** and influence the **monsoon**.
Blocked winter air keeps north India **3-8 degC warmer** than places on the same latitude.
Summer moist maritime air from the **Indian Ocean** is fed by the low-level **Somali Jet**.

18.s: Which of the following best describes an air mass?
o: A narrow boundary zone between two contrasting air masses
A cloud formed when water vapour condenses
A weather system formed only over oceans
A large body of air with relatively uniform temperature and humidity
18.x: An air mass is a large body of air with fairly uniform temperature and humidity. A narrow boundary between air masses is a front.
18.tq: Discriminate air mass from front.
n: An air mass is a large body of air with relatively uniform temperature and humidity. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 55-58]
xs: An air mass is **a large body of air with relatively uniform temperature and humidity** — option **(4)**.
It forms over a **source region** with **uniform surface properties**, which may be **land or ocean** — so not "only over oceans".
A **narrow boundary zone** between two air masses is a **front**, not an air mass.
xa: Air masses are **classified** by the **temperature and moisture** of their **source regions**.
**Bergeron** code: first letter = moisture (**c** dry, **m** moist); second = thermal source (**T, P, A, E**).
Air masses control **temperature, humidity, stability and precipitation**.

18.s:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Source Region)
a. Tropical Ocean
b. Tropical Land
c. Polar Ocean
d. Polar Land

List-II (Air Mass)
i. cT
 ii. mT
 iii. cP
 iv. mP
18.x: Tropical ocean gives mT, tropical land cT, polar ocean mP and polar land cP, giving a-ii, b-i, c-iv, d-iii.
18.tq: Read m for maritime and c for continental.
n: Tropical-ocean air masses are designated mT, meaning maritime Tropical. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 55-58]
Tropical-land air masses are designated cT, meaning continental Tropical. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 55-58]
Polar-ocean air masses are designated mP, meaning maritime Polar. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 55-58]
Polar-land air masses are designated cP, meaning continental Polar. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 55-58]
A source region may be land or ocean. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 55-58]
Air masses are classified on the basis of the temperature and moisture content of their source regions. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 55-58]
xs: The correct match is **a-ii, b-i, c-iv, d-iii** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Tropical ocean** → **mT** (warm, moist); **tropical land** → **cT** (warm, dry).
**Polar ocean** → **mP** (cold, moist); **polar land** → **cP** (cold, dry).
xa: **Arctic/Antarctic** → **cA** or **cAA**, extremely cold and dry.
**Equatorial oceans** → **mE**, hot and very humid.
cT source: **Sahara, Arabia**; cP source: **Siberia, Canada**.
⚠ First letter = **moisture**, not temperature.

18.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: Passage over a warm surface makes an air mass warmer and more unstable.
Passage over an ocean causes an air mass to lose moisture.
Passage over land makes an air mass drier.
Passage over a cold surface makes an air mass cooler and more stable.
18.x: Option B is incorrect: passing over an ocean adds moisture to an air mass. Warm surfaces make it unstable, land drier and cold surfaces stable.
18.tq: Check each statement for a reversed effect.
n: An air mass becomes warmer and more unstable when it passes over a warm surface. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 55-58]
An air mass becomes cooler and more stable when it passes over a cold surface. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 55-58]
An air mass gains moisture when it passes over an ocean. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 55-58]
An air mass loses moisture and becomes drier when it passes over land. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 55-58]
xs: The incorrect statement is **passage over an ocean causes an air mass to lose moisture** — option **(2)**.
Over an **ocean** an air mass **gains moisture**; over **land** it **loses moisture** and becomes **drier**.
Over a **warm surface** it becomes **warmer, more unstable**; over a **cold surface** **cooler, more stable**.
xa: Cold air over a warmer surface → **convection, cumulus, showers**.
Warm air over a colder surface → **fog, stratus, drizzle**.
**Vertical mixing** alters the **temperature and humidity profile**.

18.s:
Assertion (A): An air mass loses its original characteristics as it moves away from its source region.
Reason (R): It exchanges heat and moisture with the new surfaces it passes over.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
18.x: Both are true and R explains A: a moving air mass is warmed or cooled and gains or loses moisture over new surfaces, so it is modified and loses its source-region character.
18.tq: Ask what changes an air mass once it leaves its source.
n: An air mass loses its original characteristics as it moves away from its source region. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 55-58]
Vertical mixing alters the temperature and humidity profile of an air mass. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 55-58]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
An air mass **travels away** from its source and **gets modified**, losing its **original characteristics**.
It is **heated or cooled from below** and **gains or loses moisture** over new surfaces.
xa: Over an **ocean** it **gains moisture**; over **land** it **becomes drier**.
Over a **warm surface** → **more unstable**; over a **cold surface** → **more stable**.
**Dust particles** act as **condensation nuclei** (hygroscopic nuclei).

18.s: Air masses exert major control over which combination of atmospheric conditions?
o: Only wind direction and cloud colour
18.x: Air masses control temperature, humidity, stability and precipitation of the places they cross.
18.tq: Recall the influence of air masses.
n: Air masses control temperature, humidity, stability and precipitation. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 55-58]
xs: Air masses control **temperature, humidity, stability and precipitation** — option **(3)** is correct.
An air mass has **relatively uniform temperature and humidity** acquired over its **source region**.
The other options are partial lists; ocean currents and landforms are not air-mass controls in the notes.
xa: A **new air mass** can cause a **sudden rise or fall** in temperature.
**Seasonal shifts** in air masses give **seasonal climatic changes** — e.g. **monsoon winds**.
Persistent influence creates **maritime** and **continental climates**.

18.s:
Consider the following statements about the climatic effects of air masses:
1. Persistent air-mass influence creates characteristic regional climates such as maritime and continental climates.
2. Air masses and fronts can produce cold waves, heat waves, thunderstorms and blizzards.
3. Monsoon winds are an example of seasonal shifts in air masses producing seasonal climatic change.
4. A new air mass changes the temperature of a place only gradually, never suddenly.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
18.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct: monsoons are seasonal air-mass shifts, lasting air-mass influence gives maritime and continental climates, and air masses and fronts bring cold waves, heat waves, thunderstorms and blizzards. Statement 4 is wrong: a new air mass can cause a sudden rise or fall in temperature. So '1 and 3 only' misses statement 2, and the options with statement 4 are wrong.
18.tq: Air-mass change = sudden temperature jump; seasonal shift = monsoon.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
1: **persistent air-mass influence** creates **maritime** and **continental climates**.
2: air masses and fronts can produce **cold waves, heat waves, thunderstorms and blizzards**.
3: **seasonal shifts** in air masses give **seasonal climatic changes** — e.g. **monsoon winds**.
4 is wrong: a **new air mass** can cause a **sudden rise or fall** in temperature.
xa: A stalled **heat dome** caused a record early heatwave in **Western Europe** (**27 May 2026**).
**AP angle:** **SW monsoon** = summer maritime air; **NE monsoon** = winter air returning over the **Bay of Bengal**.
Winter **anticyclonic** cell over India → **clear skies**, low humidity, large daily temperature range.

18.s:
Assertion (A): The meeting of two air masses with different temperature and humidity forms a front.
Reason (R): Lighter warmer air is forced to rise over denser colder air.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
18.x: Both are true and R explains A: where contrasting air masses meet, warm air rises over cold air along a sloping boundary, the front.
18.tq: Check whether R is the cause of A.
n: A front forms when two air masses with different temperatures and humidity meet. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 55-58]
Lighter, warmer air is forced to rise over denser, colder air at a front. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 55-58]
A front is a boundary zone between two contrasting air masses. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 55-58]
Uplift at a front forces air to rise. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 55-58]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
A **front** forms when **two air masses** of **different temperature and humidity** meet.
**Lighter, warmer air** is **forced to rise** over **denser, colder air**, creating the sloping boundary.
xa: **Cold air** always forms a **wedge** under the warm air.
**Frontal uplift** produces **cyclonic or frontal rainfall**.
**Frontogenesis** = formation or sharpening of a front.

18.s: Along what feature do mid-latitude cyclones form?
18.x: Mid-latitude cyclones form along fronts where warm and cold air masses meet.
18.tq: Recall where cyclones form.
n: Mid-latitude cyclones form along fronts. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 55-58]
xs: Mid-latitude cyclones form along **fronts** — option **(4)** is correct.
A **front** is the **boundary zone** between **two contrasting air masses**.
**Bjerknes' polar front theory**: temperate (wave) cyclones form along the **polar front**.
xa: **Frontal uplift** produces **cyclonic or frontal rainfall**.
**Occluded front** is the **last stage** of a **temperate cyclone**.
Western disturbances reach north-west India at the **occluded-front stage**.

18.s:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I (Front Type)
a. Warm front
b. Cold front
c. Occluded front
d. Stationary front

List-II (Description and Outcome)
i. Cold air undercuts warm air; steep uplift
 ii. Neither air mass advances; prolonged cloudy and rainy conditions
 iii. Warm air advances over cold air; gradual uplift
 iv. Cold front overtakes warm front; complex weather and often prolonged precipitation
18.x: At a warm front warm air rises gently over cold, at a cold front cold air undercuts warm steeply, an occluded front forms when the cold front overtakes the warm and a stationary front does not move, giving a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii.
18.tq: Discriminate the four types of front.
n: A warm front forms when warm air advances over cold air. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 55-58]
A warm front produces gradual uplift. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 55-58]
A cold front forms when cold air undercuts warm air. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 55-58]
A cold front produces steep uplift. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 55-58]
An occluded front forms when a cold front overtakes a warm front. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 55-58]
An occluded front produces complex weather. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 55-58]
An occluded front often produces prolonged precipitation. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 55-58]
A stationary front produces prolonged cloudy and rainy conditions. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 55-58]
xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Warm front** = warm air advances over cold air, **gradual** uplift; **cold front** = cold air **undercuts** warm air, **steep** uplift.
**Occluded front** = **cold front overtakes warm front**, complex weather; **stationary front** = **neither air mass advances**, prolonged cloudy, rainy conditions.
xa: ⚠ **Cold** front = **steep**, short heavy showers; **warm** front = **gentle**, prolonged light rain.
Approaching warm front: **cirrus → cirrostratus → altostratus → nimbostratus**.
Cold front passage brings **cumulonimbus**, heavy showers, thunder, then cold clear air.
**Arcus (shelf/roll) clouds** form along cold fronts.

19.s: Which one of the following is the most essential oceanic condition for the formation of a tropical cyclone?
o: Sea-surface temperature above about 26.5–27°C over a large area
Sea-surface temperature below 10°C over a narrow area
19.x: Tropical cyclones require a large warm ocean surface, generally with sea-surface temperature above about 26.5–27°C. Moisture and low wind shear are also favourable conditions.
19.tq: Use the basic-condition recall method and reject reversed environmental requirements.
xs: The key oceanic condition is **sea-surface temperature above about 26.5–27°C** over a **large area** — option **(3)**.
Tropical cyclones form **only over warm oceans** and draw their energy from them.
They need **high humidity** and **low vertical wind shear** — so "no moisture" and "very high shear" are wrong; cold seas (below 10°C) cannot feed them.
xa: Other favourable conditions: enough **Coriolis force**, a **pre-existing weak low**, and **upper-level divergence**.
Belt: roughly **5-30° N and S**, western parts of tropical oceans.
They do not form within about **5°** of the equator, nor in the **South Atlantic** and **south-east Pacific**.

19.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the formation of tropical cyclones:
1. A pre-existing weak low-pressure system or low-level cyclonic circulation is favourable for their formation.
2. Upper-level divergence supports their development.
3. Large vertical variation in wind speed is essential for their formation.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
19.x: A pre-existing low-level disturbance and upper-level divergence favour tropical cyclone formation. Low vertical wind shear, not large wind variation with height, is required.
19.tq: Find the reversed condition in statement 3 and select the coded combination.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: a **pre-existing weak low / low-level cyclonic circulation** is favourable.
Statement 2 correct: **upper-level divergence** supports development.
Statement 3 wrong: they need **low vertical wind shear** (small variation in vertical wind speed), not large.
xa: Also needed: **SST above 26.5 °C** (some notes: above **27**), **high humidity** in lower and middle troposphere, enough **Coriolis force**.
**Marine heatwaves** raise TC winds by up to **20%** and rain by up to **12%**.
The **South Atlantic** has no cyclones partly because of **strong shear** and cold water.

19.s: Tropical cyclones generally originate in which belt of the tropical oceans?
o: Between 30° and 60° latitudes in both hemispheres
Within 5° of the equator over all ocean basins
Roughly between 5° and 30° latitudes in both hemispheres, especially over the western parts of tropical oceans
19.x: The usual belt of origin is approximately 5°–30° north and south, particularly in the western parts of tropical oceans.
19.tq: Distinguish the broad confinement belt from the narrower practical genesis belt.
xs: They form roughly between **5° and 30°** latitudes in both hemispheres, especially over the **western parts of tropical oceans** — option **(4)**.
Within **5°** of the equator the **Coriolis force is negligible**, so option (2) is wrong; **30-60°** is the temperate cyclone zone.
xa: The APPSC **2022** key gave the belt as **between 30° N and 30° S**.
Temperate cyclones occur at **35-65°**, along the **polar front**.
Trade winds push tropical cyclones west onto **eastern coasts**.

19.s: Which pair of oceanic regions is noted for the absence of tropical cyclone formation?
o: Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea
South-west Indian Ocean and western Pacific
19.x: Tropical cyclones do not normally form in the South Atlantic and south-east Pacific, where cool waters and strong vertical wind shear are unfavourable.
19.tq: Use region-pair discrimination rather than assuming every tropical ocean basin produces cyclones.
xs: Tropical cyclones do not form in the **South Atlantic** and **south-east Pacific** — option **(4)**.
Reason: **cold waters** and **strong wind shear** there.
The **Bay of Bengal**, Arabian Sea, **North Atlantic** (hurricanes) and **NW Pacific** (typhoons) all produce cyclones.
xa: Regional names: **Hurricane** — North Atlantic, NE Pacific; **Typhoon** — NW Pacific, South China Sea.
**Willy-willy** — Western Australia; **Baguio** — Philippines.
Cyclone **Idai** (**2019**) formed in the **SW Indian Ocean**, hitting Mozambique, Zimbabwe, Malawi.

19.s: A tropical cyclone weakens after landfall primarily because it:
o: Receives excessive moisture from the land surface
Enters a region of stronger Coriolis force
Is cut off from its warm, moist oceanic energy source
19.x: Landfall cuts the cyclone off from the warm ocean and its moisture supply, causing the system to lose energy and weaken.
19.tq: Identify the causal link between landfall and loss of the oceanic energy source.
xs: After landfall a cyclone is **cut off from its warm, moist oceanic energy source** — option **(4)**.
Cyclones form **only over warm oceans** and draw energy from them, so on land they lose energy.
Land does not supply excess moisture, and the system does not turn into an anticyclone.
xa: Tropical cyclones **die on land** in days; temperate cyclones live longer and **cross continents**.
**Storm surge** — sea water pushed ashore by winds and low pressure — is the **biggest killer**.
AP landfall: **Montha** (**Oct 2025**) on the **Kakinada coast**.

19.s: Tropical cyclones originate and intensify over which of the following?
19.x: Tropical cyclones form only over warm oceans (SST above about 26.5 °C over a large area) and draw their energy from them (APPSC-GS 2025). They do not form over rivers or lakes, and cold currents suppress them, so the other options are wrong.
19.tq: Cyclone fuel = warm ocean, never rivers/lakes.
xs: Tropical cyclones form and intensify only over **warm oceans** — option **(2)** (APPSC-GS **2025**).
They do **not** form over **rivers or lakes**; they need **SST above 26.5 °C** over a large sea surface.
Cold waters (as in the **South Atlantic**) prevent them.
xa: ⚠ Temperate cyclones can **originate over land and sea**; tropical ones **only over the sea**.
The **Bay of Bengal** produces **75-80%** of cyclones affecting India (warmer SSTs, funnel shape).
**Marine heatwaves** raise TC winds by up to **20%** and rain by up to **12%**.

19.s:
Consider the following statements about the structure of a tropical cyclone:
1. The eye is calm and clear, with sinking air and the lowest pressure.
2. The strongest winds and heaviest rain occur in the eye.
3. Rain bands are spiral bands of cloud and rain outside the eyewall.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
19.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is wrong: the strongest winds and heaviest rain are in the eyewall, the ring of towering cumulonimbus around the calm eye. So '1 only' misses statement 3, while '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' include the false statement 2.
19.tq: Eye = calm; eyewall = fiercest.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(3)**.
Statement 1 correct: the **eye** is **calm, clear**, with **sinking air** and the **lowest pressure**.
Statement 2 wrong: the **strongest winds and heaviest rain** are in the **eyewall**, the ring of towering **cumulonimbus**.
Statement 3 correct: **rain bands** are spiral cloud bands **outside the eyewall**.
xa: ⚠ **Eye** = calm, lowest pressure; **eyewall** = strongest winds.
The eye is about **20-50 km** across.
Cyclones are steered by **mid/upper-troposphere winds**.

19.s: In which direction do tropical cyclones rotate in the Northern and Southern Hemispheres respectively?
19.x: Because of Coriolis deflection, tropical cyclones rotate anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere.
19.tq: Use the hemisphere pair to avoid reversing the Coriolis-based circulation.
xs: Tropical cyclones rotate **anticlockwise** in the NH and **clockwise** in the SH — option **(1)**.
This is due to **Coriolis deflection** around a **low-pressure centre**.
xa: ⚠ **Anticyclones** do the reverse: **clockwise in the NH**, anticlockwise in the SH.
Anticyclones have **high pressure** at the centre with **outward, sinking** winds.
No cyclones within about **5°** of the equator — Coriolis negligible.

19.s: Which statement correctly explains the usual movement of tropical cyclones over the oceans?
o: They remain stationary because steering winds are absent.
Westerlies move every tropical cyclone directly towards the equator.
Trade winds push them eastward, while westerlies always move them towards the south-west.
Trade winds generally push them westward, while westerlies may recurve mature storms towards the north-east.
19.x: Trade winds steer tropical cyclones westward towards eastern continental coasts. In mature systems, westerlies may recurve them towards the north-east.
19.tq: Follow the steering-wind sequence from initial westward movement to later recurvature.
xs: **Trade winds** push cyclones **westward** onto **eastern coasts**, while **westerlies** recurve mature storms **north-east** — option **(4)**.
Cyclones are steered by **mid/upper-troposphere winds**, so they are not stationary.
xa: Tropical cyclones move **east to west** (trade winds); temperate ones **west to east** (westerlies).
**10 of 14** recent storms in the notes were **Bay of Bengal** storms striking India's **east coast**.
Arabian Sea storms (**Ockhi, Tauktae, Biparjoy**) hit the west.

19.s:
Consider the following statements about cyclone wind thresholds:
1. The IMD classifies a system as a cyclonic storm when winds reach 62 km/h (34 knots).
2. A hurricane begins at a sustained wind speed of about 62 km/h.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
19.x: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is wrong: a hurricane begins at about 119 km/h; 62 km/h is the IMD cyclonic-storm threshold. So '2 only', 'Both' and 'Neither' are wrong.
19.tq: 62 km/h = IMD cyclonic storm; 119 km/h = hurricane.
xs: Only statement **1** is correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: IMD calls it a **cyclonic storm** at **62 km/h (34 knots)**.
Statement 2 wrong: a **hurricane** begins at **119 km/h**, not 62.
xa: Cyclones are **named from the Cyclonic Storm** category (**62-88 km/h**).
**Super Cyclonic Storm**: **222 km/h and above**.
**Saffir-Simpson** scale rates hurricanes in **categories 1-5**.

19.s:
Consider the following statements about weather scales:
1. The Beaufort scale measures wind force from 0 to 12 by its observed effects at sea and on land.
2. The Enhanced Fujita scale classifies tornadoes by their sustained wind speed.
3. A gale is a strong wind of Beaufort force 8, about 62–74 km/h.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
19.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is wrong: the (Enhanced) Fujita scale rates tornadoes EF0–EF5 by the damage caused; Saffir-Simpson rates hurricanes by sustained wind. So '1 only' misses statement 3, while '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' include the false statement 2.
19.tq: Fujita = damage; Saffir-Simpson = wind; Beaufort = observed effects.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(4)**.
Statement 1 correct: **Beaufort** measures **wind force 0-12** from observed effects at sea/land.
Statement 2 wrong: **Enhanced Fujita** rates tornadoes **EF0-EF5** by **damage caused**, not wind speed.
Statement 3 correct: a **gale** is **Beaufort 8**, about **62-74 km/h**.
xa: ⚠ **Saffir-Simpson** = hurricanes; **Fujita** = tornadoes; **Beaufort** = wind force.
Saffir-Simpson grades hurricanes **1-5** by **sustained wind speed** (PYQ **2025**).
**Storm surge** is the biggest killer in a cyclone.

19.s: Which of the following statements regarding a super typhoon is correct?
o: It has sustained winds of about 240 km per hour and is equivalent to a strong Category 4 or Category 5 storm.
It is a tornado with an EF5 damage rating.
It forms only over the western Australian landmass.
It is defined by winds below 62 km per hour and corresponds to Beaufort force 4.
19.x: A super typhoon has sustained winds of about 240 km per hour and is comparable to a strong Category 4 or Category 5 storm.
19.tq: Use the defining speed and category equivalence to reject nearby storm terms.
xs: A **super typhoon** has sustained winds of about **240 km/h (150 mph)** — a **strong category 4 or 5** storm — option **(1)**.
It is a **NW Pacific** storm (typhoon), not a tornado (EF scale) or a Western Australian system (**willy-willy**).
xa: **Super Typhoon Bavi** was the **3rd category-5** storm of **2026**.
**Typhoon** region: **NW Pacific**, South China Sea (e.g. **Typhoon Noul**, Guangdong).
A **hurricane** begins at **119 km/h**.

19.s:
Consider the following statements about the IMD cyclone scale:
1. Cyclones are given names from the Cyclonic Storm category (62–88 km/h) onwards.
2. A storm with maximum sustained winds of 100 km/h is a Very Severe Cyclonic Storm.
3. A Super Cyclonic Storm has winds of 222 km/h and above.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
19.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is wrong: 100 km/h falls in the Severe Cyclonic Storm range (89–117 km/h); Very Severe starts at 118 km/h. So '1 only' misses statement 3, while '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' include the false statement 2.
19.tq: Named from 62 km/h; Severe 89–117; Very Severe 118–166.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: names are given from the **Cyclonic Storm** (**62-88 km/h**) category.
Statement 2 wrong: **100 km/h** is a **Severe Cyclonic Storm** (**89-117**); Very Severe is **118-166**.
Statement 3 correct: **Super Cyclonic Storm** = **222 km/h and above**.
xa: **Depression 31-49**, **Deep Depression 50-61**, **Extremely Severe 167-221** km/h.
Names come from **IMD (RSMC New Delhi)** using lists from member countries.
IMD cyclonic storm = **62 km/h (34 knots)**.

19.s:
Match the following IMD categories with their wind-speed ranges:

a. Depression
i. 118–166 km/h
b. Deep Depression
ii. 31–49 km/h
c. Very Severe Cyclonic Storm
iii. 50–61 km/h
d. Extremely Severe Cyclonic Storm
iv. 167–221 km/h

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
19.x: Depression corresponds to 31–49 km/h, Deep Depression to 50–61 km/h, Very Severe Cyclonic Storm to 118–166 km/h and Extremely Severe Cyclonic Storm to 167–221 km/h.
19.tq: Begin with the low-speed categories and use the non-overlapping ranges to eliminate codes.
xs: Correct matching: **a–ii, b–iii, c–i, d–iv** — option **(1)**.
**Depression 31-49**; **Deep Depression 50-61**; **Very Severe CS 118-166**; **Extremely Severe CS 167-221** km/h.
xa: **Cyclonic Storm 62-88** (named from here); **Severe CS 89-117**.
**Super Cyclonic Storm**: **222** km/h and above.
⚠ A **hurricane** begins at **119 km/h** — close to the Very Severe CS lower bound (**118**).

19.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Saffir-Simpson scale classifies hurricanes into categories 1 to 5 by sustained wind speed.
2. Storm surge, the abnormal rise of sea water pushed ashore by cyclone winds and low pressure, is the biggest killer in a cyclone.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
19.x: Both statements are correct: the Saffir-Simpson scale rates hurricanes (categories 1-5 by sustained wind; PYQ 2025), and storm surge is the biggest killer. So '1 only', '2 only' and 'Neither' are wrong. Tornadoes are rated on the (Enhanced) Fujita scale, and wind force on the Beaufort scale.
19.tq: Saffir-Simpson = hurricanes; Fujita = tornadoes; surge kills most.
xs: **Both** statements are correct — option **(3)**.
Statement 1: **Saffir-Simpson** classifies **hurricanes** in **categories 1-5** by **sustained wind speed** (PYQ **2025**).
Statement 2: **Storm surge** — abnormal sea-water rise pushed ashore by winds and low pressure — is the **biggest killer**.
xa: ⚠ **Fujita / Enhanced Fujita** = tornadoes (EF0-EF5 by damage); **Beaufort** = wind force (0-12).
A **hurricane** begins at **119 km/h**.
**"Zero casualty"** approach since **Phailin** (**2013**).

19.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes a tornado from a hurricane?
o: A tornado is generally a small, short-lived funnel associated with a thunderstorm, whereas a hurricane is much wider and may last for days.
A tornado is hundreds of kilometres wide and forms only over warm oceans.
A hurricane is a land-based funnel lasting only a few minutes.
Both phenomena have the same size, duration and place of origin.
19.x: Tornadoes are small, funnel-shaped and usually short-lived, while hurricanes may be hundreds of kilometres wide, last for days and form over warm oceans.
19.tq: Compare the phenomena across size, duration and place of formation.
xs: A **tornado** is a **small, minutes-long funnel** from a **thunderstorm**; a **hurricane** is **hundreds of km wide** and **lasts days** — option **(1)**.
Tornadoes form **mostly over land** (USA); hurricanes form over **warm ocean** — options (2)-(4) reverse or equate these.
xa: USA's **"tornado alley"** is the classic tornado region.
Tornadoes are rated on the **Enhanced Fujita** scale (**EF0-EF5**, by damage).
**Waterspout** = tornado-like funnel over water (Brahmaputra, **Barpeta**, Assam).

19.s: A tornado-like funnel that forms over a water body is known as a:
19.x: A waterspout is a tornado-like funnel over water. A waterspout was observed over the Brahmaputra in Barpeta, Assam, on 26 August 2026.
19.tq: Discriminate between land-based tornadoes and their water-based counterpart.
xs: A tornado-like funnel over water is a **waterspout** — option **(1)**.
One was seen over the **Brahmaputra** in **Barpeta, Assam** (**26 Aug 2026**).
**Nor'westers** are pre-monsoon storms of eastern India; **storm surge** is a sea-water rise; a **gale** is a Beaufort **8** wind.
xa: **Tornadoes** = land-based; **hurricanes, typhoons, cyclones** = ocean-born.
Tornado: small, **minutes-long** funnel from a thunderstorm.
Tornado scale: **Fujita / Enhanced Fujita** (by damage).

19.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Hurricane — North Atlantic and north-east Pacific
Typhoon — north-west Pacific and South China Sea
Baguio — North Indian Ocean and South Pacific
Cyclone — North Indian Ocean and South Pacific
19.x: Baguio is a regional name used in the Philippines; the North Indian Ocean and South Pacific use the term cyclone.
19.tq: Look for the regional name placed in the wrong basin.
xs: **Baguio — North Indian Ocean and South Pacific** is wrongly matched — option **(3)**.
**Baguio** is the name used in the **Philippines**; the North Indian Ocean and South Pacific use **cyclone**.
The rest are right: **hurricane** — North Atlantic, NE Pacific; **typhoon** — NW Pacific, South China Sea.
xa: **Willy-willy** — **Western Australia**.
**Tornado** — small violent funnel over **land** (USA "tornado alley").
Example typhoon: **Typhoon Noul**, **Guangdong** (2026).

19.s: Which one of the following is a characteristic feature of temperate cyclones?
o: A clear frontal system involving warm and cold fronts
Movement exclusively from east to west
19.x: Temperate cyclones possess a clear frontal system, including warm and cold fronts; an occluded front may also develop.
19.tq: Identify the precise positive feature while rejecting the familiar but reversed statement.
xs: Temperate cyclones have a **clear frontal system** with **warm and cold fronts** — option **(1)**.
⚠ "They do not have a clear frontal system" was the **incorrect** statement in APPSC **2024**.
They form over **land and sea** (not only warm seas) and move **west to east**, not east to west.
xa: Fronts: **warm, cold, occluded**.
They cover a **larger area** with **gentler winds** than tropical cyclones.
Rain is spread over a **wide area and longer period**.

19.s:
Consider the following statements about temperate cyclones:
1. They may originate over both land and sea.
2. They generally cover a larger area than tropical cyclones.
3. Their winds are usually more intense than those of tropical cyclones.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
19.x: Temperate cyclones can originate over land and sea and cover a larger area. Their winds are generally gentler than those of tropical cyclones, making statement 3 false.
19.tq: Check each comparison separately, especially the reversed intensity claim.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: temperate cyclones **originate over land and sea** (PYQ **2024**).
Statement 2 correct: they cover a **larger area** than tropical cyclones.
Statement 3 wrong: their **winds are weaker**; tropical cyclones are **smaller and very intense**.
xa: They move **west to east** with the westerlies and **cross continents**.
Latitude: **35-65°** vs **5-30°** for tropical cyclones.
They have a **clear frontal system** (APPSC **2024** trap).

19.s: Which of the following comparisons between tropical and temperate cyclones is correct?
o: Tropical cyclones move west to east, whereas temperate cyclones move east to west.
Tropical cyclones have clear fronts, whereas temperate cyclones have none.
Tropical cyclones originate over land and sea, whereas temperate cyclones originate only over warm seas.
Tropical cyclones are smaller and more intense, whereas temperate cyclones are larger and generally gentler.
19.x: Tropical cyclones are smaller and more intense, while temperate cyclones cover larger areas and generally have gentler winds. The other options reverse the stated distinctions.
19.tq: Compare size, intensity, origin, fronts and movement as a single feature set.
xs: **Tropical cyclones are smaller and more intense**; **temperate cyclones are larger and gentler** — option **(4)**.
The other options reverse facts: tropical move **east to west**, temperate **west to east**; tropical have **no fronts**; tropical form **only over warm seas**.
xa: Tropical: **5-30°**; temperate: **35-65°**.
Tropical cyclones live **days** and **die on land**; temperate ones **cross continents**.
Temperate fronts: **warm, cold, occluded**.

19.s:
Consider the following statements about Western Disturbances:
1. They originate in the Mediterranean region and are steered by the westerlies and the Subtropical Westerly Jet.
2. They affect north-western India mainly during summer.
3. Their rainfall decreases from west to east across the north-western plain.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
19.x: Statement 1 is correct: Western Disturbances are extratropical storms from the Mediterranean steered by the westerlies and the STJ. Statement 2 is wrong: they affect NW India mainly in WINTER, bringing rain for Rabi crops and snow on the mountains. Statement 3 is correct: their rainfall decreases from west to east. Hence 1 and 3 only.
19.tq: WD = Mediterranean, winter, Rabi rain, weakens eastward.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — so option **(3)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: Western Disturbances **originate in the Mediterranean** and are **steered by the westerlies** and the **Subtropical Westerly Jet**.
Statement 2 is wrong: they occur mainly in **winter**, not summer.
Statement 3 is correct: their **rainfall decreases from west to east** across the **northwestern plain**.
xa: They bring **winter rainfall** and **snowfall** to mountains — important for **Rabi crops**.
They reach NW India in winter at the **occluded stage**.
Temperate cyclones occur at about **35°–65°** in both hemispheres and move **west to east**.

19.s: A farmer in north-western India receives moderate winter rainfall of about 10–15 cm that benefits rabi crops. This rainfall is most likely associated with:
19.x: Western disturbances bring winter rainfall of about 10–15 cm to north-western India, which is beneficial for rabi cultivation.
19.tq: Identify the weather system from its season, region and agricultural effect.
xs: Winter rain of **10–15 cm** that helps **rabi** crops in NW India comes from **western disturbances** — option **(4)**.
They originate in the **Mediterranean** and are carried by the **sub-tropical westerly jet**, reaching NW India in **winter**.
**Kaal Baisakhi** is a **pre-monsoon** storm of **Bihar, Odisha, West Bengal, Assam**, not a winter rain of the north-west.
xa: They arrive at the **occluded stage** of the temperate cyclone.
**Aandhi** = summer dust storm of the dry north-west plains.
Temperate cyclones give rain over a **wide area and longer period**, with weaker winds.

19.s: Which of the following weather conditions is generally associated with the sinking air of an anticyclone?
o: Strong inward convergence and cloud development
Persistent uplift, heavy rain and thunderstorms
19.x: Sinking and diverging air in a high-pressure system generally produces clear, dry, calm and settled weather.
19.tq: Infer surface weather from the vertical movement of air in a high-pressure system.
xs: Sinking air of an anticyclone gives **clear, dry, calm (settled)** weather — option **(1)**.
Air sinks and **diverges** outward, so there is no uplift, convergence or cloud building.
xa: **Cold-core polar highs** (**Siberian, Canadian, Antarctic**) bring **fog and frost**.
**Heat dome**: stalled warm high traps hot air.
Anticyclone rotation: **clockwise in the NH**.

19.s: Kaal Baisakhi or Nor'westers are local storms associated with which group of regions?
o: Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand
The dry plains of north-western India only
Bihar, Odisha, West Bengal and Assam
19.x: Kaal Baisakhi or Nor'westers occur in Bihar, Odisha, West Bengal and Assam and approach from the north-west.
19.tq: Match the regional storm name with its geographical distribution.
xs: **Kaal Baisakhi / Nor'westers** occur in **Bihar, Odisha, West Bengal and Assam** — option **(4)**.
They are **pre-monsoon** storms approaching from the **north-west**.
The dry plains of north-west India get **Aandhi** (dust storms); Karnataka gets **cherry/coffee blossoms**.
xa: In **Assam** they are called **"tea showers"**.
**Hailstorms** also come with pre-monsoon convective weather.
Thunderstorms grow from **cumulonimbus** clouds up to **15 km** tall.

19.s:
Consider the following pairs (Local storm — Feature):
1. Cherry or coffee blossoms — showers aiding coffee flowering in Kerala
2. Aandhi — summer dust storm of the dry north-western plains
3. Hailstorms — pre-monsoon convective weather
Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
19.x: Pair 2 is correct: Aandhi is the dust-laden summer storm of the dry NW plains. Pair 1 is wrong: cherry or coffee blossoms aid coffee flowering in KARNATAKA (mango showers are the Kerala-Karnataka showers for mangoes). Pair 3 is correct: hailstorms belong to pre-monsoon convective weather. Hence 2 and 3 only.
19.tq: Coffee blossoms = Karnataka; mango showers = Kerala/Karnataka; Aandhi = NW dust.
xs: Pairs **2 and 3** are correctly matched — so option **(2)** is correct.
Pair 1 is wrong: **cherry/coffee blossoms** aid coffee flowering in **Karnataka**, not Kerala.
Pair 2 is correct: **Aandhi** = **summer dust storm** of the dry plains of **north-west India**.

xa: **Kaal Baisakhi / Nor'westers**: pre-monsoon storms of **Bihar, Odisha, West Bengal, Assam**; "tea showers" in Assam.
**Cloudburst**: Himalaya, **June-August**, ~**100 mm/hour** over **20-30 sq km**.
**Damini App** gives lightning alerts in **15** languages; **104** detection locations.

19.s:
Consider the following statements about thunderstorms:
1. They grow from cumulonimbus clouds that may reach up to about 15 km.
2. They develop best in stable, cold and dry air.
3. Thunder is the sound of air expanding explosively after being heated by a lightning stroke.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
19.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is wrong: thunderstorms grow in unstable, moist air. So '1 only' misses statement 3, while '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' include the false statement 2.
19.tq: Thunderstorms need unstable, moist air.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: thunderstorms grow from **cumulonimbus** clouds up to **15 km** tall.
Statement 2 wrong: they grow in **unstable, moist** air, not stable dry air.
Statement 3 correct: **thunder** is air **expanding explosively** after heating by a **lightning** stroke.
xa: Lightning alerts: **Damini App**, in **15** languages.
Detection network: **104** lightning detection locations.
**Kaal Baisakhi** and hailstorms are pre-monsoon convective storms.

19.s: Which of the following statements about a cloudburst is correct?
o: It is a dry dust storm of the north-western plains during summer.
It is a tropical cyclone covering hundreds of kilometres over the ocean.

19.s: The 'Damini' mobile application in India is used to provide alerts about:
19.x: Damini App gives lightning alerts in 15 languages, backed by a network of 104 lightning detection locations. It is not the app for cyclone landfall, earthquake or tsunami warnings.

19.s:

19.s: According to an INCOIS study of 1995-2019, how does El Nino affect post-monsoon cyclones in the Bay of Bengal?

El Nino shifts all of them to the Arabian Sea

19.s: India's “zero casualty” approach to cyclones has been followed since which cyclone?
19.x: The zero-casualty approach to cyclones in India is stated to have been followed since Phailin.

xs: India's **"zero casualty"** approach dates from **Phailin** — option **(4)**.

**Damini** is the **lightning-alert** app; **Sagar Bandhu** was India's operation for **Ditwah** in Sri Lanka.

19.s:
Consider the following statements about anticyclones:
I. They have a high-pressure centre.
II. Air moves outward from the centre.
III. They are associated with descending air.
IV. They generally produce stormier and cloudier weather.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
19.x: I, II and III are correct: anticyclones have a high-pressure centre with sinking air flowing outward. IV is false because they bring calm, clear weather.
19.tq: Discriminate cyclone from anticyclone weather.
n: An anticyclone has a high-pressure centre. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
Air moves outward in an anticyclone. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
Air descends in an anticyclone. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
Cyclonic weather is cloudier and stormier. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
Anticyclonic weather is generally clearer. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
An anticyclone has a high-pressure centre. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
An anticyclone has outward-moving air. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
The major mechanism of anticyclones is subsidence. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
Anticyclones are generally associated with clear skies. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
xs: Statements **I, II and III** are correct — so option **(4)** is correct.
I and II: an **anticyclone** is a **high-pressure centre** with **outward-moving air**.
III: in an anticyclone air **descends** (**sinking, diverging winds**).
IV is wrong: anticyclones bring **generally clear skies** — **clear, dry, calm** weather; cyclones are **cloudier and stormier**.
xa: Rotation: **clockwise** in the **NH**, **anticlockwise** in the **SH**.
Main mechanism: **subsidence**; fronts are **not characteristic**.
**Heat dome:** a stalled warm high traps hot air (**27 May 2026**).

19.s:
How many of the following are described as local or very local atmospheric disturbances?
1. Thunderstorm
2. Tornado / Twister
3. Cloudburst
4. Local squall / local storm
19.x: All four are local disturbances: thunderstorms, tornadoes, cloudbursts and local squalls.
19.tq: Discriminate local from large-scale disturbances.
n: A thunderstorm is local in scale. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
A tornado or twister is very local in scale. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
A cloudburst is local in scale. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
A local squall or local storm involves sudden, violent, gusty wind associated with a storm. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
A cloudburst is intense localized rainfall. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
xs: **All four** are local/very local disturbances — option **(4)** is correct.
**Thunderstorm** = **local** violent convective storm; **tornado/twister** = **very local** funnel-shaped disturbance.
**Cloudburst** = **intense localized rainfall** (local); **local squall/storm** = sudden, violent, gusty wind.
xa: **Tropical**, **temperate cyclones** and **anticyclones** are **large-scale**.
**Western Disturbance** is **regional**, affecting **northwest India**.
Tornado clouds: **cumulonimbus supercell**.

19.s:
Assertion (A): The Northern Hemisphere rotation of an anticyclone is clockwise.
Reason (R): An anticyclone is a high-pressure centre with outward-moving air.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
19.x: Both are true but R does not explain A: high pressure with outflow does not by itself give the direction; the Coriolis force makes it clockwise in the north.
19.tq: Check whether R is the cause of A.
n: An anticyclone has a high-pressure centre. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
Air moves outward in an anticyclone. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
Anticyclones rotate clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
An anticyclone has a high-pressure centre. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
An anticyclone has outward-moving air. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
xs: **Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A** — option **(2)**.
A is true: an anticyclone rotates **clockwise in the NH** (**anticlockwise** in the SH).
R is true: it is a **high-pressure centre** with **outward-moving air** — but that does not set the direction of rotation.
xa: Cyclones rotate **anticlockwise in the NH**; deflection comes from the **Coriolis** force.
Anticyclone air **descends**; weather is generally **clearer**.
**Cold-core polar highs:** **Siberian, Canadian, Antarctic** → fog and frost.

19.s:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(a) Tropical cyclone
(b) Temperate or extratropical cyclone
(c) Anticyclone
(d) Thunderstorm

List-II
(i) Large-scale low-pressure system over warm tropical oceans
(ii) Large-scale system associated with air-mass interaction
(iii) Large-scale high-pressure system with outward-moving air
(iv) Local violent convective storm with lightning and thunder
19.x: A tropical cyclone is a low over warm seas, a temperate cyclone comes from air-mass interaction, an anticyclone is a high with outflow and a thunderstorm is a local convective storm, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
19.tq: Recall the definition of each disturbance.
n: A tropical cyclone is a low-pressure system over warm tropical oceans. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
A tropical cyclone is large-scale. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
A temperate or extratropical cyclone is large-scale. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
An anticyclone is large-scale. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
Tropical cyclones occur mainly in the tropics. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
The major mechanism of thunderstorms is strong convection. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
xs: The correct match is **a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Tropical cyclone** = large-scale **low over warm tropical oceans**; **temperate cyclone** = **air-mass interaction**.
**Anticyclone** = **high-pressure centre** with **outward-moving air**; **thunderstorm** = **local violent convective storm** with **lightning and thunder**.
xa: **Tornado** = **violently rotating**, **funnel-shaped**, very local.
Fronts are **characteristic** only of **temperate cyclones**.
Tropical cyclone mechanism: **warm ocean plus convection**; anticyclone: **subsidence**.

19.s:
Assertion (A): Severe thunderstorms or supercells create tornado potential.
Reason (R): The major mechanism of tornadoes is severe rotating convection.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
19.x: Both are true and R explains A: tornadoes spin out of severe rotating convection, which supercells provide.
19.tq: Check whether R is the cause of A.
n: Severe thunderstorms or supercells create tornado potential. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
The major mechanism of tornadoes is severe rotating convection. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
**Strong wind shear** produces **severe thunderstorms or supercells**, which **create tornado potential**.
The tornado's major mechanism is **severe rotating convection**, which supercells supply.
xa: **Gulf of Mexico** supplies **warm, moisture-rich air** to the tornado-prone USA.
Tornado winds: **105 to 322 km/h**; measured on the **Fujita / Enhanced Fujita Scale**.
**Waterspout** = tornado-like funnel over water (**Brahmaputra**, Barpeta, Assam).

19.s:
How many of the following atmospheric disturbances do not characteristically have fronts?
1. Tropical cyclone
2. Anticyclone
3. Thunderstorm
4. Tornado
19.x: None of the four has fronts: tropical cyclones, anticyclones, thunderstorms and tornadoes. Fronts belong to temperate cyclones.
19.tq: Recall which systems have fronts.
n: Fronts are not characteristic of tropical cyclones. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
Fronts are not characteristic of anticyclones. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
Fronts are not characteristic of thunderstorms. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
Fronts are not characteristic of tornadoes. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
xs: **All four** lack characteristic fronts — option **(4)** is correct.
For **tropical cyclones**, **anticyclones**, **thunderstorms** and **tornadoes**, fronts are **not characteristic**.
Fronts are **characteristic** only of **temperate cyclones** (air-mass interaction).
xa: ⚠ "Temperate cyclones **do not have a clear frontal system**" was the incorrect statement (**APPSC 2024**).
Temperate cyclones can originate over **land and sea**; tropical ones **only over the sea**.
Temperate cyclones cover a **larger area** than tropical cyclones.

19.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Tropical cyclone
(b) Temperate cyclone
(c) Ordinary thunderstorm
(d) Tornado

List-II
(i) Rotating cumulonimbus supercell
(ii) Stratiform and cumuliform clouds
(iii) Cumulonimbus and rainbands
(iv) Short-lived single-cell cumulonimbus

Options:
19.x: Tropical cyclones have cumulonimbus walls and rainbands, temperate cyclones stratiform and cumuliform cloud along fronts, an ordinary thunderstorm a short-lived single-cell cumulonimbus, and tornadoes form from rotating supercells, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
19.tq: Recall the clouds of each disturbance.
n: The major cloud associated with tropical cyclones is cumulonimbus and rainbands. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
Temperate cyclones have stratiform and cumuliform clouds. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
Tornadoes are associated with cumulonimbus supercell clouds. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Tropical cyclone** = **cumulonimbus and rainbands**; **temperate cyclone** = **stratiform and cumuliform** clouds.
**Ordinary thunderstorm** = **cumulonimbus**; **tornado** = **cumulonimbus supercell**.
xa: **Anticyclones** generally have **clear skies**.
Thunderstorms grow from cumulonimbus up to **15 km** tall.
**Thunder** = sound of air **expanding explosively** after heating by lightning.

19.s: Which of the following statements about tropical cyclone structure is incorrect?
o: The eye is a central region of comparatively light winds and fair weather.
The eyewall is the zone of strongest winds, heavy rainfall and thunderstorms.
The centre is the region of highest pressure in the cyclone.
Spiral rainbands are curved cloud bands producing rain and wind.
19.x: Option C is incorrect: the centre of a cyclone has the lowest pressure, not the highest. The calm eye, violent eyewall and spiral rainbands are right.
19.tq: Check for a reversed pressure.
n: The eye of a tropical cyclone is the central region of comparatively light winds and fair weather. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
The eyewall is the most intense zone of a tropical cyclone. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
The eyewall has strong winds, heavy rainfall, and thunderstorms. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
Spiral rainbands are curved cloud bands that produce rain and wind. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
The centre of a tropical cyclone is the region of lowest pressure. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
A cyclone has a low-pressure centre. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
xs: The incorrect statement is **the centre is the region of highest pressure** — option **(3)**.
The **centre** is the region of **lowest pressure**.
The **eye** has **light winds, fair weather**; the **eyewall** is the **most intense zone**; **spiral rainbands** produce rain and wind.
xa: Eye: calm, clear, **sinking air**, **20-50 km** across.
⚠ **Eye** = calm, lowest pressure; **eyewall** = **strongest winds and heaviest rain**.
Rotation: **anticlockwise in the NH**, **clockwise in the SH**.

19.s:
Assertion (A): Tropical cyclones generally do not form exactly at the Equator.
Reason (R): The Coriolis force is too weak near the Equator.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
19.x: Both are true and R explains A: within about 5° of the Equator the Coriolis force is too weak to set the air spinning.
19.tq: Check whether R is the cause of A.
n: Sufficient distance from the Equator allows the Coriolis force to become effective for tropical cyclone formation. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
The Coriolis force is too weak near the Equator for tropical cyclones to form exactly there. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
The Coriolis force provides and maintains rotational circulation in a tropical cyclone. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
The Coriolis force provides rotation in tropical cyclones. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
The **Coriolis force** is **too weak near the Equator** for tropical cyclones to **form exactly there**.
Cyclones need **sufficient distance from the Equator** so the Coriolis force **becomes effective**.
xa: They do not form within about **5 deg of the equator**.
Belt: between **30 deg N and 30 deg S** (**APPSC 2022**); roughly **5-30° N and S**.
Also absent in the **South Atlantic** and **south-east Pacific** (cold waters, strong shear).
Need **SST above 26.5 °C** and **low vertical wind shear**.

19.s:

(b) Typhoon

List-II

n: A tropical cyclone is called a hurricane in the USA and the Atlantic region. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
A tropical cyclone is called a typhoon in China and the western Pacific. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]

xs: The correct match is **a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Hurricane** = **USA / Atlantic**; **typhoon** = **China / western Pacific**.

19.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. In India, a tropical cyclone is called a cyclone.
II. Air moves inward in a cyclone.
III. Air rises in a cyclone.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
19.x: All three are correct: in India the storm is simply called a cyclone, and its air flows inward and rises.
19.tq: Recall the air flow of a cyclone.
n: A tropical cyclone is called a cyclone in India. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
Air moves inward in a cyclone. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
Air rises in a cyclone. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
xs: All three statements **I, II and III** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
I: in India the storm is called a **cyclone** — the **common name** for a **tropical cyclone**.
II and III: in a cyclone air moves **inward** and **rises**.
xa: Anticyclone air moves **outward** and **descends**.
Cyclones are **cloudier and stormier**; anticyclones generally **clearer**.
⚠ India does **not** get **hurricanes**.

19.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Temperate cyclones are associated with the interaction of contrasting air masses.
Statement B: Temperate cyclones generally move from east to west under the influence of westerlies.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
19.x: A is true: temperate cyclones form where contrasting air masses meet. B is false because the westerlies carry them from west to east.
19.tq: Check each statement for a reversed direction.
n: Temperate or extratropical cyclones generally move from west to east. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
The key mechanism of temperate or extratropical cyclones is the interaction of contrasting air masses. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
A temperate or extratropical cyclone is a mid-latitude cyclone associated with air-mass interaction. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
Westerlies are the main wind influence on temperate or extratropical cyclones. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
The major mechanism of temperate cyclones is air-mass interaction and fronts. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
xs: **Statement A is true, Statement B is false** — option **(3)** is correct.
A is true: temperate cyclones arise from **interaction of contrasting air masses**, associated with **fronts**.
B is false: under the **westerlies** they move **from west to east**.
xa: They occur at about **35°–65°** in both hemispheres.
Tropical cyclones move **east to west** with the **trade winds**.
Indian example: the **Western Disturbance**.

19.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Warm, moisture-rich air from the Gulf of Mexico
(b) Cold, drier continental air
(c) Atmospheric instability
(d) Strong wind shear

List-II
(i) Undercuts the warm air along a cold front or dry line
(ii) Makes thunderstorms rotate as supercells
(iii) Supplies warm, moisture-rich air to the tornado-prone USA
