19.x: Gulf of Mexico air supplies warmth and moisture, cold dry continental air undercuts it along fronts, instability drives strong updrafts, and wind shear makes storms rotate as supercells, giving a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii.
19.tq: Assign each ingredient its job: moisture, lift, updraft or rotation.
n: The Gulf of Mexico supplies warm, moisture-rich air to the tornado-prone USA. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
Cold, drier continental air contributes to tornado formation in the tornado-prone USA. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
Atmospheric instability contributes to tornado formation in the tornado-prone USA. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
Strong wind shear produces severe thunderstorms or supercells in the tornado-prone USA. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Gulf of Mexico** supplies **warm, moisture-rich air** to the tornado-prone **USA**; **cold, drier continental air** undercuts it.
**Atmospheric instability** drives strong upward convection; **strong wind shear** produces **supercells**.
xa: Tornado wind speeds: **105 to 322 km/h**.
Tornadoes last a **few minutes**, rarely more than **15–20 minutes**.
Tornado = **land-based**; hurricanes, typhoons, cyclones = **ocean-born**.

19.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: The Saffir-Simpson Scale is used for hurricanes in the Atlantic and Pacific.
The Beaufort Scale measures earthquake intensity from I to XII.
The International Nuclear Event Scale has levels from 0 to 7.
The Fujita or Enhanced Fujita Scale measures tornado wind speed and damage.

19.tq: Match each scale to its hazard.
n: The Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale is used for hurricanes. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale applies to hurricanes and tropical cyclones in the Atlantic and Pacific. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The Fujita/Enhanced Fujita (F/EF) Scale is used for tornadoes. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The Fujita/Enhanced Fujita (F/EF) Scale measures tornado wind speed and damage. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The Beaufort Scale is used for wind and storms. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The Beaufort Scale measures wind force. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The Beaufort Scale ranges from 0 to 12. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The Beaufort Scale indicates general wind strength. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The International Nuclear Event Scale ranges from Level 0 to Level 7. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The Modified Mercalli Intensity Scale is used for earthquakes. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The Modified Mercalli Intensity Scale measures earthquake intensity. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The Modified Mercalli Intensity Scale ranges from I to XII. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The MSK-64 Scale is used for earthquakes. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The MSK-64 Scale measures earthquake intensity. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The MSK-64 Scale ranges from I to XII. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
xs: The incorrect statement is **the Beaufort Scale measures earthquake intensity from I to XII** — option **(2)**.
The **Beaufort Scale** measures **wind force** from **0 to 12**.
Earthquake intensity **I to XII** is measured on the **Modified Mercalli (MMI)** and **MSK-64** scales.
Saffir-Simpson (hurricanes), **INES** (**0 to 7**) and **Fujita** (tornadoes) are correctly stated.
xa: **INES** was set up by the **IAEA** (**1990**).
**Richter Scale** — **logarithmic**, **Charles Richter**, **1935**.
⚠ **Saffir-Simpson** = hurricanes; **Fujita** = tornadoes; **Beaufort** = wind force.

19.s:
Assertion (A): The Moment Magnitude Scale is preferred over the Richter Scale for large earthquakes.
Reason (R): The Moment Magnitude Scale is the modern standard for measuring earthquake magnitude.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
19.x: Both are true: the moment magnitude scale is preferred for big quakes and is the modern standard. Being the standard does not explain why it suits big quakes (Richter saturates at high values), so R does not explain A.
19.tq: Ask whether a status explains a technical reason.
n: The Moment Magnitude Scale is the modern standard. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The Moment Magnitude Scale is preferred over the Richter Scale for large earthquakes. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The Moment Magnitude Scale measures earthquake magnitude. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
xs: **Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A** — option **(2)**.
A is true: the **Moment Magnitude Scale (Mw)** is **preferred over Richter** for **large earthquakes**.
R is true: it is the **modern standard** — but being the standard does not explain why it suits large quakes.
xa: **Richter Scale** measures **magnitude** (energy released); **logarithmic**, developed in **1935**.
**MMI** measures **intensity** — **observed effects and damage**, **I to XII**.
**MSK-64** is used in **India** and **many European countries**.

19.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. The Indian Cyclone Intensity Scale is used by the IMD.
II. Its categories progress from Depression and Deep Depression to Cyclonic Storm, Severe, Very Severe, Extremely Severe and Super Cyclonic Storm.
III. The Saffir-Simpson Scale categorises hurricanes from Category 1 to Category 5.
IV. The Indian Cyclone Intensity Scale measures earthquake intensity from I to XII.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
19.x: I, II and III are correct: the IMD scale runs from depression and deep depression to super cyclonic storm, and Saffir-Simpson runs Categories 1–5. IV is false because quake intensity I–XII is MMI or MSK-64.
19.tq: Keep wind scales and earthquake scales apart.
n: The Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale has categories from Category 1 to Category 5. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The Indian Cyclone Intensity Scale is used for cyclones in India. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The Indian Cyclone Intensity Scale measures wind speed. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]

The Indian Cyclone Intensity Scale categories progress from Depression to Cyclonic Storm to Severe Cyclonic Storm to Very Severe Cyclonic Storm to Extremely Severe Cyclonic Storm to Super Cyclonic Storm. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The Indian Cyclone Intensity Scale is used by the IMD. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The Modified Mercalli Intensity Scale is used for earthquakes. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The Modified Mercalli Intensity Scale measures earthquake intensity. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The Modified Mercalli Intensity Scale ranges from I to XII. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The MSK-64 Scale is used for earthquakes. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The MSK-64 Scale measures earthquake intensity. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The MSK-64 Scale ranges from I to XII. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
xs: Statements **I, II and III** are correct — so option **(3)** is correct.
I and II: the **Indian Cyclone Intensity Scale** is used by the **IMD**, from **Depression → Cyclonic Storm → Severe → Very Severe → Extremely Severe → Super Cyclonic Storm**.
III: **Saffir-Simpson** categorises hurricanes **Category 1 to 5**.
IV is wrong: earthquake intensity **I to XII** is **MMI** or **MSK-64**.
xa: IMD classifies by **maximum sustained wind**, a **3-minute average**.
**Extremely Severe Cyclonic Storm** was **introduced in 2015**.
Naming begins at **Cyclonic Storm** (**62 km/h**, **34 knots**).

19.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Fujita/Enhanced Fujita Scale
(b) Richter Scale
(c) Moment Magnitude Scale
(d) Modified Mercalli Intensity Scale

List-II
(i) Ranges from F0/EF0 to F5/EF5
(ii) Developed by Charles Richter in 1935

19.x: Fujita runs F0/EF0 to F5/EF5, Richter was devised in 1935, moment magnitude is written Mw, and the Modified Mercalli scale is MMI. The answer is a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.

n: The Fujita/Enhanced Fujita (F/EF) Scale ranges from F0/EF0 to F5/EF5. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
Charles Richter developed the Richter Scale in 1935. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The Moment Magnitude Scale is denoted by Mw. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The Modified Mercalli Intensity Scale is abbreviated MMI. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]

xa: Richter and Mw measure **magnitude**; MMI measures **intensity** (**I to XII**).

19.s:
Assertion (A): Earthquake intensity on the Modified Mercalli Intensity Scale is based on observed effects and damage.
Reason (R): Intensity measures how strongly shaking is felt at a particular place, unlike magnitude, which measures the energy released at the source.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
19.x: Both are true and R explains A: because intensity describes the shaking felt at a place rather than energy at the source, the Mercalli scale rates it from observed effects and damage.
19.tq: Contrast intensity with magnitude to see why effects are used.
n: Earthquake intensity on the Modified Mercalli Intensity Scale is based on observed effects and damage. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The Modified Mercalli Intensity Scale is based on human observation and damage. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
**MMI** measures **intensity** — **observed effects and damage**, based on **human observation**.
**Magnitude** (Richter, Mw) measures **energy released**; intensity describes shaking felt at a place, hence observation-based.
xa: MMI range: **I to XII**.
**MSK-64** is the other intensity scale, used in **India**.
**Richter** is **logarithmic**, developed in **1935**.

19.s: Which of the following scales is used in India and many European countries?
19.x: The MSK-64 intensity scale is used in India and much of Europe. MMI is used mainly in the USA.
19.tq: Discriminate MSK-64 from MMI.
n: The MSK-64 Scale is used in India and many European countries. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
xs: **MSK-64 Scale** is used in India and many European countries — option **(2)** is correct.
**MSK-64** measures **earthquake intensity**, **I to XII**.
**MMI** is based on **human observation and damage**; **Mw** measures **magnitude**; **Fujita** rates **tornadoes**.

xs: The incorrect statement is **India gets hurricanes in the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea** — option **(3)**.

19.x: I and II are correct: Category 1 is 119–153 km/h and Category 3 is 178–208 km/h. III is false because 209–251 km/h is Category 4; Category 5 starts at 252 km/h.
19.tq: Recall the Saffir-Simpson bands.
n: Category 1 hurricanes have wind speeds of 119–153 km/h. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 16-19]
Category 1 hurricanes cause minimal damage. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 16-19]

Category 3 hurricanes cause extensive damage. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 16-19]

Category 4 hurricanes cause extreme damage. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 16-19]

Category 5 hurricanes cause catastrophic damage. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 16-19]
xs: Statements **I and II** are correct — so option **(1)** is correct.

xa: **Category 2** = **154–177 km/h**, **moderate** damage.

19.s:

o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true

n: A hurricane is a large, rotating tropical storm system. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 16-19]
A hurricane has sustained winds of at least 119 km/h (74 mph). [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 16-19]
A wind speed of 119 km/h (74 mph) is the minimum for classification as a hurricane, typhoon, or cyclone. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 16-19]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are true** — option **(1)** is correct.
A **hurricane** is a **large, rotating tropical storm** with sustained winds of at least **119 km/h (74 mph)**.
**74 mph** is the **minimum** for a **hurricane, typhoon or cyclone**.
xa: Hurricanes are **measured** on the **Saffir–Simpson Wind Scale**.
**North Atlantic** cyclones are called **hurricanes**.
Rotation: **counter-clockwise** in the **NH**, **clockwise** in the **SH**.

19.s: The Northwest Pacific region associated with typhoons includes:
o: The North Atlantic, South Atlantic and Indian Ocean
The Caribbean Sea, Gulf of Mexico and Northeast Pacific
East Asia, the Philippines and Japan
The Bay of Bengal, Arabian Sea and South Pacific
19.x: The north-west Pacific, home of typhoons, covers East Asia, the Philippines and Japan.

n: The Northwest Pacific includes East Asia, the Philippines, and Japan. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 16-19]
xs: Typhoon region covers **East Asia, the Philippines and Japan** — option **(3)** is correct.
**Typhoons** = **Northwest Pacific**; also **China**, **western Pacific**, **South China Sea**.
**Caribbean, Gulf of Mexico, Northeast Pacific** = **hurricanes**; **Bay of Bengal, Arabian Sea, South Pacific** = **cyclones**.
xa: **Baguio** = **Philippines** name.
Example: **Typhoon Noul**, **Guangdong** (**27 Jul 2026**).
**Super Typhoon Bavi** = 3rd category-5 storm of **2026**.

19.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: The East Coast is more vulnerable to cyclones than the West Coast.
Statement B: The vulnerable East Coast includes Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, West Bengal and Tamil Nadu.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
19.x: Both are true: the east coast, including Odisha, AP, West Bengal and Tamil Nadu, is more cyclone-prone than the west coast.

n: The East Coast is more vulnerable to cyclones than the West Coast. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 34-37]
The vulnerable East Coast includes Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, West Bengal, and Tamil Nadu. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 34-37]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are true** — option **(1)** is correct.
The **East Coast** is **more vulnerable** than the **West Coast** — **Bay of Bengal : Arabian Sea** ratio about **4:1**.
The East Coast includes **Odisha**, **Andhra Pradesh**, **West Bengal**, **Tamil Nadu**.
xa: **Bay of Bengal** produces **75-80%** of cyclones affecting India — warmer SSTs, enclosed funnel shape.
**Arabian Sea:** fewer but more intense (**Tauktae**, **Biparjoy**).
Nearly **5,900 km** of coast is directly exposed to cyclones.
Season is **bimodal**: main peak **post-monsoon (Oct-Dec)**, secondary **pre-monsoon (Apr-May)**.

19.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. A Depression has wind speeds of 31–49 km/h.
II. A Cyclonic Storm has wind speeds of 62–88 km/h.
III. An Extremely Severe Cyclonic Storm has wind speeds of 118–166 km/h.
IV. A Super Cyclonic Storm has wind speeds below 222 km/h.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
19.x: I and II are correct: a depression is 31–49 km/h and a cyclonic storm 62–88 km/h. III is false because 118–166 km/h is a very severe storm; an extremely severe storm is 167–221 km/h. IV is false because a super cyclonic storm is 222 km/h or more.
19.tq: Recall the IMD wind bands.
n: An IMD depression has wind speed of 31–49 km/h. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 34-37]
An IMD cyclonic storm has wind speed of 62–88 km/h. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 34-37]
An IMD very severe cyclonic storm has wind speed of 118–166 km/h. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 34-37]
An IMD extremely severe cyclonic storm has wind speed of 167–221 km/h. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 34-37]
An IMD super cyclonic storm has wind speed of at least 222 km/h. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 34-37]
An IMD depression has wind speed of 17–27 knots. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 34-37]
An IMD cyclonic storm has wind speed of 34–47 knots. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 34-37]
An IMD very severe cyclonic storm has wind speed of 64–89 knots. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 34-37]
An IMD extremely severe cyclonic storm has wind speed of 90–119 knots. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 34-37]
An IMD super cyclonic storm has wind speed of at least 120 knots. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 34-37]
xs: Statements **I and II** are correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
I: **Depression** = **31–49 km/h**; II: **Cyclonic Storm** = **62–88 km/h**.
III is wrong: **118–166 km/h** is **Very Severe**; **Extremely Severe** = **167–221 km/h**.
IV is wrong: **Super Cyclonic Storm** = **222 km/h or more**.
xa: **Low Pressure Area** = less than **31 km/h** (weakest).
**Deep Depression** = **50–61 km/h**; **Severe Cyclonic Storm** = **89–117 km/h**.
Naming begins at **Cyclonic Storm** (**34 knots**).

19.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: A Super Cyclonic Storm has a wind speed of 222 km/h or more.
The Extremely Severe Cyclonic Storm category was introduced in 2015.

An Extremely Severe Cyclonic Storm has a wind speed of 167–221 km/h.

n: A Severe Cyclonic Storm has a wind speed of 89–117 km/h. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 65-66]
A Very Severe Cyclonic Storm has a wind speed of 118–166 km/h. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 65-66]

A Very Severe Cyclonic Storm has a wind speed of 64–89 knots. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 65-66]

xs: The incorrect statement is **a Very Severe Cyclonic Storm has a wind speed of 89–117 km/h** — option **(3)**.
**89–117 km/h** is a **Severe Cyclonic Storm**; **Very Severe** = **118–166 km/h**.
**Super Cyclonic Storm** = **222 or more**; **Extremely Severe** = **167–221 km/h**, introduced **2015**.
xa: IMD speeds are a **3-minute average** of maximum sustained wind.
**Cyclonic Storm** = **62–88 km/h** — **naming begins**.

19.s:

The IMD classification differs from the Saffir–Simpson Scale. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 65-66]
The Saffir–Simpson Scale is used for hurricanes. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 65-66]

19.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Hudhud
(b) Fani
(c) Amphan

List-II
(i) West Bengal, 2020
(ii) Odisha, 2019; gold-standard evacuation of approximately 1.2 million people

Options:
19.x: Hudhud (2014) badly damaged Visakhapatnam, Fani (2019) hit Odisha with a model evacuation of about 1.2 million, and Amphan (2020) hit West Bengal. The answer is a-iii, b-ii, c-i.

19.s:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
 a. Tornado appearance
 b. Tornado duration
 c. Tornado movement speed
 d. Tornado wind speed

List-II
 i. Usually a few minutes, rarely more than 15–20 minutes

 iv. Stationary or up to about 90–100 km/h
19.x: A tornado looks like a funnel cloud, lasts a few minutes, moves at up to about 90–100 km/h, and has winds of 105–322 km/h. The answer is a-ii, b-i, c-iv, d-iii.
19.tq: Match each feature to its value.
n: Tornado wind speeds range from 105 to 322 km/h. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 14-16]
A tornado has a funnel-shaped cloud appearance. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 14-16]
A tornado usually lasts for a few minutes. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 14-16]
A tornado rarely lasts more than 15–20 minutes. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 14-16]

A tornado can travel at speeds of up to approximately 90–100 km/h. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 14-16]
xs: The correct match is **a-ii, b-i, c-iv, d-iii** — so option **(4)** is correct.

xa: Wind can **exceed 300 km/h** in severe cases.

Tornado: small, minutes-long; hurricane: **hundreds of km** wide, lasts days.

19.s: How many categories are included in the Enhanced Fujita (EF) Scale?
19.x: The Enhanced Fujita scale has six categories, EF0 to EF5.
