xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: waves carry **energy, not water**; particles move in small **circles**; **wind** supplies the energy.
Statement 2 is wrong: **wave height** = **crest to trough**; time between crests is the **period**.
Statement 3 is correct: **wavelength** = **crest to crest**.
xa: **Swells** = slow, steady, long-period waves from **distant storms**.
**Breakers** form when depth < **half the wavelength**.
**Kallakkadal** = Kerala swell surge from storms ~**10,000 km** away, most frequent **pre-monsoon**.
**Rip currents** flow **away from shore** in narrow, fast channels.

24.s: Which one of the following statements regarding swells is correct?
o: They are short, steep waves produced immediately by local winds.
They are narrow channels of water flowing away from the shore.
They occur only when the sea floor is vertically displaced.
They are slow, steady, long-period waves that originate from distant storms.
24.x: Swells are long-period waves generated by storms far from the place where they are observed. Narrow channels flowing away from shore are rip currents.
24.tq: Use the origin and period of a wave to identify a swell.
xs: **Swells** are **slow, steady, long-period waves** that come from **distant storms** — option **(4)**.
Short, steep waves from **local winds** are young wind waves, not swells.
Narrow channels flowing **away from shore** are **rip currents**; sea-floor displacement produces a **tsunami**.
xa: **Kallakkadal** (Kerala swell surge): long-period swells (**30-300 s**) from southern Indian Ocean storms ~**10,000 km** away.
Kallakkadal is most frequent in the **pre-monsoon** season.
**INCOIS** set up a second **Coastal Flood Monitoring System** at **Kollam** harbour for Kallakkadal forecasts.

24.s: A wave approaching a shore generally breaks when:
o: Its crest becomes equal to its trough
The wind ceases in the open ocean
The water depth becomes less than half the wavelength
The water depth becomes greater than the wavelength
24.x: Near the shore, friction slows the wave. It breaks when the water depth is less than half its wavelength.
24.tq: Recall the threshold ratio used to identify the formation of breakers.
xs: A wave breaks when the **water depth becomes less than half the wavelength** — option **(3)**.
Near the shore, waves **slow by friction** with the sea floor; these are **breakers**.
Crest and trough are the **top** and **bottom** of a wave; they never become "equal", so option (1) is meaningless.
xa: **Wavelength** = crest to crest; wave **height** = crest to trough; **period** = time between crests.
**Rip currents**: narrow, fast channels flowing **away from shore** as shoreward water escapes through a narrow path.
**ISRO** project: **AI + satellite** tools to detect **rip currents** for beach safety.

24.s: Kallakkadal, observed along the Kerala coast, is associated with:
o: A tidal bore caused by the full Moon
Long-period swell surges from storms in the southern Indian Ocean
Short wind waves generated within the Arabian Sea
A sudden vertical displacement of the sea floor near Kerala
24.x: Kallakkadal is a swell surge produced by long-period swells generated by storms in the southern Indian Ocean.
24.tq: Link the regional term with its specific wave phenomenon and source.
xs: **Kallakkadal** is caused by **long-period swell surges** from **storms in the southern Indian Ocean** — option **(2)**.
These swells (**30-300 s**) travel ~**10,000 km** to reach the **Kerala** coast; most frequent **pre-monsoon**.
It is not local wind waves (those are short and steep) nor a sea-floor displacement (that is a **tsunami**).
xa: **Swells** = slow, steady, **long-period** waves from **distant storms**.
**INCOIS** (Hyderabad) issues **swell-surge** alerts and has a **Coastal Flood Monitoring System** at **Kollam** harbour.
⚠ A **storm surge** is different: a weather-driven rise from **winds + pressure changes**.

24.s:
Consider the following statements about tsunamis:
1. Tsunamis are caused by sudden vertical displacement of the sea floor by an earthquake, landslide or volcano.
2. 'Tsunami' is a Japanese word meaning 'harbour wave'.
3. Tsunamis have short wavelengths and travel slowly, like ordinary wind waves.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
24.x: Statement 2 is correct: tsunami means 'harbour wave' in Japanese. Statement 1 is correct: it is set off by sudden displacement of the sea floor, not by wind. Statement 3 is wrong: tsunamis have extremely long wavelengths and can travel at up to 800 km/h in the deep ocean. So '2 only' misses statement 1, and options with statement 3 are wrong.
24.tq: Tsunami = sea-floor jolt, very long wavelength, up to 800 km/h.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: a tsunami comes from **sudden vertical displacement of the sea floor** (**quake, landslide, volcano**).
Statement 2 is correct: **tsunami** = **"harbour wave"** in **Japanese**.
Statement 3 is wrong: tsunamis have **extremely long** wavelengths and travel up to **800 km/h** in deep ocean.
xa: Tsunamis have **different causes** from **ordinary wind-driven waves**.
**ITEWS** (INCOIS) warns within **10 minutes**.
ITEWS uses **Bottom Pressure Recorders** and coastal **tide gauges**.

24.s: Which one of the following correctly describes a rip current?
o: A tidal current flowing only towards the beach
A broad current flowing parallel to the coastline
A deep-ocean current caused exclusively by salinity differences
A narrow, fast channel flowing away from the shore
24.x: A rip current is a narrow and fast-moving channel of water flowing away from the shore.
24.tq: Discriminate the exact direction and form of a rip current from other coastal currents.
xs: A **rip current** is a **narrow, fast channel flowing away from the shore** — option **(4)**.
It forms when **shoreward water escapes through a narrow path**, so it flows seaward, not towards the beach.
Density/salinity-driven flow is the deep **thermohaline** circulation, not a rip current.
xa: **ISRO** project uses **AI + satellite** tools to detect **rip currents** for **beach safety**.
**Breakers**: waves break near shore when **depth < half the wavelength**.
**Tidal currents** form when tidal water is channelled into **bays/estuaries**.

24.s: Which one of the following best describes a tide?
o: An irregular rise of sea level caused by storm winds
A permanent increase in sea level caused by melting ice
A circular movement of ocean water caused by the Coriolis force
A periodic rise and fall of sea level occurring once or twice a day
24.x: A tide is the periodic rise and fall of sea level, generally occurring once or twice a day. Storm surges are irregular and weather-driven phenomena.
24.tq: Use the precise definition and distinguish tides from storm surges.
xs: A **tide** is the **periodic rise and fall of sea level once or twice a day** — option **(4)**.
It is caused by the **gravitational pull of the moon** (greater) and **sun** (lesser), countered by **centrifugal force**.
An irregular rise from storm winds is a **storm surge** — weather-driven, irregular, **unlike tides**.
xa: High tides recur about every **12 h 25 min**.
**Semi-diurnal** (two highs + two lows a day) is the **most common** type.
Tidal energy: **tidal range** (barrage across an estuary) vs **tidal stream** (underwater turbines).

24.s:
With reference to the causes of tides, consider the following statements:
1. The gravitational pull of the Moon is greater than that of the Sun in producing tides.
2. Centrifugal force acts in opposition to gravitational attraction.
3. The vertical component of tide-generating force is more important than the horizontal component.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
24.x: The Moon has the greater tidal influence, and centrifugal force counters gravitational attraction. The horizontal components of the tide-generating force are more significant than the vertical component, making statement 3 false.
24.tq: Identify the incorrect comparison of horizontal and vertical components.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: the **moon's** pull is **greater**, the **sun's** lesser.
Statement 2 correct: **centrifugal force counters gravity**.
Statement 3 wrong: the **horizontal components** of tide-generating force matter **more than the vertical**.
xa: **Tide-generating force** = gravitational attraction − centrifugal force.
⚠ **Direct tide** = gravity (moon side); **indirect tide** = centrifugal force (opposite side).
**Perigean tides**: moon **closest** to the earth → unusually high tides.

24.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The tidal bulge on the side opposite to the Moon is associated with centrifugal force.
2. The bulge facing the Moon is called the indirect tide.
3. Two tidal bulges are formed on opposite sides of the Earth.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
24.x: The opposite-side bulge is associated with centrifugal force and the two bulges occur on opposite sides. The bulge facing the Moon is the direct tide, not the indirect tide.
24.tq: Spot the swapped meaning in a confusable pair.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 correct: the bulge on the **opposite side** comes from **centrifugal force** (the **indirect tide**).
Statement 2 wrong: the bulge **facing the moon** is the **direct tide** (gravitational attraction).
Statement 3 correct: there are **two tidal bulges** on opposite sides of the earth.
xa: **Bulge height** is higher over **wide continental shelves**, lower at **mid-ocean islands**.
**Spring tide**: sun, moon and earth **in a line** (**new moon and full moon**) — highest range.
**Neap tide**: sun and moon at **right angles** (first/third quarter) — lowest range.

24.s:
Consider the following statements about tides and related sea-level changes:
1. Tidal bulges are higher over wide continental shelves than at mid-ocean islands.
2. Tidal water channelled into bays and estuaries forms tidal currents.
3. Storm surges are periodic rises of sea level caused by the pull of the moon and sun.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
24.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: storm surges are caused by winds and pressure changes; they are weather-driven and irregular, unlike tides. So 1 and 2 only (A); options B, C and D each include the false statement 3.
24.tq: Tides = astronomical and periodic; surges = weather-driven and irregular.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: bulges are **higher over wide continental shelves**, lower at **mid-ocean islands**.
Statement 2 correct: tides channelled into **bays/estuaries** form **tidal currents**.
Statement 3 wrong: **storm surges** are caused by **winds + pressure changes** — weather-driven and **irregular**, unlike tides.
xa: **Bay of Fundy** (Canada) has the **world's greatest tidal range**.
**Gulf of Khambhat**: **5-10 m** range, potential ~**7,000 MW**.
At **Chandipur (Odisha)** the sea recedes **several km** at low tide.

24.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Type of tide)
A. Semi-diurnal
B. Diurnal
C. Mixed
D. Spring

List-II (Characteristic)
1. One high tide and one low tide a day
2. Tides of unequal height
3. Two high tides and two low tides a day
4. Highest tidal range

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
24.x: Semi-diurnal tides have two highs and two lows; diurnal tides have one high and one low; mixed tides are unequal in height; spring tides have the highest range.
24.tq: Start from the sure frequency pair and eliminate the remaining codes.
xs: Correct code: **A-3, B-1, C-2, D-4** — option **(1)**.
**Semi-diurnal** = **two high + two low** tides a day (most common); **Diurnal** = **one high + one low** a day.
**Mixed** = tides of **unequal height**; **Spring** = **highest range** (highest high, lowest low).
xa: Spring tide: sun, moon and earth **in a line** — at **new moon and full moon**.
**Neap tide**: sun and moon at **right angles**, ~**7 days** after spring — **lowest range**.
High tides recur about every **12 h 25 min**.

24.s: The interval between successive high tides is approximately
24.x: High tides recur at approximately 12 hours and 25 minutes. The lunar influence makes the interval longer than 12 hours.
24.tq: Recall the distinctive numerical interval rather than the rounded solar day.
xs: High tides recur about every **12 hours 25 minutes** — option **(1)**.
Most coasts get **semi-diurnal** tides: **two high + two low** tides a day.
**7 days** is the gap between a **spring** and the following **neap** tide, not between high tides.
xa: **Diurnal** tide = one high + one low a day; **mixed** = unequal heights.
⚠ **Spring** = sun, moon, earth in a line (new/full moon); **Neap** = right angles (first/third quarter).
**Perigean tides**: moon **closest** → unusually high.

24.s: Perigean tides are unusually high because the Moon is
o: at right angles to the Sun
24.x: Perigean tides occur when the Moon is closest to the Earth, thereby increasing its gravitational tidal influence.
24.tq: Link the astronomical term with its distance condition.
xs: **Perigean tides** are unusually high because the moon is **closest to the earth** — option **(4)**.
The **moon's** gravitational pull has the **greater** effect on tides, so a nearer moon raises them more.
Sun and moon at **right angles** give **neap tides** — the **lowest** range, not high tides.
xa: **Spring tides**: sun, moon and earth **in a line** — **new moon and full moon** — highest range.
**Tide-generating force** = gravitational attraction − centrifugal force.
Bulge facing the moon = **direct tide**; opposite = **indirect tide** (centrifugal).

24.s: At which of the following Indian locations is a tidal range of about 5–10 metres found, along with significant tidal-energy potential?
24.x: The Gulf of Khambhat has a tidal range of about 5–10 metres and an estimated tidal-energy potential of approximately 7,000 MW.
24.tq: Distinguish closely related Indian tidal-energy sites using the range figure.
xs: The **Gulf of Khambhat** (Gujarat) has a tidal range of **5-10 m** — option **(1)**.
Its tidal potential is ~**7,000 MW**, among the world's most significant.
**Gulf of Kutch** has **5-8 m**; the **Sundarbans** ~**5 m**; at **Chandipur** the sea recedes **several km** at low tide.
xa: **Bay of Fundy** (Canada) has the **world's greatest tidal range**.
Tidal energy: **tidal range** (barrage across an estuary) vs **tidal stream** (underwater turbines).
Bulges are higher over **wide continental shelves** — as in the Gujarat gulfs.

24.s: The world's greatest tidal range is associated with the
24.x: The Bay of Fundy in Canada is known for the world's greatest tidal range.
24.tq: Test the superlative location directly while using other major sites as distractors.
xs: The **Bay of Fundy** in **Canada** has the **world's greatest tidal range** — option **(1)**.
The Indian sites are smaller: **Gulf of Khambhat 5-10 m**, **Gulf of Kutch 5-8 m**, **Sundarbans ~5 m**.
xa: **Gulf of Khambhat** potential ~**7,000 MW** of tidal power.
**Chandipur (Odisha)**: sea recedes **several km** at low tide.
**Spring tides** (new and full moon) give the **highest range**; **neap tides** the lowest.

24.s: Tidal energy can be harnessed through
o: only wind turbines placed on beaches
barrages across estuaries and underwater turbines
desalination plants located on continental shelves
24.x: Tidal energy is harnessed through tidal-range systems, such as barrages across estuaries, and tidal-stream systems using underwater turbines.
24.tq: Distinguish the two technological methods from unrelated coastal infrastructure.
xs: Tidal energy is harnessed by **barrages across estuaries** and **underwater turbines** — option **(3)**.
**Tidal range** systems use a **barrage across an estuary**; **tidal stream** systems use **underwater turbines**.
Beach wind turbines, inland river dams and desalination plants are not tidal-energy technologies.
xa: **Gulf of Khambhat** has a potential of ~**7,000 MW**, among the world's most significant.
**Bay of Fundy** (Canada) has the **world's greatest tidal range**.
Tidal water channelled into **bays/estuaries** forms **tidal currents**.

24.s:
Consider the following statements regarding ocean currents:
1. Solar heating contributes to the movement of ocean currents.
2. Wind and gravity influence ocean currents.
3. The Coriolis force deflects moving water to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere.
4. Density differences have no role in the movement of ocean currents.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
24.x: Solar heating, wind, gravity, the Coriolis force and density differences all influence ocean currents. Therefore, statement 4 is false.
24.tq: Reject the absolute negative statement when the process has several recognised causes.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(1) 1, 2 and 3 only**.
Drivers of currents: **solar heating, wind, gravity** and the **Coriolis force** (right in **N hemisphere**, left in **S**).
Statement 4 wrong: **density differences** do matter — saltier, colder water sinks, driving deep **thermohaline** circulation.
xa: An ocean current = a **steady volume of water** moving along a **set path**.
**Trade winds** drive equatorial currents **westward**; **westerlies** drive drifts **eastward**.
**Gyres** form from winds, **Coriolis force** and **land barriers**.

24.s: Which planetary winds primarily drive the equatorial ocean currents westward?
24.x: Trade winds push surface water westward and drive the equatorial currents. Westerlies generally drive oceanic drifts eastward.
24.tq: Use the wind-direction relationship to distinguish trade winds from westerlies.
xs: **Trade winds** push the equatorial currents **westward** — option **(2)**.
**Westerlies** drive the oceanic **drifts eastward**, the opposite direction.
**Monsoon winds** reverse the **North Indian Ocean** currents seasonally; they are not the planetary driver of equatorial currents.
xa: Water piled up on the **western side** by trades flows back east as the **Equatorial Counter Current** through the **doldrums**.
**Wind friction** pushes surface water — the basis of wind-driven currents.
ENSO: during **La Nina** trade winds **strengthen**; during **El Nino** they **weaken or reverse**.

24.s: With reference to the role of solar heating in ocean circulation, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: Solar heating stops the movement of surface water in the tropics.
Solar heating causes water near the equator to contract and sink.
Water near the equator expands, creating a slight slope down which water flows under gravity.
Solar heating makes polar water flow towards the equator along the surface.
24.x: Solar heating expands equatorial water and creates a slight surface slope. Gravity pulls water down this gradient.
24.tq: Apply the cause-and-effect chain: heating, expansion, slope and gravity.
xs: **Water near the equator expands**, creating a **slight slope** down which water flows under **gravity** — option **(3)**.
So solar heating does not stop surface flow, and equatorial water **expands** rather than contracts and sinks.
Polar water moves towards the equator **at depth and slowly** (cold water sinks at the poles), not as warm surface flow.
xa: **Density differences**: saltier, colder water is **denser → sinks**; lighter water rises → **thermohaline** circulation.
Warm currents move from the **equator towards the poles** along the surface.
**Coriolis force** deflects currents **right in the N hemisphere**, **left in the S**.

24.s:
Consider the following statements regarding density-driven ocean circulation:
1. Saltier water is denser than less salty water.
2. Colder water tends to sink.
3. Density differences help drive deep thermohaline circulation.
4. Cold water sinking at the poles moves rapidly towards the equator.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
24.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Cold water sinks at the poles and moves slowly towards the equator, so statement 4 is false.
24.tq: Find the incorrect statement by checking the qualitative word describing speed.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(1) 1, 2 and 3 only**.
Statements 1 and 2: **saltier, colder water is denser** and **sinks**; lighter water rises.
Statement 3: these density differences drive the **deep (thermohaline) circulation**.
Statement 4 wrong: cold water sinking at the poles moves **slowly**, not rapidly, to the equator.
xa: Other drivers: **solar heating, wind, gravity, Coriolis force**.
**Cold currents** move from poles towards the equator, usually along **west coasts**.
**Upwelling** brings **cold, nutrient-rich** water up — e.g. **Peru/Humboldt**, **Somalia/Findlater**.

24.s: The Equatorial Counter Current is best described as a current that flows:
o: From south to north only in the Indian Ocean
From north to south along the western coasts of continents
From east to west between the polar currents
From west to east between the North and South Equatorial Currents
24.x: The Equatorial Counter Current flows west to east between the North and South Equatorial Currents. It returns water piled up in the west through the calm doldrums belt.
24.tq: Identify the current by its position and direction rather than by its name alone.
xs: The **Equatorial Counter Current** flows **west to east** between the **North and South Equatorial Currents** — option **(4)**.
**Trade winds** pile water on the **western side**; it flows back east through the calm **doldrums** belt.
The equatorial currents themselves flow **westward**; west-coast equatorward flows are **cold currents**.
xa: **Trade winds** → equatorial currents westward; **westerlies** → drifts eastward.
North Atlantic gyre: **N. Equatorial - Gulf Stream - N. Atlantic Drift - Canary**.
Gyres run **clockwise** in the Northern Hemisphere, **anticlockwise** in the Southern.

24.s:
With reference to ocean currents, consider the following statements:
1. Warm currents generally flow from the equator towards the poles.
2. Cold currents generally carry polar water towards the equator.
3. Warm currents usually occur along the western coasts of continents in low and middle latitudes.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
24.x: Warm currents generally move poleward from the equator, while cold currents carry polar water equatorward. In low and middle latitudes, warm currents usually flow along the eastern coasts of continents, so statement 3 is false.
24.tq: Watch for the reversed east-coast/west-coast comparison in a geography statement.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: **warm currents** flow from the **equator towards the poles**.
Statement 2: **cold currents** flow from the **poles towards the equator**.
Statement 3 wrong: warm currents usually run along **east coasts** (low-mid latitudes); **cold** ones along **west coasts**.
xa: Cold west-coast currents **chill/dry** coastal lands → **deserts** (Atacama-Humboldt, Namib-Benguela, Sonoran-California).
**North Atlantic Drift** keeps **NW Europe** mild and ports like **Murmansk** ice-free.
Warm + cold meeting points = **fishing grounds** (Grand Banks, Japan).

24.s:
Consider the following statements about oceanic gyres:
1. They are large circular current systems formed by winds, the Coriolis force and land barriers.
2. They occur only in the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans.
3. They circulate clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and anticlockwise in the Southern Hemisphere.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
24.x: Statement 1 is correct: gyres are large circular systems shaped by winds, the Coriolis force and land barriers. Statement 3 is correct: they turn clockwise in the north and anticlockwise in the south. Statement 2 is wrong: gyres occur in every ocean basin, e.g. the South Indian Ocean gyre. So '1 only' misses statement 3, and options with statement 2 are wrong.
24.tq: Gyres: clockwise north, anticlockwise south, every basin.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: **gyres** are large **circular current systems** formed by **winds, Coriolis force and land barriers**.
Statement 2 is wrong: gyres exist in **every ocean basin** — e.g. the **South Indian Ocean** gyre.
Statement 3 is correct: **clockwise in the NH**, **anticlockwise in the SH**.
xa: **North Atlantic gyre:** N. Equatorial – **Gulf Stream** – N. Atlantic Drift – **Canary**.
**South Indian Ocean gyre:** South Equatorial → **Agulhas** → West Wind Drift → **West Australian**.
**Sargasso Sea** = calm centre of the North Atlantic gyre — "**sea without shores**".

24.s: Which one of the following forms the northern boundary of the Sargasso Sea?
24.x: The Sargasso Sea is bounded by the North Atlantic Drift in the north, the Gulf Stream in the west, the Canary Current in the east and the North Equatorial Current in the south.
24.tq: Test one boundary of a current-defined region.
xs: The **North Atlantic Drift** forms the **northern** boundary of the **Sargasso Sea** — option **(4)**.
Other boundaries: **Gulf Stream (W)**, **Canary Current (E)**, **North Equatorial Current (S)**.
xa: The Sargasso Sea is the only sea bounded by **currents, not land** — "sea without shores".
It is the calm centre of the **North Atlantic gyre**; calm, warm, salty, with floating **Sargassum** seaweed.
The **North Atlantic Drift** (Gulf Stream extension) keeps **NW Europe** mild and **Murmansk** ice-free.

24.s: The Sargasso Sea is unusual because it is
o: the only sea bounded by ocean currents rather than land
a sea enclosed entirely by coral reefs
the only sea located in the Southern Hemisphere
24.x: The Sargasso Sea lies in the North Atlantic and is bounded by currents rather than land. It is also calm, warm, salty and rich in floating Sargassum weed.
24.tq: Use the distinctive geographical exception in the definition.
xs: The **Sargasso Sea** is the **only sea bounded by currents rather than land** — option **(2)**.
It lies in the **North Atlantic** (Northern Hemisphere) and is full of floating **Sargassum** seaweed — so options (1) and (4) are wrong.
xa: Boundaries: **Gulf Stream (W)**, **North Atlantic Drift (N)**, **Canary (E)**, **North Equatorial Current (S)**.
It is the calm centre of the **North Atlantic gyre**; calm, **warm, salty**.
Called the **"sea without shores"**.

24.s: Which one of the following ocean currents is correctly classified as a cold current of the Indian Ocean?
24.x: The West Australian Current is a cold current of the Indian Ocean. Agulhas and Mozambique are warm Indian Ocean currents, while Brazil is a warm South Atlantic current.
24.tq: Use current type and ocean together to eliminate reversed classifications.
xs: The **West Australian Current** is a **cold** current of the **Indian Ocean** — option **(4)**.
**Agulhas** (SE Africa) and **Mozambique** (Mozambique Channel) are **warm** Indian Ocean currents.
The **Brazil Current** is a **warm** current of the **South Atlantic**.
xa: South Indian Ocean gyre: **South Equatorial → Agulhas → West Wind Drift → West Australian** (anticlockwise).
**Agulhas and Brazil** are NOT cold — the non-cold pair (**UPPSC 2025**).
**Humboldt** is not warm among Agulhas, Brazil, Kuroshio (**APPSC G1 2019**).

24.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Humboldt — Cold current of the South Pacific
2. Falkland — Cold current of the South Atlantic
3. Kuroshio — Cold current of the North Pacific
Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
24.x: Humboldt and Falkland are correctly matched with their oceans and cold classification. Kuroshio is a warm current of the North Pacific, not a cold current.
24.tq: Check both the current type and the ocean before selecting the coded combination.
xs: Pairs **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Pair 1 correct: **Humboldt (Peruvian)** is a **cold** South Pacific current (Peru-Chile).
Pair 2 correct: **Falkland** is a **cold** South Atlantic current (Argentina).
Pair 3 wrong: **Kuroshio** is a **warm** North Pacific current (off **Japan**); the cold one there is **Oyashio (Kurile)**.
xa: **Kuroshio + Oyashio** meet off **Japan** → rich fishing ground.
**Humboldt** → **Atacama** desert and **Peru** upwelling fisheries.
North Pacific gyre: **N. Equatorial - Kuroshio - N. Pacific Drift - California**.

24.s: Which one of the following is the correct classification of the Agulhas, Brazil and Humboldt currents respectively?
24.x: The Agulhas and Brazil currents are warm currents, whereas the Humboldt or Peruvian Current is a cold current.
24.tq: Separate the two warm-current examples from the South Pacific cold-current exception.
xs: **Agulhas warm, Brazil warm, Humboldt cold** — option **(1)**.
**Agulhas** is a warm Indian Ocean current (SE Africa); **Brazil** a warm South Atlantic current.
**Humboldt (Peruvian)** is a **cold** South Pacific current off Peru-Chile.
xa: "**Humboldt** is not warm (among Agulhas, Brazil, Kuroshio)" — **APPSC G1 2019**.
"**Agulhas and Brazil** are NOT cold" — **UPPSC 2025**.
Humboldt causes the **Atacama** desert and **Peru** upwelling fisheries.

24.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Norwegian Current — Warm current of the North Atlantic
Florida Current — Warm current of the North Atlantic
Labrador Current — Warm current off north-western Africa
Gulf Stream — Warm current of the North Atlantic
24.x: The Labrador Current is a cold current off the coast of Canada in the North Atlantic. The Canary Current, not the Labrador Current, flows off north-western Africa and is also cold.
24.tq: Find the wrong coast and type combination rather than relying on the current name alone.
xs: **Labrador Current — warm current off NW Africa** is wrongly matched — option **(3)**.
**Labrador** is a **cold** current off **Canada** (North Atlantic); the current off **NW Africa** is the cold **Canary**.
**Norwegian**, **Florida** and **Gulf Stream** are all **warm** North Atlantic currents — correctly matched.
xa: **Gulf Stream + Labrador** meet at the **Grand Banks, Newfoundland** → fishing ground and **fog**.
**Gulf Stream / North Atlantic Drift** runs off the **USA east coast → NW Europe**.
**Benguela** does not flow in the North Atlantic — an asked odd-one-out.

24.s: Which one of the following pairs consists entirely of cold currents?
24.x: Humboldt (South Pacific, Peru-Chile) and Benguela (South Atlantic, Namibia) are both cold currents. Agulhas, Brazil, Kuroshio, Florida, Mozambique and Norwegian are all warm, so options A, B and C contain no cold current.
24.tq: Classify both members of each pair before choosing the all-cold combination.
xs: **Humboldt and Benguela** are both **cold** currents — option **(4)**.
**Humboldt** (South Pacific, Peru-Chile) and **Benguela** (South Atlantic, Namibia) both flow along **west coasts**.
**Agulhas, Brazil, Kuroshio, Florida, Mozambique, Norwegian** are all **warm** — so options (1)-(3) fail.
xa: Cold west-coast currents create deserts: **Atacama** (Humboldt), **Namib/Kalahari** (Benguela).
Other cold currents: **Falkland, Labrador, Canary, California, Oyashio, West Australian**.
**Agulhas and Brazil** = the non-cold pair (**UPPSC 2025**).

24.s: Which one of the following statements about the Indian Ocean circulation is correct?
o: The South Indian Ocean has a permanent clockwise gyre.
The North Indian Ocean currents reverse direction seasonally with the monsoon winds.
The North Indian Ocean has permanent gyres that do not respond to monsoon winds.
Both the North and South Indian Ocean currents reverse direction every six months.
24.x: The North Indian Ocean is unique among the major oceans in having currents that reverse seasonally with the monsoon winds. The South Indian Ocean has a permanent anticlockwise gyre.
24.tq: Use the unique seasonal-reversal feature to distinguish the North Indian Ocean from steady oceanic gyres.
xs: **North Indian Ocean currents reverse direction with the monsoon winds** — option **(2)**.
This is unique, unlike the **steady gyres** of the Atlantic and Pacific — so option (3) is wrong.
The **South Indian Ocean** has a **permanent anticlockwise** gyre — not clockwise, and it does not reverse.
xa: Summer: **SW Monsoon Current** flows **clockwise**; winter: **NE Monsoon Current** flows **anticlockwise**.
South Indian Ocean gyre: **South Equatorial → Agulhas → West Wind Drift → West Australian**.
**Findlater Current** (Arabian Sea) is tied to the **Somali Jet** and also reverses with the monsoon.

24.s: During the southwest monsoon, which one of the following combinations is correct?
o: Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal circulation is anticlockwise; WICC flows southward; EICC flows northward
Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal circulation is anticlockwise; WICC flows northward; EICC flows southward
Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal circulation is clockwise; WICC flows southward; EICC flows northward
Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal circulation is clockwise; WICC flows northward; EICC flows southward
24.x: During the southwest monsoon, the circulation in the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal is clockwise. The West India Coastal Current flows southward, while the East India Coastal Current flows northward.
24.tq: Read all three seasonal directions together; one reversed component makes a combination false.
xs: SW monsoon: circulation **clockwise**, **WICC southward**, **EICC northward** — option **(3)**.
The **SW Monsoon Current** flows **eastward**; the WICC flows **equatorward**.
The EICC flows northward in **Feb-Sep**, strongest **pre-monsoon**; anticlockwise circulation is the **NE monsoon** pattern.
xa: NE monsoon (winter): **anticlockwise**; **NE Monsoon Current** westward; WICC **northward (Nov-Feb)**; EICC **southward (Oct-Dec)**.
WICC flowing **northward (poleward) in Nov-Feb** was the **APPSC GS 2018** key.
**Findlater Current**: SW monsoon **upwelling off the Horn of Africa** → good fishing.

24.s:
Consider the following statements about the West India Coastal Current (WICC):
1. It flows northward from November to February.
2. It flows southward during the southwest monsoon.
3. Its northward flow is described as poleward.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
24.x: The WICC flows northward, or poleward, during November–February and turns southward during the southwest monsoon. All three statements are correct.
24.tq: Combine the seasonal dates, direction and geographic description before selecting the code.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: the **WICC** flows **northward** in **November-February**.
Statement 2: it turns **southward** during the **SW monsoon**.
Statement 3: the northward flow is **poleward** (the southward one equatorward).
xa: This WICC fact was the **APPSC GS 2018** key.
The **EICC** also reverses: **northward Feb-Sep**, **southward Oct-Dec**.
North Indian Ocean: SW monsoon **clockwise**, NE monsoon **anticlockwise**.

24.s:
Consider the following statements about the Findlater Current:
1. It is an Arabian Sea current tied to the Somali Jet and reverses with the monsoon winds.
2. During the SW monsoon it causes coastal upwelling off the Horn of Africa, giving good fishing.
3. Its upwelling zone is large, so it has a stronger effect on the Indian monsoon than the IOD.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
24.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: the upwelling zone is small, so its effect on the Indian monsoon is limited, unlike the IOD. Hence 1 and 2 only (B); A misses the true statement 2; C and D include the false statement 3.
24.tq: Findlater = Somali Jet + Horn of Africa upwelling; small zone, limited monsoon effect.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: the **Findlater Current** (Arabian Sea) is tied to the **Somali Jet** and **reverses** with the monsoon.
Statement 2: in the SW monsoon it causes **coastal upwelling off the Horn of Africa** (good fishing).
Statement 3 wrong: the upwelling zone is **small**, so its effect on the Indian monsoon is **limited**, unlike the **IOD**.
xa: **Somalia/Findlater** upwelling and **Peru/Humboldt** upwelling both support fisheries.
Upwelling brings **cold, nutrient-rich** water to the surface.
**NIOT** OMNI buoys feed **IOD** monitoring.

24.s:
Consider the following statements about the meeting of warm and cold ocean currents:
1. The Grand Banks near Newfoundland are rich fishing grounds where the Gulf Stream meets the Labrador Current.
2. The rich fishing grounds off Japan are formed by the meeting of the Kuroshio and Benguela currents.
3. Fog forms frequently near Newfoundland because warm and cold currents meet there.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
24.x: Statement 1 is correct: Gulf Stream (warm) + Labrador (cold) meet at the Grand Banks. Statement 2 is wrong: off Japan the Kuroshio meets the Oyashio; Benguela is a South Atlantic current. Statement 3 is correct: fog forms where warm and cold currents meet, e.g. Newfoundland. Hence 1 and 3 only (C); A and B include statement 2, D includes it too.
24.tq: Japan pair = Kuroshio + Oyashio; Atlantic pair = Gulf Stream + Labrador.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(3) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1: at the **Grand Banks, Newfoundland**, the warm **Gulf Stream** meets the cold **Labrador** → fishing ground.
Statement 2 wrong: off **Japan** the **Kuroshio** meets the **Oyashio**; **Benguela** is a **South Atlantic** current.
Statement 3: **fog** forms where warm and cold currents meet, e.g. **Newfoundland**.
xa: Where warm + cold currents meet, **plankton flourishes** → fishing grounds.
**Upwelling** fisheries: **Peru** (Humboldt), **Somalia** (Findlater).
**North Atlantic Drift** keeps **NW Europe** mild and ports like **Murmansk** ice-free.

24.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Desert / region)

**El Nino**: warm water replaces the cold Peruvian current, **suppressing upwelling** → **fewer phytoplankton**.

24.s: Upwelling of cold, nutrient-rich water is particularly important for fisheries in
o: the central areas of all deserts
Norway and the United Kingdom only

xs: **Upwelling** of cold, nutrient-rich water supports fisheries in **Peru and Somalia** — option **(2)**.
**Peru** upwelling is linked to the **Humboldt** current; **Somalia** upwelling to the **Findlater** current.
**Newfoundland** is a fishing ground from **warm + cold currents meeting** (Gulf Stream + Labrador); **Murmansk**, **Norway** and the **UK** are kept mild by the **North Atlantic Drift**.

24.s: The mild climate of north-western Europe and the ice-free condition of ports such as those in Norway and Murmansk are associated with the
24.x: The North Atlantic Drift, an extension of the Gulf Stream, carries warm water towards north-western Europe and helps keep its coasts mild and ports ice-free in winter.
24.tq: Match a climatic effect and location with the responsible warm current.
xs: The **North Atlantic Drift** keeps **NW Europe** mild and ports ice-free in winter, e.g. **Murmansk** — option **(1)**.

**California**, **Oyashio** and **Benguela** are all **cold** currents — they cannot warm Europe.

North Atlantic gyre: **N. Equatorial - Gulf Stream - N. Atlantic Drift - Canary**.

24.s:
Consider the following statements about El Nino:
1. It strengthens the upwelling of cold water off Peru.
2. A warm current flows south along the Peru coast, replacing the cold Peruvian current.
3. It recurs about every 3-7 years, and its name means 'the Christ child'.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
24.x: Statement 2 is correct: El Nino replaces the cold Peruvian current with warm water off Peru. Statement 3 is correct: it recurs about every 3-7 years and the name means 'the Christ child'. Statement 1 is wrong: El Nino suppresses upwelling, so phytoplankton and fish catches fall. So '2 only' misses statement 3, and options with statement 1 are wrong.
24.tq: El Nino = warm Peru coast, no upwelling, every 3-7 years.
xs: Statements **2 and 3** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is wrong: in El Nino **upwelling is suppressed** off Peru — **fewer phytoplankton**.
Statement 2 is correct: a **warm current** flows south along the **Peru** coast, replacing the **cold Peruvian current**.
Statement 3 is correct: it recurs about every **3-7 years**; name = **"Christ child"**.
xa: **La Nina:** **trade winds strengthen**, eastern Pacific cooler, strong upwelling.
**Bjerknes feedback:** weaker easterlies → warm water slides east → trades weaken further.
El Nino: Indian monsoon **delayed, weakened**; **6 of 10** El Nino years brought deficient rain.
**Negative SOI** = El Nino; **positive SOI** = La Nina.

24.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. During La Nina, upwelling in the eastern Pacific is generally strong.
2. La Nina is usually associated with good rainfall over India.
3. During La Nina, trade winds are weaker than usual.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
24.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Trade winds are stronger than usual during La Nina, so statement 3 is false.
24.tq: Check each phase-specific feature before selecting the coded combination.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: in **La Nina** the eastern Pacific is **cooler** with **strong upwelling**.
Statement 2: La Nina **usually** brings **good rain** to India.
Statement 3 wrong: during La Nina trade winds are **stronger** than usual; they **weaken or reverse** in El Nino.
xa: **Positive SOI** = La Nina; sustained **negative SOI** = El Nino.
El Nino: eastern Pacific warmer, **upwelling suppressed**, **fewer phytoplankton**.
El Nino weakens and delays the Indian monsoon (**drought risk**).

24.s: Who described the Southern Oscillation in 1920?
24.x: Sir Gilbert Walker described the Southern Oscillation in 1920.
24.tq: Match the scientific concept with its associated investigator and year.
xs: **Sir Gilbert Walker** described the **Southern Oscillation** in **1920** — option **(1)**.
The Southern Oscillation is the atmospheric pressure seesaw between **Tahiti** and **Port Darwin**.
xa: ⚠ **Walker** = Southern Oscillation; El Nino mechanism disrupts the **Walker circulation**.
**Bjerknes feedback**: weaker easterlies → warm water slides east → trades weaken further.
ENSO: **El Nino/La Nina** = oceanic component; **Southern Oscillation** = atmospheric counterpart.

24.s: Which one of the following correctly explains the relationship between ENSO and the Southern Oscillation?
o: El Nino and La Nina are the oceanic side, while the Southern Oscillation is the atmospheric side.
El Nino and La Nina are the atmospheric side, while the Southern Oscillation is the oceanic side.
All three are unrelated Atlantic Ocean phenomena.
The Southern Oscillation is a permanent ocean current in the Pacific.
24.x: El Nino and La Nina describe the oceanic component of ENSO, while the Southern Oscillation describes its atmospheric pressure component.
24.tq: Separate the oceanic and atmospheric components of a coupled phenomenon.
xs: **El Nino/La Nina** are the **oceanic** component of ENSO; the **Southern Oscillation** is the **atmospheric** counterpart — option **(1)**.
Option (2) reverses the two sides; ENSO is a **Pacific** phenomenon, not Atlantic.
The Southern Oscillation is a **pressure seesaw** (Tahiti vs Port Darwin), not an ocean current.
xa: **SOI** = pressure difference **Tahiti minus Darwin**.
Sustained **negative SOI = El Nino**; **positive SOI = La Nina**.
Described by **Sir Gilbert Walker** in **1920**.

24.s: The Bjerknes feedback during El Nino involves:
o: Sinking of cold polar water that reverses the monsoon
Weaker easterlies allowing warm water to move eastward, which weakens the trade winds further
Cooling of the eastern Pacific causing stronger upwelling
Strengthening easterlies that push warm water westward
24.x: Weaker easterlies allow warm western-Pacific water to slide eastward. This further weakens the trades, forming a positive feedback known as the Bjerknes feedback.
24.tq: Identify the reinforcing feedback rather than a simple one-way ocean-current change.
xs: **Bjerknes feedback**: **weaker easterlies** let warm water move **east**, which **weakens the trades further** — option **(2)**.
The chain: warm **western-Pacific** water slides east → **Walker circulation** disrupted → sinking air over the **Indian Ocean** = high pressure.
Stronger easterlies and eastern-Pacific cooling with strong upwelling describe **La Nina**, not this El Nino feedback.
xa: El Nino: trade winds **weaken or reverse**; Indian monsoon **delayed, weakened**.
**Kelvin wave**: an eastward warm wave tracked by **Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich** — an early El Nino signal.
**Super El Nino**: SST anomaly above **+2.0 deg C** in the central Pacific.

24.s: Which one of the following is the usual effect of El Nino on the Indian summer monsoon?
o: It strengthens and advances the monsoon in every case.
It produces good rainfall because of stronger trade winds.
It has no relationship with Indian rainfall.
It delays and weakens the monsoon, increasing drought risk.
24.x: El Nino is generally associated with a delayed and weakened Indian monsoon and an increased risk of deficient rainfall.
24.tq: Apply the phase-to-monsoon relationship without treating it as an absolute rule.
xs: **El Nino** usually **delays and weakens** the Indian monsoon, raising **drought risk** — option **(4)**.
**6 of 10** El Nino years brought **deficient** Indian rainfall.
Good rain from stronger trade winds is the **La Nina** pattern.
xa: Mechanism: Walker circulation disrupted → **sinking air over the Indian Ocean** = high pressure.
**IMD** warned in **May 2026** that a developing **super El Nino** could weaken the **2026** SW monsoon.
INCOIS study: **El Nino may reduce** post-monsoon (Oct-Dec) cyclones in the **Bay of Bengal**.

Consider the following statements about the Southern Oscillation (SO):
1. It is an atmospheric pressure seesaw between the Pacific and Indian Oceans.
2. The Southern Oscillation Index is the pressure difference Tahiti minus Darwin.
3. A sustained negative SOI indicates La Nina.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
24.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: a sustained negative SOI indicates El Nino; a positive SOI indicates La Nina. Hence 1 and 2 only (A); B, C and D each include the false statement 3.
24.tq: SOI = Tahiti minus Darwin; negative = El Nino, positive = La Nina.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: the SO is an atmospheric pressure **seesaw between the Pacific and Indian Oceans**.
Statement 2: **SOI** = pressure difference **Tahiti minus Darwin**.
Statement 3 wrong: a sustained **negative SOI = El Nino**; a **positive SOI = La Nina**.
xa: Described by **Sir Gilbert Walker** in **1920**.
ENSO: El Nino/La Nina = **oceanic**; Southern Oscillation = **atmospheric**.
High pressure over the equatorial South Pacific ↔ low pressure over the South Indian Ocean, and vice versa.

2. Under the IMD definition, El Nino is declared when the central equatorial Pacific is at least 0.5 degC warmer than average for five consecutive overlapping three-month periods.

24.x: Statement 1 is wrong: El Nino and La Nina are climate patterns, not storms (the false statement in RPSC 2024). Statement 2 is correct: this is the IMD 0.5 degC criterion. Statement 3 is correct: a Super El Nino exceeds +2.0 degC. So 2 and 3 only; A, C and D all include the false statement 1.
24.tq: ENSO = climate pattern, not storm; 0.5 degC El Nino, >2.0 degC super.
xs: Statements **2 and 3** are correct — option **(2) 2 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 wrong: El Nino and La Nina are **climate patterns**, not storms — the false statement in **RPSC 2024**.
Statement 2: **IMD** declares El Nino when the central equatorial Pacific is at least **0.5 deg C** warmer for five consecutive overlapping three-month periods.
Statement 3: a **Super El Nino** has an SST anomaly above **+2.0 deg C** in the central Pacific.
xa: El Nino recurs about every **3-7 years**.
**Kelvin wave** along the equatorial Pacific = early El Nino signal.

24.s:
How many of the following statements about ocean currents are correct?
1. Warm currents warm adjoining coastal air.
2. Cold currents cool the adjoining coast.
3. Cold currents can suppress convection.
4. Warm currents always produce arid west-coast climates.
24.x: Three are correct: warm currents warm the coast, cold currents cool it and suppress convection. Statement 4 is false because cold currents, not warm, help make west-coast deserts.
24.tq: Discriminate warm from cold currents.
n: Warm currents warm adjoining coastal air. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Cold currents cool adjoining coasts. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Cold currents can suppress convection. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Cold currents combined with subtropical highs are often associated with arid west-coast climates. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
xs: **Only three** statements (1, 2, 3) are correct — option **(3)**.
1: **warm currents** **warm adjoining coastal air**.
2 and 3: **cold currents** **cool adjoining coasts** and can **suppress convection**.
4 is wrong: **cold currents** with **subtropical highs** give **arid west-coast climates**, not warm currents.
xa: Desert examples: **Atacama** (Humboldt), **Namib/Kalahari** (Benguela), **Sonoran** (California).
**North Atlantic Drift** keeps **NW Europe** mild and ports like **Murmansk** ice-free.
Warm currents **increase moisture availability**.

24.s:
Assertion (A): Ocean currents influence climate.

o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
24.x: Both are true and R explains A: by carrying heat from low to high latitudes, currents warm or cool the coasts they pass.

n: Ocean currents redistribute heat. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
Ocean currents influence climate. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
Ocean currents **redistribute heat** and thereby **influence climate**.
Warm currents can **warm** and cold currents **cool** **adjacent coastal areas**.
xa: Warm currents move **toward higher latitudes**; cold currents **toward lower latitudes**.
Warm currents usually run along **east coasts**; cold along **west coasts**.
Where **warm + cold currents meet**, **plankton** flourishes and **fog** forms (e.g. **Newfoundland**).

24.s: Which ocean-water phenomenon involves horizontal movement and has major impacts on climate, fisheries and navigation?
24.x: Ocean currents are horizontal movements that affect climate, fisheries and navigation. Tides are vertical changes in level.
24.tq: Discriminate currents, tides and waves.
n: Ocean currents involve horizontal movement of water. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 72-74]
Ocean currents affect climate, fisheries, and navigation. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 72-74]
Ocean currents produce horizontal water movement. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 72-74]
Ocean currents affect climate, fisheries, and navigation. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 72-74]
xs: **Ocean currents** — option **(2)** is correct.
Currents are **continuous directed**, **horizontal movement** of water affecting **climate, fisheries and navigation**.
**Tides** are **vertical, periodic** changes in water level; **waves** are **oscillatory** movements.
xa: Current drivers: **winds**, **density differences**, **Coriolis force**, **pressure differences**.
Currents are **relatively continuous**; tides **highly periodic**; waves **variable**.
**Tsunamis** have **different causes** from wind-driven waves.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
o: I, III, IV and V only
I, II, III, IV and V

24.tq: Recall the features of waves.
n: Waves are oscillatory movements of water. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 72-74]
Wind is the main driver of waves. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 72-74]
Tsunamis have different causes from ordinary wind-driven waves. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 72-74]
Waves mainly transfer energy. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 72-74]
Wave timing is variable. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 72-74]
xs: All five statements **I, II, III, IV and V** are correct — option **(3)**.
Waves are **oscillatory movements** of water that **mainly transfer energy**; **wind** is the **main driver**.
**Tsunamis** have **different causes** from wind-driven waves; wave **timing** is **variable**.
xa: A key effect of waves is **coastal erosion** and **deposition**.
**Largest waves** occur in the **open ocean**.

24.s:
Assertion (A): Tides cause vertical and periodic changes in water level.
Reason (R): Tides are highly periodic.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
24.x: Both are true but R does not explain A: being periodic describes tides; the Moon's and Sun's gravity causes the rise and fall.

Tides involve vertical and periodic water-level changes. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 72-74]

24.s: According to the stated IMD criterion, El Nino is identified when the central equatorial Pacific is at least:

2. Warm water piled up in the western Pacific shifts eastward.

25.s: During El Nino, rising air shifts eastward and air descends over the Indian Ocean. This generally produces:
o: No change in Indian monsoon conditions
High pressure and a delayed or weak Indian monsoon
Low pressure and a stronger Indian monsoon
High pressure and exceptionally heavy monsoon rainfall

A **positive IOD** can **offset** El Nino (as in **1997**).

25.s: Which sequence correctly represents the normal Walker circulation over the tropical Pacific?
o: Rising air over the cool east, sinking air over the warm west, and westerly surface winds
Rising air over the warm west, sinking air over the cool east, and easterly surface trade winds

**Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich** tracks **Kelvin waves** — early El Nino signal.

2. It is measured by the Southern Oscillation Index.
3. It develops in April-May and peaks in October.

Statement 3: it develops in **April-May** and **peaks in October**.

25.s: Which one of the following statements best describes the relationship between the Indian Ocean Dipole and ENSO?
o: The IOD and ENSO are identical phenomena occurring in different oceans.

A negative IOD always offsets La Nina.
The IOD runs independently of ENSO, and a positive IOD can offset an El Nino.

25.tq: Reject absolute words such as “always” and distinguish two coupled-ocean climate phenomena.
xs: The **IOD runs independently of ENSO**, and a **positive IOD can offset El Nino** — option **(4)**.
Proof: in **1997** a strong positive IOD saved India from drought despite a **Super El Nino**.
So the IOD is a **separate phenomenon** — not identical to ENSO nor always caused by it.
xa: Some notes link **positive IOD with La Nina** and **negative IOD with El Nino**.
⚠ **Positive IOD** = more rain over India; **negative IOD** = reduced rain.
Measured by the **Dipole Mode Index (DMI)**.

25.s: Which condition is characteristic of a negative Indian Ocean Dipole?
o: Warmer western Arabian Sea and increased rainfall over India
Warmer eastern Pacific and stronger Peru upwelling
Cooler western Arabian Sea and warmer eastern pole, with reduced Indian rainfall
Cooler western and eastern poles with no monsoon effect
25.x: In a negative IOD, the western Arabian Sea is cooler and the eastern pole is warmer, resulting in reduced rainfall over India.
25.tq: Identify the reversed SST pattern and its linked rainfall effect.
xs: **Negative IOD** = **cooler western (Arabian Sea)**, **warmer eastern pole**, **reduced Indian rainfall** — option **(3)**.
A warmer western Arabian Sea with more rain is the **positive IOD**.
Eastern-Pacific warming and Peru upwelling belong to **ENSO**, not the IOD.
xa: IOD develops **April-May**, peaks in **October**.
Some notes link **negative IOD** with **El Nino**.
**NIOT OMNI buoys** off **Nellore** support IOD monitoring.

25.s: The strong positive IOD in 1997 is significant because it:
o: Caused drought in India despite a weak La Nina
Saved India from drought despite a Super El Nino
Produced the first recorded Madden-Julian Oscillation
25.x: The strong positive IOD in 1997 helped save India from drought even though a Super El Nino was present.
25.tq: Use an exceptional case to test interaction between climate drivers.
xs: In **1997** a strong **positive IOD** **saved India from drought despite a Super El Nino** — option **(2)**.
A positive IOD brings **more rain** over India and **can offset El Nino**.
xa: IOD develops **April-May**, peaks in **October**.
The IOD **runs independently of ENSO**.
Positive IOD: winds blow **east to west** (Bay of Bengal to Arabian Sea).

25.s: Which of the following statements regarding the Madden–Julian Oscillation is correct?
o: It is a westward-moving belt of clouds beginning over the Pacific Ocean and recurring every 5–10 days.
It is a seasonal reversal of winds confined to the Arabian Sea.
It is an eastward-moving belt of clouds and rain beginning over the tropical Indian Ocean and recurring every 30–60 days.
It is a stationary pressure belt over the subtropical Atlantic Ocean.
25.x: The MJO is an eastward-moving belt of clouds and rain that starts over the tropical Indian Ocean and recurs every 30–60 days.
25.tq: Combine movement, place of origin and recurrence interval to identify the exact phenomenon.
xs: The **MJO** is an **eastward-moving** belt of clouds and rain that starts over the **tropical Indian Ocean** and recurs every **30-60 days** — option **(3)**.
It is not westward, not from the Pacific, and not every 5-10 days; it is not a seasonal Arabian Sea wind reversal.
xa: Identified by **Madden and Julian, 1971-72**.
Convection rises up to **10 km**; it fades in the **eastern Pacific** but circles the globe aloft.
It shifts the heavy-rain zone eastward → **active/break spells** of the monsoon.

25.s:
Which of the following correctly describes the vertical and horizontal behaviour of the Madden-Julian Oscillation?
1. Its convection can rise up to 10 km.
2. It fades in the eastern Pacific but circles the globe aloft.
3. It shifts the heavy-rain zone eastward.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
25.x: The MJO convection rises up to 10 km, weakens in the eastern Pacific while continuing aloft around the globe, and shifts the heavy-rain zone eastward.
25.tq: Combine vertical extent, movement and rainfall-zone displacement.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: MJO convection rises up to **10 km**.
Statement 2: it **fades in the eastern Pacific** but **circles the globe aloft**.
Statement 3: it **shifts the heavy-rain zone eastward**.
xa: The shift produces **active/break spells** of the monsoon.
Periodicity: every **30-60 days**.
Identified by **Madden and Julian, 1971-72**.

25.s: The Madden-Julian Oscillation is associated with which monsoon pattern?
o: The complete absence of monsoon variability
Only winter snowfall in North India
Active and break spells of the monsoon
25.x: By shifting the zone of heavy rain eastward, the MJO contributes to active and break spells of the monsoon.
25.tq: Connect a moving atmospheric pulse with its practical weather effect.
xs: The **MJO** causes **active and break spells** of the monsoon — option **(4)**.
It does this by **shifting the heavy-rain zone eastward**.
xa: MJO recurs every **30-60 days** and moves **eastward**.
It begins as a warm pool in the tropical **Indian Ocean**.
Convection up to **10 km**; fades in the **eastern Pacific** but circles the globe aloft.

25.s: In its April 2026 forecast, the India Meteorological Department projected the southwest monsoon at what level of the Long Period Average?
25.x: The IMD forecast projected a below-normal monsoon at 92% of the Long Period Average, whose reference value was stated as 87 cm.
25.tq: Distinguish closely spaced percentage figures in a forecast question.
xs: IMD's **April 2026** forecast put the monsoon at **92% of LPA** — option **(1)**.
The **LPA** is **87 cm**; the forecast was **below normal** due to a developing **El Nino**.
xa: It was the first "below normal" April warning in **11 years**.
El Nino gives a **delayed/weak Indian monsoon** via high pressure over the Indian Ocean.
Weak monsoon years hit **rain-fed Rayalaseema** farming.

25.s: Which inference regarding El Nino and Bay of Bengal cyclones is supported by the INCOIS study?
o: El Nino may reduce post-monsoon Bay of Bengal cyclones.
El Nino always increases post-monsoon Bay of Bengal cyclones.
El Nino shifts all Bay of Bengal cyclones to the Arabian Sea.
El Nino has no relationship with Bay of Bengal cyclones.
25.x: The study indicated that El Nino may reduce the number of post-monsoon Bay of Bengal cyclones.
25.tq: Use the cautious wording ‘may’ and distinguish a possible tendency from an absolute rule.
xs: The **INCOIS** study says **El Nino may reduce** post-monsoon Bay of Bengal cyclones — option **(1)**.
ENSO governs the number of **post-monsoon (Oct-Dec)** Bay of Bengal cyclones.
**La Nina** goes the other way: **more floods and severe cyclones** in the Bay of Bengal.
xa: INCOIS is in **Hyderabad**.
Fewer/more Bay of Bengal cyclones affect **coastal AP**.
El Nino weakens the **Walker circulation** and shifts it eastward.

25.s:
Arrange the following developments in chronological order:
A. Identification of the Indian Ocean Dipole
B. Last El Nino mentioned in the record
C. First description of the Southern Oscillation by Walker

Choose the correct sequence.
25.x: Walker first described the Southern Oscillation in the 1920s, the Indian Ocean Dipole was identified in 1999, and the last El Nino mentioned was in 2023–24.
25.tq: Anchor the sequence using the 1920s, 1999 and 2023–24 time markers.
xs: Order: **C, A, B** — option **(2)**.
**C**: **Walker** described the **Southern Oscillation** in the **1920s**.
**A**: the **IOD** was identified in **1999**; **B**: the last El Nino was **2023-24**.
xa: **Madden and Julian** identified the **MJO** in **1971-72** — between Walker and the IOD.
**2025** was the **warmest La Nina year on record**.
IMD's **April 2026** forecast was the first "below normal" April warning in **11 years**.

26.s:
Consider the following statements about marine ecosystems:
1. They cover about 71% of Earth's surface.
2. Rivers and freshwater lakes are marine ecosystems.
3. They hold about 97% of Earth's water.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
26.x: Statement 1 is correct: marine ecosystems cover about 71% of the surface. Statement 3 is correct: they hold about 97% of Earth's water. Statement 2 is wrong: rivers and freshwater lakes are freshwater (lotic and lentic) ecosystems, not marine. So '1 only' misses statement 3, and options with statement 2 are wrong.
26.tq: 71% of surface, 97% of water.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: marine ecosystems cover about **71%** of Earth's surface.
Statement 2 is wrong: **rivers and freshwater lakes** are **lentic/lotic freshwater** ecosystems, **not marine**.
Statement 3 is correct: they hold ~**97%** of Earth's water.
xa: Marine: **coral reefs**, **hydrothermal vents**, **estuaries**, **mangroves**, **seagrass beds**, **kelp forests**.
**Neritic** zone: over the **continental shelf** to about **200 m** — **richest fishing zone**.
**Epipelagic (sunlit)** zone holds the **highest percentage of marine life**.

26.s: Which one of the following is a marine ecosystem associated with chemosynthetic life?
26.x: Hydrothermal vents are marine ecosystems that support chemosynthetic life, unlike rivers and freshwater lakes.
26.tq: Use the distinctive biological process to identify the ecosystem.
xs: **Hydrothermal vents** are marine ecosystems with **chemosynthetic** life — option **(3)**.
**Rivers** and **freshwater lakes** are freshwater (lotic/lentic) ecosystems, **not marine**; a glacial pond is freshwater too.
xa: Other marine ecosystems: **coral reefs, intertidal zone, estuaries, salt marshes, mangroves, seagrass beds, kelp forests**.
Ocean **primary producers** are **phytoplankton** (diatoms, dinoflagellates, cyanobacteria).
The **aphotic** zone is dark with **no photosynthesis**.

26.s: The littoral or intertidal zone lies between the
o: sunlit and dark zones of the ocean
sea floor and the deepest ocean trench
continental shelf and the open ocean
26.x: The littoral or intertidal zone is the area between the high-tide and low-tide marks.
26.tq: Recall the physical boundaries of the intertidal zone.
xs: The **littoral / intertidal** zone lies between the **high-tide and low-tide marks** — option **(4)**.
Sunlit vs dark is the **photic/aphotic** divide; shelf vs open ocean is the **neritic/oceanic** divide.
xa: **Neritic** zone: from the **high-water line** over the continental shelf to about **200 m**.
**Benthic** = the **sea floor** and its organisms.
**Oceanic** = open ocean **beyond the shelf**.

26.s: The neritic zone extends from the high-water line over the continental shelf to approximately
26.x: The neritic zone extends from the high-water line across the continental shelf to about 200 metres depth.
26.tq: Associate the neritic zone with the continental shelf and its approximate depth.
xs: The **neritic zone** reaches about **200 m** depth over the **continental shelf** — option **(4)**.
It starts at the **high-water line**.
xa: The neritic shelf zone is the **richest fishing zone**.
The **photic (euphotic)** zone is the sunlit upper layer (~**200 m**) where photosynthesis occurs.
Corals grow in **clear, shallow, sunlit** water, usually < ~**50 m**.

26.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Pelagic — sea floor and its organisms
26.x: The photic or euphotic zone is the sunlit upper layer in which photosynthesis occurs. The pelagic zone is the open water column, the benthic zone is the sea floor, and the aphotic zone is dark.
26.tq: Match each oceanic term with its precise spatial meaning.
xs: **Photic — zone where photosynthesis occurs** is correctly matched — option **(3)**.
**Benthic** is the **sea floor** and its organisms (not the water column); the **aphotic** zone is **dark**, not sunlit.
So "pelagic — sea floor" and "aphotic — sunlit" are wrong pairings.
xa: Photic (euphotic) = sunlit upper layer, about **200 m**.
**Epipelagic (sunlit)** zone holds the **highest percentage** of marine life.
**Aphotic** = dark zone below, **no photosynthesis**.

26.s: The richest fishing zone among the following is generally the
26.x: The neritic zone over the continental shelf is generally the richest fishing zone.
26.tq: Link shallow continental-shelf waters with high fisheries productivity.
xs: The **neritic shelf zone** is the richest fishing zone — option **(3)**.
It extends from the **high-water line** over the **continental shelf** to about **200 m**.
The **aphotic** zone is dark with no photosynthesis, so it cannot be the richest.
xa: **Upwelling** zones (Peru-Chile, California, Namibia, Somalia, Kerala) are also rich fisheries.
**Epipelagic (sunlit)** zone holds the most marine habitats/life.
**Phytoplankton** are the ocean's main **primary producers**.

26.s: Which ocean zone holds the highest percentage of marine habitats and life?
26.x: The epipelagic (sunlit) zone holds the highest percentage of marine habitats and life, because light there allows photosynthesis. The aphotic zone is dark with no photosynthesis, and the abyssal and hadal zones on the deep sea floor and in trenches support far less life.
26.tq: Sunlit epipelagic = most marine life.
xs: The **epipelagic (sunlit)** zone holds the **highest percentage** of marine habitats/life — option **(1)**.
Light there allows **photosynthesis**; the **aphotic** zone is dark with **no photosynthesis**.
xa: The **photic (euphotic)** layer is about **200 m** deep.
**Phytoplankton** (diatoms, dinoflagellates, cyanobacteria) are the main primary producers.
The **neritic shelf zone** is the richest fishing zone.

26.s: Approximately how much of Earth’s oxygen is produced by the oceans, mainly through phytoplankton?
26.x: The oceans, mainly through phytoplankton, produce about half or more than half of Earth’s oxygen, exceeding the contribution of all rainforests combined.
26.tq: Select the approximate share rather than confusing oceanic production with rainforest production.
xs: Oceans, mainly via **phytoplankton**, produce **about half (50%+)** of Earth's oxygen — option **(2)**.
That is **more than all rainforests combined**.
xa: Phytoplankton = **diatoms, dinoflagellates, cyanobacteria**.
**El Nino** suppresses Peru upwelling → **fewer phytoplankton**, fishery collapse.
Marine ecosystems cover about **71%** of Earth's surface.

26.s: Upwelling along a coast generally occurs when:
o: Tides permanently stop vertical movement of seawater
Warm surface water sinks because of intense evaporation
River water pushes all subsurface water into the open ocean
Winds push surface water offshore and cold, nutrient-rich subsurface water rises
26.x: Coastal upwelling occurs when winds drive surface water away from the coast, allowing cold, nutrient-rich subsurface water to rise.
26.tq: Use the direction of surface-water movement to identify the upwelling mechanism.
xs: **Upwelling**: winds push **surface water offshore** and **cold, nutrient-rich subsurface water rises** — option **(4)**.
Result: a **plankton boom** and **rich fisheries**.
xa: Upwelling zones: **Peru-Chile** (Humboldt), **California**, **Namibia** (Benguela), **Somalia** (Findlater), **Kerala**.
**El Nino** **suppresses** the Peru upwelling.
Kerala upwelling supports **oil sardine and mackerel**.

26.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Upwelling zone)
a. Peru–Chile
b. California
c. Namibia
 d. Somalia/Horn of Africa

List-II (Associated current or season)
i. Benguela Current
 ii. Findlater Current and southwest monsoon
 iii. Humboldt Current
 iv. California Current

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
26.x: Peru–Chile is associated with the Humboldt Current, California with the California Current, Namibia with the Benguela Current, and Somalia with the Findlater Current and southwest monsoon.
26.tq: Start from the sure current–coast pairs and eliminate codes containing a wrong association.
xs: Correct code: **a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii** — option **(1)**.
**Peru-Chile** — **Humboldt** (anchoveta fishery); **California** — **California current**.
**Namibia** — **Benguela**; **Somalia/Horn of Africa** — **Findlater current, SW monsoon**.
xa: **Kerala / SW India** upwelling: **SW monsoon** — **oil sardine and mackerel**.
Upwelling: winds push surface water offshore → cold, nutrient-rich water rises.
**El Nino** suppresses Peru upwelling → fishery collapse.

26.s:
Consider the following statements about upwelling off Kerala and southwest India:
1. It is associated with the southwest monsoon.
2. It supports oil sardine and mackerel fisheries.
3. It is caused by the Benguela Current.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
26.x: Kerala and southwest India experience upwelling associated with the southwest monsoon, supporting oil sardine and mackerel fisheries. The Benguela Current is associated with Namibia.
26.tq: Separate the correct seasonal and fisheries links from the swapped-current statement.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: Kerala/SW India upwelling comes with the **SW monsoon**.
Statement 2: it supports **oil sardine and mackerel** fisheries.
Statement 3 wrong: the **Benguela** current is linked to **Namibia (SW Africa)**, not Kerala.
xa: **Somalia/Horn of Africa** upwelling: **Findlater** current, SW monsoon.
**Peru-Chile** upwelling: **Humboldt** (anchoveta fishery).
AP fisheries depend on **Bay of Bengal plankton** productivity, now threatened by **marine heatwaves**.

26.s: El Niño can cause a collapse of the Peru fishery because it:
o: Strengthens Peru upwelling and eliminates all nutrients
Suppresses Peru upwelling, reducing phytoplankton and fish food
Stops all ocean circulation in the Pacific Ocean
Increases cold-water upwelling and causes excessive shell formation
26.x: El Niño suppresses the Peru upwelling system, reducing phytoplankton abundance and thereby contributing to fishery collapse.
26.tq: Trace the sequence from climate event to upwelling, phytoplankton and fisheries.
xs: **El Nino suppresses Peru upwelling**, reducing **phytoplankton** and fish food — option **(2)**.
No upwelling → no nutrient-rich water → **fewer phytoplankton** → **fishery collapse**.
It does not strengthen upwelling or increase cold water — that is the opposite of El Nino.
xa: The Peru-Chile upwelling is tied to the **Humboldt** current — the **anchoveta** fishery.
Since **1998** every strong El Nino has coincided with a **global bleaching event**.
Phytoplankton are the ocean's main **primary producers**.

26.s:
Consider the following statements regarding coral reef distribution:
1. Coral reefs are generally found between about 30°N and 30°S.
2. Zooxanthellae live in symbiotic association with corals.
3. Coral reefs generally require water temperatures below 20°C.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
26.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because coral reefs generally require warm water above about 20°C.
26.tq: Reject the reversed temperature condition while retaining the latitude and symbiosis facts.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: reefs lie mostly within the **tropics**, roughly **30°N-30°S**.
Statement 2: **zooxanthellae** live in **mutualistic symbiosis** with corals.
Statement 3 wrong: corals need **warm water above ~20°C**, not below.
xa: Minimum about **20-21 °C**; optimum **23-25 °C**.
Water must be **clear, shallow, sunlit** (usually < ~**50 m**), sediment-free, normal salinity.
Reefs avoid **muddy river mouths**.

26.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Type of reef)
a. Fringing reef
b. Barrier reef
c. Atoll

List-II (Characteristic)
i. Ring reef enclosing a central lagoon
ii. Grows close to the shore
iii. Runs parallel to the coast and is separated from it by a lagoon

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
26.x: A fringing reef grows close to the shore, a barrier reef is separated from the coast by a lagoon, and an atoll encloses a central lagoon.
26.tq: Start with the sure pair and eliminate codes containing a wrong reef characteristic.
xs: Correct code: **a-ii, b-iii, c-i** — option **(1)**.
**Fringing reef** grows **close to the shore**; **barrier reef** runs **parallel to the coast**, separated by a wide, deep **lagoon**.
**Atoll** = **ring-shaped reef** enclosing a lagoon, with no central island.
xa: Fringing: **Gulf of Mannar**, **Gulf of Kutch**.
Barrier: **Great Barrier Reef** (Australia) — Queensland, Coral Sea.
Atoll: **Lakshadweep** — India's only true atolls.

26.s: The Great Barrier Reef is correctly described as a:
o: Fringing reef in the Gulf of Mannar
Barrier reef off Queensland in the Coral Sea
Fringing reef off the coast of Maharashtra
26.x: The Great Barrier Reef is a barrier reef located off Queensland in the Coral Sea and extends for about 2,300 km.
26.tq: Discriminate among reef types by matching the named example with its location.
xs: The **Great Barrier Reef** is a **barrier reef** off **Queensland** in the **Coral Sea** — option **(3)**.
**Lakshadweep** has **atolls**; the **Gulf of Mannar** has **fringing** reefs; **Malvan** (Maharashtra) has patchy reefs.
xa: **UNESCO World Heritage Site 1981**.
World's **largest** reef, followed by the **Mesoamerican Barrier Reef**.

26.s: The mutualistic association between coral polyps and zooxanthellae is correctly described by which one of the following?
o: Zooxanthellae destroy coral tissues and prevent calcification
Corals provide food and colour, while zooxanthellae provide calcium carbonate
Zooxanthellae provide food and colour, while corals provide shelter and nutrients
Both organisms independently obtain all their nutrients from seawater
26.x: Zooxanthellae photosynthesise and supply food and colour to corals. The coral provides them with shelter and nutrients.
26.tq: Test the reciprocal benefits in a symbiotic relationship.
xs: **Zooxanthellae** supply **food and colour**; the **coral** gives **shelter and nutrients** — option **(3)**.
The algae **photosynthesise** to supply food/energy; option (2) reverses the roles.
The coral, not the algae, builds the **calcium carbonate** skeleton.
xa: This is **mutualistic symbiosis** (**mutualism**).
**Bleaching** = corals turn **white after expelling zooxanthellae** and lose pigments.
Bleached coral is **stressed, not necessarily dead**.

26.s:
With reference to coral reef growth conditions, consider the following statements:
1. Coral reefs generally require warm water, with a minimum temperature of about 20–21°C.
2. The optimum temperature for coral growth is approximately 23–25°C.
3. Coral reefs generally flourish in clear, shallow and sunlit water.
4. Heavy sediment deposition at muddy river mouths favours coral reef growth.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
26.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Heavy sediment and freshwater from muddy river mouths generally inhibit coral reef growth.
26.tq: Identify the environmental requirement and reject the reversed condition.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(1) 1, 2 and 3 only**.
Statements 1-2: minimum about **20-21 °C**, optimum **23-25 °C**.
Statement 3: corals need **clear, shallow, sunlit** water.
Statement 4 wrong: corals **avoid muddy river mouths**; they need **sediment-free** water.
xa: That is why most of India's **east coast** (West Bengal, Odisha, **Andhra Pradesh**) has **no reefs**.
Depth usually < ~**50 m**; normal salinity.
Location: mostly within **30°N-30°S**.

26.s: Coral reefs are called the ‘Rainforests of the Sea’ primarily because they
o: support exceptionally high marine species richness despite occupying less than one per cent of the ocean floor
are found only near tropical rainforests
receive the highest rainfall among all marine ecosystems
cover most of the ocean floor and contain only tropical plants
26.x: Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor but support more than 25 per cent of all marine species, giving them exceptionally high species richness.
26.tq: Distinguish an ecological epithet from a literal geographical association.
xs: Reefs are **"Rainforests of the Sea"** because they cover **< 1% of the ocean floor** yet support **> 25% of all marine species** — option **(1)**.
The epithet is about **species richness**, not rainfall or being near rainforests.
xa: With tropical rainforests, reefs have the **highest species richness**.
Roles: **break wave power during storms**, preventing **coastal erosion**.
**APPSC 2024** paired the epithet with "breaks wave power" — both true, but the second does not explain the first.

26.s: Which one of the following is NOT a role of coral reefs?
o: Increasing coastal erosion by amplifying storm waves
