26.x: Coral reefs break storm waves and thereby help prevent coastal erosion. They also provide nursery grounds and support fisheries and tourism.
26.tq: Find the option that reverses a stated ecological function.
xs: **Increasing coastal erosion by amplifying storm waves** is **not** a reef role — option **(3)**.
Reefs do the opposite: they **break wave power during storms**, **preventing coastal erosion**.
They also provide **nursery/spawning grounds**, **fisheries**, **tourism** and biodiversity.
xa: Reefs protect coasts from **storm surges**.
NGT cleared the **₹92,000-crore Great Nicobar project** (Feb 2026) — **coral loss** is the core objection.
**MPAs**, no-fishing zones and sanctuaries help reefs **recover**.

26.s:
Assertion (A): Coral reefs are called the 'Rainforests of the Sea'.
Reason (R): Coral reefs break wave power during storms and prevent coastal erosion.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
26.x: Both statements are true (APPSC 2024). Reefs are called 'Rainforests of the Sea' because they cover under 1% of the ocean floor yet support over 25% of marine species, i.e. their species richness, not their wave-breaking role. So R does not explain A; options C and D are wrong because both A and R are true.
26.tq: Rainforest epithet = biodiversity, not storm protection.
xs: **Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation** — option **(2)**.
A is true because reefs cover **< 1% of the ocean floor** yet hold **> 25%** of marine species — **species richness**.
R is true (reefs **break wave power**, preventing **coastal erosion**) but it does not explain the epithet (**APPSC 2024**).
xa: Other services: **nurseries/spawning grounds**, fisheries, tourism, protection from **storm surges**.
With tropical rainforests, reefs have the **highest species richness**.

26.s: Which one of the following sets contains only recognised true coral reef areas in India?
o: Godavari Delta, Mahanadi Delta, Malvan and West Bengal
Sundarbans, Krishna Delta, Chilika and Gulf of Kutch
West Bengal, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh and Lakshadweep
Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Kutch, Lakshadweep and Andaman and Nicobar Islands
26.x: India’s recognised true reef areas include the Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Kutch, Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep. Patchy reefs also occur at Malvan in Maharashtra.
26.tq: Select the complete valid geographical set while rejecting sediment-rich east-coast locations.
xs: **Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Kutch, Lakshadweep, Andaman & Nicobar** are true reef areas — option **(4)**.
Most of the **east coast** (**West Bengal, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh**) has **no reefs** — heavy river sediment + freshwater.
**Malvan** (Maharashtra) has only **patchy reefs**.
xa: **Andaman & Nicobar** = **highest diversity**; **Lakshadweep** = only true **atolls**.
**Gulf of Mannar** (TN), **Gulf of Kutch** (Gujarat) = true reefs.
⚠ **AP** has **no true coral reefs**.

26.s: Coral reefs are absent along most parts of the east coast of India mainly because of
o: absence of sunlight throughout the year
excessively high salinity near all river mouths
heavy river sediment and freshwater input
extremely cold ocean currents and permanent sea ice
26.x: Most of the east coast, including West Bengal, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh, lacks reefs because heavy river sediment and freshwater inhibit coral growth.
26.tq: Connect a physical coastal condition with the geographical distribution of reefs.
xs: Most of India's **east coast** lacks reefs because of **heavy river sediment and freshwater** — option **(3)**.
Corals need **clear, sediment-free** water of **normal salinity** and avoid **muddy river mouths**.
xa: No-reef states: **West Bengal, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh**.
AP fisheries depend on **Bay of Bengal plankton** productivity, threatened by **marine heatwaves**.
The east coast exception: **Gulf of Mannar** (TN) has true reefs.

26.s: Which one of the following is correctly associated with the Gulf of Mannar Biosphere Reserve?
o: It is India’s only true atoll system and has no islands
It is India’s first national coral reef research institute
It is located on the Andhra coast and consists only of freshwater wetlands
It is India’s first marine biosphere reserve and includes coral reefs, mangroves and seagrass beds
26.x: The Gulf of Mannar Biosphere Reserve is India’s first marine biosphere reserve. It includes islands, estuaries, beaches, coral reefs, salt marshes, mangroves, seagrass beds and dugongs.
26.tq: Match the reserve with its status and ecosystem composition.
xs: The **Gulf of Mannar Biosphere Reserve** is India's **first marine biosphere reserve**, with **coral reefs, mangroves, seagrass beds** — option **(4)**.
It also has islands, estuaries, beaches, salt marshes, and **dugongs** in its seagrass beds.
India's **only true atolls** are in **Lakshadweep**; the **first coral reef research institute** is at **Chidiyatapu**; it is in **TN**, not AP.
xa: Gulf of Mannar is a **true reef** of the **fringing** type.
**Feb 2025** bleaching hit the **Gulf of Mannar** and **Palk Bay**.
**National Coral Reef Research Institute** = **Chidiyatapu, South Andaman**.

26.s:
Which of the following statements about the Great Barrier Reef is correct?
1. It is situated along the north-eastern coast of Australia.
2. It is approximately 2,300 km long.
3. It contains about 3,000 reefs and 900 islands.
4. It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1981.

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
26.x: All four statements are correct. The Great Barrier Reef lies off north-eastern Australia, is about 2,300 km long, includes approximately 3,000 reefs and 900 islands, and became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1981.
26.tq: Combine location, scale, composition and heritage-status facts in one coded question.
xs: All four statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
The **Great Barrier Reef** lies off **Queensland, Australia** (Coral Sea), ~**2,300 km** long.
It has ~**3,000 reefs + 900 islands** and became a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** in **1981**.
xa: Area ~**344,400 sq km**; ~**1,500** fish + **400+** coral species.
It is the **world's largest** reef, followed by the **Mesoamerican Barrier Reef**.
Type: **barrier reef** — parallel to the coast, separated by a wide, deep lagoon.

26.s:
With reference to coral reefs in India, consider the following statements:
1. The Andaman and Nicobar region has the highest diversity among the Indian reef regions listed.
2. Coral reefs occur in the Gulf of Mannar and the Gulf of Kutch.
3. Malvan is a coral-reef region in Maharashtra.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
26.x: All three statements are correct. Indian reef regions include the Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Kutch, Andaman and Nicobar, Lakshadweep and Malvan; the Andaman and Nicobar region has the highest diversity among them.
26.tq: Test a complete regional list through the ‘all statements’ option.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: **Andaman & Nicobar** has the **highest diversity**.
Statement 2: **Gulf of Mannar** (TN) and **Gulf of Kutch** (Gujarat) have **true reefs**.
Statement 3: **Malvan** (Maharashtra) has **patchy reefs**.
xa: **Lakshadweep** = India's only true **atolls**.
India's first **National Coral Reef Research Institute**: **Chidiyatapu, South Andaman**.
**Andaman** mass bleaching was linked to about a **2°C rise** in Indian Ocean temperature.

26.s: India's first National Coral Reef Research Institute is located at:
26.x: India's first National Coral Reef Research Institute is located at Chidiyatapu in South Andaman.
26.tq: Apply the location-based institutional association.
xs: India's first **National Coral Reef Research Institute** is at **Chidiyatapu, South Andaman** — option **(4)**.
**Malvan** (Maharashtra) has patchy reefs; **Lakshadweep** has India's only atolls; **Gulf of Mannar** has India's first **marine biosphere reserve**.
xa: **Andaman & Nicobar** has the **highest reef diversity** in India.
**CMLRE Kochi** studies **EEZ** living resources.
Andaman mass bleaching: about a **2°C rise** in Indian Ocean temperature (**UPPSC 2024** key).

26.s: Which one of the following is regarded as the strongest global driver of coral loss in the context of coral bleaching?
o: Rising sea-surface temperature and marine heatwaves
26.x: Rising sea-surface temperature and marine heatwaves are currently the strongest global drivers of coral loss associated with bleaching.
26.tq: Identify the dominant driver among several environmental factors.
xs: **Rising SST and marine heatwaves** are now the **strongest global driver** of coral loss — option **(3)**.
They are the **primary cause** of bleaching.
Normal tides are not a driver — though **extremely low tides** are listed as a trigger.
xa: Other triggers: **pollution and runoff, high UV, disease, storms/cyclones, ocean acidification**.
Also: **crown-of-thorns starfish**, coral mining, tourism.
GCRMN 2026: in **2024**, **87%** of reefs faced unprecedented heat stress.

26.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I: Global bleaching event

a. First
b. Second
c. Third
d. Fourth

List-II: Year or period

i. 1998
ii. 2010
iii. 2014–2017
iv. 2023–mid-2025

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
26.x: The first global event occurred in 1998, the second in 2010, the third during 2014–2017, and the fourth from 2023 to about mid-2025.
26.tq: Start with the certain year-event pair and complete the chronological matching.
xs: Correct code: **a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv** — option **(1)**.
1st **1998** (strong El Nino); 2nd **2010**; 3rd **2014-2017** (**68.2%** of reef areas hit).
4th: **2023 - ended ~mid-2025** — the fastest and most extensive.
xa: The 4th hit **84%** of reef areas in **83** countries (NOAA).
Since **1998** every strong **El Nino** has coincided with a global bleaching event.
Large-scale bleaching takes **more than 15 years** to recover from.

26.s: Since 1998, every strong El Niño has coincided with
o: the disappearance of all marine heatwaves
the formation of new atolls in the Pacific Ocean
the complete recovery of coral reefs
26.x: Every strong El Niño since 1998 has coincided with a global coral bleaching event.
26.tq: Identify the stated recurring relationship between El Niño and bleaching.
xs: Since **1998**, every strong **El Nino** has coincided with a **global coral bleaching event** — option **(4)**.
The first global event (**1998**) itself came with a **strong El Nino**.
xa: Recovery from large-scale bleaching takes **more than 15 years**.
El Nino also suppresses **Peru upwelling** → fishery collapse.

26.s:
With reference to coral bleaching, consider the following statements:
1. Bleaching occurs when coral polyps expel their symbiotic zooxanthellae.
2. A bleached coral is necessarily dead.
3. Loss of pigments accompanies bleaching.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
26.x: Coral bleaching involves expulsion of zooxanthellae and loss of pigments. A bleached coral is stressed but is not necessarily dead.
26.tq: Find the false absolute statement; ‘necessarily dead’ reverses the distinction between stress and death.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1: bleaching = polyps **expel symbiotic zooxanthellae** (**APPSC-G2 2017**).
Statement 2 wrong: bleached coral is **stressed, not necessarily dead** (but prone to starvation/disease).
Statement 3: corals turn **white** and **lose pigments**.
xa: Primary cause: **rising SST / marine heatwaves**.
**INCOIS** issues **coral bleaching** and algal bloom alerts.
Zooxanthellae normally supply the coral's **food and colour**.

26.s: Which one of the following is NOT identified as a factor that can contribute to coral bleaching?
26.x: Pollution, extreme low tides and ocean acidification are recognised contributors to coral bleaching. Increased carbonate availability is not listed as a bleaching factor.
26.tq: Eliminate the three recognised stressors and identify the reversed carbonate claim.
xs: **Increase in carbonate availability** is **not** a bleaching factor — option **(3)**.
In fact **ocean acidification** **lowers** carbonate ions, which harms corals — and acidification **is** a trigger.
**Extremely low tides** and **pollution and runoff** are listed triggers.
xa: Other triggers: **high UV, disease, storms/cyclones, crown-of-thorns starfish, coral mining, tourism**.
Primary cause: **rising SST and marine heatwaves**.
**Harmful algal blooms** also block sunlight for corals and seagrass.

26.s: The mass coral bleaching in the Andaman region was linked to approximately what rise in Indian Ocean temperature?
26.x: The Andaman mass bleaching was linked to an approximately 2°C rise in Indian Ocean temperature.
26.tq: Use the specific temperature figure rather than the general marine-heatwave threshold.
xs: The **Andaman** mass bleaching was linked to about a **2°C** rise in Indian Ocean temperature — option **(3)**.
This was the **UPPSC 2024** key; rising SST is the **primary cause** of bleaching.
xa: **Andaman & Nicobar** has India's **highest reef diversity**.
**Feb 2025** bleaching also hit the **Gulf of Mannar, Palk Bay, Lakshadweep, Gulf of Kachchh**.
India's first **National Coral Reef Research Institute** is at **Chidiyatapu, South Andaman**.

26.s:
Consider the following statements about ocean acidification:
1. It necessarily affects cloud formation.
2. It is the fall in the pH of seawater (normally alkaline, about 8.1) caused by uptake of carbon dioxide.
3. It is called the 'evil twin of global warming' or 'the other CO2 problem'.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
26.x: Statement 2 is correct: acidification is falling ocean pH from CO2 uptake; seawater is alkaline at about pH 8.1. Statement 3 is correct: it is nicknamed the 'evil twin of global warming'. Statement 1 is wrong: acidification harms corals and calcareous organisms but does not necessarily affect cloud formation. So '2 only' misses statement 3, and options with statement 1 are wrong.
26.tq: Acidification hits calcifiers (corals, plankton, shellfish), not clouds.
xs: Statements **2 and 3** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is wrong: acidification does **not necessarily affect cloud formation**.
Statement 2 is correct: it is **falling ocean pH** (seawater alkaline, **pH ~8.1**) from **CO2 uptake**.
Statement 3 is correct: called the **"evil twin of global warming"** / **"the other CO2 problem"**.
xa: CO2 + water → **carbonic acid** → carbonate ions fall → **calcifiers** (corals, plankton, shellfish) struggle.
Oceans absorb about **30-40%** of anthropogenic CO2.
Acidity is up **30%** since the Industrial Revolution; may rise **150%** by **2100**.
Worst areas: **cold temperate seas** and the melting **Arctic**.

26.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the chemical basis of ocean acidification:
1. Carbon dioxide reacts with water to form carbonic acid.
2. Carbonic acid yields bicarbonate and hydronium ions.
3. The concentration of carbonate ions declines.
4. Calcifying organisms find it easier to build calcium carbonate shells.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
26.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is false because declining carbonate ions make calcium carbonate shell formation more difficult for corals, plankton and shellfish.
26.tq: Find the statement that reverses the effect of declining carbonate ions.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(1) 1, 2 and 3 only**.
Statement 1: **CO2 + water → carbonic acid**.
Statement 2: carbonic acid yields **bicarbonate + hydronium ions**.
Statement 3: **carbonate ions fall**; so statement 4 is wrong — calcifiers find it **harder** to build **calcium carbonate** shells.
xa: Calcifiers hit: **corals, plankton and shellfish**.
Seawater is **alkaline**, **pH ~8.1**; acidification = falling pH from **CO2** uptake.
Epithets: **"evil twin of global warming"** / **"the other CO2 problem"**.

26.s: Approximately what proportion of anthropogenic carbon dioxide is absorbed by the oceans?
26.x: The oceans absorb approximately 30–40% of anthropogenic carbon dioxide; another cited estimate places the uptake above 25%.
26.tq: Use the middle numerical range carefully rather than confusing it with the alternative lower estimate.
xs: Oceans absorb about **30-40 percent** of anthropogenic **CO2** — option **(3)**.
Some notes put it at **>25%**.
xa: Ocean acidity is up **30%** since the **Industrial Revolution**.
Acidity may rise **150%** by **2100**.
Worst areas: **cold temperate seas** and the **melting Arctic**.

26.s: Ocean acidification is expected to be more severe in cold temperate seas primarily because:
o: Cold water contains no carbonate ions
Cold seas have permanently higher salinity than tropical seas
Cold water has higher carbon dioxide solubility
26.x: Carbon dioxide is more soluble in cold water, making cold temperate seas particularly vulnerable to acidification. The melting Arctic is also identified as a region of concern.
26.tq: Link the regional pattern to the physical property of gas solubility.
xs: Cold temperate seas acidify more because **cold water has higher CO2 solubility** — option **(4)**.
The **melting Arctic** is the other worst-hit area.
Salinity, sunlight or an absence of carbonate ions are not the reasons given.
xa: Chemistry: **CO2 + water → carbonic acid → bicarbonate + hydronium**; **carbonate ions fall**.
Normal seawater **pH ~8.1** (alkaline).
Oceans absorb about **30-40%** of anthropogenic CO2.

26.s:
Consider the following statements about harmful algal blooms:
1. When a bloom dies and decomposes, oxygen is stripped from the water, creating dead zones.
2. The Gulf of Mexico dead zone is linked to runoff from the Mississippi.
3. Blooms increase sunlight reaching corals and seagrass, aiding their growth.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
26.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: blooms block sunlight for corals and seagrass. Hence 1 and 2 only (A); B, C and D include the false statement 3.
26.tq: Nutrients -> bloom -> decay -> no oxygen -> dead zone; blooms shade the seabed.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: a dying, decomposing bloom **strips oxygen** → **dead zones**.
Statement 2: the **Gulf of Mexico** dead zone comes from **Mississippi** runoff.
Statement 3 wrong: blooms **block sunlight** for corals and seagrass.
xa: Another dead zone: **Chesapeake Bay**.
Cause: excess **nitrogen and phosphorus** (farm runoff, sewage) → **eutrophication**.
**INCOIS** issues **algal bloom** and coral bleaching alerts.

26.s:
With reference to red tides, consider the following statements:
1. They are toxic algal blooms.
2. They are mostly associated with dinoflagellates.
3. They may discolour water.
4. They may kill fish and contaminate shellfish.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
26.x: Red tides are toxic blooms, mostly involving dinoflagellates, that can discolour water, kill fish and contaminate shellfish.
26.tq: Use the inclusive option when every listed characteristic belongs to the same phenomenon.
xs: All four statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
A **red tide** is a **toxic bloom**, mostly of **dinoflagellates**.
It **discolours water**, **kills fish** and **contaminates shellfish**.
xa: Dinoflagellates are also among the ocean's **primary producers** (phytoplankton).
Harmful algal blooms → decomposition → **dead zones**.
**INCOIS** issues algal bloom alerts.

26.s: The Aichi Target 11 under the Convention on Biological Diversity envisaged protection of what proportion of coastal and marine areas by 2020?
26.x: Aichi Target 11 set the goal of protecting 10 per cent of coastal and marine areas by 2020.
26.tq: Distinguish the Aichi target from the later 30x30 framework.
xs: **Aichi Target 11** (CBD, **2011-2020**) aimed to protect **10 per cent** of coastal and marine areas by **2020** — option **(2)**.
**30%** belongs to the later **30x30** target (by **2030**).
xa: 30x30: **30%** of land + **30%** of oceans by 2030 — **Kunming-Montreal GBF**, **COP15**, **Dec 2022**, **Target 3**.
**MPAs**, no-fishing zones and sanctuaries help reefs **recover**.
Recovery from large-scale bleaching takes **more than 15 years**.

26.s: The 30x30 target under Target 3 of the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework seeks to protect by 2030
26.x: The 30x30 target seeks protection of 30 per cent of land and 30 per cent of oceans by 2030. It was adopted under the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework at COP15 in December 2022.
26.tq: Use the numerical phrase itself to distinguish the target’s two components.
xs: **30x30** = protect **30% of land and 30% of oceans** by **2030** — option **(4)**.
It is **Target 3** of the **Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework**, adopted at **COP15**, **Dec 2022**.
xa: Earlier target: **Aichi Target 11** — **10%** of coastal and marine areas by **2020**.
**MPAs**, no-fishing zones and sanctuaries help reefs recover.
Since **2010** major reef disturbances recur every **4-6 years**.

26.s: Which one of the following current-affairs pairs is correctly matched?
o: Pavona clavus — artificial reef modules off Ramanathapuram
D-COIN — oil sardine fishery off Kerala
PMMSY — coral colony near Kadmat Island
Pavona clavus — giant potato patch coral colony near Kadmat Island, Lakshadweep
26.x: A giant Pavona clavus (potato patch coral) colony was reported near Kadmat Island, Lakshadweep. Options A and C mismatch Pavona clavus and PMMSY, and B wrongly pairs D-COIN with the oil sardine fishery.
26.tq: Separate the species-location pair from the programme-location pair.
xs: **Pavona clavus** — giant **potato patch coral** colony near **Kadmat Island, Lakshadweep** — option **(4)**.
Option (1) gives Pavona clavus the wrong place; option (3) pairs the Kadmat colony with the wrong name.
xa: **Lakshadweep** has India's **only true atolls**.
**Feb 2025** bleaching also hit **Lakshadweep**.
Atoll = **ring-shaped** reef enclosing a lagoon, no central island.

26.s: The National Green Tribunal’s clearance of the ₹92,000-crore Great Nicobar project included a direction to:
o: Protect and regenerate coral reefs through the Environment Ministry
Remove all coral reefs before project construction
Suspend all marine research in the Nicobar Islands
Transfer coral-reef protection exclusively to the Fisheries Ministry
26.x: The NGT clearance directed the Environment Ministry to protect and regenerate coral reefs; coral loss remained a central objection to the project.
26.tq: Identify the authority’s actual environmental direction instead of an extreme or transferred power.
xs: The NGT directed the **Environment Ministry** to **protect and regenerate coral reefs** — option **(1)**.
The **₹92,000-crore Great Nicobar project** was cleared in **Feb 2026**; **coral loss** remains the core objection.
xa: **Andaman & Nicobar** has India's **highest reef diversity**.
**Andaman** mass bleaching was linked to about a **2°C rise** in Indian Ocean temperature.
Reefs **break wave power**, preventing coastal erosion.

26.s:
With reference to Andhra Pradesh, consider the following statements:
1. Andhra Pradesh has no true coral reefs.
2. Its fisheries depend partly on plankton productivity in the Bay of Bengal.
3. Marine heatwaves threaten this plankton-supported fisheries base.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
26.x: All three statements are correct: Andhra Pradesh has no true coral reefs, while its fisheries rely on Bay of Bengal plankton productivity that is threatened by marine heatwaves.
26.tq: Combine the regional exception with the linked fisheries and climate relationship.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: **AP has no true coral reefs** — **heavy river sediment + freshwater** on the east coast.
Statements 2-3: AP fisheries depend on **Bay of Bengal plankton productivity**, now threatened by **marine heatwaves**.
xa: Other east-coast states without reefs: **West Bengal, Odisha**.
**Phytoplankton** are the ocean's main **primary producers**.
⚠ Highest diversity = **Andaman & Nicobar**; only atolls = **Lakshadweep**; AP = **no reefs**.

26.s: Which of the following statements about coral reefs is incorrect?
o: They are mainly distributed in tropical and semi-tropical waters.
Coral reefs are formed through consolidation of the skeletons of marine organisms or coral polyps.
They are typically found around 25°N–25°S, with some extension to about 30°.
They are generally poor in biodiversity because they occur only in shallow marine settings.
26.x: Option D is incorrect: coral reefs are among the richest ecosystems on Earth. They grow in warm waters of about 25°N–25°S from polyp skeletons.
26.tq: Check for a reversed property.
n: Coral reefs form through consolidation of the skeletons of marine organisms and coral polyps. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
Coral reefs are distributed mainly in tropical and semi-tropical waters. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
Coral reefs are typically found around 25°N–25°S. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
Some coral reefs extend to approximately 30° latitude. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
Coral reefs are extremely rich marine habitats. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
xs: The incorrect statement is that reefs are **generally poor in biodiversity** — option **(4)**.
Coral reefs are **highly diverse** marine ecosystems — **extremely rich marine habitats**.
They lie mainly in **tropical and semi-tropical waters**, around **25°N–25°S** (some to ~**30°**), formed from **coral polyp skeletons**.
xa: **"Rainforests of the Sea"**: under **1%** of the ocean floor, over **25%** of marine species.
Polyps live in **mutualism** with **zooxanthellae** algae.
Need warm water (**above ~20 deg C**), **clear, shallow, sunlit** water.

26.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Phytoplankton are primary producers.
II. Zooplankton are animal plankton and form part of the food chain.
III. Nekton are organisms associated with the ocean bottom.
IV. Benthos are actively swimming organisms.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
26.x: I and II are correct: phytoplankton are producers and zooplankton animal plankton. III and IV are swapped: nekton swim actively and benthos live on the bottom.
26.tq: Check for swapped definitions.
n: Phytoplankton are primary producers. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
Zooplankton are animal plankton. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
Zooplankton are part of the food chain. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
Nekton are actively swimming organisms. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
Benthos are organisms associated with the ocean bottom. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
xs: Statements **I and II** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
I: **phytoplankton** are **primary producers**.
II: **zooplankton** are **animal plankton**, part of the **food chain**.
III and IV are swapped: **nekton** are **actively swimming**; **benthos** are **associated with the ocean bottom**.
xa: **Plankton** = organisms that **drift** with water.
Phytoplankton include **diatoms, dinoflagellates, cyanobacteria**.
Oceans, mainly phytoplankton, produce **about half** of Earth's **oxygen**.

26.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Main distribution of coral reefs
(b) Typical latitude of coral reefs
(c) Major concentration areas
(d) Biodiversity of coral reefs

List-II
(i) Extremely rich marine habitats
(ii) Mainly tropical and semi-tropical waters
(iii) Around 25°N–25°S, with some extension to about 30°
(iv) Australia, Indonesia and the Philippines
26.x: Coral reefs are mainly in tropical and semi-tropical waters, around 25°N–25°S, concentrated in Australia, Indonesia and the Philippines, and are extremely rich habitats, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i.
26.tq: Recall the features of coral reefs.
n: Coral reefs are distributed mainly in tropical and semi-tropical waters. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
Coral reefs are typically found around 25°N–25°S. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
Some coral reefs extend to approximately 30° latitude. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
Coral reefs are extremely rich marine habitats. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
Australia is a major concentration of coral reefs. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
Indonesia is a major concentration of coral reefs. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
The Philippines is a major concentration of coral reefs. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
xs: The correct match is **a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Distribution** = **tropical and semi-tropical waters**; **latitude** = around **25°N–25°S**, some to ~**30°**.
**Major concentrations** = **Australia, Indonesia, Philippines**; **biodiversity** = **extremely rich marine habitats**.
xa: **Great Barrier Reef** (Queensland) is the **largest coral reef system**, ~**2,300 km** long; **UNESCO** site **1981**.
India: **Andaman & Nicobar** = **highest diversity**; **Lakshadweep** = only true **atolls**.
**Andhra Pradesh** has **no reefs** — heavy river sediment.
⚠ Other notes give **30 deg N-30 deg S**.

27.s:
Consider the following statements regarding India's disaster vulnerability:
1. About 58.6% of India's landmass faces moderate-to-very-high earthquake risk.
2. More than 40 million hectares, approximately 12% of the area, is flood-prone.
3. About 68% of the cultivable area is vulnerable to drought.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
27.x: All three are correct: about 58.6% of the landmass faces moderate-to-very-high earthquake risk, over 40 million ha (~12%) is flood-prone, and about 68% of the cultivable area is drought-vulnerable.
27.tq: Check each numerical statement independently before selecting the coded combination.
xs: All three statements are correct — so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: about **58.6%** of India's landmass faces **moderate-to-very-high earthquakes** (NDMA).
Statement 2 is correct: more than **40 million ha (~12%)** of India is **flood-prone**.
Statement 3 is correct: about **68%** of the **cultivable area** is drought-vulnerable.
xa: About **5,700 km** of the old **7,516.6 km** coastline is exposed to **cyclones and tsunamis**.
**Assam** alone has **31.05 lakh ha** of flood-prone area.
⚠ The coastline was remeasured to **11,098.81 km** (MHA, **Dec 2024**) — older hazard shares still use the old base.
**World Risk Index 2025:** India is the **2nd most vulnerable** country, after the **Philippines**.

27.s: According to the World Risk Index 2025, India is the world's second most vulnerable country after which country?
27.x: The World Risk Index 2025 places India as the second most vulnerable country, after the Philippines.
27.tq: Direct ranking recall.
xs: In the **World Risk Index 2025**, India is the **2nd most vulnerable** country, after **the Philippines** — so option **(4)** is correct.
India's risk is dominated by **floods and storms**, while **China and Indonesia** face higher **seismic** risk.
xa: India loses about **0.4% of GDP every year** to disasters (1990-2024).
About **58.6%** of the landmass faces moderate-to-very-high earthquakes; ~**68%** of cultivable area is drought-vulnerable.
Core formula: **Hazard x Vulnerability = Disaster**.

27.s: Which of the following hazard-to-region associations is correctly matched?
o: Cyclones — east coast; drought — Rajasthan and the Deccan interior
Drought — Western Ghats; earthquakes — east coast only
27.x: Cyclones are especially associated with the east coast, while drought is prominent in Rajasthan and the Deccan interior. Floods affect the Brahmaputra-Ganga plains, earthquakes the Himalaya and Kutch, and landslides the Himalaya and Western Ghats.
27.tq: Check both hazard and regional setting in each pair.
xs: **Cyclones — east coast** and **drought — Rajasthan + Deccan interior** are both correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Option (1) is wrong: **earthquakes** belong to the **Himalaya + Kutch**, and the **Brahmaputra-Ganga plains** are the **flood** region.
Option (3) is wrong: **landslides** occur in the **Himalaya + Western Ghats**; **Kutch** is an earthquake zone.
Option (4) is wrong: the **Western Ghats** are a landslide zone, and earthquakes are not tied to the east coast.
xa: Full NDMA map: **Floods** → Brahmaputra-Ganga plains; **Earthquakes** → Himalaya + Kutch; **Landslides** → Himalaya + Western Ghats.
The **east coast** gets far more cyclones than the west; **Andhra Pradesh** is the most cyclone-prone state.
**Drought-prone regions** also include Kutch-Saurashtra, Marathwada-Vidarbha, interior Karnataka and **Rayalaseema** (AP).

27.s: Which organisation publishes the annual Global Report on Internal Displacement?
27.x: The Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre, headquartered in Geneva, publishes the annual Global Report on Internal Displacement.
27.tq: Match the report with its specialised international institution.
xs: The **Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre (IDMC)**, based in **Geneva**, publishes the annual **Global Report on Internal Displacement** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The IDMC tracks people displaced within their own countries; disasters displace **millions** every year.
xa: **Water-related disasters worldwide (2025):** about **5,000 deaths** and **8 million** displaced.
**Emerging Asia (OECD):** about **100 disasters a year** affecting about **80 million** people.
India's main risk drivers are **floods and storms**.

27.s:
Consider the following statements about India's disaster losses:
1. India loses about 0.4% of its GDP every year to disasters (1990-2024).
2. Droughts and earthquakes are the principal drivers of India's disaster risk.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
27.x: Statement 1 is correct: the economic loss is about 0.4% of GDP a year (1990-2024). Statement 2 is wrong: the risk drivers are FLOODS AND STORMS. Hence 1 only; the other options accept the wrong drivers or reject the correct loss figure.
27.tq: India's risk = floods + storms; loss about 0.4% of GDP a year.
xs: Only **statement 1** is correct — so option **(1) 1 only** is the answer.
Statement 1 is correct: India's **economic loss** from disasters is about **0.4% of GDP every year** (**1990-2024**).
Statement 2 is wrong: the **risk drivers** are **floods and storms**, not droughts and earthquakes.
xa: **2025 toll:** about **331** days of climate impacts and **over 4,000 deaths**; heaviest toll in **HP** and **Uttarakhand**.
**IDMC** (Geneva) publishes the annual **Global Report on Internal Displacement**.
**Emerging Asia (OECD):** about **100** disasters a year affecting about **80 million** people.
**World Risk Index 2025:** India is the **2nd most vulnerable** country, after the **Philippines**.

27.s: In 2025, the heaviest toll from climate-induced disasters in India was reported in:
27.x: More than 4,000 deaths were reported in India from climate-induced disasters in 2025, with the heaviest toll in Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand.
27.tq: Link the national figure with the specifically identified regional concentration.
xs: The heaviest 2025 toll from climate-induced disasters was in **Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand** — so option **(2)** is correct.
In **2025**, India saw about **331 days** of climate impacts and **over 4,000 deaths** from climate-induced disasters.
xa: **2025 flash floods** at **Dharali and Harsil** (Uttarkashi) diverted the **Bhagirathi**.
**Mandi (HP)** got nearly **20 times** its normal rain in 2025.
The **Dharali flood (5 Aug 2025)** came from an **ice-patch collapse on the Srikanta glacier** (ISRO study).

27.s:
Which of the following sets contains only causes of floods identified for India?
1. Heavy or prolonged rainfall
2. Poor drainage and low infiltration
3. Deforestation and dam failure
4. Siltation resulting from soil erosion
27.x: Heavy rainfall, poor drainage, low infiltration, deforestation, dam failure and siltation from soil erosion are all recognised causes of floods.
27.tq: Check whether each listed causal factor belongs to the same hazard rather than selecting a partial combination.
xs: All four are recognised causes of floods — so option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4** is correct.
**Heavy/prolonged rainfall, poor drainage, deforestation and dam failure** are the APPSC 2025 key causes.
**Low infiltration** and **siltation from soil erosion** are further causes, along with storm surges and snow/ice melt.
xa: **Assam:** **800 sq km** of upstream **Nagaland** forest was cleared in **2013-23**, causing faster runoff.
**Rashtriya Barh Ayog** assessed about **40 million ha** as flood-prone.
Flood types: **riverine, flash, coastal, urban**.

27.s: Riverine flooding in the Krishna-Godavari region may become particularly severe when water is released simultaneously from:
27.x: Flooding in the Krishna-Godavari region can be especially severe when Srisailam, Nagarjuna Sagar and Hirakud release water together.
27.tq: Test the linked dam names through a same-basin and downstream-impact association.
xs: Krishna-Godavari delta floods are worst when **Srisailam, Nagarjuna Sagar and Hirakud** release water together — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Hirakud** is in **Odisha**; the **Krishna-Godavari deltas** are AP's main riverine-flood zone.
xa: AP faces three hazards: **coastal cyclones, delta floods and Rayalaseema drought**.
**Urban flooding** in AP hits **Vijayawada** (Budameru rivulet), Visakhapatnam and Guntur.
Flood control is a **state subject**, supported by the Centre through **FMBAP**.

27.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Rashtriya Barh Ayog is the National Flood Commission.
2. The Rashtriya Barh Ayog assessed about 40 million hectares as flood-prone.
3. Flood control is a Union subject, with States only implementing central schemes.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
27.x: Statement 1 is correct: Rashtriya Barh Ayog = National Flood Commission. Statement 2 is correct: it assessed about 40 million ha as flood-prone. Statement 3 is wrong: flood control is a State subject; the Centre only supports States through FMBAP. So '1 only' misses 2, while '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' include the false statement 3.
27.tq: Flood control = State subject; Centre helps via FMBAP.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — so option **(2) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: **Rashtriya Barh Ayog** is the **National Flood Commission** (set up **1976**; some notes give **1980**).
Statement 2 is correct: it assessed about **40 million ha** as flood-prone.
Statement 3 is wrong: flood control is a **state subject**; the Centre only supports states through **FMBAP**.
xa: The **Expert Committee for Scientific Assessment of Flood-Prone Areas** was set up in **2012** by the **Ministry of Water Resources**.
**India-China ELM** on flood data held its **16th meeting** in **Apr 2025**.
**India-Bhutan JGE** held its **11th meeting** in **May 2025**.

27.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
27.x: Flood insurance is a non-structural measure. Dams and reservoirs, and channel and drainage improvement are structural measures, while flood-plain zoning is non-structural.
27.tq: Find the classification reversal by comparing physical construction with policy and financial tools.
xs: **Flood insurance** is a **non-structural** measure, so "Flood insurance—structural measure" is wrongly matched — option **(1)** is correct.
**Channel and drainage improvement** and diversion are **structural** measures, so option (2) is correctly matched.
Non-structural measures are **flood-proofing, flood fighting and flood insurance**.
xa: Flood control is a **state subject**; the Centre supports states via **FMBAP**.
**Rashtriya Barh Ayog** (National Flood Commission) assessed about **40 million ha** as flood-prone.
Flood types: **riverine, flash, coastal and urban**.

27.s: Which sequence correctly explains the formation of a glacial lake outburst flood?
o: Glacier retreat → enlargement of a proglacial lake → bursting of the lake → flood
Deforestation → oceanic tide → lake freezing → flood
River siltation → volcanic eruption → glacier advance → flood
Rain shadow → soil erosion → sea-level fall → flood
27.x: Glacier retreat can enlarge proglacial lakes; when the lake bursts, the stored water produces a glacial lake outburst flood.
27.tq: Arrange the causal chain from environmental change to disaster occurrence.
xs: A GLOF forms by **glacier retreat → enlargement of a proglacial lake → bursting of the lake → flood** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**GLOF** = **glacial lake outburst flood**: glacier retreat enlarges proglacial lakes that later burst.
xa: **Nepal** saw catastrophic GLOF flash floods on **26 Aug 2026**; UNDP counts **26 GLOFs since the 1970s**.
The world has lost **9,500+ Gt** of glacier mass since **1975**.
**Central Himalaya** glacier area is down **>20%** in three decades.

27.s:
Consider the following statements about the Dharali flash flood of 5 August 2025 in Uttarakhand:
1. The flash floods at Dharali and Harsil diverted the Alaknanda river.
2. An ISRO study attributed it to the collapse of an ice patch on the Srikanta glacier.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
27.x: Statement 2 is correct: ISRO linked the Dharali flood to an ice-patch collapse on the Srikanta glacier. Statement 1 is wrong: the Dharali-Harsil floods diverted the BHAGIRATHI, not the Alaknanda. Hence 2 only.
27.tq: Dharali (Uttarkashi) = Srikanta glacier + Bhagirathi.
xs: Only **statement 2** is correct — so option **(1) 2 only** is the answer.
Statement 2 is correct: an **ISRO study** traced the Dharali flood (**5 Aug 2025**) to an **ice-patch collapse on the Srikanta glacier**.
Statement 1 is wrong: the **Dharali and Harsil** (Uttarkashi) flash floods diverted the **Bhagirathi**, not the Alaknanda.
xa: **Mandi (HP)** got nearly **20 times** normal rain in **2025**.
**Kedarnath (June 2013):** a **cloudburst** and a **GLOF** contributed.
**Nepal:** catastrophic GLOF flash floods on **26 Aug 2026**; **26 GLOFs since the 1970s** (UNDP).
Central Himalaya **glacier area** down **>20%** in three decades.

27.s: The India Meteorological Department provides flash-flood guidance not only for India but also to which group of neighbouring countries?
27.x: IMD supplies flash-flood guidance for India and neighbouring Bangladesh, Bhutan and Nepal.
27.tq: Match the agency with the correct cross-border service recipients.
xs: **IMD** gives flash-flood guidance for India and its neighbours **Bangladesh, Bhutan and Nepal** — so option **(1)** is correct.
These neighbours share Himalayan and Bengal-delta river basins with India.
xa: **Cloudburst (IMD):** about **100 mm per hour** over a small area (**~20-30 sq km**).
**India-Bhutan JGE** on floods held its **11th meeting** in **May 2025**; **India-China ELM** its **16th** in **Apr 2025**.
**ITWS** warns **25** Indian Ocean countries of tsunamis within **10 minutes**.

27.s: Which statement best describes the monsoon paradox in the Hindu Kush-Himalaya region?
o: Seasonal rainfall is increasing uniformly while cloudbursts are declining.
Seasonal rainfall is declining or becoming erratic while short, intense cloudbursts are increasing.
Cloudbursts occur only during winter and are unrelated to monsoon behaviour.
Both seasonal rainfall and short-duration rainfall are declining at the same rate.
27.x: The HKH monsoon paradox refers to declining or erratic seasonal rainfall occurring alongside an increase in short, intense cloudbursts.
27.tq: Identify the contrasting trends within the same climatic system.
xs: The HKH **monsoon paradox**: **seasonal rainfall is declining or erratic while short, intense cloudbursts are increasing** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It is a paradox because total seasonal rain falls even as extreme short bursts rise.
xa: **Cloudburst (IMD):** about **100 mm per hour** over ~**20-30 sq km**.
**GLOFs:** glacier retreat enlarges proglacial lakes that burst.
The world has lost **9,500+ Gt** of glacier mass since **1975**.

27.s: Cloudbursts in the Eastern Ghats agency areas of Andhra Pradesh are particularly hazardous because they can:
o: Eliminate monsoon breaks throughout the State
Produce only inland droughts without runoff
Cause flash floods in narrow valleys
27.x: Cloudbursts in Andhra Pradesh's Eastern Ghats agency areas can rapidly generate flash floods in narrow valleys.
27.tq: Apply the hazard mechanism to the specified terrain and regional setting.
xs: Cloudbursts in AP's **Eastern Ghats** agency areas **cause flash floods in narrow valleys** — so option **(4)** is correct.
A cloudburst is about **100 mm per hour** over a small area, so steep narrow valleys flood quickly.
xa: AP's three hazards: **coastal cyclones, delta floods and Rayalaseema drought**.
**Vijayawada** floods are linked to the **Budameru** rivulet.
AP coast has seen **62+ cyclonic events** in four decades.

27.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Mumbai — 26 July 2005 urban flood
2. Chennai — December 2015 urban flood
3. Vijayawada — Budameru-related urban flooding
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
27.x: All three pairs are correctly matched. The Vijayawada case is associated with flooding linked to the Budameru rivulet.
27.tq: Use a familiar pair to eliminate mismatched city-event combinations.
xs: All three pairs are correctly matched — so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
**Mumbai** flooded on **26 July 2005**; **Chennai** in **Dec 2015**.
**Vijayawada** floods are linked to the **Budameru rivulet**.
xa: Urban flood causes: **unplanned concretisation**, blocked drains, encroached lakes and extreme rainfall.
**AP City Flood Alert** uses satellite **DEM** plus ~**30 years** of Budameru data.
It gives **48-hour rainfall** forecasts and **6-hour flash-flood** warnings.

27.s:
Consider the following statements about Andhra Pradesh's AI-based City Flood Alert platform (July 2026):
1. It is to be implemented first in Vijayawada and later in all ULBs.
2. It gives 24-hour rainfall forecasts and 12-hour flash-flood warnings.
3. It was developed by RTGS and APSDMA with IIT Gandhinagar.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
27.x: Statement 3 is correct: RTGS, APSDMA and IIT Gandhinagar built it. Statement 2 is NOT correct: it gives 48-hour rainfall forecasts and 6-hour flash-flood warnings. Statement 1 is correct: it starts in Vijayawada (Budameru data) and later covers all ULBs. So only statement 2 is incorrect.
27.tq: City Flood Alert = 48 h rain + 6 h flash flood, Vijayawada first.
xs: Only **statement 2** is NOT correct — so option **(2) 2 only** is the answer.
Statement 2 is wrong: the platform gives **48-hour rainfall** forecasts and **6-hour flash-flood** warnings.
Statement 1 is correct: it starts in **Vijayawada**, later **all ULBs**.
Statement 3 is correct: it is an **AI platform** by **RTGS + APSDMA + IIT Gandhinagar**.
xa: It uses **satellite DEM** plus about **30 years** of **Budameru** data.
**Vijayawada** floods come from the **Budameru rivulet**; Visakhapatnam and Guntur are other AP flood cities.
Urban floods come under the **Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs**.

27.s:
Match the type of drought with its meaning:
a. Hydrological drought
b. Agricultural drought
c. Socio-economic drought

i. Soil-moisture deficit causing crop failure
ii. Water and food shortage hitting livelihoods and markets
iii. Fall in surface and groundwater after prolonged deficiency
Select the correct answer.
27.x: Hydrological drought is the fall in rivers, reservoirs and aquifers (iii); agricultural drought is a soil-moisture deficit causing crop failure (i); socio-economic drought is water/food shortage hitting livelihoods and markets (ii). So a-iii, b-i, c-ii. The second option swaps hydrological and agricultural; the third swaps agricultural and socio-economic; the fourth swaps hydrological and socio-economic.
27.tq: Hydrological = water bodies; agricultural = soil moisture; socio-economic = people and markets.
xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-i, c-ii** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Hydrological** drought (a) = **fall in surface and groundwater** after prolonged deficiency (iii).
**Agricultural** drought (b) = **soil-moisture deficit** causing crop failure (i).
**Socio-economic** drought (c) = **water/food shortage** hitting livelihoods and markets (ii).
xa: **Meteorological** drought = rainfall well below the **long-period average** over a period.
**Ecological** drought = ecosystem productivity collapses.
About **68%** of cultivable area is drought-vulnerable.

27.s:
Consider the following statements regarding ecological drought:
1. It involves a collapse of ecosystem productivity.
2. It is associated with environmental distress.
3. It is defined exclusively by a decline in rainfall below the long-period average.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
27.x: Ecological drought involves collapsing ecosystem productivity and environmental distress. Statement 3 describes meteorological drought, not ecological drought.
27.tq: Find the statement that swaps the defining indicator of one drought type with another.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — so option **(1) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
Statements 1 and 2 are correct: **ecological drought** means **ecosystem productivity collapses** with **environmental distress**.
Statement 3 is wrong: rainfall below the long-period average defines **meteorological** drought.
xa: **Hydrological** drought: fall in surface and groundwater after prolonged deficiency.
**Agricultural** drought: soil-moisture deficit causing crop failure.
Drought effects include **land degradation**, desertification and **ecosystem damage**.

27.s:
Which of the following climatic conditions can trigger or intensify drought in India?
1. Irregular or delayed monsoon
2. Monsoon breaks
3. El Nino conditions
4. High temperature and evaporation
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
27.x: Irregular or delayed monsoon, monsoon breaks, El Nino, and high temperature with enhanced evaporation are all drought triggers.
27.tq: Test a complete cause-list, including both atmospheric and heat-related triggers.
xs: All four can trigger or intensify drought — so option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4** is correct.
Climatic triggers: **irregular or delayed monsoon**, monsoon failure, **monsoon breaks** and **high temperature**.
**El Nino:** **6 of 10** El Nino years depressed Indian rain; **high heat + evaporation** speed soil-moisture loss.
xa: Normal SW-monsoon rainfall: **868.6 mm** (**1971-2020** base).
About **68%** of the cultivable area is drought-vulnerable.
Drought-prone: Western Rajasthan, Kutch-Saurashtra, Marathwada-Vidarbha, interior Karnataka, **Rayalaseema**.

27.s: Which one of the following is NOT a long-term consequence of recurrent droughts?
o: A sustained increase in farm output
27.x: Droughts generally reduce farm output; they contribute to groundwater depletion, land degradation, desertification and distress migration.
27.tq: Identify the reversed trend in a list of long-term consequences.
xs: **A sustained increase in farm output** is not a drought effect — so option **(3)** is correct.
Droughts cause **lower farm output**, not higher.
The real long-term effects are **groundwater depletion**, **land degradation and desertification** and **rural (distress) migration**.
xa: Drought also brings **rural indebtedness** and **ecosystem damage**.
In **Rayalaseema**, **deep borewells** cause severe groundwater depletion.
About **68%** of the cultivable area is drought-vulnerable.

27.s: Rayalaseema is highly drought-prone mainly because of which combination of factors?
o: Frequent storm surges, tidal bores and mangrove expansion
Permanent high rainfall, waterlogging and salinity alone
Excessive snowfall, glacier retreat and coastal inundation
Failure of the monsoon, crop loss, distress migration and severe groundwater depletion
27.x: Rayalaseema faces monsoon failure, crop losses, distress migration and severe groundwater depletion, aggravated by deep borewells. The North-East monsoon is particularly important in the region.
27.tq: Combine several linked causes and consequences in a region-specific scenario.
xs: Rayalaseema is drought-prone due to **failure of the monsoon, crop loss, distress migration and severe groundwater depletion** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Deep borewells** cause the severe groundwater depletion.
Some notes stress failure of the **North-East monsoon** in Rayalaseema.
xa: **Rayalaseema drought** is one of AP's three hazards, with **coastal cyclones** and **delta floods**.
Other drought-prone regions: Western Rajasthan, Kutch-Saurashtra, Marathwada-Vidarbha, interior Karnataka.
Hazard → region: **drought** → **Rajasthan + Deccan interior**.

27.s: Which of the following is NOT listed among the drought-prone regions of India?
27.x: Lower Assam is flood-prone (Brahmaputra plains), not drought-prone. The drought-prone regions listed are western Rajasthan, Kutch-Saurashtra, Marathwada-Vidarbha, interior Karnataka and Rayalaseema.
27.tq: Find the geographically misplaced region in a regional classification.
xs: **Lower Assam** is not a drought-prone region — so option **(2)** is correct.
Assam is **flood-prone**: **31.05 lakh ha** of flood-prone area, in the **Brahmaputra-Ganga plains** flood belt.
**Interior Karnataka, Western Rajasthan and Kutch-Saurashtra** are listed drought-prone regions.
xa: Others listed: **Marathwada-Vidarbha** and **Rayalaseema** (AP).
Hazard → region: **drought** → **Rajasthan + Deccan interior**.
About **68%** of cultivable area is drought-vulnerable.

27.s: The term ‘tsunami’ is derived from which combination of Japanese words and meanings?
27.x: In Japanese, ‘tsu’ means harbour and ‘nami’ means wave; hence tsunami literally means ‘harbour wave’.
27.tq: Test the exact meaning of a look-alike term rather than accepting the familiar but incorrect ‘tidal wave’.
xs: **Tsu = harbour, nami = wave** ("harbour wave") — so option **(1)** is correct.
The word is **Japanese**.
xa: A tsunami is a **series of waves** from **sudden vertical displacement of the ocean floor**.
⚠ **Trap:** a tsunami is not a "**tidal wave**" — tides come from **gravitational pull**.
Main cause: **undersea earthquakes** at **subduction zones**.

27.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes a tsunami from a tidal wave?
o: A tsunami results from sudden displacement of the ocean floor, whereas tides result mainly from gravitational pull.
A tsunami consists of a single wave, whereas tides always consist of multiple waves.
A tsunami is confined to shallow water, whereas tides occur only in deep oceans.
A tsunami is caused by gravitational attraction, whereas a tidal wave is caused by earthquakes.
27.x: Tsunamis are generated by sudden displacement of the ocean floor, usually due to tectonic activity. Tides are produced mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon and the Sun.
27.tq: Separate two commonly confused terms by matching each with its actual cause.
xs: A tsunami comes from **sudden displacement of the ocean floor**, while tides come from **gravitational pull** — so option **(1)** is correct.
⚠ Calling a tsunami a "**tidal wave**" is a trap.
Option (2) is wrong: a tsunami is a **series of waves**, not a single wave.
xa: Causes: mainly **undersea earthquakes**, also volcanic eruptions, **submarine landslides** and asteroid impacts.
Deep ocean: speed up to **800 km/h**, height **under 1 m**.
Warning sign: sudden **receding of sea water**.

27.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the causes of tsunamis:
1. Subduction-related undersea earthquakes are the chief cause of tsunamis.
2. Submarine landslides and volcanic eruptions can also generate tsunamis.
3. Asteroid or meteorite impacts in the ocean can produce tsunamis.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
27.x: All three statements are correct. Tsunamis may result from tectonic earthquakes, submarine landslides, volcanic eruptions and large asteroid or meteorite impacts.
27.tq: Use the inclusive option after checking whether every listed triggering mechanism is supported.
xs: All three statements are correct — so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: the main cause is **undersea earthquakes**, chiefly at **subduction zones**.
Statement 2 is correct: **volcanic eruptions** and **submarine landslides** can also cause tsunamis.
Statement 3 is correct: **asteroid/meteorite impacts** are also listed.
xa: Definition: series of waves from **sudden vertical displacement of the ocean floor**.
Most tsunamis affecting India originate in the **Indian Ocean** (**Sumatra-Andaman / Sunda** subduction zone).
The **Makran zone** threatens the **west coast**.

27.s:
Consider the following statements about tsunami waves:
1. In the deep ocean a tsunami has a very long wavelength and a height usually under 1 m.
2. In the deep ocean it can travel at about 700-800 km/h.
3. On entering shallow coastal water the wave speeds up, which is why its height falls.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
27.x: Statement 1 is correct: deep-ocean tsunamis have very long wavelength and low height (under 1 m). Statement 2 is correct: speed reaches ~700-800 km/h. Statement 3 is wrong: near the coast the wave slows and its height rises sharply (shoaling). So '1 only' misses 2, while '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' include the false statement 3.
27.tq: Near the coast: speed down, height up (shoaling).
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — so option **(2) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: in the deep ocean a tsunami has a **very long wavelength** and height **under 1 m**.
Statement 2 is correct: deep-ocean speed is about **700-800 km/h**.
Statement 3 is wrong: near the coast the wave **slows down** and its **height rises sharply** (**shoaling**).
xa: Near the coast it causes **massive inundation**.
Warning signs: sudden **receding of sea water**, rapid sea-level rise, earthquake shaking.
**ITWS** warns **25** Indian Ocean countries within **10 minutes**.

27.s: Tsunamis affecting India mostly originate from which combination of regions?
o: Bering Sea and Gulf of Mexico
27.x: Most tsunamis affecting India originate in the Indian Ocean, particularly from the Sunda-Andaman subduction zone; the Makran zone poses a threat to India’s west coast.
27.tq: Start from the sure geographical source and distinguish the eastern and western Indian Ocean threat zones.
xs: Tsunamis affecting India mostly come from the **Sunda-Andaman** and **Makran** subduction zones — so option **(2)** is correct.
Most originate in the **Indian Ocean** (APPSC 2025 key), at the **Sumatra-Andaman (Sunda) subduction zone**.
The **Makran zone** threatens India's **west coast**.
xa: **Andaman & Nicobar** is the **very high** risk zone, being near the Sunda subduction zone.
The **2004** tsunami was triggered by the **Sumatra-Andaman earthquake**, **Mw ~9.1**.
**NIOT Nellore**'s **OMNI buoys** feed the tsunami warning system.

27.s: Which of the following is the correct order of tsunami risk zones from highest to moderate risk in India?
o: Tamil Nadu—Andaman and Nicobar—Kerala, Karnataka, Goa, Maharashtra and Gujarat
Andhra Pradesh and Odisha—Gujarat and Maharashtra—Andaman and Nicobar
Kerala, Karnataka, Goa, Maharashtra and Gujarat—Tamil Nadu—Andaman and Nicobar
Andaman and Nicobar—Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Puducherry and Odisha—Kerala, Karnataka, Goa, Maharashtra and Gujarat
27.x: Andaman and Nicobar Islands are in the very-high-risk zone; Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Puducherry and Odisha are in the high-risk zone; Kerala, Karnataka, Goa, Maharashtra and Gujarat are in the moderate-risk zone.
27.tq: Read the risk classification from highest to moderate without reversing the geographical grouping.
xs: The order is **Andaman & Nicobar → TN, AP, Puducherry, Odisha → Kerala, Karnataka, Goa, Maharashtra, Gujarat** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Very high:** **Andaman & Nicobar**, near the **Sunda subduction zone**.
**High:** Tamil Nadu, **Andhra Pradesh**, Puducherry, Odisha; **Moderate:** Kerala, Karnataka, Goa, Maharashtra, Gujarat.
xa: ⚠ Very high risk = **A&N**; worst hit in **2004** = **Tamil Nadu** (**Nagapattinam**).
The **Makran zone** threatens the west coast.
**ITWS** warns **25** Indian Ocean countries within **10 minutes**.

27.s:
With reference to the Indian Ocean tsunami of 26 December 2004, consider the following statements:
1. It was triggered by an earthquake near the Sumatra-Andaman region.
2. The earthquake had a magnitude of approximately 9.1.
3. Nagapattinam was the worst-affected district in Tamil Nadu.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
27.x: The 26 December 2004 tsunami was generated by an approximately magnitude 9.1 Sumatra-Andaman earthquake, and Nagapattinam was the worst-affected district in Tamil Nadu.
27.tq: Combine event, magnitude and location facts; the all-inclusive option is correct when each detail fits.
xs: All three statements are correct — so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: the **26 Dec 2004** tsunami was triggered by the **Sumatra-Andaman earthquake**.
Statement 2 is correct: its magnitude was **Mw ~9.1**.
Statement 3 is correct: **Nagapattinam** was the worst-hit district of **Tamil Nadu**.
xa: **Tamil Nadu** was the **worst-hit state** (APPSC 2025 key).
Also hit: **A&N Islands, Kerala, AP, Puducherry**.
⚠ Very high risk zone = **A&N**, but worst hit in 2004 = **Tamil Nadu**.

27.s: Which Indian State was the worst hit by the Indian Ocean tsunami of 26 December 2004?
27.x: Tamil Nadu was the worst-hit State, with Nagapattinam the worst-affected district. Andhra Pradesh and Kerala were also hit but less severely; Odisha was not among the main affected areas listed.
27.tq: 2004 tsunami worst hit: Tamil Nadu (Nagapattinam).
xs: **Tamil Nadu** was the worst-hit state in the **26 Dec 2004** tsunami — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Nagapattinam** was the worst district/coast (APPSC 2025 key).
**Andhra Pradesh** and **Kerala** were also hit, along with A&N Islands and Puducherry, but less than Tamil Nadu.
xa: The trigger was the **Sumatra-Andaman earthquake**, **Mw ~9.1**.
⚠ Very high risk zone = **A&N**; worst hit in 2004 = **Tamil Nadu**.
High-risk zone: Tamil Nadu, **Andhra Pradesh**, Puducherry, Odisha.

27.s:
Consider the following statements about storm surges:
1. Sea-level rise can increase their coastal-flooding impact.
2. They can cause permanent inundation of low-lying coastal land.
3. They are produced exclusively by rainfall over the sea.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
27.x: Sea-level rise magnifies storm-surge impacts and may result in permanent inundation of low-lying land. Storm surges are not produced exclusively by rainfall.
27.tq: Reject the absolute causal claim and retain the two linked coastal effects.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: with **sea-level rise**, surges cause more **coastal flooding**.
Statement 2: they can cause **permanent inundation** of low-lying land.
Statement 3 wrong: surges are pushed by **cyclone winds + low pressure**, not by rainfall alone.
xa: Cyclones affect **13 coastal states/UTs** and **84 coastal districts**.
The **east coast** gets far more cyclones than the west.
AP coast: **62+ cyclonic events** in four decades.

27.s: Which of the following combinations represents components of coastal defence against storm surges?
o: Mangroves, coastal shelter belts, dune stabilisation and seawalls
Glaciers, aquifers and inland reservoirs only
Deep borewells, contour ploughing and check dams only
27.x: Mangroves and shelter belts anchor sediment and buffer storm surges, while dune stabilisation and seawalls strengthen coastal defence.
27.tq: Match protective measures with the hazard they mitigate.
xs: **Mangroves, coastal shelter belts, dune stabilisation and seawalls** form coastal defence — option **(1)**.
Mangroves and shelter belts **anchor sediment** and **buffer storm surges**.
Glaciers, aquifers, borewells, check dams and desert landforms have nothing to do with surge defence.
xa: Storm surge = abnormal sea-level rise from **cyclone winds + low pressure**.
Very high tsunami risk zone: **Andaman & Nicobar**.
AP faces **coastal cyclones, delta floods and Rayalaseema drought**.

27.s: The remeasurement that produced the revised coastline length was undertaken by the:
o: India Meteorological Department with the Geological Survey of India
National Disaster Management Authority with the Indian Coast Guard
Central Water Commission with the Forest Survey of India
National Hydrographic Office with the Survey of India
27.x: The revised coastline was measured by the National Hydrographic Office in association with the Survey of India.
27.tq: Identify the correct institutional pair and avoid swapping neighbouring technical agencies.
xs: The coastline was remeasured by the **National Hydrographic Office** with the **Survey of India** — option **(4)**.
It was reported by the **MHA** in **Dec 2024** (remeasurement **2023-24**).
xa: New length **11,098.81 km**, up from **7,516.6 km** (+~**47.7%**) — **only the method changed**, not the land.
**Gujarat** is first (**2,340.62 km**); **Tamil Nadu** second; **AP** third (**1,053.07 km**).
**GSI** is the nodal agency for **landslide** studies — a different body.

27.s:
Consider the following statements about India's remeasured coastline (2023-24):
1. The coastline rose from 7,516.6 km to 11,098.81 km because the measurement method changed, not the land.
2. Gujarat has the longest revised coastline.
3. Under the revised figures Andhra Pradesh has the second-longest coastline and the longest on the east coast.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
27.x: Statement 1 is correct: only the method changed. Statement 2 is correct: Gujarat ranks first (2,340.62 km). Statement 3 is wrong: Tamil Nadu is now second, and Andhra Pradesh (1,053.07 km) is third, so AP is not the longest on the east coast. So '1 only' misses 2, while '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' include the false statement 3.
27.tq: Revised order: Gujarat 1, Tamil Nadu 2, Andhra Pradesh 3.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: **7,516.6 km → 11,098.81 km** — only the **method changed**, not the land.
Statement 2: **Gujarat** is first with **2,340.62 km**.
Statement 3 wrong: **Tamil Nadu** is now **second**; **AP** (**1,053.07 km**) is **third**, so not the longest on the east coast.
xa: ⚠ Older notes and **APSDMA's "second"** carry the old ranking.
AP's rank **3** is from **APSES 2024-25**.
Remeasured by the **National Hydrographic Office** with the **Survey of India**; reported by **MHA**, **Dec 2024**.

27.s: Which of the following correctly describes the cyclone vulnerability of India?
o: Cyclones affect 13 coastal States or Union Territories and 84 coastal districts; Andhra Pradesh is identified as the most cyclone-prone state.
Cyclones affect only 9 coastal States and Andhra Pradesh is least affected on the east coast.
Cyclones affect 13 inland States and 84 districts, with Rajasthan as the most cyclone-prone state.
Cyclones affect 84 Union Territories and 13 coastal districts, with the west coast receiving most cyclones.
27.x: Cyclones affect 13 coastal States or Union Territories and 84 coastal districts. Andhra Pradesh is identified as the most cyclone-prone state, and the east coast receives far more cyclones than the west.
27.tq: Use composition, number and east-west comparison together.
xs: Cyclones affect **13 coastal states/UTs** and **84 coastal districts**; **AP** is the **most cyclone-prone state** — option **(1)**.
The **east coast** gets far more cyclones than the west, so options (2)-(4) are wrong; Rajasthan is a **drought** region.
xa: AP coast: **62+ cyclonic events** in four decades.
Cyclone/tsunami exposure: ~**5,700 km** of the old **7,516.6 km** coastline.
**Mangroves** buffer storm surges.

27.s:
Consider the following statements about landslides and avalanches in India:
1. Landslides occur mostly in hilly terrain.
2. The major landslide zones are the Himalaya and the Eastern Ghats.
3. Avalanches occur in the snow-bound Himalaya, such as Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
27.x: Statement 1 is correct: landslides are mostly a hilly-terrain hazard. Statement 2 is wrong: the major landslide zones are the Himalaya and the Western Ghats (Kerala, Konkan, Nilgiris), not the Eastern Ghats. Statement 3 is correct: avalanches hit the snow-bound Himalaya. So '1 only' misses 3, while '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' include the false statement 2.
27.tq: Landslides: Himalaya + WESTERN Ghats.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1: landslides occur mostly in **hilly** terrain (**APPSC 2025** key).
Statement 2 wrong: the zones are the **Himalaya** and the **Western Ghats** (Kerala, Konkan, Nilgiris), not the Eastern Ghats.
Statement 3: **avalanches** hit the snow-bound Himalaya — **J&K, Ladakh, HP, Uttarakhand**.
xa: Himalayan landslide states: **J&K, HP, Uttarakhand, NE**.
**GSI** is the nodal agency for landslide studies.
Causes: unregulated construction, **deforestation + road widening**, **cloudbursts and deglaciation**.

27.s: Which of the following factors contributes to the increasing frequency of landslides?
o: Increase in forest cover on vulnerable slopes
27.x: Unregulated construction on unstable slopes is one of the factors increasing landslide frequency. Deforestation, road widening, cloudbursts and deglaciation are other cited factors.
27.tq: Select the human activity that increases slope instability.
xs: **Unregulated construction on unstable slopes** raises landslide frequency — option **(1)**.
Example: the **HP flash floods 2023**.
More forest cover or less road widening would reduce, not raise, landslides — **deforestation + road widening** are the causes.
xa: **Char Dham** road widening: **43 ha** diverted, ~**7,000 deodars** approved for felling (**23 Jan 2026**).
**Cloudbursts and deglaciation** also add to landslides.
Nodal agency: **GSI**.

27.s:
Arrange the following disasters in chronological order:
A. Latur earthquake
B. Bhuj earthquake
C. Odisha super cyclone
D. Indian Ocean tsunami
27.x: The correct sequence is Latur earthquake in 1993, Odisha super cyclone in 1999, Bhuj earthquake in 2001 and Indian Ocean tsunami in 2004.
27.tq: Fix the earliest and latest events, then arrange the middle events by year.
xs: Order: **A, C, B, D** — option **(1)**.
**Latur (Killari)** earthquake **30 Sep 1993** → **Odisha super cyclone Oct 1999** → **Bhuj** earthquake **26 Jan 2001** → **Indian Ocean tsunami 26 Dec 2004**.
xa: **Bhopal gas leak**: **1984**, Madhya Pradesh.
**Kedarnath floods**: **June 2013**; **Kerala floods**: **Aug 2018**.
**Chamoli glacier burst**: **2021**, Uttarakhand.

27.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
27.x: The Chamoli glacier burst of 2021 occurred in Uttarakhand, not Himachal Pradesh. The other three pairs are correctly matched.
27.tq: Find the wrong place in a disaster-year-location chain.
xs: **Chamoli glacier burst — 2021 — Himachal Pradesh** is wrong — option **(4)**.
Chamoli is in **Uttarakhand**, not HP.
The others are right: **Kerala floods Aug 2018**, **Bhuj 26 Jan 2001 (Kutch)**, **Kedarnath June 2013 (Uttarakhand)**.
xa: **Dharali flash flood**: **5 Aug 2025**, **Uttarkashi**, Uttarakhand.
**Kedarnath** cloudburst: **June 2013**.
**Central Himalaya** glacier area down **>20%** in three decades.

27.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Chernobyl — Pripyat, Ukraine — 26 April 1986
2. Fukushima Daiichi — earthquake and tsunami followed by reactor meltdowns — 11 March 2011
3. Bhopal gas leak — Madhya Pradesh — 1987
How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
27.x: Pair 1 is correct: Chernobyl's reactor No. 4 exploded at Pripyat, Ukraine (then USSR), on 26 April 1986. Pair 2 is correct: Fukushima Daiichi (Japan, 11 March 2011) followed an earthquake-tsunami that caused reactor meltdowns. Pair 3 is wrong: the Bhopal gas leak was in 1984. So only two pairs are correct.
27.tq: Bhopal 1984, Chernobyl 1986, Fukushima 2011.
xs: Pairs **1** and **2** are correct — so option **(2) Only two** is the answer.
Pair 1 is correct: **Chernobyl** (Pripyat, Ukraine, then USSR) — **Reactor No. 4** explosion on **26 Apr 1986**.
Pair 2 is correct: **Fukushima Daiichi** (Japan, **11 Mar 2011**) — **earthquake-tsunami** led to **reactor meltdowns**.
Pair 3 is wrong: the **Bhopal gas leak** (Madhya Pradesh) was in **1984**, not 1987.
xa: **Nuclear hazards:** plant accidents plus **improper disposal of radioactive waste**.
**HSDPR scheme (2021-26):** **2 tertiary and 10 secondary** CBRN medical management centres.
**NIDM Southern Campus** is at **Kondapalli, AP**.
Nuclear and radiological emergencies come under the **Department of Atomic Energy (DAE)**.

27.s: The NIDM Southern Campus at Kondapalli is associated with which activity?
o: Conducting crop-weather surveys in drought-prone districts
Forecasting earthquakes in the Eastern Ghats
Preparing safety audits for chemical corridors and port clusters
Monitoring ocean currents in the Bay of Bengal
27.x: The NIDM Southern Campus at Kondapalli, Andhra Pradesh, prepares safety audits for chemical corridors and port clusters.
27.tq: Identify the institution from its specialised function.
xs: **NIDM Southern Campus, Kondapalli (AP)** prepares **safety audits for chemical corridors and port clusters** — option **(3)**.
Ocean monitoring belongs to bodies like **NIOT Nellore** (OMNI buoys), not NIDM.
xa: **HSDPR** (2021-26): **2 tertiary and 10 secondary** CBRN centres.
**Bhopal gas leak** (**1984**) is India's classic industrial disaster.
AP's three hazards: **coastal cyclones, delta floods, Rayalaseema drought**.

27.s: Apart from accidents at nuclear power plants such as Chernobyl and Fukushima, which of the following is identified as a source of nuclear hazards?
27.x: Nuclear hazards arise from plant accidents and from improper disposal of radioactive waste. Solar panels, check dams and shelter belts carry no radioactive risk.
27.tq: Nuclear hazards = plant accidents + radioactive waste disposal.
xs: Besides plant accidents, **improper disposal of radioactive waste** is a nuclear hazard — option **(1)**.
Solar panels, check dams and shelter belts carry no radioactive risk.
xa: **Chernobyl**: **26 Apr 1986**, Reactor No. 4 explosion.
**Fukushima Daiichi**: **11 Mar 2011**, earthquake-tsunami → meltdowns.
**HSDPR** scheme builds **CBRN** medical management centres.

27.s: Which of the following pairs of historic disaster and country is correctly matched?
27.x: The 1970 Bhola cyclone struck East Pakistan, now Bangladesh. The 1931 Yellow River (Huang He) flood was in China, the 365 CE Crete tsunami in Greece, and the 2011 Tohoku tsunami in Japan.
27.tq: Bhola 1970 = Bangladesh; Huang He 1931 = China.
xs: **Bhola cyclone (1970) — East Pakistan, now Bangladesh** is correctly matched — option **(1)**.
**Yellow River (Huang He) flood 1931** was in **China**; **Crete tsunami 365 CE** in **Greece**; **Tohoku 2011** in **Japan**.
xa: **Solomon Islands tsunami**: **2007**.
Tohoku tsunami triggered the **Fukushima** meltdowns.
**World Risk Index 2025**: India **2nd**, after the **Philippines**.

27.s:
Consider the following statements about India's notified-disaster list:
1. The addition of heatwaves and lightning raised the list from 12 to 14 for the 2026-31 award period.
2. The addition was made on the recommendation of the Fifteenth Finance Commission.
3. Droughts, hailstorms, frost/cold waves and pest attacks are handled by the Agriculture Ministry, the rest by the Ministry of Home Affairs.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
27.x: Statement 1 is correct: heatwaves and lightning took the list from 12 to 14 (Aug 2026, for 2026-31). Statement 2 is wrong: it was on the Sixteenth Finance Commission's recommendation. Statement 3 is correct: those four go to the Agriculture Ministry, the rest to MHA. So '1 only' misses 3, while '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' include the false statement 2.
27.tq: 2026-31 award period = 16th Finance Commission.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1: **heatwaves and lightning** took the list from **12 to 14** (**Aug 2026**), for **2026-31**.
Statement 2 wrong: it was on the **16th Finance Commission**'s recommendation, not the Fifteenth.
Statement 3: **droughts, hailstorms, frost/cold waves, pest attacks** → **Agriculture Ministry**; the rest → **MHA**.
xa: Disaster = **Hazard x Vulnerability**.
India's economic loss from disasters: about **0.4% of GDP** a year (**1990-2024**).
**2025**: **over 4,000 deaths** from climate-induced disasters; heaviest toll in **HP and Uttarakhand**.

27.s: A region has a high level of hazard but very low vulnerability. According to the relationship used in disaster studies, which of the following best describes the likely outcome?
o: It will necessarily become a major disaster.
The hazard alone does not determine a disaster; disaster risk depends on the interaction of hazard and vulnerability.
It will be classified as a drought-prone region only.
It will automatically be free from all hazards.
27.x: The relationship is expressed as Hazard × Vulnerability = Disaster. Therefore, a hazard does not necessarily produce a major disaster when vulnerability is very low.
27.tq: Translate the formula into a practical situation rather than treating hazard as synonymous with disaster.
xs: A hazard alone does not make a disaster; it depends on **hazard and vulnerability** together — option **(2)**.
The relation is **Hazard x Vulnerability = Disaster**, so very low vulnerability keeps the disaster small.
A hazard never makes a place "free from hazards", nor is it automatically drought-prone.
xa: India is **2nd most vulnerable** in the **World Risk Index 2025**.
Floods, droughts, cloudbursts = **hydro-meteorological**; tsunamis = **geological** hazards.
India's risk drivers: **floods and storms**.

27.s: Which of the following institutions and instruments are associated with the tsunami warning system serving the Indian region?
o: Agriculture Ministry and automated rain gauges only
Central Water Commission and glacier monitors only
IMD Hyderabad and Doppler weather radars only
27.x: NIOT Nellore’s OMNI buoys provide inputs to the tsunami warning system. The other combinations substitute institutions or instruments not identified for this function.
27.tq: Use the institution–instrument association to reject substitutions involving nearby disaster-management bodies.
xs: **NIOT Nellore's OMNI buoys** feed the **tsunami warning system** — option **(2)**.
The other bodies (Agriculture Ministry, CWC, IMD radars) are not named for this role.
xa: **ITWS** warns **25** Indian Ocean countries within **10 minutes**.
Tsunami warning signs: sudden **receding of sea water**, rapid sea-level rise, earthquake shaking.
AP is in the **high** tsunami risk zone, with TN, Puducherry and Odisha.

27.s:
Assertion (A): Andhra Pradesh has a geographically differentiated pattern of hydrological-disaster vulnerability.
