Reason (R): Its coastal belt, deltaic plains and Rayalaseema region are respectively associated with cyclones and storm surges, floods and droughts.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
27.x: Both statements are true, and the regional association given in the Reason directly explains why Andhra Pradesh has a differentiated disaster-vulnerability pattern.
27.tq: Check whether the Reason explains the geographic pattern asserted, rather than merely being a related fact.
xs: **Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
AP faces three hazards: **coastal cyclones** (and surges), **delta floods**, **Rayalaseema drought**.
This regional split is exactly why AP's vulnerability is **geographically differentiated**.
xa: AP is the **most cyclone-prone state** — **62+ cyclonic events** in four decades.
**Krishna-Godavari** delta floods are worst when **Srisailam, Nagarjuna Sagar** or **Hirakud** release water together.
**Rayalaseema**: deep borewells → **severe groundwater depletion**.

27.s: India's tsunami warning system (ITWS) is able to issue warnings to how many Indian Ocean countries, and within what time?
27.x: The ITWS warns 25 Indian Ocean countries within 10 minutes. 13 is the number of coastal States/UTs affected by cyclones, and the other combinations alter the country count or response time.
27.tq: ITWS: 25 countries, 10 minutes.
xs: **ITWS** warns **25** Indian Ocean countries within **10 minutes** — option **(1)**.
**13** is the number of coastal states/UTs hit by cyclones, not ITWS countries.
xa: **NIOT Nellore's OMNI buoys** feed the tsunami warning system.
Tsunamis mostly originate in the **Indian Ocean** — **Sumatra-Andaman (Sunda)** subduction zone (**APPSC 2025** key).
The **Makran** zone threatens the **west coast**.

27.s:
Assertion (A): A cloudburst has a strong potential to cause flash floods.
Reason (R): A cloudburst involves highly localized and extremely intense rainfall, resulting in rapid runoff.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
27.x: Both are true and R explains A: a cloudburst dumps very intense rain on a small area, so runoff surges and causes a flash flood.
27.tq: Check whether R is the cause of A.
n: A cloudburst consists of extremely intense localized rainfall. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
A cloudburst produces very intense rainfall over a small area. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Cloudbursts are highly localized. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Cloudbursts are extremely intense. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Cloudbursts produce rapid runoff. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Cloudbursts have strong flash-flood potential. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
A cloudburst causes flash floods. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
A cloudburst is **extremely intense, highly localized** rainfall, giving **rapid runoff** and a **strong flash-flood potential**.
In the secondary-hazard chain, **Cloudburst → Flash flood**.
xa: **IMD:** at least **100 mm (10 cm)** in **one hour** over about **20–30 square kilometres**.
Cloudbursts mostly occur at **1,000 to 2,500 metres** in mountains.
Ordinary heavy rainfall may **cover a larger area** and be **prolonged**; its runoff **depends on duration and intensity**.
**Flash flood → Landslide** is the next link in the secondary-hazard chain.

27.s:
Which of the following statements are correct?
I. Siltation reduces channel depth and capacity.
II. Deforestation increases runoff.
III. Poor drainage causes water to accumulate.
IV. Embankment failure prevents water from escaping the channel.
27.x: I, II and III are correct: silt reduces channel capacity, deforestation raises runoff and poor drainage lets water pool. IV is false because a failed embankment lets water escape.
27.tq: Check each statement for a reversed effect.
n: Siltation reduces channel depth or capacity. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Embankment failure allows water to escape the channel. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Deforestation increases runoff. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Poor drainage causes water to accumulate. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
xs: **I, II and III** are correct — option **(4) I, II and III only**.
**Siltation** reduces **channel depth or capacity**; **deforestation** increases **runoff**; with **poor drainage** water **accumulates**.
IV is wrong: in **embankment failure** water **escapes the channel**.
xa: **Urbanisation** increases runoff through **impervious surfaces**.
**Floodplain encroachment** increases **human exposure**; **snowmelt** causes a **sudden increase in river flow**.
**APPSC 2025 key causes:** **heavy/prolonged rainfall, poor drainage, deforestation, dam failure**.
**Dam failure** causes a **sudden downstream discharge**.

27.s:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(a) River flood
(b) Flash flood
(c) Urban flood
(d) Drought

List-II
(i) Sudden high-intensity runoff or discharge
(ii) Prolonged water deficit
(iii) River discharge exceeding channel capacity
(iv) Rainfall combined with inadequate urban drainage
27.x: A river flood is discharge exceeding the channel, a flash flood sudden intense runoff, an urban flood rain with poor drainage and a drought a long water deficit, giving a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii.
27.tq: Recall the definition of each hazard.
n: A river flood occurs when river discharge exceeds channel capacity. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
A flash flood involves sudden high-intensity runoff or discharge. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
An urban flood results from rainfall combined with inadequate urban drainage. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
A drought is a prolonged water deficit. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii** — option **(1)**.
**River flood** — river **discharge exceeds channel capacity**; **flash flood** — **sudden high-intensity runoff**.
**Urban flood** — **rainfall with inadequate urban drainage**; **drought** — a **prolonged water deficit**.
xa: **Cloudburst:** extremely intense localized rainfall → **flash floods** and **landslides**.
**Dam failure:** sudden water release → **catastrophic downstream flooding**.
**Coastal flooding:** **storm surge**, tidal or wave action on a **low-lying coast** → inundation, **salinity**.
**Drought** is **slow-onset** — a **creeping emergency**.

27.s:
Match the primary event in List-I with its associated secondary hazard in List-II.

List-I
(a) Cloudburst
(b) Dam failure
(c) River flood
(d) Coastal flood

List-II
(i) Salinity intrusion
(ii) Bank erosion
(iii) Flash flood
(iv) Catastrophic flooding below a breached reservoir
27.x: A cloudburst triggers flash floods, a dam failure floods the land below the breached reservoir, river floods cause bank erosion, and coastal floods bring salinity intrusion, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
27.tq: Link each event with the hazard it most directly sets off.
n: A cloudburst causes a flash flood as a secondary hazard. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
A flash flood causes a landslide as a secondary hazard. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
A river flood causes bank erosion as a secondary hazard. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
A coastal flood causes salinity intrusion as a secondary hazard. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
A cloudburst causes flash floods. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i** — option **(3)**.
**Cloudburst → flash flood**; **dam failure → downstream flash flooding**.
**River flood → bank erosion**; **coastal flood → salinity intrusion**.
xa: **Flash flood → landslide**; **urban flood → traffic or infrastructure collapse**.
**Flood → water contamination**, **disease risk**, **crop or livelihood loss**.
**Rapid-onset:** cyclone, flood, tsunami; **slow-onset:** drought.

27.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) River flood
(b) Cloudburst
(c) Urban flood
(d) Dam failure

List-II
(i) Infrastructure disruption
(ii) Landslides
(iii) Catastrophic downstream flooding
(iv) Crop damage
27.x: River floods damage crops, cloudbursts trigger landslides, urban floods disrupt infrastructure and dam failure causes catastrophic floods downstream, giving a-iv, b-ii, c-i, d-iii.
27.tq: Recall the main impact of each hazard.
n: A river flood causes crop damage. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
An urban flood disrupts infrastructure. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
A cloudburst causes landslides. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
A dam failure causes catastrophic downstream flooding. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
xs: The correct match is **a-iv, b-ii, c-i, d-iii** — option **(4)**.
**River flood** → **crop damage**; **cloudburst** → **landslides**.
**Urban flood** → **disrupts infrastructure**; **dam failure** → **catastrophic downstream flooding**.
xa: River floods also cause **inundation** and **property damage**.
**Flash flood** effect: **very rapid destruction**.
**Drought** affects **agriculture**, **water supply** and **ecosystems**.
An **earthquake** is a **geological** disaster, not hydrological.

27.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Coastal flooding can result when storm surge, tidal action or wave action combines with a low-lying coast.
Statement B: Coastal flooding can cause both inundation and salinity.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
27.x: Both are true: surge, tides or waves on a low coast cause coastal floods, which bring both inundation and salinity.
27.tq: Check each statement separately.
n: Coastal flooding results from storm surge, tidal action, or wave action affecting a low-lying coast. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Coastal flooding causes inundation. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Coastal flooding causes salinity. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are true** — option **(1)**.
Coastal flooding arises from **storm surge**, **tidal action** or **wave action** affecting a **low-lying coast**.
Its effects are **inundation** and **salinity**.
xa: **Coastal flood → salinity intrusion** (secondary hazard).
A **cyclone** produces a **storm surge**; a **high tide** gives a **higher baseline water level**.
**Sea-level rise** increases coastal exposure; a **low-lying delta** suffers **greater inundation**.

27.s:
Consider the following statements about flash floods:
I. Debris is a main danger associated with flash floods.
II. Flash floods are associated with landslides.
III. Flash floods are associated with erosion.
IV. Flash floods are associated with infrastructure damage.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
27.x: All four are correct: flash floods carry debris and cause landslides, erosion and damage to infrastructure.
27.tq: Recall the impacts of flash floods.
n: Debris is a main danger associated with flash floods. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Flash floods are associated with landslides. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Flash floods are associated with erosion. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Flash floods are associated with infrastructure damage. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
xs: **All four** statements are correct — option **(3) I, II, III and IV**.
The **main dangers** of flash floods are **high flow velocity** and **debris**.
Flash floods are **associated with landslides**, **erosion** and **infrastructure damage**.
xa: Flash floods have a **very rapid onset** and a **very short warning time**.
**Triggers:** intense rainfall or a **cloudburst**, **sudden water release**, **steep terrain**.
**Vulnerable:** **mountains**, **steep catchments** and **urban areas**.

27.s: Which of the following statements regarding the causes of urban flooding is incorrect?
o: Wetland destruction can contribute to urban flooding.
Wetland restoration can contribute to urban flooding.
Encroachment of drains can contribute to urban flooding.
27.x: Option B is incorrect: restoring wetlands reduces urban flooding because wetlands store water. Wetland loss, paved surfaces and blocked drains add to it.
27.tq: Check for a reversed effect.
n: Encroachment of drains causes urban flooding. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Wetland destruction causes urban flooding. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Impervious surfaces cause urban flooding. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Wetland protection preserves natural storage. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Wetlands store excess water. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
xs: **Wetland restoration can contribute to urban flooding** is the incorrect statement — option **(2)**.
**Wetland destruction** (not restoration) is a cause of urban flooding; **wetlands store excess water**.
**Impervious surfaces** increase runoff and **encroachment of drains** causes flooding — both correct.
xa: Other urban-flood causes: **poor storm-water drainage**, **unplanned urbanisation**, **floodplain construction**.
**Urban green infrastructure** increases **infiltration** and reduces **runoff**.
**Prep:** unplanned **concretisation**, blocked drains/canals, **encroached lakes**.
Urban-flood cities: **Mumbai**, **Chennai**, **Bengaluru**, **Hyderabad**, **Delhi**.

27.s: Which of the following areas is identified as highly vulnerable to flash floods?
o: Mountains, steep catchments and urban areas
Low-lying deltas and agricultural plains only
27.x: Flash floods threaten mountains, steep catchments and cities, where water gathers fast. Prolonged deficit describes drought.
27.tq: Relate terrain to the speed of runoff.
n: Mountains are vulnerable to flash floods. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Steep catchments are vulnerable to flash floods. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Urban areas are highly vulnerable to flash floods. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
xs: **Mountains, steep catchments and urban areas** are highly vulnerable to flash floods — option **(2)**.
A **prolonged water deficit** describes **drought**, not flash floods.
**Steep terrain** is itself a flash-flood trigger.
xa: Main dangers: **high flow velocity** and **debris**.
Cloudburst-prone: the **Himalayan region** and the windward **Western Ghats**.
Flash floods occur in **Himalayan regions** and **urban areas** (types-of-flood table).

27.s: Which of the following statements regarding coastal flooding is incorrect?
o: High tide creates a higher baseline water level.
Heavy coastal rainfall can cause drainage congestion.
Sea-level rise leads to lower coastal exposure.
27.x: Option C is incorrect: sea-level rise increases coastal exposure. High tides, heavy rain and cyclone surges all add to coastal flooding.
27.tq: Check for a reversed effect.
n: A cyclone produces a storm surge. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
A high tide produces a higher baseline water level. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Heavy coastal rainfall causes drainage congestion. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Sea-level rise increases coastal exposure. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
xs: **Sea-level rise leads to lower coastal exposure** is incorrect — option **(3)**; sea-level rise **increases** coastal exposure.
A **high tide** gives a **higher baseline water level**; **heavy coastal rainfall** causes **drainage congestion**.
A **cyclone** produces a **storm surge** — correct.
xa: **Storm surge:** abnormal sea-level rise pushed by **cyclone winds + low pressure**.
**Mangroves** with coastal shelter belts **buffer storm surges**.
**Salinity intrusion** hits **agriculture** and **water**.

27.s:
Consider the following statements about flash floods:

I. They have a very rapid onset.
II. They may be triggered by intense rainfall or cloudbursts.
III. They may be triggered by sudden water release.
IV. Steep terrain can trigger them.
V. They generally have a very short warning time.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
o: II, III, IV and V only
I, II, III, IV and V
27.x: All five are correct: flash floods start very fast with little warning, triggered by intense rain, cloudbursts, sudden releases or steep terrain.
27.tq: Recall the features of flash floods.
n: Flash floods have a very rapid onset. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Intense rainfall or a cloudburst can trigger a flash flood. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Sudden water release can trigger a flash flood. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Steep terrain can trigger a flash flood. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Flash floods have a very short warning time. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
A cloudburst causes flash floods. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
xs: **All five** statements are correct — option **(4) I, II, III, IV and V**.
Flash floods have a **very rapid onset** and a **very short warning time**.
**Triggers:** **intense rainfall** or a **cloudburst**, **sudden water release** and **steep terrain**.
xa: Vulnerable: **mountains**, **steep catchments**, **urban areas**.
Main dangers: **high flow velocity** and **debris**.
**IMD** gives **flash-flood guidance** for India and neighbours (**Bangladesh**, **Bhutan**, **Nepal**).

27.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Cloudbursts are highly localized, whereas ordinary heavy rainfall may cover a larger area.
Statement B: Cloudbursts are sudden, whereas ordinary heavy rainfall can be prolonged.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
27.x: Both are true: cloudbursts are sudden and very local, while ordinary heavy rain can cover wider areas and last longer.
27.tq: Discriminate cloudburst from heavy rain.
n: Cloudbursts are highly localized. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Ordinary heavy rainfall may cover a larger area. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Cloudbursts are sudden. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Ordinary heavy rainfall can be prolonged. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are true** — option **(1)**.
Area: a cloudburst is **highly localized**; ordinary heavy rainfall may **cover a larger area**.
Timing: a cloudburst is **sudden**; ordinary heavy rainfall **can be prolonged**.
xa: Intensity: cloudburst **extremely intense**; ordinary rain has **varying intensity**.
Flood potential: cloudburst has **strong flash-flood potential**; ordinary rain **depends on basin conditions**.
**HKH "monsoon paradox":** seasonal rain erratic while short, intense cloudbursts rise.

27.s:
How many of the following factors can cause urban flooding?
I. Poor storm-water drainage
II. Unplanned urbanisation
III. Low-lying terrain
IV. Floodplain construction
V. High tides or storm surges
27.x: All five cause urban flooding: poor storm drains, unplanned growth, low ground, floodplain building and high tides or surges.
27.tq: Recall the causes of urban flooding.
n: Poor storm-water drainage causes urban flooding. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
High tides or storm surge cause urban flooding. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Unplanned urbanisation causes urban flooding. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Low-lying terrain causes urban flooding. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Floodplain construction causes urban flooding. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
xs: **All five** factors cause urban flooding — option **(3) All five**.
Causes include **poor storm-water drainage**, **unplanned urbanisation**, **low-lying terrain** and **floodplain construction**.
**High river discharge**, **high tides or storm surge** also flood cities.
xa: Other causes: **intense rainfall**, **cloudbursts**, **cyclone rainfall**, **encroachment of drains**, **wetland destruction**.
Major urban floods: **Mumbai 2005** (**944 mm** in **24 hours**), **Chennai 2015**.
**AP City Flood Alert:** **48-hour rainfall** forecasts + **6-hour flash-flood** warnings.

27.s:
Consider the following statements about the causes of dam failure:
1. A weak foundation, material failure and design failure are structural causes of dam failure.
2. Sedimentation increases the storage capacity of a dam.
3. Overtopping occurs when water exceeds the dam crest.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
27.x: Statement 1 is correct: weak foundation, material and design failure are the structural causes. Statement 2 is wrong: sedimentation REDUCES dam storage capacity. Statement 3 is correct: overtopping means water exceeds the dam crest. Hence 1 and 3 only.
27.tq: Sedimentation shrinks a reservoir; overtopping = over the crest.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(3) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 is correct: **weak foundation**, **material failure** and **design failure** are **structural** causes.
Statement 2 is wrong: **sedimentation reduces** dam storage capacity.
Statement 3 is correct: **overtopping** is when water **exceeds the dam crest**.
xa: **Natural causes:** an **extreme flood exceeding design capacity**, **landslides**, **earthquakes**, **extreme rainfall**.
**Management causes:** **improper reservoir management**, **poor inspection**, **poor maintenance**.
Dam failure → **catastrophic downstream flooding**.

27.s:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(a) Nuclear and radiological emergencies
(b) Forest fire
(c) Urban floods
(d) Drought

List-II
(i) Department of Atomic Energy
(ii) Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change

(iv) Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare
27.x: Atomic Energy is nodal for nuclear and radiological emergencies, the Environment Ministry for forest fires, Housing and Urban Affairs for urban floods and Agriculture for drought, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
27.tq: Recall the nodal ministry for each hazard.
n: The Department of Atomic Energy is the nodal department for nuclear disasters. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #17 · pp 41-43]
The Department of Atomic Energy is the nodal department for radiological disasters. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #17 · pp 41-43]
The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change is the nodal ministry for forest fire. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #17 · pp 41-43]
The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change is the nodal ministry for chemical disasters. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #17 · pp 41-43]
xs: The correct match is **a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv** — option **(2)**.
**Nuclear and radiological emergencies** — **Department of Atomic Energy**; **forest fire** — **Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change**.
**Urban floods** — **Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs**; **drought** — **Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare**.
xa: **Agriculture Ministry** also handles **hailstorms**, **frost and cold waves**, **pest attacks**.
**MoEFCC** also handles **industrial and chemical disasters**.
**Floods and GLOFs** — **Ministry of Jal Shakti** (with the **CWC**).

27.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Urban Flood
(b) Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF)
(c) Landslide
(d) Biological Disasters / Epidemics

List-II
(i) Ministry of Mines
(ii) Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
(iii) Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs
(iv) Ministry of Jal Shakti
27.x: Urban floods come under Housing and Urban Affairs, glacial lake outbursts under Jal Shakti, landslides under Mines, and epidemics under Health. The answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
27.tq: Match each hazard to its ministry.
n: The nodal ministry for urban floods is the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 63-65]
The nodal ministry for Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs) is the Ministry of Jal Shakti. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 63-65]
The nodal ministry for landslides is the Ministry of Mines. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 63-65]
The nodal ministry for biological disasters and epidemics is the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 63-65]
xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii** — option **(4)**.
**Urban flood** — **Housing and Urban Affairs**; **GLOF** — **Ministry of Jal Shakti**.
**Landslide** — **Ministry of Mines**; **epidemics** — **Ministry of Health and Family Welfare**.
xa: ⚠ Landslide nodal **ministry** is **Mines**; the nodal **agency** is the **GSI**.
**Avalanches** — **Ministry of Defence**.
**Earthquakes, cyclones, tsunamis** — **MoES** with **IMD**.

27.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: Forest Fire is assigned to the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change.
Civil Aviation Accidents are assigned to the Ministry of Civil Aviation.
Rail Accidents are assigned to the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways.
Oil Spills are assigned to the Ministry of Defence through the Indian Coast Guard.
27.x: Option C is incorrect: rail accidents come under the Ministry of Railways. Road Transport handles road accidents.
27.tq: Match each hazard to its ministry.
n: The nodal ministry for forest fires is the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 63-65]
The nodal ministry for civil aviation accidents is the Ministry of Civil Aviation. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 63-65]
The nodal ministry for rail accidents is the Ministry of Railways. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 63-65]
The nodal ministry for road accidents is the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 63-65]
The nodal ministry for oil spills is the Ministry of Defence (Indian Coast Guard). [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 63-65]
xs: **Rail accidents assigned to the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways** is incorrect — option **(3)**.
**Rail accidents** come under the **Ministry of Railways**; **road accidents** under **Road Transport and Highways**.
**Forest fire** — **MoEFCC**; **civil aviation accidents** — **Ministry of Civil Aviation**; **oil spills** — **Defence (Indian Coast Guard)** — all correct.
xa: **Avalanches** also come under the **Ministry of Defence**.
**Nuclear and radiological** emergencies — **DAE**.
**Biological disasters** — **Ministry of Health and Family Welfare**.

27.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Disaster/Hazard)
(a) Earthquake

Codes:
27.x: Earth Sciences is nodal for earthquakes, Jal Shakti for floods, Agriculture for drought and Defence for avalanches, giving a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv.
27.tq: Recall the nodal ministry for each hazard.
n: The nodal ministry for earthquakes is the Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES). [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 63-65]
The nodal ministry for cyclones and tornadoes is the Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES). [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 63-65]
The nodal ministry for tsunamis is the Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES). [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 63-65]
The nodal ministry for floods is the Ministry of Jal Shakti. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 63-65]
xs: The correct match is **a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv** — option **(1)**.
**Earthquake** — **MoES**; **flood** — **Ministry of Jal Shakti**.
**Drought** — **Agriculture and Farmers Welfare**; **avalanche** — **Ministry of Defence**.
xa: **MoES** with **IMD** handles **cyclone** and **earthquake forecasting**; also **tsunamis**.
**Urban floods** — **Housing and Urban Affairs** (not Jal Shakti).
Avalanche technical agency: **DGRE** (earlier **SASE**) under **DRDO**.

27.s: Which of the following is the nodal ministry for industrial and chemical disasters?
o: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
27.x: The Environment, Forest and Climate Change Ministry is nodal for industrial and chemical disasters.
27.tq: Match each hazard to its ministry.
n: The nodal ministry for industrial and chemical disasters is the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 63-65]
xs: **Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change** is nodal for **industrial and chemical disasters** — option **(3)**.
**Ministry of Mines** handles **landslides**; **Health and Family Welfare** handles **biological disasters and epidemics**.
**Ministry of Defence** handles **avalanches** and **oil spills**.
xa: **MoEFCC** is also nodal for **forest fires**.
**Bhopal gas leak** — **1984**, **Madhya Pradesh**.
**NIDM Southern Campus (Kondapalli)** prepares safety audits for **chemical corridors** and port clusters.

27.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: Floods affect about 10% of India's area.
Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal are among the next most affected states.
The flood-prone area estimated by the Rashtriya Barh Ayog is about 49 million hectares.
Assam and Bihar are the worst-affected states.
27.x: Option C is incorrect: the Rashtriya Barh Ayog put the flood-prone area at about 40 million hectares. About 49 million hectares is a more recent estimate.
27.tq: Discriminate the RBA figure from the recent one.
n: Flood-affected areas cover about 10% of India. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
Assam and Bihar are the worst-affected states by floods in India. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal are the next most affected states by floods in India. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
The Rashtriya Barh Ayog estimated India’s flood-prone area at approximately 40 million hectares. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
Recent estimates place India’s flood-prone area at up to approximately 49 million hectares. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
xs: **Rashtriya Barh Ayog estimate of about 49 million hectares** is incorrect — option **(3)**.
The **Rashtriya Barh Ayog** put the flood-prone area at about **40 million hectares**; **recent estimates** go up to about **49 million hectares**.
Floods affect about **10%** of India; **Assam** and **Bihar** worst, then **Uttar Pradesh** and **West Bengal** — correct.
xa: Rashtriya Barh Ayog (National Flood Commission) set up **1976** (some notes give **1980**).
**Expert Committee for Scientific Assessment of Flood-Prone Areas** — **2012**.
**Assam** alone: **31.05 lakh ha** flood-prone.
Flood control is a **state subject**; Centre helps through **FMBAP**.

27.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Riverine or fluvial floods result from the overflow of rivers due to heavy monsoon rainfall.
II. Urban floods may result from poor drainage, heavy rain and encroachment on wetlands.
III. Glacial Lake Outburst Floods result from storm surge and high tides.
IV. Coastal floods may be caused by storm surge, cyclones and high tides.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
27.x: I, II and IV are correct: river floods follow heavy monsoon rain, urban floods come from poor drainage and lost wetlands, and coastal floods from surges and tides. III is false because GLOFs come from glacial lakes bursting.
27.tq: Match each flood type to its cause.
n: Riverine or fluvial floods result from the overflow of rivers due to heavy monsoon rainfall. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
Urban floods result from poor drainage, heavy rain, and encroachment on wetlands. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
Coastal floods result from storm surges, cyclones, and high tides. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
Glacial Lake Outburst Floods result from the bursting of glacial lakes. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
xs: **I, II and IV** are correct — option **(1) I, II and IV only**.
**Riverine/fluvial** floods: **overflow of rivers** from **heavy monsoon rainfall**; **urban floods**: **poor drainage**, heavy rain, **encroachment on wetlands**.
**Coastal floods**: **storm surges**, **cyclones**, **high tides**.
III is wrong: **GLOFs** come from the **bursting of glacial lakes**.
xa: GLOF-prone: **Himalayan states** — **Uttarakhand**, **Sikkim**.
Riverine floods hit the **Ganga**, **Brahmaputra**, **Kosi** and **Godavari** basins.
Flash floods: **sudden intense rainfall** or **cloudbursts** in **Himalayan regions** and **urban areas**.

27.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Flood water flows in rivers, streams and other water bodies and cannot be contained.
Statement B: Floods are rapid-onset disasters.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
27.x: Both are true: flood water spills out of rivers and water bodies and cannot be held, and floods are rapid-onset disasters.
27.tq: Recall the nature of floods.
n: Flood water flows in rivers, streams, and other water bodies and cannot be contained. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
Floods are rapid-onset disasters. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are true** — option **(1)**.
A flood is water in **rivers, streams and other water bodies** that **cannot be contained**, overflowing onto **normally dry land**.
A flood is a **rapid-onset** disaster.
xa: ⚠ Sources differ: the **Prep** notes call floods **slow-onset** and season-predictable.
Floods are the **most frequent** natural disaster in **India**.
**Causes:** **excess rainfall**, **river overflow**; aggravated by **poor drainage**, **urbanization**, **poor planning**.

27.s:
How many of the following statements about floods are correct?

1. Floods are the most frequent natural disaster in India.
2. Floods cause damage worth thousands of crores annually.
3. Floods cause significant loss of life annually.
4. Floods cause significant loss of crops annually.
27.x: All four are correct: floods are India's most frequent disaster and cause huge yearly losses of money, lives and crops.
27.tq: Recall the flood impacts.
n: Floods are the most frequent natural disaster in India. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
Floods cause damage worth thousands of crores annually. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
Floods cause significant loss of life annually. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
Floods cause significant loss of crops annually. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
xs: **All four** statements are correct — option **(4) All four**.
Floods are the **most frequent natural disaster** in **India**.
**Annual losses:** damage worth **thousands of crores**, significant **loss of life** and of **crops**.
xa: Flood-affected area: about **10%** of India.
Flood-prone area: about **40 million hectares** (Rashtriya Barh Ayog); recent estimates up to **49 million hectares**.
India loses about **0.4% of GDP** a year to disasters; drivers are **floods and storms**.

27.s:
Assertion (A): Flash floods result from sudden intense rainfall or cloudbursts.
Reason (R): Himalayan regions and urban areas commonly experience flash floods.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
27.x: Both are true: flash floods come from sudden heavy rain or cloudbursts, and they are common in the Himalaya and in cities. Where they happen does not explain their cause, so R does not explain A.
27.tq: Ask whether a place explains a cause.
n: Flash floods result from sudden intense rainfall or cloudbursts. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
Himalayan regions commonly experience flash floods. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
Urban areas commonly experience flash floods. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
xs: **Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A** — option **(2)**.
A is true: flash floods result from **sudden intense rainfall** or **cloudbursts**.
R is true: **Himalayan regions** and **urban areas** commonly see flash floods — but where they occur does not explain their **cause**.
xa: Flash floods are **very rapid onset** with a **very short warning time**.
Main dangers: **high flow velocity** and **debris**.
Cloudbursts: at least **100 mm** in **one hour** (IMD).

27.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Heavy rainfall
(b) Prolonged rainfall
(c) Landslide
(d) Poor drainage

List-II
(i) Can contribute to flooding
(ii) Can cause heavy landslides
(iii) Can block rivers and cause downstream havoc

27.x: Heavy rain can cause flooding, prolonged rain landslides, landslides can block rivers and cause havoc downstream, and poor drainage worsens urban floods. The answer is a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
27.tq: Match each factor to its effect.

xs: **"Only structural measures, not non-structural"** is the incorrect statement — option **(2)**.
**NDMA guidelines** cover **risk zonation**, **early warning**, and **both structural and non-structural** mitigation measures.
xa: **Structural** avalanche measures: **snow bridges**, **snow nets**, **retaining walls**, **galleries**.
**Non-structural:** **hazard zonation mapping**, **restricted movement**, **training**, **awareness**.
**Nodal ministry:** **Ministry of Defence**.

27.s:
Consider the following statements about the Defence Geoinformatics Research Establishment (DGRE):
1. It develops avalanche mitigation technologies.
2. The daily avalanche warning bulletins during winter are issued by the Border Roads Organisation, not by DGRE.
3. It functions under DRDO and conducts avalanche forecasting, research and hazard mapping.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
27.x: Statement 3 is correct: DGRE (earlier SASE) works under DRDO and does forecasting, research and hazard mapping. Statement 2 is wrong: DGRE itself issues the daily avalanche warning bulletins in winter; the BRO builds and maintains roads and protection structures. Statement 1 is correct: DGRE develops mitigation technologies. Hence 1 and 3 only.
27.tq: DGRE (ex-SASE, DRDO) = forecasts, bulletins, mapping, mitigation tech; BRO = roads.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 is correct: **DGRE develops mitigation technologies**.
Statement 2 is wrong: **DGRE** itself issues the **daily avalanche warning bulletins** in **winter**; the **BRO** builds roads and protection structures.
Statement 3 is correct: DGRE functions under **DRDO** and does **forecasting**, **research** and **hazard mapping**.
xa: DGRE was **earlier known** as the **Snow and Avalanche Study Establishment (SASE)**.
**BRO** constructs and maintains **roads** and installs **protection structures** in avalanche-prone areas.
Nodal ministry for avalanches: **Ministry of Defence**.

27.s: An avalanche is best defined as:
o: Breaking and sliding of rocks only along a fault
Rapid flow of water and silt through a river valley
Rapid flow of snow, ice, and debris down a mountain slope
Sudden movement of molten rock from a volcanic slope
27.x: An avalanche is a rapid flow of snow, ice and debris down a mountain slope. Option B is a flash flood and option D a lava flow.
27.tq: Recall the definition of an avalanche.
n: An avalanche is a rapid flow of snow, ice, and debris down a mountain slope. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
xs: An avalanche is a **rapid flow of snow, ice and debris down a mountain slope** — option **(3)**.
It is a **geological** and **snow-related** natural hazard.
xa: In India avalanches occur mainly in the **Himalayan region**, in **high-altitude areas**.
⚠ A **landslide** is the mass movement of **rocks, debris or earth** down slopes or riverbanks.
**Slab avalanche** is the **most dangerous type**.

27.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: The Ministry of Defence is the nodal ministry for avalanche management.
DGRE functions as the key technical agency for avalanche-related work.
The Ministry of Home Affairs is the nodal ministry for avalanche management.
DGRE was earlier known as the Snow and Avalanche Study Establishment.
27.x: Option C is incorrect: the Ministry of Defence is the nodal ministry for avalanches, with DGRE (formerly SASE) as the technical agency.
27.tq: Match each hazard to its ministry.
n: The nodal ministry for avalanche management is the Ministry of Defence. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
The key technical agency for avalanche management is the Defence Geoinformatics Research Establishment (DGRE). [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
The Defence Geoinformatics Research Establishment was earlier known as the Snow and Avalanche Study Establishment (SASE). [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
xs: **Ministry of Home Affairs as nodal ministry for avalanches** is incorrect — option **(3)**.
The **Ministry of Defence** is the **nodal ministry** for avalanches.
**DGRE** is the **key technical agency**, **earlier known** as **SASE** — correct.
xa: DGRE functions under **DRDO**; issues **daily avalanche warning bulletins** in **winter**.
**Oil spills** also come under **Defence** (**Indian Coast Guard**).
**Landslides** — **Ministry of Mines**.

27.s:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(a) Slab Avalanche
(b) Loose Snow Avalanche
(c) Ice Avalanche
(d) Rock / Debris Avalanche

List-II
(i) Involves ice masses from glaciers
(ii) Small slide of dry, powdery snow
(iii) Mixture of rock, soil and snow
(iv) Large cohesive slab of snow that breaks off and slides
27.x: A slab avalanche is a large snow slab breaking off, a loose-snow avalanche is a small dry slide, an ice avalanche comes from glaciers, and a debris avalanche mixes rock, soil and snow. The answer is a-iv, b-ii, c-i, d-iii.
27.tq: Match each avalanche type to its description.
n: A slab avalanche occurs when a large cohesive slab of snow breaks off and slides. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
A loose snow avalanche, also called a sluff, consists of small slides of dry, powdery snow. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
An ice avalanche involves ice masses from glaciers. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
A rock or debris avalanche consists of a mixture of rock, soil, and snow. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
xs: The correct match is **a-iv, b-ii, c-i, d-iii** — option **(1)**.
**Slab** — a **large cohesive slab** of snow **breaks off and slides**; **loose snow (sluff)** — **small slides** of **dry, powdery snow**.
**Ice** — **ice masses from glaciers**; **rock/debris** — a **mixture of rock, soil and snow**.
xa: ⚠ The **slab avalanche** is the **most dangerous type**.
**Steep slopes** of **30°–45°** are a natural cause.
**Weak snow layers** form through a **temperature gradient**.

27.s:
Consider the following statements about avalanche causes:

I. Heavy snowfall is a natural cause.
II. Skiing and mountaineering are human or other causes.
III. Wind loading is a natural cause.
IV. Artificial triggering through explosives is a natural cause.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
27.x: I, II and III are correct: heavy snow and wind loading are natural causes, and skiing and climbing are human causes. IV is false because explosive triggering is a human cause.
27.tq: Sort the causes into natural and human.
n: Heavy snowfall is a natural cause of avalanches. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
Wind loading is a natural cause of avalanches. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
Skiing is a human or other cause of avalanches. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
Mountaineering is a human or other cause of avalanches. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
Artificial triggering using explosives is a human or other cause of avalanches. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
xs: Statements **I, II and III** are correct — option **(2) I, II and III only**.
**Heavy snowfall** and **wind loading** are **natural** causes; **skiing** and **mountaineering** are **human/other** causes.
IV is wrong: **artificial triggering using explosives** is a **human/other** cause.
xa: Other natural causes: **weak snow layers**, **steep slopes** of **30°–45°**, **earthquakes**, **rain falling on snow**.
Other human causes: **road construction**, **deforestation**, **climate change effects**.
**J&K** is the **most affected** avalanche region.

27.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: The Border Roads Organisation constructs and maintains roads in avalanche-prone areas and installs protection structures.
Statement B: Snow bridges, snow nets, retaining walls and galleries are structural measures for avalanche management.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
27.x: Both are true: the BRO builds and maintains roads in avalanche zones and puts up protection, and snow bridges, nets, walls and galleries are structural measures.
27.tq: Recall the avalanche structural measures.
n: The Border Roads Organisation (BRO) constructs roads in avalanche-prone areas. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
The Border Roads Organisation maintains roads in avalanche-prone areas. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
The Border Roads Organisation installs protection structures in avalanche-prone areas. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
Snow bridges are structural measures for avalanche management. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
Snow nets are structural measures for avalanche management. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
Retaining walls are structural measures for avalanche management. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
Galleries are structural measures for avalanche management. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are true** — option **(1)**.
The **BRO** constructs and maintains **roads** and installs **protection structures** in avalanche-prone areas.
**Snow bridges**, **snow nets**, **retaining walls** and **galleries** are **structural** measures.
xa: **Non-structural:** **hazard zonation mapping**, **restricted movement**, **training**, **awareness**.
**DGRE** (under **DRDO**) issues **daily avalanche warning bulletins** in **winter**.
**NDMA guidelines:** **risk zonation**, **early warning**, structural and non-structural mitigation.

27.s: Which type of avalanche is considered the most dangerous?
27.x: The slab avalanche, where a large block of snow breaks away, is the most dangerous type.
27.tq: Recall the most dangerous avalanche.
n: A slab avalanche is the most dangerous type of avalanche. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
xs: The **slab avalanche** is the **most dangerous type** — option **(1)**.
A **large cohesive slab** of snow **breaks off and slides**.
**Loose snow avalanche (sluff)** involves only **small slides** of **dry, powdery snow**.
xa: **Ice avalanche:** **ice masses** from **glaciers**.
**Rock/debris avalanche:** a mixture of **rock**, **soil** and **snow**.
**Weak snow layers** from a **temperature gradient** cause avalanches.

27.s:
Consider the following statements about natural causes of avalanches:
I. Weak snow layers caused by a temperature gradient can cause avalanches.
II. Steep slopes of 30°–45° can cause avalanches.
III. Earthquakes and seismic activity can cause avalanches.
IV. A rapid temperature rise can cause avalanches.
V. Rain falling on snow can cause avalanches.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
o: I, II, III, IV and V
II, III, IV and V only
27.x: All five are natural causes: weak snow layers, slopes of 30–45°, earthquakes, sudden warming and rain on snow.
27.tq: Recall the natural causes of avalanches.
n: Weak snow layers caused by a temperature gradient are a natural cause of avalanches. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
Steep slopes of 30°–45° are a natural cause of avalanches. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
Earthquakes and seismic activity are natural causes of avalanches. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
A rapid temperature rise is a natural cause of avalanches. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
Rain falling on snow is a natural cause of avalanches. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
xs: **All five** are natural causes — option **(1) I, II, III, IV and V**.
Natural causes: **weak snow layers** from a **temperature gradient**, **steep slopes** of **30°–45°**, **earthquakes and seismic activity**.
Also **a rapid temperature rise** and **rain falling on snow**.
xa: Other natural causes: **heavy snowfall**, **wind loading**.
**Human/other causes:** **skiing**, **mountaineering**, **road construction**, **explosives**, **deforestation**.
**Structural** measures: **snow bridges**, **snow nets**, **retaining walls**, **galleries**.

27.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Jammu and Kashmir

List-II
(i) Most affected region among avalanche-prone areas
(ii) High-altitude avalanche-prone zones
(iii) Avalanche-prone areas in Himachal Pradesh
(iv) Avalanche-prone areas in Uttarakhand
27.x: J&K is the worst affected, Ladakh has high-altitude avalanche zones, Lahaul-Spiti and Kinnaur are in Himachal Pradesh, and the high Garhwal and Kumaon Himalaya are in Uttarakhand. The answer is a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
27.tq: Match each area to its tag.
n: Jammu and Kashmir is the most affected region among the avalanche-prone areas of India. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
Ladakh has high-altitude avalanche-prone zones. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
Lahaul-Spiti in Himachal Pradesh is an avalanche-prone area. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
Kinnaur in Himachal Pradesh is an avalanche-prone area. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
Rohtang Pass in Himachal Pradesh is an avalanche-prone area. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
Chamba in Himachal Pradesh is an avalanche-prone area. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
xs: The correct match is **a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv** — option **(1)**.
**J&K** — the **most affected** region; **Ladakh** — **high-altitude** zones.
**Lahaul-Spiti and Kinnaur** — **Himachal Pradesh**; **higher reaches of Garhwal and Kumaon** — **Uttarakhand**.
xa: HP also has **Rohtang Pass** and **Chamba**.
**Sikkim** and **Arunachal Pradesh** have **high-altitude Himalayan stretches**.
Avalanches mainly occur in the **Himalayan region**, in **high-altitude areas**.

27.s:
How many of the following nature-based flood-management pairs are correctly matched?
I. Wetlands — Store excess water
II. Mangroves — Buffer coastal hazards
III. Forests — Decrease infiltration and interception
IV. Riparian vegetation — Stabilise banks
27.x: Three are correct: wetlands store water, mangroves buffer coasts and riparian plants hold banks. III is false because forests increase infiltration and interception.
27.tq: Check each pair for a reversed effect.
n: Wetlands store excess water. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Mangroves buffer coastal hazards. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Forests increase infiltration. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Forests increase interception. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Riparian vegetation stabilises banks. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
xs: Pairs **I, II and IV** are correct — option **(3) Only three**.
**Wetlands** store excess water; **mangroves** buffer coastal hazards; **riparian vegetation** stabilises banks.
Pair III is wrong: **forests increase infiltration and interception**.
xa: **Floodplains** provide **temporary water storage**.
**Urban green infrastructure** increases **infiltration** and reduces **runoff**.
**Mangroves** with shelter belts **buffer storm surges**.

27.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Developer of the unique flood hazard atlas
(b) Basis of the atlas
(c) Period covered
(d) Intended purpose

List-II
(i) 2000–2018
(ii) Odisha

(iv) More efficient flood management
27.x: Odisha made the flood hazard atlas, based on satellite images of past floods from 2000 to 2018, to manage floods better. The answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv.
27.tq: Match each item to its detail.
n: Odisha developed a unique flood hazard atlas. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
The Odisha Flood Hazard Atlas is based on historical flood inundation captured through satellite imagery. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
The Odisha Flood Hazard Atlas covers the period from 2000 to 2018. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
The Odisha Flood Hazard Atlas is intended to help manage floods more efficiently. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
xs: The correct match is **a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv** — option **(4)**.
**Odisha** made a **unique flood hazard atlas** based on **historical flood inundation** captured through **satellite imagery**.
It covers **2000 to 2018** and aims to **manage floods more efficiently**.
xa: **GIS** deals with **spatial data** — can **model**, **analyse** and **display** community vulnerability.
**Hirakud (Odisha)** releases worsen **Krishna-Godavari delta** floods together with **Srisailam** and **Nagarjuna Sagar**.
Flood control is a **state subject**; Centre supports through **FMBAP**.

27.s:
Assertion (A): A tsunami is a natural disaster.
Reason (R): The term tsunami originated in the Japanese language.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
27.x: Both are true: a tsunami is a natural disaster, and the word is Japanese ('harbour wave'). Where the word comes from does not explain the classification, so R does not explain A.
27.tq: Ask whether a word's origin explains a fact.
n: A tsunami is a natural disaster. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 10-14]
The term tsunami originated in Japanese. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 10-14]
xs: **Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A** — option **(2)**.
A tsunami is a **natural disaster**: **large waves** from **sudden movements of the ocean floor**.
The term is **Japanese** — **"tsu" = harbour + "nami" = wave**; the word's origin does not explain why it is a disaster.
xa: Most commonly caused by an **earthquake beneath the sea**.
Other triggers: **landslides**, **volcanic eruptions**, **explosions**, **bolide impacts**.
⚠ **Trap:** not a **"tidal wave"** — tides come from **gravitational pull**.

27.s:
How many of the following are non-structural measures for avalanche management?
1. Hazard zonation mapping
2. Restricted movement
3. Training
4. Awareness
27.x: All four are non-structural avalanche measures: hazard zoning, restricted movement, training and awareness.
27.tq: Discriminate structural from non-structural measures.
n: Hazard zonation mapping is a non-structural measure for avalanche management. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
Restricted movement is a non-structural measure for avalanche management. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
Training is a non-structural measure for avalanche management. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
Awareness is a non-structural measure for avalanche management. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
xs: **All four** are non-structural avalanche measures — option **(4) All four**.
Non-structural: **hazard zonation mapping**, **restricted movement**, **training** and **awareness**.
xa: **Structural:** **snow bridges**, **snow nets**, **retaining walls**, **galleries**.
**BRO** installs **protection structures** in avalanche-prone areas.
**DGRE** undertakes **hazard mapping** and issues **daily warning bulletins**.

28.s: An earthquake occurring in an uninhabited desert, without causing damage to people or property, is best classified as a:
28.x: A hazard is a potentially damaging event. It becomes a disaster when it interacts with a vulnerable population or exposed assets.
28.tq: Apply the hazard–disaster distinction to a concrete situation.
xs: An earthquake in an **empty desert** is a **hazard**, not a disaster — option **(4)**.
A **hazard** is a **potentially damaging event**; it becomes a **disaster** only when it meets a **vulnerable population**.
**Vulnerability** = exposure + inability to cope; **risk** = likelihood of loss — neither describes the event itself.
xa: **Hazard x Vulnerability = Disaster**.
**Sec. 2(d)** of the DM Act: disaster = catastrophe causing substantial loss **beyond the community's coping capacity**.
Earthquakes are a **geological** hazard (with landslides, volcanoes, tsunamis).

28.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Under Section 2(d) of the DM Act, 2005, a disaster is a catastrophe causing substantial loss beyond the coping capacity of the State Government.
2. Disaster risk rises with hazard, exposure and vulnerability, and falls with coping capacity.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
28.x: Statement 2 is correct: risk rises with hazard, exposure and vulnerability and falls with coping capacity. Statement 1 is wrong: Section 2(d) defines a disaster as a catastrophe causing substantial loss beyond the coping capacity of the AFFECTED COMMUNITY, not the State Government. Hence 2 only.
28.tq: Sec 2(d): beyond the community's coping capacity.
xs: Only **statement 2** is correct — option **(1) 2 only**.
Statement 2 is correct: **risk** rises with **hazard, exposure, vulnerability** and falls with **coping capacity**.
Statement 1 is wrong: **Sec. 2(d)** defines disaster as a catastrophe causing substantial loss beyond the **community's coping capacity**, not the State Government's.
xa: **Hazard x Vulnerability = Disaster**.
**Vulnerability** = **exposure + inability to cope**.
An **earthquake in an empty desert** is a **hazard**, not a disaster.
**Hazard types:** geological, hydro-meteorological, biological (**epidemics**, **pest attacks**).

28.s: Which of the following is NOT identified as a community vulnerability factor?
28.x: Kutcha housing, weak health infrastructure and weak early warning increase vulnerability. High crop-insurance coverage tends to reduce vulnerability.
28.tq: Reverse the vulnerability indicators and identify the protective condition.
xs: **High crop-insurance coverage** is **not** a vulnerability factor — option **(2)**.
The listed factor is **low** crop-insurance cover; high cover reduces vulnerability.
**Kutcha housing**, **thin health infrastructure** and **weak early warning** are listed factors.
xa: Also listed: **dependence on farm labour**.
Risk **falls** with **coping capacity**.
Biological hazards: **epidemics, pest attacks**.

28.s:
Consider the following statements about flood forecasting in India:
1. Scientific flood forecasting in India began in 1958.
2. It was begun by the then Central Water & Power Commission, now the Central Water Commission.

28.tq: 1958, CWPC, Yamuna at Delhi.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statements 1-2: scientific flood forecasting began in **1958** under the then **Central Water & Power Commission** (now **CWC**) — **APPSC 2025** key.
Statement 3 wrong: it started on the **Yamuna at Delhi**, not the Ganga at Patna.
xa: **CWC** remains the warning agency for **river floods**.
⚠ Tsunami = **INCOIS**; landslides = **GSI**; river floods = **CWC**.
**1987**: Disaster Management Institute, **Bhopal**, after the gas tragedy.

28.s: The High Powered Committee on Disaster Management constituted in 1999 was chaired by:
o: The Chairman of the Central Water Commission
28.x: The High Powered Committee on Disaster Management constituted in 1999 was chaired by J. C. Pant.
28.tq: Match a committee with its chairperson, a common APPSC trap.
xs: The **1999 High Powered Committee** on DM plans was chaired by **J.C. Pant** — option **(3)**.
It was part of the background to the **DM Act 2005**, along with the **National Committee** after the **2001 Gujarat earthquake**.
xa: **1990s**: **DM Cell under the Ministry of Agriculture** (UN IDNDR).

28.s:
Consider the following statements about the Sendai Framework:
1. It covers 2015-2030 and followed the Hyogo Framework of 2005-2015.
2. Its priorities include understanding disaster risk and investing in disaster risk reduction.
3. Its goal is universal access to multi-hazard early warning by 2025.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
28.x: Statement 1 is correct: Sendai 2015-2030 succeeded Hyogo 2005-2015. Statement 2 is correct: understanding risk and investing in DRR are two of its four priorities (with risk governance and preparedness/Build Back Better). Statement 3 is wrong: the early-warning goal is for 2030. So '1 and 2 only'; '1 only' misses 2, and the options with 3 include the false statement.
28.tq: Sendai = 2015-2030; early warning for all by 2030.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(3) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: **Sendai 2015-2030** followed **Hyogo 2005-2015**.
Statement 2: its **4 priorities** include **understanding risk** and **investing in DRR** (plus risk governance and preparedness/"Build Back Better").
Statement 3 wrong: the goal of **universal multi-hazard early warning** is for **2030**, not 2025.
xa: Sendai was adopted at **Sendai, Japan**.
**NDMP 2016** was India's first national plan aligned with Sendai; revised **NDMP 2019**.
**Build Back Better** is part of the **recovery and reconstruction** phase.

28.s: The Disaster Management Cell established in the 1990s in response to the UN International Decade for Natural Disaster Reduction was placed under the:
28.x: In the 1990s, a Disaster Management Cell was established under the Ministry of Agriculture in response to the UN International Decade for Natural Disaster Reduction.
28.tq: Use the responsible ministry as the distinguishing institutional detail.
xs: The **1990s** DM Cell was under the **Ministry of Agriculture** — option **(1)**.

**MHA** became the **nodal ministry** later, under the **DM Act 2005**.
xa: **Dec 2020**: a **DM Cell in MoHFW**.
**1999**: **High Powered Committee** chaired by **J.C. Pant**.
**1958**: scientific flood forecasting by the then **Central Water & Power Commission**.

28.s:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
A. Sendai Framework
B. National Policy on Disaster Management
C. National Centre for Disaster Management at IIPA

28.x: The correct sequence is 1995 National Centre for Disaster Management, 2005 Disaster Management Act, 2009 National Policy on Disaster Management and 2015 Sendai Framework.

28.s:
Consider the following statements about the National Disaster Management Plan (NDMP):
1. The first NDMP was issued in 2016 and revised in 2019 in alignment with the Sendai Framework.
2. The short-, medium- and long-term time frames of NDMP 2016 are 3, 7 and 12 years respectively.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

28.tq: NDMP: 2016 first, 2019 revised; 5-10-15 years.
xs: Only **statement 1** is correct — option **(1) 1 only**.
Statement 1 is correct: the first **NDMP** came in **2016**, revised **NDMP 2019** aligned to **Sendai**.
