n: Mixed farming combines crops and livestock on the same farm. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 23-25]
Mixed farming is highly mechanised. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 23-25]
Mixed farming is practised in Western Europe. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 23-25]
Mixed farming is practised in the eastern United States. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 23-25]
Mixed farming is practised in Argentina. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 23-25]
Mixed farming is practised in south-eastern Australia. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 23-25]
Mixed farming is practised in New Zealand. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 23-25]
Mixed farming is practised in South Africa. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 23-25]
xs: All four statements — **I, II, III and IV** — are correct, so option **(3)** is correct.
I and II: **mixed farming** **combines crops and livestock** on the same farm and is **highly mechanised**.
III: it is practised in **Western Europe**, the **eastern United States** and **Argentina**.
IV: also in **south-eastern Australia**, **New Zealand** and **South Africa**.
xa: Mixed farming is also found in **NW Europe** and **eastern North America**.
**Dairy farming** specialises in **milk** and needs **refrigeration and transport**.
**Livestock ranching** is large-scale commercial rearing on **ranches**.

80.s:
How many of the following are regions where dairy farming is practised?

2. Denmark
3. The Netherlands
4. New Zealand
5. The Midwest of the United States
6. South-eastern Australia
80.x: All six are dairy regions: north-western Europe, Denmark, the Netherlands, New Zealand, the US Midwest and south-eastern Australia.
80.tq: Count each listed region carefully.
n: Dairy farming is practised in north-western Europe. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 23-25]
Dairy farming is practised in Denmark. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 23-25]
Dairy farming is practised in the Netherlands. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 23-25]
Dairy farming is practised in New Zealand. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 23-25]
Dairy farming is practised in the Midwest of the United States. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 23-25]
Dairy farming is practised in south-eastern Australia. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 23-25]
xs: All **six** listed are dairy regions — option **(3)**.
Dairy farming is practised in **north-western Europe** — **Denmark**, the **Netherlands**.
It is also practised in **New Zealand**, the **Midwest** of the US and **south-eastern Australia**.
xa: Dairy farming **specialises in milk production**.
It **requires refrigeration and transport**.
**New Zealand** also has **mixed farming** and **livestock ranching**.

80.s: Mediterranean agriculture is practised in which of the following regions?
80.x: South-western Australia has a Mediterranean climate and Mediterranean farming. The Pampas are grain and ranching lands, New Zealand is dairy, and the eastern United States has mixed farming.
80.tq: Recall where each farming type occurs.
n: Mediterranean agriculture is practised in south-western Australia. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 23-25]
xs: Mediterranean agriculture is practised in **south-western Australia** — option **(2)**.
Other Mediterranean regions: the **Mediterranean Basin**, **California**, **Central Chile**, the **Cape Province**.
The **Pampas** are a **commercial grain** and **ranching** region; the **eastern United States** has **mixed farming**.
**New Zealand** is linked with **dairy**, mixed farming and ranching.
xa: Mediterranean agriculture specialises in **fruits, olives, grapes, citrus**; includes **viticulture**.
Whittlesey: Mediterranean areas have **winter rain**.
**Dairy** regions include **south-eastern Australia**, not the south-west.

81.s: Which of the following combinations regarding wheat cultivation is correct?
o: Zaid crop; hot nights and waterlogged soils
Perennial crop; uniform rainfall throughout the year
Rabi crop; cool growing season, 50–75 cm rainfall and warm sunny ripening
Kharif crop; very high humidity and rainfall above 150 cm
81.x: Wheat is a rabi crop requiring a cool growing season, about 50–75 cm rainfall and warm, sunny conditions during ripening.
81.tq: Match the crop season with its growth and ripening requirements.
xs: Wheat is a **rabi** crop needing a **cool growing season**, **50-75 cm** rainfall and **bright warm sun at ripening** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Wheat is not kharif: very high humidity and heavy rainfall describe **rice** (above **100 cm**), which is the **kharif** cereal.
Wheat is the **2nd** most important cereal in India, grown on the alluvium of the **Ganga-Satluj plains**.
xa: Wheat also grows on the **black soil of the Deccan** — the APPSC-G1 2024 trap called it unsuitable, which is incorrect.
⚠ Rice **above 100 cm** vs wheat **50-75 cm**; rice = **kharif**, wheat = **rabi**.
Leading wheat states (2026 order): **Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Punjab, Haryana**.
India is **2nd** in the world in wheat with **117.94 MMT**.

81.s: Which one of the following cereals ranks first in India in terms of importance and is a staple food for more than half of the country's population?
81.x: Rice is the first-ranking cereal in India and is the staple food of more than half of the country's population.
81.tq: Use the rank and population-share clue to identify the cereal.
xs: **Rice** is India's **1st** cereal and the staple of **over half of India** — option **(4)** is correct.
**Wheat** is the **2nd** most important cereal; **maize** and **millets** are kharif crops of lesser rank.
Rice needs **20-35°C** (above **25°C** ideal), high humidity and **above 100 cm** rainfall.
xa: **West Bengal** is the "**Rice Bowl of India**" and the largest producer.
India (**150.18 MT**) has now **surpassed China** (**145.28 MT**) as the world's largest rice producer.
India is the **largest rice exporter**, with **~40%** of world trade.
Rice suits **clayey/loamy**, deltaic and coastal alluvium soils.

81.s: Rice is especially suited to which of the following soil and geographical environments?
o: Clayey or loamy soils of deltaic and coastal alluvial areas
Laterite soils of upland plateaus only
81.x: Rice is well suited to clayey or loamy soils, particularly the deltaic and coastal alluvium.
81.tq: Match the crop with its characteristic soil and landform.
xs: Rice suits **clayey or loamy soils** of **deltaic and coastal alluvium** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Sandy soils** of the driest tracts suit **bajra**, not rice; **red soils** are linked with **ragi**.
Rice needs **above 100 cm** rainfall, so desert and arid soils are unsuitable.
xa: **AP and TN rice deltas** gained in the Green Revolution through irrigation.
Wheat grows on the alluvium of the **Ganga-Satluj plains** and the **black soil of the Deccan**.
**Lower Gangetic Plains** (West Bengal) zone: **rice, jute**.
AP paddy output **127.15 lakh MT** (2024-25).

81.s: Which one of the following statements regarding wheat cultivation in India is NOT correct?
o: It requires a cool growing season and bright warm sunshine at the time of ripening.
It is mainly a rabi crop.
Wheat is the second most important cereal in India.
The black-soil region of the Deccan is unsuitable for wheat cultivation.
81.x: The statement is NOT correct. Wheat is grown not only in the Ganga-Satluj plains but also in the black-soil region of the Deccan.
81.tq: Find the reversed suitability statement, especially where a known crop-soil association is denied.
xs: The NOT-correct statement is that the **black-soil region of the Deccan is unsuitable for wheat** — option **(4)**; black soil does suit wheat.
Statements 1-3 are true: wheat needs a **cool growing season** and **bright warm sun at ripening**, is a **rabi** crop and the **2nd** most important cereal.
This was the **APPSC-G1 2024** trap: black soil is listed with **cotton, jowar, oilseeds** as a wheat-suitable soil.
xa: Wheat's main belt is the **Ganga-Satluj plains** (Indo-Gangetic "**wheat bowl**").
Wheat rainfall: **50-75 cm**.
Wheat states: **UP, MP, Punjab, Haryana** (2026 order).
The first Green Revolution phase (mid-1960s-1980s) was largely **wheat**.

81.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Pulses — high-moisture crop requiring continuous heavy rainfall
Millets — mainly kharif crops suited to dryland and rainfed tracts
Wheat — crop of hot and humid monsoon season
Rice — crop requiring low-input dryland conditions
81.x: Millets are mostly kharif crops and are climate-resilient, low-input crops of dryland and rainfed tracts.
81.tq: Eliminate pairs that reverse the characteristic climate or season of the crop.
xs: **Millets** are **mostly kharif**, **climate-resilient, low-input** crops of **dryland/rainfed tracts** — option **(2)** is correct.
Pulses are **rain-fed, low-moisture** crops, not heavy-rainfall crops; wheat is **rabi**, not monsoon.
Rice needs **above 100 cm** rainfall or irrigation, not dryland conditions.
xa: Some millets are **rabi in the south**.
Major millets: **Bajra** (~**60%** of India's millet output), **Jowar**, **Ragi**; minor: foxtail, little, kodo, proso.
India is the **largest millet producer**, **42.75%** of world output (**18.59 MMT**).
**2023** was the UN **International Year of Millets**; millets branded **Shree Anna**.

81.s: Which one of the following pairs of food crop and its characteristic growing condition is correctly matched?
o: Bajra — red soils of humid tracts
Ragi — sandy soils of the driest tracts
Pulses — fix atmospheric nitrogen and are used in crop rotation
Rice — less than 50 cm rainfall without irrigation
81.x: Pulses are leguminous and fix atmospheric nitrogen, which is why they are used in rotation. Bajra suits the driest conditions and sandy soils, not humid red soils; ragi is associated with red soils; rice needs above 100 cm of rainfall or irrigation.
81.tq: Pulses = nitrogen fixers; bajra = sandy, driest; ragi = red soils.
xs: **Pulses** **fix atmospheric nitrogen** and are **used in rotation** — option **(3)** is correct.
**Bajra** suits the **driest** tracts and **sandy soils**; **ragi** suits **red soils** — options 1 and 2 swap them.
**Rice** needs **above 100 cm** rainfall or irrigation, not under 50 cm.
xa: A **pulse-cereal rotation** leaves fixed nitrogen for the next crop.
**Intercropping** example: **tur with jowar or maize**.
Pulses grow in **both seasons**: kharif (**tur/arhar**) and rabi (**gram**).
**Rajasthan** leads bajra; **Karnataka** leads ragi.

81.s:
Arrange the following wheat-producing states in descending order of production:
A. Haryana
B. Madhya Pradesh
C. Uttar Pradesh
D. Punjab
81.x: The stated order is Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Punjab and Haryana.
81.tq: For an order question, first identify the leading state and then compare the middle positions.
xs: The 2026 order of wheat states is **Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Punjab, Haryana** — i.e. **C, B, D, A**, option **(1)**.
Wheat is the **2nd** cereal and a **rabi** crop of the **Ganga-Satluj plains**.
xa: **Punjab, Haryana, western UP** were the **core Green Revolution** states.
India is **2nd** in world wheat output (**117.94 MMT**).
⚠ For pulses the order starts with **MP**, then **Rajasthan**; for rice **West Bengal** leads.
Wheat also grows on the **black soil of the Deccan**.

81.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the distribution of major food crops in India:
1. Rice is produced in West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Odisha, Bihar and Tamil Nadu.
2. Wheat is chiefly associated with Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Haryana and Madhya Pradesh.
3. Rice is exclusively a rainfed crop in India.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
81.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because rice is grown with both rainfall and irrigation, including irrigated Punjab.
81.tq: Use the word exclusively as a warning and verify the crop's stated regional distribution.
xs: Statement 1 correct: rice states include **West Bengal, UP, Punjab, AP, Telangana, Odisha, Bihar, TN**.
Statement 2 correct: wheat leaders are **UP, MP, Punjab, Haryana**.
Statement 3 wrong: rice needs **above 100 cm** **or irrigation** and **Punjab** grows irrigated rice — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: **West Bengal** = "**Rice Bowl of India**", largest producer (2026).
**Rajasthan** leads **bajra**; **Karnataka** leads **ragi**.
Rice-wheat is the dominant **double cropping** system of the **Indo-Gangetic plains**.
MSP and free power favour rice-wheat, e.g. **paddy in Punjab**.

81.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Maize — Tamil Nadu; exclusively winter cultivation
Bajra — Rajasthan; driest conditions and sandy soils
Jowar — West Bengal; humid deltaic conditions
81.x: Rajasthan is the leading bajra-producing state, and bajra is suited to the driest conditions and sandy soils. Ragi is led by Karnataka, while jowar is associated mainly with Maharashtra and Karnataka.
81.tq: Check the crop-soil-climate relationship before accepting the state match.
xs: **Bajra** is led by **Rajasthan** and suits the **driest** conditions and **sandy soils** — option **(2)** is correct.
**Maize** is a **kharif** crop led by **Karnataka, MP**, not a winter crop of Tamil Nadu.
**Jowar** is led by **Maharashtra, Karnataka**; **ragi** by **Karnataka** on **red soils**.
xa: **Bajra** (pearl millet) gives ~**60%** of India's millet output.
Millet leaders: **Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Karnataka** (2026).
**Andhra Pradesh** was marked a major **jowar** state in the APPSC 2025 key.
El Nino and conflict are pushing farmers to **bajra/jowar** (2026).

81.s: Which of the following statements about maize production is correct?
o: West Bengal and Odisha lead maize production, which is concentrated only in deltaic soils.
Rajasthan and Punjab are the only leading states, and Andhra Pradesh has no significant maize region.
Tamil Nadu and Kerala lead maize production, and maize is grown only as a rabi crop.
Karnataka and Madhya Pradesh are leading states, while production is rising in the Godavari–Krishna districts of Andhra Pradesh.
81.x: Karnataka and Madhya Pradesh are listed as leading maize-producing states, with rising production in Andhra Pradesh's Godavari–Krishna districts.
81.tq: Combine the national leaders with the specified emerging regional centre.
xs: **Karnataka and Madhya Pradesh** lead maize, and output is **rising in AP's Godavari-Krishna districts** — option **(4)** is correct.
Maize is a **kharif** crop driven by **feed/starch demand**, so "only rabi" is wrong.
xa: In AP, maize is surging in **Godavari and Krishna** for **poultry feed**.
Maize is covered under **NFSNM**.
**Intercropping** example: **tur with jowar or maize**; **parallel cropping**: **maize + green gram**.
**West Bengal** leads **rice**, **Rajasthan** leads **bajra**.

81.s: Which State is known as the 'Rice Bowl of India' and is currently the largest producer of rice?
81.x: West Bengal is called the Rice Bowl of India and is the largest rice producer. Uttar Pradesh, Punjab (irrigated rice) and Andhra Pradesh are also important rice states, but none leads West Bengal.
81.tq: Rice Bowl = West Bengal (largest producer).
xs: **West Bengal** is the "**Rice Bowl of India**" and the **largest producer** (2026) — option **(3)**.
**UP, Punjab** (irrigated), **AP** are also rice states but trail West Bengal.
xa: Other rice states: **Telangana, Odisha, Bihar, TN**.
India produced **150.18 MT**, **surpassing China** as world's largest rice producer.
India is the **largest rice exporter**, **~40%** of world trade.
**Lower Gangetic Plains** zone (West Bengal): **rice, jute**.

81.s: Among the following States, which one was marked in the APPSC 2025 key as a major producer of jowar?
81.x: The APPSC 2025 key marked Andhra Pradesh as the major jowar state among the options. Rajasthan is known for bajra, West Bengal for rice and Uttar Pradesh for wheat.
81.tq: APPSC 2025: jowar → Andhra Pradesh (textbooks: Maharashtra, Karnataka).
xs: The **APPSC 2025 key** marked **Andhra Pradesh** as the major **jowar** state among UP / Rajasthan / AP / West Bengal — option **(3)**.
**Rajasthan** is the largest **bajra** state; **West Bengal** is the **rice** leader; **UP** tops **wheat**.
xa: Textbook jowar leaders: **Maharashtra, Karnataka**.
Jowar is a **kharif/rabi**, dry, rainfed crop (sorghum).
Jowar is a **major millet** with bajra and ragi.
⚠ Black soil is listed with **cotton, jowar, oilseeds** — and also suits wheat.

81.s: Which phase of agricultural development is marked by a price policy based on minimum support price and procurement?
81.x: The third phase of agricultural development is marked by a price policy based on MSP and procurement.
81.tq: Associate the policy characteristic with the correct phase of agricultural development.
xs: The **third phase** is marked by a **price policy based on MSP and procurement** (PYQ 2017) — option **(3)**.
The **first phase** (mid-1960s-1980s) was largely **wheat**; the **second phase (1980s)** spread east and west.
xa: Second-phase output growth was **3.4% vs 2.3%** earlier.
Inputs included **HYV seeds**, fertilisers, irrigation, mechanisation and **MSP**.
The New Agricultural Strategy began **1965** (dated **1968** in current notes).
Procurement is confined to **rice, wheat, sugarcane**, which use over two-thirds of India's urea.

81.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Green Revolution:
1. The first phase from the mid-1960s to the 1980s was largely centred on wheat.
2. Rice benefited in a later and wider phase.
3. Pulses and coarse cereals were the principal crops of the first phase.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
81.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because wheat was central to the first phase, while pulses and coarse cereals lagged.
81.tq: Find the crop-imbalance trap in the statement that reverses the first-phase beneficiaries.
xs: Statement 1 correct: the first phase (**mid-1960s-1980s**) was largely **wheat**.
Statement 2 correct: **rice** gained in a **later, wider phase**.
Statement 3 wrong: **pulses, oilseeds, coarse cereals lagged** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: The crops most benefited were **wheat and rice** (APPSC 2025 key).
Second phase (**1980s**): spread east and west; growth **3.4% vs 2.3%**.
Third phase: **MSP and procurement** price policy.
Crop imbalance — **pulses, oilseeds, millets neglected** — is a key limitation.

81.s:
Consider the following statements about the Green Revolution:
1. C. Subramaniam was the Union Agriculture Minister who backed the strategy.
2. Norman Borlaug, who developed Mexican dwarf wheat, received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1970.
3. M.S. Swaminathan is known as the father of the Green Revolution in India.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
81.x: Statement 2 is wrong: Borlaug (father of the Green Revolution in the world, HYV Mexican dwarf wheat) received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970, not Economics. Statement 3 is correct: Swaminathan is the father of India's Green Revolution. Statement 1 is correct: C. Subramaniam was the Union Agriculture Minister who backed it. So '1 and 3 only'.
81.tq: World = Borlaug (Nobel Peace 1970); India = Swaminathan.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct and 2 is wrong — so option **(3)** 1 and 3 only.
Statement 1 is correct: **C. Subramaniam** was the **Union Agriculture Minister** who backed the strategy.
Statement 2 is wrong: **Norman Borlaug** (HYV **Mexican dwarf wheat**) won the **Nobel Peace Prize** in **1970**, not Economics.
Statement 3 is correct: **M.S. Swaminathan** is the **Father of the Green Revolution in India**.
xa: ⚠ Father in the **world** = **Borlaug**; father in **India** = **Swaminathan**.
The Green Revolution began in **1965** as the **New Agricultural Strategy** (dated **1968** in current notes).
Inputs: **HYV seeds**, chemical fertilisers, pesticides, assured irrigation, mechanisation and **MSP**.
Crops most benefited: **wheat and rice** (APPSC **2025** key).

81.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu gained from the spread of irrigated rice cultivation.
2. The Green Revolution helped India move from PL-480 wheat imports towards food self-sufficiency.
3. The Green Revolution completely eliminated regional imbalance in Indian agriculture.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
81.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because rainfed and hill areas remained comparatively neglected, creating regional imbalance.
81.tq: Reject the absolute claim that a major agricultural transformation eliminated every imbalance.
xs: Statement 1 correct: **AP and TN rice deltas** gained via **irrigation**.
Statement 2 correct: India moved from **PL-480** wheat imports to **self-sufficiency**.
Statement 3 wrong: **regional imbalance** remained — **rainfed and hilly areas left out** — so option **(1)**, **1 and 2 only**.
xa: **Punjab, Haryana, western UP** turned from **food-deficit to surplus**.
The **eastern belt** (MP, Bihar, Odisha, WB, Assam) **lagged** in phase 1.
**BGREI** (**2010-11**) aimed to bring the Green Revolution to Eastern India.
Gains were captured by big landowners (**>10 ha**).

81.s: The New Agricultural Strategy associated with the Green Revolution in India began in:
81.x: The New Agricultural Strategy began in 1965 and combined HYV seeds, fertilisers, irrigation and minimum support price with the objective of foodgrain self-sufficiency.
81.tq: Use the strategy's starting year rather than the later year associated with the wider production surge.
xs: The **New Agricultural Strategy** began in **1965** — option **(2)**.
It brought a **mid-1960s surge** in foodgrain output.
xa: ⚠ Current notes date it **1968**.
Inputs: **HYV seeds**, chemical fertilisers, pesticides, **assured irrigation**, mechanisation, **MSP**.
Aim: **self-sufficiency in food grains**, ending dependence on **PL-480** imports.
**Borlaug** won the **Nobel Peace Prize 1970**.

81.s: The Green Revolution in India mainly increased the production of:
81.x: Wheat (first phase) and rice (later, wider phase) gained most, as in the APPSC 2025 key. Pulses, oilseeds and coarse cereals lagged; cotton and sugarcane were not the focus of the strategy.
81.tq: Green Revolution = wheat first, then rice; pulses/oilseeds left behind.
xs: The Green Revolution mainly increased **wheat and rice** (APPSC 2025 key) — option **(2)**.
**Pulses, oilseeds, coarse cereals lagged**, so options 1 and 3 are wrong.
xa: First phase largely **wheat**; rice gained in the **later, wider phase**.
It locked the north-west into **rice-wheat monoculture** and groundwater over-use.
**Cotton, jute, sugarcane** were added to **NFSM** only in **2014-15**.
⚠ Father in world = **Borlaug**; in India = **Swaminathan**.

81.s: Which one of the following was NOT a major limitation of the Green Revolution mentioned in relation to Indian agriculture?
o: Neglect of pulses, oilseeds and millets
Complete equality in the distribution of gains among all landholders
Regional imbalance affecting rainfed and hill areas
81.x: The gains were not equally distributed; big landowners benefited most. Groundwater depletion, salinity, crop imbalance and regional imbalance were recognised limitations.
81.tq: Find the statement that reverses a known limitation instead of identifying one.
xs: The odd one out is **complete equality in the distribution of gains** — option **(3)**; gains were captured by **big landowners (>10 ha)**.
Real limitations: **groundwater depletion, salinity**; **pulses, oilseeds, millets neglected**; **rainfed and hilly areas left out**.
xa: Fertiliser imbalance: N:P:K **10.9:4.1:1** vs ideal **4:2:1**.
North-west locked in **rice-wheat monoculture** and groundwater over-use.
Remedy: Swaminathan's **Evergreen Revolution**.
Only about **12%** of irrigated area uses **drip or sprinkler**.

81.s: The fertiliser-use ratio of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium cited for Indian agriculture, compared with the ideal ratio, is:
81.x: The prevailing N:P:K ratio is cited as 10.9:4.1:1, whereas the ideal ratio is 4:2:1.
81.tq: Keep the observed ratio and ideal ratio in their correct order before comparing the figures.
xs: The N:P:K ratio is **10.9:4.1:1** compared with an ideal **4:2:1** — option **(3)**.
This **fertiliser imbalance** is a listed Green Revolution limitation — excess **nitrogen**.
xa: Inputs stressed chemical fertilisers, **esp. nitrogenous**.
Rice, wheat and sugarcane use **over two-thirds of India's urea**.
Other limitations: **groundwater depletion, salinity**, crop and regional imbalance.
Remedy: **Evergreen Revolution** (Swaminathan).

81.s: Swaminathan's proposed remedy for the adverse effects and ecological limitations of the Green Revolution is known as:
81.x: The Evergreen Revolution was proposed as a sustainable corrective approach associated with M.S. Swaminathan.
81.tq: Distinguish the sustainability-oriented term from revolutions associated with fisheries, milk or broad diversification.
xs: Swaminathan's remedy is the **Evergreen Revolution** — option **(2)**.
It answers Green Revolution ills: **groundwater depletion, salinity**, **rice-wheat monoculture**, fertiliser imbalance.
xa: Swaminathan = **Father of the Green Revolution in India**.
Borlaug = Father in the **world**, **Nobel Peace Prize 1970**.
Fertiliser imbalance: **10.9:4.1:1** vs ideal **4:2:1**.
Gains went to farmers with **>10 ha**.

81.s:
Consider the following statements about BGREI (Bringing Green Revolution to Eastern India):
1. It focuses on the rice-based (rice-wheat) cropping system.
2. It was launched in 2010-11 under RKVY.
3. Its States include Punjab and Haryana.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
81.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: BGREI was launched in 2010-11 under RKVY for the rice-based cropping system. Statement 3 is wrong: it covers Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Odisha, eastern UP and West Bengal - the eastern belt that lagged in the first Green Revolution, not Punjab and Haryana. So only statement 3 is NOT correct.
81.tq: BGREI = eastern States, not the Green Revolution core.
xs: Only statement **3** is NOT correct — so option **(1)** 3 only.
Statement 1 is correct: BGREI focuses on the **rice-based (rice-wheat) cropping system**.
Statement 2 is correct: it was launched in **2010-11** under **RKVY**.
Statement 3 is wrong: its States are **Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Odisha, eastern UP** and **West Bengal** — not Punjab and Haryana.
xa: **NFSM** was launched in **2007-08** for **rice, wheat, pulses**.
In **2024-25** NFSM was renamed the **National Food Security and Nutrition Mission (NFSNM)**.
**Nutri-cereals** were added to NFSM in **2018-19**; **SMSP** (seeds) merged in **2023-24**.
⚠ **Punjab, Haryana, western UP** were the **core** Green Revolution states; the **eastern belt** lagged in phase 1.

81.s:
With reference to the National Food Security Mission (NFSM), consider the following statements:
1. It was launched in 2007-08 for rice, wheat and pulses.
2. Its initial objectives included area expansion, productivity enhancement and improvement of soil fertility.
3. Nutri-cereals were added to it in 2014-15.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
81.x: NFSM began in 2007-08 for rice, wheat and pulses, with the stated production and soil-fertility objectives. Nutri-cereals were added later, in 2018-19.
81.tq: Track the original launch year separately from later additions.
xs: Statement 1 correct: NFSM launched **2007-08** for **rice, wheat, pulses**.
Statement 2 correct: aims were **area expansion, productivity, soil fertility**.
Statement 3 wrong: **nutri-cereals** were added in **2018-19**, not 2014-15 — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: **2014-15**: coarse cereals and **cotton, jute, sugarcane** added.
**2023-24**: **SMSP** (seeds) merged in.
**2024-25**: renamed **NFSNM**.
Funds: Rs **15,166.33 crore** released 2014-15 to 2024-25.

81.s: NFSM was renamed as the National Food Security and Nutrition Mission (NFSNM) in:
81.x: NFSM was renamed the National Food Security and Nutrition Mission in 2024-25.
81.tq: Match the renamed scheme with its precise milestone year.
xs: NFSM was renamed **NFSNM** in **2024-25** — option **(3)**.
**2023-24** was the **SMSP** merger; **2018-19** added nutri-cereals.
xa: NFSNM crops: rice, wheat, pulses, maize, barley, **Shree Anna**, cotton, jute, sugarcane.
**Oilseeds/oil palm** moved to **NMEO-Edible Oils**.
AP allocation: NFSNM ₹**2,194.07 lakh** (**60:40**).
NFSM launched **2007-08**.

81.s: Which of the following is NOT included among the crops covered by NFSNM?
81.x: NFSNM covers rice, wheat, pulses, maize, barley, Shree Anna, cotton, jute and sugarcane. Oilseeds and oil palm were moved to the NMEO initiatives.
81.tq: Find the crop group transferred to a separate oil mission.
xs: **Oilseeds** are not in NFSNM — they **moved to NMEO-Edible Oils** — option **(3)**.
NFSNM covers **rice, wheat, pulses, maize, barley, Shree Anna, cotton, jute, sugarcane**.
xa: **Shree Anna** = jowar, bajra, ragi, small millets.
NMEO target: about **70 million tonnes** by **2030-31**.
Edible-oil import dependence: **63.2% (FY16) → 56.25% (FY24)**.
Renamed NFSNM in **2024-25**.

81.s: The NMEO-Oilseeds and NMEO-Oil Palm initiatives aim at approximately what level of production by 2030-31?
81.x: The two missions target about 70 million tonnes by 2030-31.
81.tq: Link the target figure with the correct mission and terminal year.
xs: **NMEO-Oilseeds and NMEO-Oil Palm** target about **70 million tonnes** by **2030-31** — option **(3)**.
Their aim is to cut **edible-oil import dependence**.
xa: Import dependence fell from **63.2% (FY16)** to **56.25% (FY24)**.
Oilseeds and oil palm were **moved out of NFSNM** into NMEO-Edible Oils.
Oilseeds were **neglected** during the Green Revolution.
Black soil is listed with **cotton, jowar, oilseeds**.

81.s: Which one of the following statements regarding recent foodgrain production in India is correct?
o: Foodgrain production reached a record 357.73 million tonnes in 2024–25.
Foodgrain production in 2024–25 remained below 250 million tonnes.
Foodgrain production was exactly equal to horticulture production in 2024–25.
Horticulture production was lower than foodgrain production in 2024–25.
81.x: India recorded 357.73 million tonnes of foodgrain production in 2024–25. Horticulture production was higher at 367.72 million tonnes.
81.tq: Select the precise current figure while rejecting changed or reversed comparisons.
xs: Foodgrains hit a record **357.73 million tonnes in 2024-25** — option **(1)**.
**Horticulture** exceeded it at **367.72 MT**, so options 3 and 4 are wrong; option 2 (below 250) is far off.
xa: Rice **150.18 MT**; wheat **117.94 MMT**; millets **18.59 MMT**.
AP foodgrains (2024-25): **161.86 lakh MT** on **37.51 lakh ha**.
Gross cropped area **219.16 MH**; net sown **141 MH** (2021-22).
India is **largest producer and consumer of pulses**.

81.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. India's rice output (150.18 MT) has surpassed China's (145.28 MT), making India the largest rice producer.
2. India is the world's largest wheat producer, with 117.94 MMT.
3. India is the largest rice exporter, with about 40 per cent of world rice trade.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
81.x: Statement 1 is correct: India's 150.18 MT exceeded China's 145.28 MT (Jan 2026). Statement 3 is correct: India is the largest rice exporter with about 40 per cent of world trade. Statement 2 is wrong: with 117.94 MMT India is 2nd in wheat. So '1 and 3 only'.
81.tq: Rice: India 1st now; wheat: India 2nd.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — so option **(3)** 1 and 3 only.
Statement 1 is correct: India's **150.18 MT** surpassed China's **145.28 MT**, making India the **largest rice producer** (5 Jan 2026).
Statement 2 is wrong: with **117.94 MMT** of wheat, India is **2nd** in the world, not the largest.
Statement 3 is correct: India is the **largest rice exporter**, with about **40%** of world trade.
xa: Record foodgrain output: **357.73 million tonnes (2024-25)**; horticulture exceeded it at **367.72 MT**.
India is the world's **largest producer and consumer of pulses**.
India is the **largest millet producer**, with **42.75%** of world output.
⚠ Sources differ: other notes rank **China ahead of India** in rice.

81.s: Which of the following correctly represents India's net sown area and gross cropped area in 2021-22?
o: Net sown area 328.7 MH; gross cropped area 77.9 MH
Net sown area 219.16 MH; gross cropped area 141 MH
Net sown area 141 MH; gross cropped area 219.16 MH
Net sown area 77.9 MH; gross cropped area 120.3 MH
81.x: India's net sown area was 141 million hectares and gross cropped area was 219.16 million hectares in 2021-22.
81.tq: Distinguish net area from gross area by identifying the larger figure as the repeatedly cropped area.
xs: Net sown area **141 MH**; gross cropped area **219.16 MH** — option **(3)**.
**328.7 MH** is the geographical area; **77.9** net irrigated; **120.3** gross irrigated.
xa: Cropping intensity **155.4%** (2021-22).
Net sown = **42.8%** of geographical area.
Gross irrigated is **54.9%** of GCA.
AP cropping intensity **1.88 in 2024-25**.

81.s: Approximately what percentage of India's net sown area is irrigated?
81.x: Only 56.4 per cent of India's net sown area is irrigated.
81.tq: Distinguish the percentage of net sown area irrigated from the percentage of gross cropped area irrigated.
xs: Only **56.4 per cent** of net sown area is irrigated (2026) — option **(3)**.
**Wells + tube wells** give **over 63%** of irrigation.
xa: About **51%** of net sown area is **rainfed**.
Net irrigated **77.9 MH**; gross irrigated **120.3 MH**.
Only about **12%** of irrigated area uses **drip or sprinkler**.
**Dryland farming**: **less than 750 mm** rainfall and no assured irrigation.

81.s: Which of the following is correctly stated about India's position in world agriculture?
o: India is the largest producer of all food grains.
India is the largest producer of pulses and millets.
India is the largest producer of oil palm and barley.
India is the largest producer of wheat and sugarcane in the world.
81.x: India is identified as the largest producer of pulses and millets. The other options make broader claims not supported by the stated facts.
81.tq: Reject an overbroad superlative and select the precisely stated crop groups.
xs: India is the **largest producer of pulses and millets** — option **(2)**.
Pulses: **largest producer and consumer**; millets: **42.75%** of world output.
In **wheat** India is only **2nd**, so option (4) is wrong.
xa: Millets: **18.59 MMT** on **12.86 million ha**.
India is now the **largest rice producer**, surpassing China.
India is the **largest rice exporter** (~**40%**).
**Bajra** gives ~**60%** of India's millet output.

81.s: The dominant cropping system of the Indo-Gangetic Plains is:
81.x: Rice-wheat is the dominant cropping system of the Indo-Gangetic Plains, with paddy followed by wheat as double cropping.
81.tq: Identify the standard regional crop sequence rather than an individual crop.
xs: **Rice-wheat** is the dominant system of the **Indo-Gangetic plains** — option **(1)**.
**Paddy followed by wheat** in one year is **double cropping**.
xa: **Punjab-Haryana** rotate **wheat, paddy, mustard, pulses**.
The system locked the **north-west** into **rice-wheat monoculture** and groundwater over-use.
**Lower Gangetic Plains** (West Bengal) = **rice, jute**; **Eastern Himalayan** = plantations, jhum.
**BGREI** focuses on the **rice-based (rice-wheat) cropping system** of Eastern India.

81.s: Intercropping is best described as:
o: Growing a crop only on fallow land
Sowing the next crop after complete removal of the previous crop
Growing one crop continuously for several years
Growing two or more crops together in definite rows
81.x: Intercropping involves growing two or more crops together in definite rows, such as tur with jowar or maize.
81.tq: Separate intercropping from mixed cropping by focusing on the definite row arrangement.
xs: **Intercropping** = **two or more crops together in definite rows** — option **(4)**.
Example: **tur with jowar or maize**.
xa: ⚠ **Mixed cropping** = seeds mixed, **no row pattern**; insures against failure.
**Parallel cropping**: crops of different growth habit, **no competition** (maize + green gram).
**Relay cropping**: next crop sown into the **standing crop** before harvest.
**Multiple/double**: crops in **succession** in one year (paddy then wheat).

81.s: Which one of the following examples represents parallel cropping?
o: Tur and jowar sown together in definite rows
Maize and green gram grown together without competition
The next crop sown into a standing crop before its harvest
Paddy followed by wheat in the same year
81.x: Parallel cropping involves two crops of different growth habit and duration growing without competition; maize plus green gram is the stated example.
81.tq: Discriminate parallel cropping from intercropping and relay cropping by its no-competition condition.
xs: **Parallel cropping** = two crops of **different growth habit and duration**, **no competition** — e.g. **maize and green gram**, option **(2)**.
Tur with jowar in rows is **intercropping**; sowing into a standing crop is **relay cropping**; paddy then wheat is **double cropping**.
xa: ⚠ **Intercropping** = in rows; **mixed cropping** = seeds mixed, no rows.
**Ratoon**: crop regrows from **stubble**; yield falls each cycle.
**Crop rotation**: fixed, planned sequence to keep soil fertile and cut pests.
Maize is a **kharif** crop led by **Karnataka, MP**.

81.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Mixed cropping involves sowing crops together without a definite row pattern.
2. Relay cropping involves sowing the next crop into the standing crop before harvest.
3. Ratoon cropping involves regrowth from stubble, and yield generally falls with each cycle.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
81.x: All three statements correctly describe mixed cropping, relay cropping and ratoon cropping respectively.
81.tq: Match each technical definition to its system before selecting the coded combination.
xs: Statement 1 correct: **mixed cropping** sows crops together, seeds mixed, **without row pattern**.
Statement 2 correct: **relay cropping** sows the next crop into the **standing crop before harvest**.
Statement 3 correct: a **ratoon** regrows from **stubble** and **yield falls each cycle** — so **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
xa: Mixed cropping **insures against failure**.
**Intercropping** keeps crops in **definite rows** (tur with jowar or maize).
**Parallel cropping**: maize + green gram, no competition.
**Double cropping**: paddy followed by wheat.

81.s: Which one of the following best describes the recent diversification of agriculture in Andhra Pradesh?
o: A complete shift from crops to mining
A movement from horticulture towards only wheat cultivation
A movement from food grains towards fruits, vegetables, spices and oil palm
A shift from agriculture towards exclusively plantation forestry

82.s: As per the APPSC 2019 key, which State is the leading producer of spices in India?

82.s: Which one of the following crops is associated with a temperature range of approximately 21–37°C, 50–70 cm rainfall and 180–200 frost-free days?

xs: **Cotton** needs **21-37°C**, **50-70 cm** rainfall and **180-200 frost-free days** — option **(4)**.
Tea needs **150-300 cm**, coffee **150-250 cm**, rubber **200-300 cm** — far wetter.
xa: Some notes give cotton **21-30°C**.

82.s:
Consider the following statements about plantation crops in India:

2. Rubber grows on the alluvial flood plains of the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta with 50-70 cm of rain.
3. Coffee needs about 15-28 degrees C, shade, 150-250 cm of rain and deep, humus-rich, well-drained soil.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
82.x: Statement 1 is correct: tea needs 20-30 degrees C, 150-300 cm rain and acidic, well-drained hill slopes. Statement 3 is correct: coffee needs 15-28 degrees C, shade, 150-250 cm rain and humus-rich soil (Western Ghats). Statement 2 is wrong: rubber needs a hot humid climate (25-35 degrees C), 200-300 cm rain and laterite soils of the Western Ghats; the delta flood plains suit jute and 50-70 cm suits cotton. So '1 and 3 only'.
82.tq: Rubber = laterite, 200-300 cm; jute = delta alluvium; cotton = 50-70 cm, black soil.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — so option **(1)** 1 and 3 only.
Statement 1 is correct: **tea** needs **20-30°C**, **150-300 cm** of rain and **acidic, well-drained hill slopes**.
Statement 2 is wrong: **rubber** needs **25-35°C**, **200-300 cm** and **laterite** soil of the **Western Ghats**; delta flood plains suit **jute**.
Statement 3 is correct: **coffee** needs **15-28°C**, **shade**, **150-250 cm** and **humus-rich** soil.
xa: **Cotton** needs **50-70 cm** of rain and **180-200 frost-free days**, on deep black **regur**.
**Sugarcane** is a long-duration crop of **10-15 months**.
Rubber leaders: **Kerala**, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka; India is **5th** in natural rubber.

Consider the following statements about sugarcane in India:

xa: **North concentration (UP-Bihar):** fertile alluvium rich in **lime + potash**, level land, compact cane blocks.
**Western UP** is the main sugar-mill belt.

84.s:

84.x: Cropping intensity was 1.88 in 2024–25 and 1.21 in 2023–24. Therefore, the figures do not refer to the same agricultural year.

xs: Statement 1 correct: AP cropping intensity was **1.88 in 2024-25** (2025-26 Survey).
Statement 2 correct: it was **1.21 in 2023-24**.
Statement 3 wrong: the two figures are for **different years** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.

AP geographical area: about **162.97 lakh ha**; under cultivation **49.55 lakh ha (30.4%)**.

84.s: Small and marginal farmers holding up to 2 hectares constitute approximately what share of India's farmers?

84.x: Statement 1 is wrong: paddy occupies about 56% of the foodgrain area. Statement 2 is correct: it contributes about 79% of foodgrain output. So '2 only'.
84.tq: Paddy: 56% of area, 79% of output - do not swap them.
xs: Statement 1 wrong: paddy covers ~**56%** of foodgrain **area**, not 79%.
Statement 2 correct: paddy gives **79%** of foodgrain **output** — so **2 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: Total foodgrains: **37.51 lakh ha**, **161.86 lakh t**.

84.s: Which of the following is NOT included among the crops identified under the 17 growth engines for raising productivity?
84.x: The 17 growth engines cover 11 crops including paddy, maize, jowar, bajra, ragi, pulses, groundnut, sunflower and sesamum. Coffee is not in this list.
84.tq: Test membership in the specified crop list and identify the horticultural distractor.
xs: **Coffee** is not among the **11 crops** of the **17 growth engines** — option **(3)**.
The 11: **paddy, maize, jowar, bajra, ragi, redgram, blackgram, bengalgram, groundnut, sunflower, sesamum**.
xa: AP targets **30% growth** in agriculture over five years.
Coffee grows in **ASR (Araku)** clusters.
Diversification is toward **oilseeds, millets, horticulture, oil palm**.
**Coarse cereals** are shrinking for **lack of MSP procurement**.

84.s: Which of the following best describes the recent direction of change in Andhra Pradesh’s cropping pattern?
o: A shift towards oilseeds, millets, horticulture and oil palm
A reduction of all horticultural cultivation
A shift exclusively towards wheat and barley
A complete shift from agriculture to mining
84.x: The cropping pattern is shifting towards oilseeds, millets, horticulture and oil palm, with productivity improvement initiatives for 11 crops.
84.tq: Select the option that captures the stated trend without an extreme word such as ‘complete’ or ‘exclusively’.
xs: AP's pattern is diversifying to **oilseeds, millets, horticulture, oil palm** — option **(1)**.
It is also moving **from food grains to fruits, vegetables, spices**.
xa: **17 growth engines** raise productivity of **11 crops**.
**Coarse cereals** shrink for **lack of MSP procurement**.
Horticulture GSDP **₹1,52,950 crore** (2024-25), **21%** growth.
Rayalaseema horticulture: **7.8 lakh ha**, GVA **Rs 76,458 crore**.

84.s: Which of the following is identified as one reason for the shrinkage of coarse cereal cultivation in Andhra Pradesh?
o: Lack of minimum support price procurement
Excessive canal irrigation in every district
84.x: Coarse cereal cultivation has been shrinking partly because of inadequate MSP procurement.
84.tq: Choose the stated economic cause and reject absolute or unsupported explanations.
xs: **Coarse cereals** are shrinking for **lack of MSP procurement** — option **(1)**.
Millets are not banned — AP is in fact diversifying **toward millets**.
xa: The **17 growth engines** cover **jowar, bajra, ragi** among **11 crops**.
Paddy dominates: **79%** of foodgrain output.
Rainfed shift crops: **black gram, green gram, groundnut, sesamum, sunflower**.
Kharif 2026 El Nino: water-budgeted shift to **pulses**.

84.s: Which district is known as the Rice Bowl of Andhra Pradesh?
84.x: East Godavari is known as the Rice Bowl of Andhra Pradesh. Its delta rice cultivation is supported by canal irrigation.
84.tq: Use the district–regional identity association, while avoiding confusion with horticulture and coffee regions.
xs: **East Godavari** is the "**Rice Bowl of AP**" (APPSC-GS 2025 key) — option **(1)**.
Paddy grows in the **Godavari and Krishna deltas** under **canal irrigation**.
xa: AP's main irrigation source = **canals**.
AP paddy: **127.15 lakh t** on **20.97 lakh ha** (2024-25).

**West Bengal** is the "Rice Bowl of India".

84.s:
Match the following crops with their principal district or region in Andhra Pradesh:

List-I (Crop)
A. Paddy
B. Groundnut
C. Tobacco
D. Coffee

List-II (District or region)
i. Anantapur
 ii. East Godavari and the Godavari–Krishna deltas
 iii. Prakasam and Guntur
 iv. Alluri Sitharama Raju district, especially Araku

Codes:
84.x: Paddy is concentrated in East Godavari and the Godavari–Krishna deltas; groundnut in Anantapur; tobacco in Prakasam and Guntur; and coffee in the ASR–Araku region.
84.tq: Start with distinctive pairs such as Anantapur–groundnut and Araku–coffee.
xs: **Paddy — East Godavari/deltas**, **Groundnut — Anantapur**, **Tobacco — Prakasam, Guntur**, **Coffee — ASR (Araku)**: **A-ii, B-i, C-iii, D-iv**, option **(1)**.
Paddy is the **delta** crop under canals, groundnut the **red-soil** Rayalaseema crop, and coffee the **Araku** hill crop.
xa: **Cotton**: Rayalaseema black soils, Guntur, Kurnool.
**Chillies**: Guntur, Krishna zone.
**Banana**: Rayalaseema clusters.
**Maize**: Godavari and Krishna, for poultry and starch.

84.s: Which one of the following combinations is correctly matched with the crop and its major area of cultivation in Andhra Pradesh?
o: Maize — confined to the coastal delta and unrelated to poultry demand
Banana — chiefly cultivated in the Araku coffee clusters
Cotton — Rayalaseema black soils, Guntur and Kurnool
Chillies — only the Alluri Sitharama Raju district
84.x: Cotton is associated with the black soils of Rayalaseema and the districts of Guntur and Kurnool. Chillies are prominent in Guntur and the Krishna zone, maize in Godavari and Krishna districts, and bananas in Rayalaseema clusters.
84.tq: Find the correctly matched crop–region pair and reject absolute location claims.
xs: **Cotton** grows on **Rayalaseema black soils** (APPSC 2025), **Guntur, Kurnool** — option **(3)**.
**Maize** is driven by **poultry and starch demand**; **banana** is in **Rayalaseema clusters**; **chillies** in **Guntur, Krishna zone**.
xa: **Coffee** = ASR (Araku) clusters.
**Groundnut** = Anantapur.
**Tobacco** = Prakasam, Guntur.
**Red soils** suit groundnut, ragi, tobacco.

84.s:
Consider the following statements regarding red soils in Rayalaseema:
1. They are suitable for groundnut.
2. They are suitable for ragi.
3. Rice and sugarcane require irrigation when cultivated in these soils.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
84.x: Red soils support groundnut, ragi and tobacco, while rice and sugarcane can be grown in them only with irrigation.
84.tq: Test the crop-soil relationship along with the irrigation qualification.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 correct: Rayalaseema **red** soils suit **groundnut, ragi**, tobacco.
Statement 3 correct: **rice/sugarcane** grow there **only with irrigation** — option **(4)**.
xa: Rainfed shift crops: **black gram, green gram, groundnut, sesamum, sunflower**.
**Cotton** grows on **Rayalaseema black soils**.
Rayalaseema micro-irrigation = **71%**.
**Groundnut** = Anantapur.

84.s: According to the classification based on Cultivable Command Area, a medium irrigation project covers:
84.x: A medium project has a CCA of 2,000–10,000 hectares; minor projects are up to 2,000 hectares and major projects exceed 10,000 hectares.
84.tq: Distinguish adjacent numerical ranges rather than relying on the project names alone.
xs: A **medium** project has a CCA of **2,000 to 10,000 hectares** — option **(2)**.
**Minor** = up to **2,000 ha**; **major** = over **10,000 ha**.
xa: AP treats **minor** irrigation as ayacut up to **5,000 acres**.
Minor irrigation gives about **65%** of India's irrigated area.
India: tube wells **47.3%**, canals **24.7%**, tanks **2.8%**.
AP main source = **canals**.

84.s: Under the Andhra Pradesh classification, minor irrigation generally refers to an ayacut of up to:
84.x: Andhra Pradesh treats an ayacut up to 5,000 acres as minor irrigation.
84.tq: Separate the state-specific ayacut limit from the CCA-based project classification.
xs: AP treats **minor irrigation** as ayacut up to **5,000 acres** — option **(3)**.
⚠ The CCA class for minor is **up to 2,000 ha** — hectares, not acres.
xa: Minor irrigation gives about **65%** of India's irrigated area.
**APMIP** (since **2003**): **2.05 lakh acres**, **75,035** farmers.
Rayalaseema micro-irrigation = **71%**.

84.s:
Consider the following statements about sources of irrigation:
1. Tanks account for under 3 per cent of India's net irrigated area.
2. In India as a whole, canals account for the largest share of net irrigated area.
3. Canals are the main source of irrigation in Andhra Pradesh.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
84.x: Statement 3 is correct: canals are AP's main source (APPSC-GS 2025 key). Statement 2 is wrong: at the all-India level tube wells lead with 47.3 per cent of net irrigated area; canals have 24.7 per cent. Statement 1 is correct: tanks give only 2.8 per cent. So '1 and 3 only'.
84.tq: AP = canals; India = tube wells (47.3%).
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — so option **(2)** 1 and 3 only.
Statement 1 is correct: **tanks** give only **2.8%** of India's net irrigated area.
Statement 2 is wrong: in India, **tube wells** lead with **47.3%**; **canals** have **24.7%**.
Statement 3 is correct: **canals** are AP's main source (APPSC-GS **2025** key).
xa: ⚠ AP main source = **canals**; India main source = **tube wells**.
**Minor irrigation:** CCA **up to 2,000 hectares**; **major** above **10,000 hectares**.
AP gross irrigated area: **32.71 lakh ha**; net irrigated **26.03 lakh ha** (2023-24).
Rayalaseema has **71%** of micro-irrigation.

84.s: The Andhra Pradesh Drought Mitigation Project (APDMP) is funded by:

84.s: Annadatha Sukhibhava is described as which of the following?

84.s: According to APSES 2025-26, Andhra Pradesh accounts for approximately what share of India’s total fish production?

xs: AP gives **nearly 29%** of India's fish (APSES 2025-26) — option **(3)**.
The earlier estimate was ~**30%** (2024-25).
xa: ⚠ **~29%** = fish production; **~32%** = seafood exports; **~70%** = shrimp in AP's export basket.

Coastline **1,053 km**.

84.s: India is described as which one of the following in relation to global fisheries?
o: The third-largest fish producer and the largest shrimp importer
The largest fish producer and the leading marine-capture country
The second-largest fish producer but a minor inland-capture country
The second-largest fish producer and a leader in inland capture fisheries
84.x: India is the world's second-largest fish producer (about 8% of world output; some sources say about 9%, FAO SOFIA 2026) and leads the world in inland capture (2.2 MT). It is not the largest producer (B), nor a minor inland-capture country (C).
84.tq: Separate the country’s global rank from its specific strength in inland capture.
xs: India is the **second-largest fish producer** and **leads inland capture** (**2.2 MT**) — option **(4)**.
India gives ~**8%** of world output (some notes ~**9%**, FAO SOFIA 2026), so it is not the largest.
xa: India is also **2nd** in aquaculture (~**12%** of global farmed output).
Inland fisheries give **>75%** of India's fish.
SOFIA 2026: aquaculture passed **100 million tonnes** = **53%** of aquatic animal output.
India 2024-25 seafood exports: **16,98,170 MT**, **₹62,408.45 crore**.

84.s: Which one of the following statements regarding Andhra Pradesh's seafood exports is correct?
o: Andhra Pradesh ranked first among States in seafood export value in 2022–23.
Andhra Pradesh contributes nearly 75% of India's total seafood exports.
Andhra Pradesh's seafood export share was about 32% only in 2024–25.
Shrimp accounts for nearly 70% of Andhra Pradesh's seafood export basket.

xs: **Shrimp** is ~**70%** of AP's seafood export basket (MPEDA) — option **(4)**.

xa: ⚠ ~**29%** is AP's share of **fish production**.
**Vannamei** shrimp is the main export item.
US tariff **50%** from Aug 2025, cut to ~**18%** in Feb 2026.
Non-US markets took ~**57%** of AP shrimp shipments.

o: Vannamei shrimp is the main export item, while black tiger shrimp brood multiplication is undertaken at the FAO centre in West Godavari
Carp is the main export item, while black tiger shrimp brood multiplication is undertaken at the MPEDA centre in Vijayawada
Vannamei shrimp is the main export item, while black tiger shrimp brood multiplication is undertaken at the MPEDA centre in Visakhapatnam

**ICAR-CMFRI** Regional Centre (Visakhapatnam) does **open-sea cage farming**.
Shrimp = ~**70%** of AP's export basket.

84.s: Andhra Pradesh ranks first in India in the production of:
84.x: Andhra Pradesh ranks first in India in fish and shrimp production (APPSC PYQ key) and is described as India's leading fisheries producer, with a 1,053 km coastline. Tea and coffee are led by Assam and Karnataka, silk by Karnataka (AP is 2nd), and jute by West Bengal.

Replacement of freshwater fisheries with marine aquaculture
Conversion of all departmental tanks into industrial zones

xs: AP's **shrimp backbone**: **Prakasam, West Godavari, East Godavari, Nellore, Krishna** — option **(1)**.

**Vannamei** is the main export species.

84.s: In India, inland fisheries contribute more than what proportion of total fish output?

xs: Inland fisheries give **>75 percent** of India's fish output — option **(3)**.

84.s:
Consider the following statements about Kolleru Lake:
1. It lies between the Krishna and Pennar deltas.
2. It is fed by the Tammileru among other streams.
3. It is the largest freshwater lake in Andhra Pradesh, about 305 sq km.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
84.x: Statement 3 is correct: Kolleru is AP's largest freshwater lake (~305 sq km; older notes say 250). Statement 1 is wrong: it lies between the Krishna and Godavari deltas (Eluru / West Godavari). Statement 2 is correct: the Tammileru is among its feeders. So '2 and 3 only'.
84.tq: Kolleru = between Krishna and Godavari deltas; Ramsar 2002.
xs: Statements **2 and 3** are correct — so option **(3)** 2 and 3 only.
Statement 1 is wrong: Kolleru lies between the **Krishna and Godavari deltas** (Eluru / West Godavari), not the Pennar.
Statement 2 is correct: it is fed by the **Tammileru** among others.
Statement 3 is correct: it is AP's **largest freshwater lake**, about **305 sq km** (older notes **250 sq km**).
xa: **Kolleru WLS** has been a **Ramsar site** since **2002**.
Breeding ground of the **spot-billed pelican**, also painted storks.
Sanctuary limit: the **+5 ft contour**.
Problem: lake bed turned into **aquaculture ponds** — the lake is shrinking and eutrophic.

84.s: Kolleru Wildlife Sanctuary is associated with which of the following bird species as a breeding ground?

xs: **Kolleru WLS** is a breeding ground of the **spot-billed pelican** — option **(4)**.
It also supports **painted storks**.
xa: **Ramsar site** since **2002**.
Sanctuary limit **+5 ft contour**.
Area ~**305 sq km**.

xs: Kolleru's sanctuary limit is the **+5 ft contour**, and it is a **Ramsar site since 2002** — option **(2)**.
The other contours (**−5**, **+10**, sea level) and years are wrong.

It is fed by the **Tammileru** among others.

84.s: The principal environmental problem caused by aquaculture encroachment in Kolleru Lake is that it:
o: Eliminates all agricultural activity in the surrounding deltas
Turns the lake bed into ponds and fields, causing shrinkage and eutrophication
Converts freshwater into saline water through tidal action
Increases the lake’s depth and improves water circulation
84.x: Aquaculture ponds and fields have occupied portions of the lake bed, causing the lake to shrink and become eutrophic.
84.tq: Apply the cause-and-effect chain from land-use change to ecological impact.
xs: The lake bed is turned into **aquaculture ponds + fields**, so the lake is **shrinking and eutrophic** — option **(2)** (AP Geography 2026).
Encroachment shrinks the lake rather than deepening it or salting it.
xa: Kolleru is a **freshwater** lake between the Krishna and Godavari deltas.
**Ramsar site** since **2002**; limit **+5 ft contour**.
Area ~**305 sq km** (older notes **250 sq km**).
Aqua farmers cite high **input and power costs** (Jun 2026).

84.s: Which one of the following correctly describes India’s position regarding the WTO Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies?

India accepted it as the 23rd member, and inland fishing is prohibited.

xs: India became the **123rd** member to accept the **WTO Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies**; **aquaculture + inland fishing** are **exempt** — option **(1)**.

India is **2nd** in aquaculture (~**12%** of global farmed output).
Inland gives **>75%** of India's fish.
AP diesel subsidy: **₹9 per litre**.

84.s:

85.s: Which statement correctly describes the location of cotton textile industries?
o: They are necessarily located at cotton-producing farms because cotton is weight-losing.
They can be located only near coalfields.
They are non-weight-losing and therefore are not bound to raw-material sites.
They are market-based because cotton gains weight during processing.
85.x: Cotton textiles are non-weight-losing industries and therefore are not necessarily tied to the location of raw cotton.
85.tq: Separate non-weight-losing cotton textiles from weight-losing industries.
xs: Cotton textiles are **non-weight-losing**, so they are **not bound to raw-material sites** — option **(3)**.
In Weber's terms **cotton** is a **pure localised** material — it loses no weight in processing.
Weight-losing (**gross**) materials are **iron ore, coal, sugarcane**, which pull plants to the raw material.
xa: **Material Index** = weight of localised raw materials / weight of finished product.
**MI > 1** → locate at raw material; **MI < 1** → at market.
**Lancashire** (Manchester) and **Osaka** are cotton-textile centres.
**Osaka** = "**Manchester of the East**".

85.s: According to Weber’s least-cost theory, an industrial firm seeks a location where the combined cost of which factors is least?
o: Raw materials, climate and exports only
85.x: Alfred Weber’s 1909 least-cost theory considers the combined transport, labour and agglomeration costs.
85.tq: Recall the three cost components of the theory.
xs: **Alfred Weber (1909)**: a firm locates where total **transport + labour + agglomeration** costs are least — option **(1)**.
This is the **least-cost theory**.
xa: ⚠ **Weber** = least cost; **Losch** = maximum profit / market area; **Isard** = substitution; **Florence** = Location Quotient.
**Locational triangle**: two raw-material sources + one market.
**Isodapanes**: lines of equal extra transport cost.
**Agglomeration economies**: savings when firms cluster.

85.s: In Weber’s locational triangle, the three vertices represent:
o: one raw-material source and two ports only
two markets and one labour centre
two raw-material sources and one market
85.x: The locational triangle consists of two raw-material sources and one market. The least-transport-cost point lies inside the triangle.
85.tq: Identify the vertices before judging the location point.
xs: Weber's **locational triangle** = **two raw-material sources and one market** — option **(4)**.
The **least-transport-cost point** lies **inside** it.
xa: **Isodapanes**: labour or agglomeration savings can pull a firm off that point.
**Material Index** decides raw-material vs market pull.
Weber's theory dates to **1909**.
**Ubiquities** (water, air) are available everywhere and do not pull location.

85.s:
Consider the following statements about Weber's least-cost theory:
1. Isodapanes are lines joining places of equal extra transport cost.
2. The Material Index is the weight of localised raw materials divided by the weight of the finished product.
3. An industry with a Material Index greater than one tends to locate near the market.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
85.x: Statement 2 is correct: MI = weight of localised raw materials / weight of finished product. Statement 3 is wrong: MI > 1 (weight-losing) pulls the industry to the RAW-MATERIAL source; MI < 1 pulls it to the market. Statement 1 is correct: isodapanes join points of equal extra transport cost. Hence 1 and 2 only.
85.tq: MI > 1 = raw material site; MI < 1 = market.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — so option **(2)** 1 and 2 only.
Statement 1 is correct: **isodapanes** are lines of **equal extra transport cost**.
Statement 2 is correct: **MI = weight of localised raw materials / weight of finished product**.
Statement 3 is wrong: **MI > 1** pulls the industry to the **raw material**; **MI < 1** pulls it to the **market**.
xa: **Locational triangle:** two raw-material sources + one market.
**Ubiquities** (water, air) are available everywhere; **pure localised** materials (cotton) lose no weight.
**Gross (weight-losing)** materials: iron ore, coal, sugarcane.
⚠ **Weber** = least cost; **Losch** = maximum profit; **Isard** = substitution.

85.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with its material category?
85.x: Water and air are ubiquitous materials available everywhere. Cotton is treated as a pure localised material, while iron ore is a gross or weight-losing material.
85.tq: Match each material with its defining category.
xs: **Water — ubiquity** is correct — option **(1)**; **ubiquities** are available everywhere.
**Cotton** is **pure localised** (not gross); **iron ore** is **gross (weight-losing)**; **air** is a **ubiquity**.
xa: Gross materials: **iron ore, coal, sugarcane**.
Pure localised materials **lose no weight**.
**MI** counts only **localised** raw materials.
Steel's inputs include **iron ore, coking coal, limestone, dolomite**.

85.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:

List-I (Theorist)
A. Edgar Hoover
B. Walter Isard
C. August Losch
D. P. Sargant Florence

List-II (Concept)
1. Location Quotient
2. Maximum-profit and market-area approach
3. Transport-cost structure and terminal costs
4. Substitution principle

Codes:
85.x: Edgar Hoover dealt with transport-cost structure and terminal costs; Walter Isard proposed the substitution principle; August Losch developed the maximum-profit and market-area approach; and P. Sargant Florence introduced the Location Quotient.
85.tq: Start from the sure pair and eliminate codes with mismatched theorist–concept relationships.
xs: **Hoover — transport-cost structure, terminal costs**; **Isard — substitution principle**; **Losch — maximum-profit / market area**; **Florence — Location Quotient**: **A-3, B-4, C-2, D-1**, option **(1)**.
⚠ **Weber** (**1909**) is the least-cost theorist and is not in this list — do not confuse him with **Losch**.
xa: **Weber (1909)** = **least-cost theory**.
Hoover favoured **ports and break-of-bulk points**.
⚠ Weber = least cost vs Losch = maximum profit.
Location Quotient = region's share of an industry vs its national share.

85.s:
Assertion (A): Ports and break-of-bulk points are favoured locations in Edgar Hoover's approach to industrial location.
Reason (R): Edgar Hoover's theory emphasises transport-cost structure and terminal costs.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
85.x: Both statements are true, and the emphasis on transport-cost structure and terminal costs explains why ports and break-of-bulk points are favoured.
85.tq: Test whether the reason directly explains the location preference stated in the assertion.
xs: Both are true and R is the correct **explanation** of A — option **(1)**.
**Edgar Hoover** stressed **transport-cost structure** and **terminal costs**, so **ports and break-of-bulk points** are favoured.
xa: **Isard**: **substitution principle**.
**Losch**: **maximum-profit / market-area** approach.
**Weber**: **least-cost** (transport + labour + agglomeration).
**Florence**: **Location Quotient**.

85.s: Which one of the following is a characteristic of footloose industries?
o: They are necessarily highly polluting heavy industries.
They are generally light, high-value and have low transport costs.
They can operate only in mining regions.
They must be located beside bulky raw materials.
85.x: Footloose industries are generally light, high-value, low in transport cost and low in pollution, and are not tied to a raw material or fixed location, e.g. diamond cutting, electronics, software and watch-making. They are not heavy polluting, mining-bound or raw-material-bound industries.
85.tq: Use the defining characteristics to eliminate location-bound industries.
xs: **Footloose industries** are **light, high-value**, with **low transport cost** and **low pollution** — option **(2)**.
They are **not tied to a raw material or a fixed location**, so options 3 and 4 are wrong.
xa: Examples: **diamond cutting**, **electronics**, **software**, **watch-making**.
PYQ (APPSC-GS 2019 key): **Diamond**.
⚠ **Steel** is the opposite — weight-losing, tied to coalfields/ore fields.
**Agglomeration economies** draw firms to clusters like **Chennai-Bengaluru**.

85.s:
Consider the following statements about agglomeration economies:
1. They are cost savings firms obtain when they cluster, through shared infrastructure, specialised suppliers and a skilled labour pool.
2. Mumbai-Pune, Chennai-Bengaluru and Delhi-NCR are examples of such clusters.
3. They explain why footloose industries such as diamond cutting must locate next to their raw materials.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
85.x: Statement 1 is correct: agglomeration economies are the savings from clustering. Statement 2 is correct: Mumbai-Pune, Chennai-Bengaluru and Delhi-NCR are the examples. Statement 3 is wrong: footloose industries like diamond cutting are by definition not tied to raw-material sites. So '1 and 2 only'.
85.tq: Agglomeration = clustering savings; footloose = not tied to raw material.
xs: Statement 1 correct: **agglomeration economies** are savings from clustering — **shared infrastructure, specialised suppliers, skilled labour pool**.
Statement 2 correct: **Mumbai-Pune, Chennai-Bengaluru, Delhi-NCR** are examples.
Statement 3 wrong: **footloose** industries like **diamond cutting** are **not tied** to raw materials — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: Weber's least-cost sum includes **agglomeration** costs.
Agglomeration savings can pull a firm off the least-transport point (**isodapanes**).
**Chennai** = "**Detroit of India**".
Footloose examples: **software, electronics, watch-making**.

85.s: Which one of the following is a correct statement regarding steel production and location?
o: Steel plants require no coking coal or limestone.
Steel is weight-gaining and plants are generally located near markets only.
Steel is a footloose industry because its raw materials are weightless.
About four tonnes of raw materials produce one tonne of steel, encouraging location near coalfields or ore fields.
85.x: Steel is weight-losing: about four tonnes of iron ore, coking coal, limestone and dolomite produce one tonne of steel. This encourages location near coalfields or ore fields.
85.tq: Apply the weight-loss principle to industrial location.
xs: About **4 tonnes of raw material** make **1 tonne of steel**, so plants sit on **coalfields/ore fields** — option **(4)**.
Inputs: **iron ore, coking coal, limestone, dolomite** — steel is **weight-losing**, not footloose or weight-gaining.
xa: **MI > 1** → locate at raw material.
**Gross** materials: iron ore, coal, sugarcane.
**TISCO Jamshedpur (1907)** = first private integrated plant.
**Chotanagpur** = "Ruhr of India".

85.s:
Consider the following statements about steel production:
1. China ranks first in the world, with over half of world steel output.
2. India ranks second, with crude steel output of 168.4 MT.
3. India's steel capacity is 300 MT and its 2030 target is 220 MT.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
85.x: Statement 1 is correct: China is first with over 50% of world steel. Statement 2 is correct: India is second with 168.4 MT of crude steel. Statement 3 is wrong: India's capacity is about 220 MT and the target is 300 MT by 2030 (the figures are reversed). So only two statements are correct.
85.tq: India steel: 168.4 MT output, 220 MT capacity, 300 MT target (2030).
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — so option **(2)** only two.
Statement 1 is correct: **China** is **1st** with over **50%** of world steel.
Statement 2 is correct: **India** is **2nd** with **168.4 MT** of crude steel.
Statement 3 is wrong: the figures are reversed — capacity is **220 MT** and the target **300 MT by 2030**.
xa: About **4 tonnes of raw material** make **1 tonne of steel** — so plants sit on coalfields/ore fields.
Steel leadership has moved to **China and India**; old Western regions (**Ruhr, Lorraine**, US Rust Belt) declined.
UPPSC **2022** key: **China** at the top.

85.tq: Rourkela = Germany; Bhilai = USSR; Bhadravati = oldest southern PSU.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — so option **(2)** only two.

Statement 3 is wrong: **VISL Bhadravati** is the **oldest** public-sector plant in the south.

India's crude steel: **168.4 MT**; capacity **220 MT**.
PSU steel plants placed away from raw-material bases: **Salem**, **Vizag**, **Vijayanagar**.

86.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
86.x: Sugar is raw-material-based because cane is weight-losing and perishable. Bakery is market-based (B wrong), iron and steel is raw-material-based, about 4 t of input per tonne (C wrong), and cement is raw-material-based on limestone, not footloose (D wrong).
86.tq: Classify industries by weight change and location tendency.
xs: **Sugar** is a **raw-material-based** industry — so option **(1)** is correct: sugarcane is **perishable** and the input is **weight-losing**.
**Bakery** is **market-based** (weight-gaining or fragile products, located near consumers).
**Iron and steel** is raw-material-based (about **4 t** of input per tonne), and **cement** is raw-material-based on **limestone** — neither is market-based or footloose.
xa: **Power-oriented**: **aluminium**, needing **14,000-15,000 kWh** per tonne.
**Footloose** examples: **software**, **electronics**, and **cotton textiles** (cotton is a "pure" material).
⚠ Both **sugar** and **iron & steel** are weight-losing, so Weber puts them near raw material (**MI > 1**).

86.s: Market-based industries are generally located near consumers because their products are:
86.x: Market-based industries such as bakeries and soft-drink production locate near consumers because their products are weight-gaining or fragile.
86.tq: Apply the product-characteristic test to market location.
xs: Market-based industries locate near consumers because their products are **weight-gaining or fragile** — option **(3)**.
Examples given: **bakery** and **soft drinks**.
**Weight-losing and perishable** inputs describe **raw-material-oriented** industries (sugar, iron & steel, cement), not market-based ones.
Dependence on cheap electricity is **power orientation** (aluminium).
xa: In Weber's theory, **MI < 1** or **ubiquitous inputs** (such as **water**) pull an industry **near the market**.
**Footloose** industries locate anywhere with **skills and links** — software, electronics, diamond polishing.
Location factors include **raw material**, **power**, **market**, **labour**, **transport**, water and **government policy**.

Statement 2: **labour** (skilled and cheap) is a location factor — correct.

xa: Full factor list: raw material, **power**, **market**, labour, **transport**, water, government policy, **clustering**, environment.

86.s:
Consider the following statements about Alfred Weber's least-cost theory:
1. Formulated in 1909, it holds that a plant first locates where total transport cost is lowest, then adjusts for labour and agglomeration.
2. A Material Index below 1, or ubiquitous inputs such as water, favours location near the market.
3. A Material Index above 1 (weight-losing inputs) pulls the industry towards the market.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
86.x: Statement 1 is correct: Weber (1909) puts least transport cost first, then labour and agglomeration. Statement 3 is wrong: MI > 1 (weight-losing, e.g. iron and steel, sugar) pulls the plant to the raw material. Statement 2 is correct: MI < 1 or ubiquitous inputs favour the market. So '1 and 2 only'.
86.tq: MI > 1 -> raw material; MI < 1 -> market; pure material -> anywhere.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — so option **(2)** 1 and 2 only.
Statement 1 is correct: **Weber (1909)** puts **least transport cost** first, then labour + agglomeration.
Statement 2 is correct: **MI < 1** or **ubiquitous inputs** (water) favour the **market**.
Statement 3 is wrong: **MI > 1** (weight-losing, e.g. **iron & steel, sugar**) pulls the plant to the **raw material**.
xa: **Pure raw material** (no weight loss, e.g. **cotton**) → free to locate anywhere.
**Footloose** = **software / diamond** (APPSC **2019**).
Steel needs about **4 t** of input per tonne.

86.s: In Weber's least-cost theory, a 'pure' raw material such as cotton, which loses no weight in processing, allows the industry to be located:
o: Anywhere between the source and the market
86.x: A pure raw material has no weight loss, so transport cost is the same whether raw material or product is moved; the plant is free to locate anywhere between source and market. Weight-losing inputs (MI > 1) pull it to the source (A); weight-gaining or ubiquitous inputs (MI < 1) pull it to the market (B); a port location (D) is not implied by the theory.
86.tq: Pure material (cotton) = free location; weight-losing = source; ubiquitous = market.
xs: A **pure raw material** such as **cotton** loses no weight, so the plant can locate **anywhere between the source and the market** — option **(3)**.
**Weight-losing** inputs (**MI > 1**) pull the plant to the raw-material source.
**MI < 1** or ubiquitous inputs (water) pull it to the market.
xa: This is why **cotton textiles** are listed as **footloose** in the orientation table.
**Alfred Weber (1909)**: least total transport cost first, then labour and agglomeration adjustments.
Iron & steel needs about **4 t** of input per tonne — a classic weight-losing case.

Consider the following statements about policy measures for balanced regional industrial growth in India:
1. The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 recognised balanced regional growth and placed public-sector units in backward regions.
2. The Fourth Five-Year Plan (1969-74) called for measures to attract industry to backward areas.
3. Public-sector plants at Salem, Visakhapatnam and Vijayanagar (Hospet) were placed right next to their raw-material sources.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
86.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct as stated. Statement 3 is wrong: Salem, Visakhapatnam and Vijayanagar were deliberately placed away from raw materials for regional balance. So B (1 and 2 only) is right; A omits statement 2, C and D wrongly include statement 3.
86.tq: Salem-Vizag-Vijayanagar = sited AWAY from raw materials (policy override).
xs: **Statements 1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: **IPR 1956** recognised balanced regional growth and placed the public sector in backward regions — correct.
Statement 2: the **Fourth Plan (1969-74)** called for attracting industry to backward areas — correct.
Statement 3 is wrong: **Salem, Vizag and Vijayanagar** plants were placed **away from** raw-material bases.
xa: This siting is called a **policy override** in India.
The Centre gave **subsidies** to units in backward areas.
**ES 2025-26**: most clusters too small, with **regulatory rigidities**.
